I've seen video reviews of products such as this BOSALY Ice Maker Machine. It promises to make ice in 9 minutes and I gotta say, it does just that. This ice maker can make two sizes of ice. In my testing, small ice cubes can be made in 9 minutes while the large one takes 11. I think it is necessary to set some expectations for this unit for those who are interested. If you know these things ahead of time, you will not be disappointed by your purchase:

This ice maker is fairly heavy, but that is to be expected because of the compressor. Also due to the compressor, this until will not work with power from a car adapter so as far as portability, you'd need to make sure there is a wall outlet or a generator that you can plug it into or you'll be draining a lot of battery power.

It must also be pointed out that the ice made by this machine is quite wet due to how the ice is made. It means that if you make ice with this machine, then put them into your freezer, you'll end up with one big lump of ice.

With that said, this machine does EXACTLY what I want it to do: make ice during a small gathering without the need for much oversight. Just make sure the water tank is filled.

Here are the features I like:
-- Portable. Be the savior of the party by bringing the ice maker for a friend's party.
-- Auto stop when the water level is low or the basket is filled.
-- Plug at the bottom allows draining of excess water.
-- FAST. 9 pieces of ice cube are made with each batch. That's enough for two cups.
-- Convenient. Make sure the machine is filled with water and plugged in. Come back once in a while to dump out the basket to make more ice or to refill the water.
-- Useful. This will definitely make a difference during a party. There are too many other things to worry about when preparing for guests.

Overall, great product.

OK - so I have a GE "Quietpower 3" or something like that dishwasher.  My wife and kids refuse to get all of the stuck on food off of the dishes before loading the dishwasher.  This causes the food to become mixed with the water, and get pumped through the pump and back through the spray arms.  Things like Rice and Stickers off of new cups and you name it clog up the arms, EXPECIALLY this center arm.  My dishwasher has a lower spinning arm on the bottom of the tub, this one attaches to the underside of the top rack, and then there is the top arm at the top of the dishwasher which is pretty useless.  I have taken the arms off at least 50 times and cleaned them by hand in the tub, soaking in vinegar, using pipe cleaners and wire to clear them out.  I finally gave up when something got caught inside that I couldn't dislodge.  THIS WORKED LIKE A CHARM.  However, here is something IMPORTANT FOR ALL TO READ.  When you take off the arm under the top rack - KEEP THE SCREW AND WASHER THAT COME OUT.  This arm does not have a new replacement screw or washer, and you'll need that to reinstall new arm.  This is not a defect or anything - It is just good information to have before you throw out the screw and washer and then have to go digging through the garbage to find it again, clean it and be able to put the new arm on.  Also - the part number from GE and the part number for this arm (and pretty much all other arms for dishwashers) do not match.  I simply eyeballed the picture and it looked identical and took a chance.  It is identical.  Works great.  Wife is happy.  I'll probably end up buying another to pre-plan for the next clog that occurs when my family decides to put a bowl full of rice into the dishwasher without rinsing it out first.

I tried to save a few bucks by buying a cheaper set of these suspension rods. They worked okay for a short while but just couldn't stabilize large loads in the washer. The slamming resumed.

I watched a few online videos and found (according to a couple of videos I found online, so take it with a grain of salt) that it's not the springs that are the key to how these rods work. It's the cap on top of the spring. The cap has a collar that fits rather tightly on the rod and slides up and down, but with some resistance. Apparently that resistance is what provides the damping and stops the slamming. When that collar loosens over time and the cap slides too easily, the slamming starts.

I saw some innovative fixes. One was to use construction adhesive around the collar to increase the friction. Another was to put a small cable tie around the collar and cinch it tightly enough to increase it.

Or you could just buy this set of replacement rods. This set works. Washer is slamming no more. Several videos are available online that show how to install them.

REVISED REVIEW: First BIG PRO. I have had this unit for over a year now and it is still going strong. This unit makes one incredible cup of coffee. Like the best cup of coffee, I've ever had from one of these single-cup units. THIS UNIT DOES ONE JOB - MAKE A GEAT CUP OF COFFEE, AND IT DOES IT VERY, VERY WELL. The unit also has a lot of desirable features: It has a much smaller footprint than many of the coffee makers out there and does not take up a huge amount of room on the counter. It also has a large water reservoir so you don't need to immediately refill it after you make a cup of coffee; it has a function for "extra hot" coffee and brew strength, a hot water feature to make soup and tea with, and a rinse function to remove coffee residue. If you intend to use the unit to make anything like soup, it should be rinsed immediately (using the rinse feature) after everybody has made their morning coffee so your soup does not have an off-taste. The coffee maker can be programmed to turn on in the morning, and off when no one is home, and includes a digital clock. The unit is fairly intuitive and easy to use. I also love that you can use your own coffee and are not forced to purchase a bunch of expensive, wasteful pods.

On the Con side, and this is a kind of a big Con, the unit is very cheaply made of lightweight plastic, including all moving parts. The underside of the brewing latch of the unit is not finished off very professionally, to the degree that when I initially opened it, I thought the top was broken and the coffee maker needed to be returned. I realized that the coffee maker was simply made that way after watching a video on YouTube of the unit being used.

Out of the box, the brewing chamber of the unit does not open or close smoothly, is very stiff and strange to open and close, and makes a sound somewhere between a squeak and a groan when the unit is opened to insert the coffee pod. The unit does become easier to open and close with use, and the sound it used to make is gone.

You will also think that the unit takes a long time to brew coffee. There is a very good reason for this; the super hot water needs to spend time with the coffee grounds to make superior tasting coffee, which it does. So, waiting the few extra seconds is definitely worth the time it takes. When you taste your coffee and want to start singing, it's so good, you'll know what I mean.

So, while I wish this unit was made of metal and was sturdy, I can't fault its performance, which is the whole point. It makes such an awesome cup of coffee that if it does die, I'll probably replace it with another unit of the same brand.

These re-usable K cup filters, made in China, are reported to be 100% BPA, LEAD, and DEHP free. They are purple "plastic" with gold mesh bottom and sides. They reportedly fit Keurig 2.0, K200, K250, K300, K350, K400, K450, K500, K550, K560 and all 1. After our K200 broke we checked the Keurig (machine) ratings and then went down to the K-50 because that Keurig seemed to have the highest ratings. These filters fit the K-50 fine. Just fill the filter with coffee, gently snap the filter top closed, place the filter in the Keurig, and press your coffee-maker button(s). You do not need to insert any kind of a paper filter into the items as they themselves are filters! Open them gently as repeated opening and closing, or forceful opening and closing will eventually result in breakage of the bendable "plastic" that functions as a hinge. Although disposable, with gentle care, these filters should certainly last long enough to be worth their cost. Of course, they are not as convenient as using actual K cups because (unless you choose to add paper filters to them), these disposable filters must be emptied of the sticking coffee grounds (which must be scooped out), and then cleaned (which is easy - just swish out in hot soapy water or squirt small amount of liquid detergent in and then turn while under hot kitchen faucet). I would advise supporting the outside of the mesh (with a light pressure) while lightly "scraping" the inside mesh to remove the used coffee grounds. A permanent filter for K coffee makers is more practical because of being easier to clean (not requiring the degree of gentle handling). However, these little disposable ones have their place too!

We have an ancient and cheap little coffee pot that we take out on occasion when we want a pot full of coffee, use out regular K cups (including many brands), and now have these disposable filters for when desiring a couple of cups of coffee and needing to consume our older ground coffee, or for when temporarily running out of "K" cups. Just as with any brand of little coffee cups for your brewer, the hot water just runs through these little filters holding your coffee. Whether using a "K" cup, other brand coffee cup, or these filters, you generally do not get a really strong cup of coffee. For that you need to actually brew your own coffee. However, if you don't have a bold button on your coffee machine and want to get a stronger cup when using these disposable filters ( or "K" cups/other brands of coffee-filled cups) you can use a small gravy ladle to catch the initial and final scoops of coffee water coming out of the coffee maker, and then transfer that less strong coffee to a second (adjacent) cup that can be emptied down your kitchen sink. Sometimes I add the used coffee grounds to my garden soil. K cups and comparable brands are convenient, but it certainly is better for the environment to use either a real coffee pot that brews coffee, permanent "K" filters filled with coffee, or disposable filters to which coffee is added.

Aftermarket replacement will save you bout $120 over the GE OEM part. Even at approx $45, I think this is overpriced for what it is, but when you need this - you will know and I will save you some time and tell you my experience on my GE Profile Side by Side unit ( the *starred* troubleshooting tips would have saved me a few days of time if I did those first):

- Symptom: the freezer and fridge will not get cold, even at the coldest settings (The freezer will be barely at 32 degrees closest to the cooling fans, Fridge will never go below 38 degrees), and the sides of the external walls will be hot to the touch. Food will spoil, frozens will be thawed, and ice cream will be soupy (that was the most obvious sign for me)

- Symptom: the cooling fan in freezer will be on 24/7 attempting to cool down. The compressor in the back will get very hot and cut off which will cause the refrigerator to be in a constant defrost mode. Both systems running and competing against each other all day will make your electric bill higher (second obivous sign for me). My unit never got quiet as the compressor and cooling fans were always humming and churning.

- Troubleshooting: Cleaning your coils will / may make your unit seem immediately cooler by 2 degrees, but it's a Pyrrhic victory, since you may think you fixed the problem, but nothing happens in the long run (you will know within 2 hours using a thermometer). But, anyway, it always and still is a good idea to clean the coils periodically.

- Troubleshooting: Emptying, defrosting and checking for ice blockages and accumulations within your appliance yeilded no discernible results other than a big waste of time and possible food spoilage

- *Troubleshooting: From researching Youtube videos, you will pull your fridge out and open up the area where the condensor fan motor is and see it barely moving/dead and probably feel (after immmediately unplugging, that it is very hot to the touch). You can run a multimeter on the part to make sure it died (most accurate confirmation), or you can run an external fan (moderately accurate confirmation - see below)

- **Troubleshooting/ Bandaid fix from another reviewer on Amazon: Suspecting that is the only part broken, you will place a floor fan in front of your fridge to blow air into the coils. within an hour temperatures will reduce to usuability and the sides of the fridge will no longer feel hot. This acutally is the cheapest immediate and potentially permanent fix, but only if you dont mind having a fan running 24/7 in the floor space in front of the fridge.

- Research on OEM part will yield results over $160, but this replacement is alot less expensive, and its decription mentioned the GE part I needed (WR60X187 -- there is another vendor on AMZ that offer what looks like the same part (descibed as "833697 Refrigerator Condenser Fan Motor Kit")) for a few dollars less but it did not specify compatibility exactly).

Install is as you see on youtube videos - you will have to unplug the fridge to remove the bad part, cut off the old wire harness end from the fridge, splice to the replacement, and reinstall (you can find a new aftermarket wire harness, but that is additional cost and not 100% compatible due to the ground wire- see note below). It will work once you restore power - that fun will be spinning fast and all will be good in your world at least for this problem. You'll be back to eating hard ice cream in no time - no more soft serve soup!

My OEM part lsted 20 years before dying, so even if I get a few years out of this one , it is worth it. My fridge is now back to the default setting (middle of the dials on both the frdge and freezer) and my freezer is running at -4 degrees Farenheit and the fridge has been clocking at 34 degrees Farenheit. Other reviewers mention noise on the aftermarket part - I did not hear anything to cause concern, but mine is a new install on a garage (non living area) refridgerator.

Note - the OEM unit and OEM harness include a ground wire (green) ~ 3 wires. The replacement has no ground ~ 2 wires. Keep this in mind and understand any potential risks of not having a ground on the replacement.

Something got sloshed over the top of the tub in our washing machine and got down in the pump and chewed it up. I knew the pump was stuck because I could hear a very slight humming sound when it tried to drain the tub. I ordered this, watched a few videos on YouTube about how to replace it...and...now I have a working washing machine again for a lot less than a repair man would charge me just to drive to the house and tell me what the problem was.

Tips:
Empty the tub as much as you can with a bucket, cups, shop-vac, soak up the water with towels...whatever you can do. There will be water you can't get out because it's below the tub, but the more you get out before you start, the less there will be that can spill all over your laundry room floor.
Rent a shop vac. Hook it to the drain hose (after you've finished getting all the water you can out of the tub) and lower it to the floor. That will get a lot of the water out of the pump and hoses below the tub.
Put some towels down on the floor. This will give you something comfy to lay on as you're working and absorb some of the water you're not going to get out of the washer any other way.

I'll get to the "Sonic Ice" part below.

The ice maker required no assembly at all when it came out of the box, but instructions in two places said it needed to sit upright before use so that the refrigerant could settle into place. Instructions plastered to the maker said 24 hours; those in the manual said 1 hour. I let it sit overnight--it was fine.

Instructions suggested cleaning out the maker with warm soapy water, and I'd say that's good advice since I found several hair-like strings of glue around some of the joints. There's a small plug on the underside to drain the water from inside once cleaning is finished.

When the lid is lifted, you look in and see a plastic basket which sits towards the top of the machine in the front half. The ice drops in here when it is formed. (The back half is where the ice makes.) The "water tank" is just the area below the basket, and when you fill it with water, you have to be sure not to let it come up to the bottom of the basket. A pump pulls the water up into the back half of the maker to make the ice, which takes maybe five minutes or so.

HERE"S THE CRUCIAL PART: There is no "freezer" aspect to this maker. Once the ice drops in the basket, it sits there until it melts back into the water tank if you don't use it. I think the maker must monitor the weight of the basket to trigger the mechanism to make more, as it will keep the basket full.

SONIC ICE? Well, sort of. It has a different shape--that hollow bullet shape--but because the maker doesn't store the ice at freezing temperatures, it's 'softer' to chew than ice from a refrigerator freezer.

VERY HAPPY WITH THE PRODUCT! It's quiet, except for those moments when the ice rattles into the basket. We turn it off at night. Keeps my wife in all the ice she can chew!

2. Once complete cycle takes just over 90 MINUTES to complete
3. There are 10 batches of ice per cycle, with each batch taking between 9-10 minutes.

While working inside an oven is never fun, this was an easy swap and worked perfectly. *Unplug the range before messing with it.* Remove the plate at the bottom of the oven with the two thumb screws at the back. Remove the silver heat spreader plate with the two screws at the front. Use a socket wrench to remove the old igniter, you may need to unscrew the bracket at the back of the oven to lift the gas bar it's connected to and lift it slightly from the rear to reach the bottom screw on the igniter. Be careful not to drop any screws. Gently pull some slack in the wire connected to the igniter, and disconnect the wire with pliers by wiggling the connector side to side. Connect the new igniter and reassemble the oven in reverse. 30 minutes, tops.

The only complaint I have is the insulation value could be a little better especially in the lid however this can be easily fixed by putting a coat or blanket over the top (making sure not to cover the compressor vents).

All in all I would highly recommend this cooler!! For the price (cheaper then a lot of quality ice chests) it’s a great buy. I hope this helps anyone on the fence.

This dryer duct cleaner was about as easy to use and worked as well as you could ask for. The segments are flexible enough to bend around 90 degree corners no problem, though it did take a little bit of finessing to get it around an S-bend in my duct. The kit seems pretty durable, and I don't forsee any issues getting several annual cleanings. 12' was not quite long enough to get my whole duct, but working from each end using a shop vac to assist (see below) took me all of maybe 20 minutes once I got the dryer moved.

In addition to following the instructions about removing the outside vent cap, I found it worked well to stick the blower hose of my shop vac into the dryer end of the duct and blow air through the duct as I worked the rotary brush through. (Just make sure to use a rag or blanket to seal up the end you're working from, so the air is actually forced through the duct) With the shop vac going, and working about 12" at a time, I ended up with a pretty good pile of lint outside that had been cleaned out!

The instructions say to wrap each joint with a piece of duct tape--that's probably a good idea, but as long as you're careful to ONLY rotate the brush clockwise, you will actually be tightening the threaded joints. Another reviewer mentioned setting the clutch on your electric drill to the lowest setting--also a very good idea, just in case the brush were to get caught on a sharp edge of duct or something.

After reading good reviews and liking the overall color and shape of this vent hood, I took a chance on it for our kitchen remodel. It came well packaged and all the steel was covered with protective plastic.

Our remodel team read the installation directions and put it up, including cutting a hole in the wall since we did not have the stove in this spot in the old kitchen. It came with two options for the stack. They used this one (the other one had vent slits). The vent hood base attaches to studs in the wall with two large bolts. Then the stack sits on the top. Behind the stack, there is an outlet our electrician installed and the plug for the hood. Also there is a plastic, accordion style tube that vents air from the stove to the outside of the house. The building inspector was not sure the plastic tube was good enough for fire code because usually you use a metal version, in case your cooking catches fire and gets sucked through the tube. A plastic tube could melt and allow fire into the walls. The contractor put fire insulation spray between the tube and the wall. The inspector said it was alright. We looked for written proof that this meets code but didn't find it.

The vent hood looks nice. I polish the steel with a little bit of baby oil on a microfiber cloth to remove grime and finger prints. I wasn't sure I liked the edge with protruding buttons. But I am used to it now and like the overall look of the vent hood.

The cost was better than anything I saw at my local store. The cost of installation exceeded the cost of the hood.

The light and fan might make this a 4 star hood. But I don't want to knock it since I have nothing to compare it to. The lighting is very important to me because it lights what I am cooking more than my overhead lighting. There are two small lights coming down. It's good but I imagine more expensive hoods have more lighting coverage. The actual fan has various settings and suits my needs for being a normal home cook. I imagine more expensive fans are bigger. I can't complain and I like the sound level for each of the fan settings.

I did not order the optional charcoal filters. The underside of the vent has three metal grates. They are very easy to remove for cleaning. That is a good design.

Overall this was a good buy. It came with a few challenges for the carpenters, fitting it into place just right and trying to align the top of the stack with our ceiling. But they got it and it works.

I recently purchased this refrigerator from Lowe's. I actually tried to shop for it on Amazon but it didn't come up when I put in the search variables. I later saw this listing. I'm glad I got it on sale from Lowe's, because otherwise I would have paid too much.

Amazon has this refrigerator listed at 16 cubic feet. Hair lists this model number as 16.4 cubic feet. Amazon lists this as 27 inches deep. Haier lists it as 26.5 inches deep. The doors curve out, so on the edges it is only 26 inches deep, maybe a quarter-inch less. The width is 32.75 inches. The reason I'm sharing these is because I needed to get it into a fairly small hole and I figure other people might want the information, too.

The hole I had to put this in was 33.25 inches, which was too narrow if I wanted to push it back all the way. So I had to pull the refrigerator away from the back wall so that the door wouldn't hit the cabinet. The doors are hinged so that they can fit in a small place, but even so you will need a 34-inch hole if you want to push this all the way back against the wall. I had to pull it out an inch so that it is 27 inches from the wall on the edges and 27.5 inches or so in the middle.

There are a couple of things I don't just love. The bottom freezer area has drawers that are only 10 inches wide. This isn't wide enough for a frozen pizza. There is a space at the top of the drawers that could have taken a shelf so that it would hold a pizza, because each side of the freezer is 12-inches wide. I think it will be a simple matter to cut out a shelf from corrugated plastic and simply lay it atop the drawer framework (there's actually plastic there to hold it, so the drawers will still be operational). This is an easy fix, so I'm surprised the manufacturer didn't do something along these lines.

The other thing I don't like so much is that there are only three shelves in the refrigerator. Only one of the shelves can be adjusted, essentially giving a choice between having the tall stuff on the bottom shelf above the vegetables or in the middle. I would very much like to have four shelves, so that two of the shelves could be fairly narrow in height, which is perfect for soda cans and just lots of stuff. As things are now I have a lot of dead space over the stuff I put in the fridge. With my configuration my shelves have a clearance of 7.75 inches, 7.25 inches, and 10.25 inches. Given that most jars and cans are only five-inches high and stuff like hamburger meat is only two-inches high, it would be really nice to have an extra shelf and less dead air space.

Also, there is no ice maker, but I knew that when I ordered it. If I could have found an equally shallow refrigerator with an ice maker for the same money I would have bought it. And that's really the selling point on the fridge. It's more shallow that any other model I could find at this price point. Every other so-called "counter-depth" refrigerator stuck out an additional three or four inches. I was important for the way my kitchen is laid out not to have a giant fridge sticking out, otherwise I wouldn't be able to open the back door. We drink a lot of coffee each month, so I am pretty reliable about monthly de-scaling as well, as I know from experience that failing to do so will greatly reduce the longevity of a Keurig coffee maker.

I never had a coffee machine with a charcoal filter before, so when the K-Supreme arrived, I decided to include replacing the filter as part of the monthly de-scaling regime.

I quickly learned that if you don't soak the filters in water for 10 minutes (as per the instructions), and then run one cup of water thru a cycle, the first several cups will have a strong brackish taste. This applies to ANY charcoal filter, including Keurig's.

If you follow these simple steps, you will find no difference between these filters and the much more expensive Keurig OEM filters. More importantly, these are cheap enough for you to include in your monthly de-scaling routine as a good way to preserve both the taste of the coffee, as well as to filter out any impurities that may otherwise make their way thru your new Keurig machine.

We have this 16” sealer as well as two 8” sealers, and seems we’re grabbing one most every day. One nice thing that many folks may not have thought of is, these sealers will seal potato chip bags! Why would you want to? Well, for us, trash food scraps can be put in empty food bags (such as from chips) and sealed, keeping any odor locked inside.

We have a new litter of kittens and there was some food that sat out too long and I didn’t want to trust. So found a chip bag, dumped the old kitten chow in (water-soaked dry food mixed with canned paté) and sealed it up. …Or at least that was the plan.

We’ve had this sealer for 3 years and I’ve never had a problem. This time, I ended up cutting my finger on a piece of metal left over from the manufacturing process. On the bottom are two oblong holes. Each hole had excess metal that was not removed. Well, guess my tough-as-leather skin is no more, cause I got a cut. First couple of days went well but today is day 3 and it’s quite painful.

To remedy the problem, I took a pair of needle nose pliers and, using the rounded nose, formed the metal fragments up into the sealer housing. Now the unit will be safe for anyone to handle….even me! LOL

As mentioned, we have this 16” sealer as well as two smaller 8” sealers. Other than this issue, can’t say enough good about them. Wonderful tools. Just too bad about the lack of Q.C. (Quality Control) during manufacturing. So I urge anyone to check their sealers and make similar ‘fixes’ as needed.

Again, the use of space is near perfect!

It's also attractive, with it's cool interior LED lighting, stainless steel exterior, and cool looking blue icon touch screen controls by the ice maker.

So far, I love the fridge!

This is a genuine FSP (Factory Specification Part) - and it fits perfectly. More importantly, it has the terminals for the belt switch. This shuts the dryer off if the drive belt breaks. Many of the cheaper non-genuine motors don't have provisions for the belt safety switch, so you have to bypass it for the dryer to run. So what happens if the belt breaks while the dryer is running? Well, since the safety is bypassed, the heater (gas flame or electric heating elements) will still be on but the drum won't be turning. This may cook your clothes, or worse yet, start a fire if the over-temp switches don't kick in on the burner or heater.

Don't cheap out, pay the extra for a genuine part.

I purchased this from another online appliance place back in late 2014.  After maybe 3 years something I had in the fridge went bad and rotted/oozed while I was on vacation.  I think its that Kambutcha junk my wife drinks.  No big deal - cleaned it up but after that the fridge was never the same.  The summer after that water would always pool at the bottom of the fridge and spill over.  I thought I had wine that was not corked shut but it turned out to be that the evaporation system was not working right ans water was pooling instead of being evaporated properly.  In the back is a small drain that was plugged up with some nasty sludge - it seems that my wife's Kambucha had evolved to something more nasty than what comes in the overpriced jug from Whole Foods!  I needed to clear the sludge plugging up the drain but to clear it completely you really need to disassemble the entire back of the fridge!  After disassembling the back (about 16-20 screws) I used an air compressor and pipe cleaners to clean all that nasty stuff out and the water could freely drain properly - my water/evap issues were solved.  Soon after my fridge would continuously alarm that the door was open and the light would come on (as if the door was open).  There was no mechanical switch to be seen so I assumed the switch must be magnetic.  As it turns out it was.  Apparently the water from my previous problem had pooled inside that folded metal seam at the bottom, rusted, and swollen that folded metal so that magnet sensor in the lower left of the fridge front could no longer sense the magnetic gasket on the door when shut.  For about a year I could wipe this all down with soapy water and it was often enough to make a better seal and trigger the sensor but eventually the rust became too much.  In the end I had to take the bottom plastic trim off and it you look top the left (if you face the fridge) on the bottom is a thin pair of wires that go to the sensor.  They un-clip easily.  If you take the longer end that runs into the computer circuit and just short out those two wires it tells the system that hte dfoor is shut.  An old school PC jumper worked perfectly to short these 2 pins for me.  The door is always shut now as far as the fridge is aware so no alarm ever.  However there is no automatic light when the door opens. but you can choose to have the light on all the time (3 small LED lights do not use much power) or leave it off all the time - or manually turn it on and off as needed with the bottom on top.  Its annoying but a lot better than contestant door open alarm beeping.  I'm annoyed that a $2K small fridge was designed in a way that this could happen.  If they just sealed that bottom lip where the sensor lived water would not have been able to get in and start to rust, however I knowledge that it started with a spill that I was responsible for (darn that Kambucha).  What did I learn?  It doesn't pay to buy higher quality appliances because all are for the most part poorly designed and there is no value in paying for an appliance brand name.  When this breaks I plan to toss it in the trash and buy the cheapest replacement I can find at Sam's or Costco, assuming it will fail in 5 years or so anyway.

I live in an apartment building with a communal laundry room. Over the years I have grown increasingly disgusted with this arrangement as people seem to be washing some very gross things and the machines are filthy. It is my concern that laundromats are not much better. I also have a great fear of getting bedbugs and what better place to get them then in a communal laundry. So I decided to research all my alternatives for doing my own laundry in my apartment. There is not enough room in my place for full appliances and I am not sure the manager even allows that. So I tried doing laundry simply by hand entirely. It was a ton of work and the worst part was dealing with the soaking wet clothes. No matter how much I hand wrung them they still were dripping all over the place and they were heavy and took forever to dry. So, I looked at all kinds of drying options. After reading all the reviews and studying up a bit on the Nina Soft Spin Dryer I took the plunge and bought it. It is the best purchase I have made in a long time. I thought the reviews were too good to be true but I must say that is not the case. I am very surprised at how well this dryer works. It has made doing hand laundry a breeze. I use an old fashioned laundry plunger. I have seen it called "the Mobilewasher" here on Amazon though I have seen it called other things on other sites. With two buckets, the Mobilewasher and the Nina Soft Dryer I am able to wash my clothes as needed for the week in a very efficient, effective and relatively fast manner. When washing clothes by hand I used to step on the clothes in the bucket (like stomping on grapes in a barrel) but found that the mobilewasher is the better and easier option. It actually takes less work. because it suctions the clothes back up after plunging them down. You can't do this with your bare feet. Anyway I digress. With this combination i can get outfits ready the night before i need them. I say the night before because the clothes will need some time to dry longer after being taken out of the Nina Soft. But they come out fairly dry and don't take long to dry. Things like towels take longer to dry than a pair of underwear. I live alone and have no children. I am a single adult and do laundry for myself only and this has been a wonderful solution. I would probably use it even if I had free and CLEAN access to the traditional washing and drying machines because it is fast! The only thing I can say is I believe I still need to go to the communal laundry to clean heavy comforters or blankets. i have not tried these things in the Nina soft but if I ever do I will come back here and update. I have washed towels, underwear, jean shorts, blouses etc and I am satisfied with the condition of all of them coming out of the Nina soft. I think my clothes are cleaner and less damaged while using this system. Definitely does not age your clothes like heat from a traditional dryer will do. I recommend it highly.

Update:

It is Now November 17th and I have been using this dryer for about a month and a half. The novelty has worn off but the practicality has not. I still highly recommend this dryer. I wanted to make a couple of recommendations. One is I have noticed that some people in their reviews state that they dump the water directly into their bathtub or shower after washing their clothes in buckets or what have you. I try to avoid this as there is some lint that collects in the water as you wash and I worry that I will clog the drains so I pour the water into the toilet. I am considering getting a screen for the shower floor. Also I saw some complaints about having to rearrange the clothes in order to get the dryer to spin correctly. I found this sort of frustrating at first too but over time you learn how to balance it as you put the clothes in. Always put the heavy clothes at the bottom and the lighter weight clothes at the top of each load. Sometimes if I have a very heavy pair of jeans that I didn't wring out much I will just dry them alone. This goes relatively fast.

The dryer doesn't get your clothes completely dry in most cases. I have had a few polyester, thin shirts that came out almost completely dry but most clothes are damp coming out of the dryer. I am okay with this. I just hang them up to dry and usually all clothes are completely dry over night. I bought this dryer after doing clothes entirely by hand and I think it is wonderful! No more dripping wet clothes hanging around. It serves my purposes well. Oh and I must mention that there are a few things I can't dry in this dryer. Comforters and I have a heavy winter jacket that I wouldn't dry in this dryer because it is too big. Other than that everything else works out fine.

First some caveats:

A) These hold less than 2 pounds of laundry...which is not much. A couple of shirts, maybe a pare of socks and underwear. It will do pants, especially if they are lightweight, but I wonder if heavy blue jeans are over the weight limit.

B) You need to manually dump the "grey water" after the wash cycle and put in fresh water for the rinse. It's a little heavy for some people.

C) There is NO SPIN cycle! These units have neither the mechanics nor the mass to spin out water! When you are done, you have wet,soggy clothes. This unit is essentially like the old ringer washers of the 40's and 50's, but without the ringer. (Anybody seen a really big salad spinner? It might just work!)

D) Use tiny amounts of soap! As in tablespoons. You will need to experiment with your brand. Too much soap will be almost impossible to rinse out!

Best uses:

You only need to wash a shirt, etc., and you have a big washer. Do it in the small one and spin it out in the big one.
You are stuck at a hotel with no fresh clothes and you really don't want to go out to some laundromat (washateria). Keep this in your trunk for those events.
You are a college student and your wardrobe is mainly t-shirts, underwear, socks and jeans.
You are in some wonderful resort and you need to get the salt out of your nice little bathing suit.

Observations: I find that my permapress shirts come out softer than when done in my old Maytag. Perhaps it has something to do with less soap? I hear that Miele washing machines do the same thing, but they are big and cost $2,000.

I'm disabled and quite weak and was worried it might be too hard to crank or just plain tiring. It's not. The trick is to get the amount of water and clothes correct. It took me a couple loads to figure it out. If it's hard to crank or feels heavy, you either need more water or fewer clothes. If you get it right, a,small load feels about the same as a large load.

In order to get the clothes clean, make sure you hear a THUNK sort of sound as you turn it, as the vacuum created inside works. If you don't hear that, it means you need more water, fewer clothes and/or you're turning it too fast.

The difference between the three models of Ivation portable mini-icemaker comes down to the number of ice cube sizes each can produce (1, 2, or 3), the relative size of the compartment lid, the control panel and its orientation (top or front-facing), and the overall size/style of the unit.
The compressor, capacity, and operation of the three models are essentially the same.

I went into more detail in my review of the 3-sizes-of-cubes model so I’m just going to recap here:

This particular model produces only one size of ice cube. My fridge built-in only makes one-size and I've never thought it a problem. The size corresponds to the 'large' size of the two-size model and the 'medium' size of the three-size model.

The ice cubes are shaped like hollowed-out rounded cones, not the semi-circular solids many refrigerator built-ins produce nor the classic cube shape you get with freezer trays.

It takes just over a 6-cup Brita pitcher-full of water to fill the icemaker to the max indicator. The compartment lid stays open by itself so pouring is comfortable.

It takes about two hours to make cubes using just about all of the water. All three units will simply detect and go into standby when the basket is full so there’s no worry about overflow. I emptied the basket twice, the first time at about the one hour mark.

All three icemaker models are very easy to operate and don’t produce excessive noise. The three-cube model has a somewhat more complex control panel with a standby/pause function and auto on/off timer. It also provides a bit more feedback in the form of troubleshooting icons.

This one-sized cube models is probably the simplest to operate and I think the appearance of the control panels is more attractive than the one on the three size model.

All three models use the same drain plug mechanism and are easy to position over a sink.

Bottom Line: All three icemaker models are well-made and attractive – although all are too large to keep permanently on our countertop. The hollow cone-shaped cubes are an acquired taste but if you entertain a lot and need to crank out more ice than the fridge can handle (or you don’t have a built-in), it’s a handy and easy-to-use addition.

This filter works as well as one would expect.  I tried one out and returned it.  Here is why. It is grossly overpriced and is essentially a duplicate of the Hario Woodneck in grind, technique and results, and the Woodneck can be bought together with 3 extra rags for less than the price of this filter alone.  Both the Hario/rag and the Chemex/Kone require a finer grind, a tad coarser than espresso, than a Chemex/paper setup because they are more porous and the water passes through much faster.  Any coarser than that and the grounds will still be foaming when you're finished, resulting in very under-extracted coffee. I purchased the LG 2040 steam washer and dryer in combination, and could not be happier! Prior to this, we owned an old whirlpool agitator washer and drier, which worked great, but after 14 years, were starting to have some issues. In researching washers and dryers, we decided to go with the steam versions due to their excellent ability to wash more efficiently, reduce wrinkles in clothing, and reduce allergens. However, never having had any experience with the steam option on washers and dryers, we were not really sure what to expect. Well, after using them for about three week now, we are very happy with the results!

The steam option on the washer (which can be difficult to fully appreciate) definitely has benefits. The primary benefit is the ability to reduce allergens on the "Allergene" setting. It is great to know that items are getting thoroughly sanitized in the wash. Steam also reduces the amount of water being used (which is already quite low in the front-loading machine). Finally, don't worry about steam shrinking the clothes. Basically, the steam comes from above, while there is cooler water in the bottom where the clothes are located. The steam gives a deeper penetration with superior cleaning, while the cooler water keeps your fabric protected. It also minimizes wrinkling problems by softening the fabric. We've had excellent results in experimenting with the steam washer option.

Another feature we love in the washer is the load sensing capability. In this process, which takes about one minute at the beginning of the cycle, the washer spins a couple of times, judging the weight of your load (the material must be dry for this to work properly), and estimating how much detergent you should use. Bottom line, this will save you lots of money on the HE detergent required for these machines. Most loads, which look like full loads due to their volume, actually only require a half measure of detergent. The machine lets you know exactly how much to put into the load before beginning the cycle. This is a genius feature!

The washer, whether using steam or normal washing procedures, is fantastic! We've had tremendous results, and our clothing has never felt cleaner and fresher. One note: the machine does wobble a bit in the spin cycle, but is overall very quiet and smooth. It will take lots of experimentation, which can be quite fun actually, to understand all the features of this washer. Highly recommended!

We have had this cooktop for more than 6 months and have enjoyed it. We installed it as part of a kitchen remodel so that we could keep some of our favorite old cookware (not induction compliant) as well as experience the benefits of induction cooking. We had decided against gas because of the heat issue--it is hot enough in Texas! (We had rented a house in Houston with Jenn-Air gas cooktop and oven, and found that the kitchen was 10 degrees hotter when either--especially the gas oven--was used.)

Wow, for cooking quality and speed, what a difference induction makes! If we had to do this over, we would purchase a hybrid again. We rarely would need all four burners anyway, so the hybrid works fine. Please be aware of the following however:
--our contractor had to install a stronger breaker to support induction cooktop
--the rim around the edge of the cooktop is annoying, making it difficult to 1) clean and 2) accommodate large pans or griddles. We knew we wouldn't like this feature when we purchased, but when it is half price, it is hard to justify paying double to eliminate the rim!
--The electronic control panel does strange things when we get it wet. I.e., When we spray the cooktop to clean it, if any measurable amount of water/cleaner/etc. lands on the control panel, all the lights start flashing and beeping. But as soon as we wipe it clean/dry, everything goes back to normal. This happens even when we "lock" the panel. Although it makes us concerned that the cooktop might not be as durable as desired, so far, so good. We might update if that status changes.

Lastly, other reviewers have mentioned humming noises. We have found the cooktop hums more during "cool down" after the traditional electric burners have been used, but it doesn't last long and isn't that loud. Overall, we would recommend this cooktop.

LG LFXS30766S. Ice dispenser was getting flaky and then stopped working. Seems to be a common problem. You can easily pull the dispenser assy out by following this YouTube video 7V37EHMJjZQ. After pulling it out noticed a lot of the screws were rusty and there was dried water crud all over the place. Not sure why that's happening, maybe due to the ice pieces falling out of the chute?

The switch contacts had a bunch of corrosion on them too, I cleaned it off and the switch still measured open (using a DMM) when pressed in. The water must have gotten inside of it and corroded the contacts. (update: I dunked the switch in WD-40 and it started working again. I still installed the new one though).

This SZM-V01-2FA-33 is the exact same part number as the existing switch. Just pull the wires off the old one, unscrew the old switch and install this one. I had to use a screw extractor as it was totally rusted out. It's a 3 x 16 mm screw, you probably want to get a new one in case yours is rusted out too. I had some screws that were 3.22 mm diameter and roughly same length that I used as I didn't want to wait for more parts, since it's plastic not a big deal.

You'll also want to clean the contacts on the switch plug. WD-40 makes a specialist contact cleaner spray (item B0BL2G25ST, or get it at Walmart) that works good. You can also use it to clean contacts on other electronics and cables, for example cell phones and cables. Be careful with the phone, don't use too much, and hold it upside down so the fluid can drip out.

In case you were wondering, it's not the same switch used on the water dispenser. That switch is SZM-V01-4FA-33 and has a semi-circle on the end of the metal piece. That switch doesn't appear to be a failure issue like the ice dispenser switch is since water doesn't get on it.

The dispenser light on mine had also burned out, it's an LED on a small board that has wires and plugs for the dispenser switches going to it. The board part number is EBR60388513, appears to be a common part for fridges that have a light there. I bought a new board assy and will fix the old one, the LED probably burned out. The board runs on +12VDC and there is a 220 ohm resistor on it. So need to find a bright white LED the same size to replace it with. I'll update my review later if I find one that works good.
(Update: I found some 5mm 75000mcd 50mA high intensity clear white LED's that should be a good replacement).

Got this for a Kirkland/Whirlpool SAWS800JQ2 washer as I thought it was going bad due to no/slow spin. This clutch has 3 pads, the stock one on the washer did too. It looks like this washer uses the thicker light blue spring after comparing it the original.

My problem ended up being the 357021 capacitor which I had also purchased not knowing exactly which part was bad.

Be sure to check the washer suspension plate or skate plate (3946509) alignment before putting the washer back upright, it probably moved while you had the washer on its side or back as it's free floating. It's a triangle shaped plate with notches on the corners, and those notches need to line up with the base posts. If you don't the washer will spin very roughly on the spin cycle, and you'll think it's the springs or the pads but it's really this plate alignment.

It's easier to align it on its side/back, if you do it after the washer is upright you have to remove the motor and lift the tub up with a piece of wood so you can move the plate.

You probably want to check or even replace those pads too, there are 3 on the plate and 3 on the base. It's actually really easy to replace them while it's on the side/back since the pressure is removed from them.

Danby DFF261BSLDB Bottom Mount Refrigerator

We bought one of these refrigerator/freezers for our basement bar area.

Pros:

- Quite attractive. It's enameled gloss black steel on the outside with stainless steel [look] doors; inside is white. Danby's web site says this about the door material: "Spotless steel finish - looks identical to real stainless steel but without the smudging"

- Energy Star rated (uses 20% less electricity than most units); we received a $100 rebate from our power company because of that fact. Check with your utility company...

- The two thermostatic controls are in the refrigerator section against the back wall, out of the way. (See Customer Images.) Many of these small refrigerators stupidly mount the control hanging down from the inside top which gets in the way of storing anything on the top shelf.

- Frost free. The unit this Danby replaced was not frost free and its freezer would accumulate ice on of its walls just from the moisture in the air. It was a royal pain to defrost and clean up the water.

- Set to 3/4 of maximum cold, the freezer gets down to -20 degrees Fahrenheit. We couldn't test how cold it would get on maximum since none of our thermometers read lower than 20 below. We leave it at about 5 below.

- With plenty of cooling to spare we keep the refrigerator section just over freezing. These units work by directly cooling the freezer at the thermostat setting, and then circulating just enough freezer air through the refrigerator section to maintain its thermostatic setting.

- Reasonably designed storage areas. Milk, orange juice, soda cans, etc., all seem to have their place. Gallon jugs even fit in the refrigerator door.

- One of the very few small unit designs with the refrigerator section on top. That was important to us.

- If you're standing right next to a unit that's on, you'll hear a very low frequency hum (emanates from the unit's rear & bottom) - but at about 8' away, that hum is nearly inaudible. So, unless you're close to it, this thing is very quiet.

- We ordered ours via the Sears web site for $420 + tax and picked it up in our SUV (to avoid a delivery charge) from the local Sears store. Locally purchased refrigerators are MUCH easer to return if they arrive defective or damaged. Since our old GE unit was reliable, we checked out the latest GE models at local appliance dealers. Unfortunately, they wanted twice as much for the new comparably sized GE units. Perhaps these GE models were "better", but you can't tell that by looking at them and their warranty was the same.

Cons:

- The two plastic slide-in vegetable crispers in the refrigerator section are cheaply constructed and should have been larger to fully use their allotted space.

Other:

- When opening the doors, the hinged side of the door pivots to the side ½" beyond the width of the unit. This makes flush installations on a hinge side impossible. So, although the unit is 23 5/8" wide, you'll need at least 24 1/4" width (24.5" is better) if either side is to be flush to a wall. We had exactly 24" available and it was really too tight. This isn't a product defect, just something to be aware of.

- In a side-wall flush installation, the doors won't open far enough to fully remove refrigerator shelves or the freezer drawer, so set them the way you want before pushing the refrigerator into place. The refrigerator comes with a fixed location glass shelf over the vegetable crisper and 2 height-adjustable shelves, which is one too many if you plan on putting tall things on more than one shelf.

- The doors come hinged on the right. For left hinging, you'll need to lay the unit on its back on the floor or have it sitting on an appliance hand truck (where it will be at a 45 degree angle). The doors can't be re-hinged if it's upright, since the freezer door hinge screws attach to the very bottom. You'll need an 8mm wrench (box, open, socket, or adjustable), Phillips and flat screwdrivers, and a drill with a 3/32" bit for pilot holes. In spite of the product handbook's drawings being way too small, any handy person should be able to do the job. If you buy the unit locally and have it delivered, that store's delivery person might rehinge the doors for you at no or minimal cost, but verify this before placing the order.

- Once it's in place, the front two legs can be adjusted for height or level with groove joint pliers (search Amazon) or a similar tool, but the rear rollers do not adjust, which is standard for refrigerators. Therefore, it's important that the floor be reasonably level where the rollers will rest. If it isn't, consider using some type of shim arrangement that won't move when the unit is pushed into place.

- If any refrigerator feet will rest on carpet, go the Home Depot or Lowes and buy a ½" thick x 2' x 2' plywood section for under the unit. (Both stores stock this size in their lumber section.) E.g., as shown in Customer Image 4, the front of our refrigerator was on a carpet; thus, the unit rocked to and fro, and made adjusting the front feet (having sunk into the carpet) all but impossible. Plywood stopped the rocking and made the front feet accessible for adjustment, but I had to construct a temporary "ramp" onto the plywood for sliding the unit into place. If you're having someone install the refrigerator, have the plywood ready.

- The model and serial number are on a sticker on the back, so write these numbers down before pushing it into place.

Measurements:

- 26 3/4" deep from the very back to the front of the doors.

- 24" deep from the very back to the front frame (where the door gasket hits).

- 59 1/4" high

- 23 5/8" wide

- Black plastic trim at the top/bottom of the doors results in the doors being 23 3/4" wide.

- Opened anywhere near 90 degrees, the doors (on the hinge side) extend out ½" beyond the side of the unit.

- With the compressor running, it draws 1.75 amps (202 watts).

My 2007 Bosch SHX99A Apexx was experiencing a no-water inflow issue after we returned home from vacation. In my 12 years of ownership, this was the first maintenance/parts failure we experienced. This is an appliance that actually makes me happy. Truly the BEST dishwasher we've ever owned.

I ran a few simple tests to confirm what could be wrong and isolated my issue down to a water inflow problem. There's really only 3 functions that can stop water from in-flowing into a dishwasher and the water inlet valve is usually the first item to check.

Knowing we had defective plumbing in our home (for 11 years until we had a small flood), which we had to fully re-pipe our home (Kitec pipes), I suspected that the debris buildup over time had finally blocked or stopped the in-flow valve's solenoid from opening/actuating the valve mechanism.

So my choices were to hire an appliance repair person which I was quoted $300 for this repair, if indeed this was the problem, or i could DIY this for less than $30 for all parts ($16 for this valve and $13 for a new braided 5' hose and 90 degree elbow, Fluidmaster B6W60 Dishwasher Connector With 3/8-Inch and 3/4-Inch Elbow Fittings, Braided Stainless Steel - 3/8 Female Compression Thread x 3/8 Female Compression Thread, 5 Ft. (60-Inch) Length, https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B005D2K6MW/ref=ppx_yo_dt_b_asin_title_o00_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1).

So I took the leap to spend $30 and attempt this fix with the help of some YouTube videos and the Bosch online repair manual.

Around 60 minutes later, we had the new valve fully installed and checked for water-tightness.

The hardest part of this repair was removing the dishwasher's internal water hose from the old valve assembly. Over time, in this case 12 years, the hose became firmly attached to the valve's connecting end.

Nothing a flat head screwdriver couldn't solve, along with a little elbow grease and safety gloves, I was able to disconnect the hose line from the old valve.

Once the hose was disconnected, I assembled the new valve with its new 90 degree elbow fitting (along with plumbers tape as required), ensuring the elbow would not be in the way of the mounting screws for the valve face-plate, reconnected the internal hose to the new valve, reconnected the hose clamp ensuring the clamp was firmly set, connected the power fitting and the ground connector, and then finally screwed the valve face-plate to the dishwasher.

Reassembly took maybe 15 minutes total. I then used a lot of electrical tape to connect the old braided supply line to the new line and snaked it through the cabinet wall pulling the old supply line out while the new line was attached. Once I had enough new hose exposed I then removed the electrical tape and connected the supply line compression ends to the hot water supply under the sink and then to the dishwasher; hand tight plus 1 full turn with an adjustable wrench.

After a water-tight connection check I ran a Party Wash cycle to check to see if the washer was working. And it was.

We finally had water in-flowing into the dishwasher and we let this cycle run in full (30 minutes). After verifying all was good, I did final parts installs (kick plate and sound deadening foam) to complete this repair.

Overall this was an easy repair. On a scale of 1-5 I'd rate this a 2. With a few simple tools and around 60-90 minutes, any handy person can make this repair and save a few hundred bucks.

I'm slowly updating the kitchen and found this Broan Evolution 2 range hood to be a good upgrade. The previous range hood was over 28 years old. So after refinishing the cabinets using General Finishes Java Gel Stain, I installed the Broan range hood. The installation was fairly straight forward, although not exactly easy. I took the following steps:

1) After unboxing, I replaced the four halogen lights with LED lights. The set I purchased was [[ASIN:B00XK8FL0S Bioluz LED 5 Pack GU10 50W Equiv Dimmable 6.5w 3000K UL listed]] The halogen lights need a quarter turn to release. Since they are flush against the underside of the hood, turning them is difficult. Luckily they provide a suction tool that you press on and twist. They came out easily. The LED replacement lights were easy to place in and twist. They were ever so slightly larger than the halogen so they protrude just a tad. It makes them easy to grab - even though some might not like the 1/8 inch they stick out. But they work really well.

2) I took off the bottom panel to get access to the inside. Since I was using this unit for RECIRCULATING air (no ducting) I had to make some easy modifications. I took off a rectangular air damper and the electrical box cover. It comes with an air diverter that must be installed. It fits over two holes. The holes don't line up perfectly, so they have to be forced a little. I put the unit over the hole nearest the motor and then forced it over the second hole. Then I pressed down until it was firmly in place. Then I put on the washers and screws. Next, I took off the small panel which opened the path to the recirculating air vent. I just removed the two screws and lifted it out. The instructions indicate to screw it down out of the way inside the unit. Now the air will be diverted to the vent that is located at the front of the unit.

3) My cabinets above the range hood had an inch ridge all the way around. The hood would rest on that ridge which meant there would be a gap of about an inch before reaching the underside of the cabinets. The screws were obviously not long enough for that. So, I cut some wood pieces and glued and screwed them to the underside of the cabinets to fill in that gap so the range hood screws can be attached to them.

4) I prepared the wiring that was coming out of the back wall where the range hood would be going. I just used the same wiring that went with the previous range hood. The Broan has two different openings for wires - one at the top and one in the back. The opening are located on the right side of the unit about 8 inches to the right of center. Unfortunately, my wires were coming out of the wall on the left side, so I had to do a little modification. The "pop-out" plug in the Broan for the wires to go through was easy to take out. I just put my screwdriver in the little slit and wiggled it back and fourth until the metal connections gave way.

5) I shut off power to that section of the kitchen. I moved the stove out of the way. This range hood weighs about 20 pounds or so. Unfortunately I had no help during installation day, so I lifted it in place and put the screws in myself. I will spare describing to you my elaborate system of boxes and books I used to prop it up enough to get those screws in. The screws were the most difficult aspect of installation. There are 5 screws - two on each side and one in the front middle. The problem is that the unit is full of very sharp sheet metal sections and diverters and you have to try to navigate in very tight places to get the screws in. What I did first was to lift the unit flush against the cabinet bottom and all the way back and then mark with a Sharpie the places for the screws on the four holes on the sides. Then I screwed in the screws halfway. I lifted the unit up - making sure the wires were coming through the hole in the back panel - and I slipped the unit over the screw heads and slid the unit back into the screw-down gaps. The two screws on the right side are fairly accessible and I could reach up with a screwdriver and tighten them down. The two screws on the left are behind the motor and VERY difficult to reach. I tried reaching up with a small screwdriver, but my hand kept hitting the sharp motor blades. However, when I used a long screw driver, I had to angle it to avoid metal parts and it wouldn't connect with the screw head well. I collected about ten different screw drivers and finally managed to find something that would work. When the screws were all in place on the sides, then I placed the screw in the hole in the front middle.

6) Next came the wiring. It was very simple - black to black, white to white, ground to ground. I used twist wire connectors. I replaced the wire cover and that rectangular damper that I took off previously. I reinstalled the bottom panel. After all of this installation around the sharp sheet metal inside the unit, I did have a few cuts and a little blood.

7) Previous to the installation I bought some filters for the bottom panels since this is NOT being ducked to the outside. Since the air is recirculated, I needed these filters to take care of the fumes and smoke from cooking. There are the filters I purchased: [[ASIN:B004AA1JXI Broan BPPF30 Non-Ducted Replacement Filters for 30-Inch QP Range Hoods, 2-Pack]]. The filters come with clips. You just clip them against the two grates that come with the unit and then snap them in place on the bottom panel.

The unit works as expected. The lights gradually get brighter or dim lower. I really like the lights. The fan was a little wobbly - not bad though. It is MUCH quieter than my old 28-year-old range hood. The low and medium settings are fine. The high might be a little loud but the high on this unit is about the same volume as my low was on my old unit. So, it's much better. One negative is that the motor is on the left side and that is where the suction is. So, if you cook on the left side, it's great. If you cook on the right side of your stove, it is much weaker.

I will update this review after I have a chance to use it more. To this point, I would give it four out of five stars. It seems to work better than my old unit and it looks very good. The somewhat difficult installation and the inefficiency of sucking up smoke and fumes from the right side of the stove is worthy of a star deduction. But so far so good.

Living in very small studio apartments over the years, they rarely come with something like a dishwasher--you're lucky to even get a stove/stovetops. One apartment didn't have a kitchen at all (not even a kitchen sink), and getting an instant pot was the best decision I ever made. This little countertop dishwasher is easily the second best decision! Instead of putting off doing dishes because I hate wrangling my tiny sink, I can just give something a quick rinse and throw it in the washer. It's a little bulky, but as long as it's close enough to plug in, and level with (or above) a drain, it's good to go on just about any level surface. I can't connect it to my water, but that's ok--I actually prefer to manually fill it from the top when I need to, and having this feature is great. I just lay the drain hose in my sink and it does its thing. Controls are easy, the cycles aren't too long, and I have yet to have any dishes that come out icky or spotty. As with a regular sized dishwasher, it's always a good idea to rinse off any food chunks from your dishes before starting, just to prolong the life of any filters, especially since this one is small. When it's done, everything dries quickly (including the machine interior).

I've only used detergent pods (the Method mineral-based ones from Target are great), so I can't speak for using powders or liquid, but I've yet to have any detergent residue, so this machine is quite thorough and efficient.

Also worth noting is that it's not super quiet, but not loud by any means. I believe it's got two rotating arms (top and bottom), but the white noise of the washer isn't something I've had a problem with, and not so noisy that it would hinder a conversation nearby.

Speaking of the washer arms, that's something to watch for. Because of the small interior of the washer, just make sure you're not putting something in that either falls below the rack, or is too tall that it blocks them. I think the max plate size is 11" and I have washed my 6qt instant pot (inner pot) AND the lid with no problem. Kinda common sense, but if you've started a cycle and water isn't swooshing against the glass door in an arc, pause and readjust. :)

The ONLY thing that I have a problem with (a barely noteworthy problem) is not even with the washer itself--the water pitcher that comes with it (for filling the tank manually) is bizarre. The tank is 5 liters. The pitcher is 1.8? That's such a weird, arbitrary volume. And it's not very pour-friendly. Maybe this varies depending on when the machine is manufactured and packed, but it seems like it's just there as a freebie until you get something else that's easier to measure and spills less while pouring.

My 10+ year old dryer, Amana Dryer Model NDE2330AYW, was working fine but emitted an exceptionally loud screeching noise when operating. Through internet research, determined the bearing in the idler level was shot and needed replacing. Ordered this replacement idler level from Pandora's OEM Appliance Parts and it arrived earlier than expected and in a sealed plastic bag indicating it was an actual Maytag OEM part (Maytag owns Amana and apparently many parts, including this one, are interchangeable between the brands). Followed the instructions on this video - youtube.com/watch?v=8AtOYoABVp0 (search youtube for "Whirlpool Dryer Idler Level Replacement") - and the repair was completed in less than 15 minutes, and the screeching is now gone. One note about the video - my dryer has screws holding the dryer top to the body, so do not try to pry the top off the body of the dryer with a putty knife or screwdriver - you need to remove the front panels first to expose the screws holding the top lid to the body.

Can only imagine what this would have cost had a repairman been called - at least $200 I'd estimate. If you are even minimally handy, you should be able to complete this repair yourself with little effort and time, for short money with great personal satisfaction and hopefully many more years of useability for your dryer.

As an alternative you could buy the idler pulley (the wheel section of the part) alone, as it comes with the replacement bearings, but then you'd have to affix it to the idler lever and that looks like it would be a bit of a pain and would save you only a couple of dollars - not worth it for me.

Original Review May 2018:
I'm on the fence with this thing. I had serious doubts when I read the reviews and watched a couple videos, but decided to pick one up and see for myself. Overall, sure it does make a slightly better cup with less particularities required for a "non modded" (as it were) Aeropress. But it costs just shy of the Aeropress itself which I find a tad ridiculous. If it were 10 bucks, I'd recommend it, but at 25.... mmmmmmm not really. Why?

It simplifies the inversion method, and gives you a very nice metal filter, but it's really just more rubber to eventually fail (and it will - its rubber and it's under pressure and exposed to 212 degrees at each and every use) and only achieves marginally better results than what you'll get employing good techniques and timings with the Aeropress solo. The "crema" everyone reports is not crema. Sorry. It is merely bubbles that are created in the brew itself when the pressured stream jets into the vessel. When you dump the grinds, you'll find any crema there is up at the top of them, just like they always are with an Aeropress (it still makes me sad - can't I scrape them off into my brew? can't I lick at them?), but what's below is scant little of that if any and what you actually see it light foam from stream itself.
Is it easier? Yes.
Is it better coffee? Mmmm.... yes, a bit.
Is it worth the cost? Not really.
If you have 25 to blow, go for it. Or you could put it to a better use. I may return mine. Maybe you can get that one from an Amazon warehouse deal?

The overall issue was that the dryer would not heat. I took the front off and could see that the igniter would come on for about 5 seconds, shut off and repeat. I read a lot of articles and watched videos and found that the most common parts to fail in this case were the therma fuse, therma sensors, flame sensor, gas valve solenoids, gas valve and control board – in that order.

I found that the sensors are safely and easily tested with a volt/multimeter. In my case they all tested “good” so everything was pointing to the more expensive control board or gas valve. I wasn’t sure of myself so I as I indicated, I ordered this part and found that it didn’t help. From there, not wanting to touch the gas valves, I ordered a control board. My model has two boards – one in front with the buttons and knobs and another one behind it with some wire connectors and circuitry. I ordered the board with the circuitry and that fixed the issue. ~$110

When we entertain and have the inevitable ton of leftovers, or when we stock up on cheese / yogurt / cake / potato salad etc. deals at the store - we need a reliable "overflow" fridge BUT we don't want to have the space usage and electric bill of a full blown 2nd fridge. THIS SUMMIT Model # FF61 IS THE ANSWER!

THIS "FREEZERLESS" FRIDGE SIZE / PRODUCT IS KIND OF UNIQUE IN THE MARKETPLACE from what I can tell:

We used to have small Magic Chef 4.4 cu foot fridge for this purpose but the Summit being slightly larger and NOT HAVING A FREEZER makes all the difference in the world.

First of all, that one extra Cubit Foot of space (5.5 vs. 4.4) means....

You'll want to apply a hack I did to the top of the glass shelve that is right above the crisper drawer: apply 2 pieces of tape on each side of the glass that crosses over and sticks to the fridge unit white plastic. Why do this? Because there's a tendency for the cripser shelf to make the glass come with you, i.e. out towards you when you pull the white plastic crisper shelf. NOTE: This issue is * NOT * a big deal. The "fix" I mention is an enhancement you can opt to do that takes all of 2 minutes.

HOW WELL DOES IT COOL FOR IT'S INTENDED PURPOSE? GREAT. We have thermostat set slightly past half way mark and cheese, yogurt, pies, etc are kept perfectly cool.

NO MOTOR NOISE, HUM or VIBRATION that I can hear.

SUMMARY: My family * LOVES * this fridge. It's well made, cute, and keeps our perishables and pop cold. I can really recommend this.

Most importantly to me, is that their humidity numbers are almost identical and I've found in the past that temperature is easy for these things to get right and often they are way off. Then you have to GENTLY pry tabs that are along all 4 sides of the back cover to release it. If you're not very careful, you'll break it. I did a lot of research before I bought this and for there Fisher and paykel refrigerators, there isn't enough information a available. First, if you are interested in these and want specs and useful info, contact the company directly, they have a pdf pamphlet of their models that is very helpful. I had space restrictions so I did not have many options. Ideally, I wouldn't have spent nearly two grand on a less than luxury refrigerator. That said, I know that the simpler something is, the less can go wrong. So I ordered a model with no water hook ups. I also looked for a long time for a great price and found plessers.com has the best deal, 5% off if you order with a salesperson over the phone, a free 10 year warranty, free shipping and no tax. If you can wait two weeks, it's a huge savings!
That said, I wanted to mention some discoveries since I received this unit. I read in a few reviews of other models similar to this that the covered drawers on the top of the door don't stay up, they do if they are rotated fully. Also, I wanted to tell you the door is actually magnetic, something none of my other stainless appliances can boast. The interior vegetable drawers are a little difficult to access if the door is only opened 90 degrees. The smaller bin will need to be removed before the larger can be if you want to remove them from the refrigerator with the door only open at 90 degrees. I know some people will have that set up and it shows such a set up in the diagrams. The bins are also fairly small compared to many other brands, but easily accessible and make good use of space. Another weird thing about the drawers is the plastic lid that maintains moisture and seals the vegetable bins... I think it's a little cheap to put thin, bendable plastic in a refrigerator this expensive. I hope it works well but I will be very careful not to squish larger items that may touch or bend the sealing system. Nowhere have I seen anyone mention this weird feature. Most crisper bins have a lever on the drawer handle that moderates humidity, though not well. There are very specific instructions for removal and cleaning of this plastic seal, so save your manual. Another thing, the door will not fit a gallon of milk, no way, the jug pictured in product photos is from New Zealand and is likely metric and thin. That is what this refrigerator is designed for, metric stuff. I don't like keeping my milk in the door anyway, so I am not disappointed by this. Milk should be in the coldest part of the refrigerator where cold air pools, not in a door where temperatures are most variable. The unit overall is really nice, aluminum and stainless features on the interior make me feel appreciative, I really dislike plastic on shelves. The shelves are also really easy to adjust! Not kidding, having had a typical Kenmore with the metal triangular struts that fit into tracks in the back, this system is almost funny how easy it is-it's clearly the best designed refrigerator for adjusting shelves out there.
The unit isn't really loud when it is at maximum power like other reviews complained of...I'm not that picky though-I have toddlers and nothing quieter than clanging symbols really bothers me now. This refrigerator fits wonderfully into the space my previous dinosaur overcrowded. Hope this helps others decide on their next refrigerator purchase. I will update with performance as time goes by.

The store I purchased it from (Lowe's) did not have any such solution. Neither did Bed Bath & Beyond or Ace hardware. I finally found a 5 pack of safety 1st stove knob covers at Home Depot. Like many others, my Maytag fridge just up and died one day. The fridge was about five years old and never gave me a problem. There were no warning signs or anything. I took a risk and I'm glad I did! Local repair shops couldn't get the part for at least a week and who knows what they would have charged. This board came in about 36 hours after I ordered. It took me maybe 15 minutes to pull the old board and hook in the new one. Programming was a small pain as it didn't want to take the code at first, but once it did, everything fired back up and in about 24-48 hours, everything was cooled down and working as it should. It has been over a week since I installed the board and it is still running. I lost some food, but it gave me an excuse to clean everything, so silver lining. And $200 is way better than buying a new fridge (and who knows how long it would take to get one, given how messed up the supply chains still are). If your fridge has power and the front panel is either dead or glitched out, this may be the part for you, and it has to be among one of the easiest DIY fixes ever.
