After years of use, it would not only no longer fully close using gravity, but even when we pushed the door shut, it frequently bounced off and 're-opened'.  The parts in the kit did fit perfectly, and appeared to be a duplicate of the replaced parts.  It worked similar to new (would gravity close from about 1/4 open) for about a month before we noticed the issue seems to be returning.  After about 4 weeks of use, the door will no longer close using the CAM and gravity alone.  I suspect it is the quality of the plastic parts as noted by another reviewer.  It's not hard to install, but it will require you to fully remove the door to remove and replace the cam assembly.  In my case for just the frig side door, that's the bracket/brace that bolts to the top of the door/frig.  Once unbolted, the door can be lifted up and removed completely from the frig.  Replace the parts and then re-assemble.  A second person is helpful to hold the door upright while you reassemble to top bracket (the last step).  I will try to find an actual OEM for next time as I don't like doing this and failure after one month is unacceptable.

The bibs are about the same thickness and durability of heavy duty aluminum foil. They're not industrial strength aluminum, but they aren't designed to be, as they're disposable. My gas stove has different sizes of burners, and one of the burners was too large for the bib. To make it fit, I simply cut out more of a circle on the inside of the bib until it fit on the specific burner. To further help prevent messes, I placed some heavy duty strength aluminum foil in the center of my cooktop between the burners. Some people might think it looks tacky, but I don't care at all - what I care about is preventing caked on mess on my cooktop, and these bibs are great for doing that.

So, I have been very happy with this machine. It looks nice and is fairly quiet. Since I am a DIY'er, and I won't have to hassle with the warranty stuff and the repairmen.

========UPDATE ON THE WATER WALL WAND==========
The lower moving arm is tricky. It does not move back and forth continuously during the wash cycle, so, it is easy to think that is it not moving at all. This arm moves once at the very start of the cycle, as a self test, so try and catch it there to see if it moves. If you block it with an object in the lower rack extending beneath the basket, the machine won't cycle, but will blink on and off. Putting a big dirty bowel in the lower rack is also a way to test the lower arm.
There is way this arm may not work and be hard to figure out. There is a magnet in the arm which, when the arm is fully back at the rest position, tells the machine where it is. Magnets may degrade over time and the machine may not detect that the arm is fully retracted. I put two of those small, silver, "super magnets" on the bottom of the arm where the factory installed magnet is. They just stick there. Having done that, and being careful about objects in the lower rack not extending through the basket and blocking the arm (they may get dislodged during the cycle and block the arm), I have not seen issues with the "water wall" wand.

============Update Fall 2020======================
The water wall arm stopped working. The motor that drives it was broken. There is a good U-tube video about this There is a cheap plastic part in the motor casing that breaks, disconnecting the motor from the moving arm. I had previously purchased another brand of water filter for my refrigerator, and it worked great. There were no install issues whatsoever. For example, there is a plastic piece that holds the butt end of the filter. You slide it over the filter end, turn the assembly until the plastic piece is facing the 12:00 to 1:00 position, insert, push slightly and turn clockwise. The plastic piece ends up being parallel to the floor (pointing at the 3:00 and 9:00 positions).

The install on this brand didn't go that easy. I tried the method noted above and couldn’t get the assembly to lock in place. I didn’t want to push for fear that I would crack or damage something inside the refrigerator. I first thought the filter might be too long, but it was the same length. I then oriented the old and new filter in the same manner and laid them side by side. The problem was evident almost immediately. There are locating tabs / tangs near the tip of the filter, and the ones on the new filter were offset a few degrees from the old filter.

This meant that I had to rotate the assembly around until I felt the tabs ease into place. When all was said and done, the assembly had to be inserted at the 10:00 position and after locking into place, the assembly was pointing at the 1:00 position. This isn’t a big deal to folks who don’t expect things to go back the same way as before, but it is to others. And I admit, the symmetry of the plastic piece lining up with the air vent slots at the bottom of the refrigerator is appealing. Now, it’s sitting at an offset of 30 degrees or so.

It’s also a big deal to folks who don’t take the time to figure out why something isn’t working. They very well could damage their refrigerator if they try to force it. And to be honest, I don’t understand why the offset even exists. The manufacturer likely created a drawing from which to build the filter molds, and they should have used an OEM filter to make that drawing.

The reason why the tabs are offset is a mystery. But what’s done is done in that you can’t change the mold easily, so you’re going to get a replacement that is slightly different than OEM.

UPDATE 4.4.18: I just added a second Proteus sensor at our second location, and it couldn’t have been easier. What's nice is that I can use the same account as I did for the original sensor, even though it’s on a different WiFi network. I just set this device up. It was pretty straighforward, but you need to have the provided temperature extension plugged in and should have your WiFi setter open in your phone or tablet before you plug in the sensor. If your WiFi setter doesn’t immediately pick up the Proteus WiFi signal, try pressing the black button next to the temperature sensor jack for several seconds, and the device will reset and should get the Proteus network to appear. You need to enter your account info (email and password) on their website and then log in. You will see your sensor with the temp and humidity readout. You can then do your alert settings for low and high temp and humidity %, etc., and add additional emails addresses, and cell phone numbers (for texts, if you want). Mine started recording the temp and humidity with great accuracy. I plugged mine into an UPS battery backup, so it will still work, if there is a power outage (my WiFi router is also plugged into the same UPS). Parents have had a Netatmo weather station for years and love it. I don't need a sensor to tell me if it's raining outside, but I liked the idea of tracking indoor temp/humidity/CO2. I was on the fence for a long time and finally decided to buy during a Black Friday sale ($75).

Let's start with the good. The setup was really easy, a lot less painful than other internet-of-things you've used. The app UI will be familiar to anyone who has used Netatmo before - I love that you can easily look at historical data. I think the design is quite elegant, even if the rose-gold-and-white wouldn't be my first choice.

The bad is that the whole product feels limited:
* you can get notifications to your phone, but you can't easily configure what alerts to get or what threshold to be triggered. You can NOT turn off the notification for when you check the room quality on the sensor itself.
* the product advertises "air quality", but only shows CO2. I was expecting a wider range of measurements so I could learn about what pollutants are drifting in from the city.
* there is no "so what?" in the app. If my CO2 level is a little too high, what can I do about it? I'm thinking about how tools like FitBit have more elaborate explanations for the factors you should pay attention to.
* but the WORST part about this product is the lack of integration to services like IFTTT. I simply do not understand why this integration is still missing - it really frustrates me that I cannot use this as a sensor to automatically trigger things like turning on a humidifier or changing a thermostat.

For $75 I figure I might as well hang on to it and hope that one day they enable integrations. But if I could go back in time, I would not buy this product again. There's nothing particularly special or unique about it and there's no integration to give it more functionality.

I purchased the 4-faucet model of this about a month ago. Here are my impressions so far:

First, this "homebrew" package is an absolute steal of a deal, even if you do not plan to use ball-lock style kegs. When you are looking at commercial kegerators, once you go past single faucet models, pretty much every manufacturer sells them with just the tower, faucets, and beer lines. No taps, no CO2 bottle, no air lines, no CO2 manifold. The price of that stuff really adds up, and this kit here gives you a significant discount vs. buying that stuff individually, and none of it is low-end kit. You're getting a dual gauge regulator, not a single-gauge. You're getting a metal CO2 manifold/splitter, not a plastic one. And the red CO2 bottle is so beautiful that I almost want to set it on top of the machine so everyone can look at it. You're not going to be able to piece that together for the price of this kit from anywhere, including from this vendor.

If you want to convert a couple of the taps to a standard tap, the ball lock taps are threaded, and an adapter to adapt it to a normal sankey-style connection costs $5-$10 (look for beer tailpiece with 1/4" MFL). There is clearance within the fridge for the air hose-to-adapter-to-sankey tap configuration without having to resort to a low-profile sankey tap, though you'll have to tilt the keg to get it through the door because it will be slightly taller than the door opening when configured like this. Also, the beer lines of this kit come set up for normal sankey taps, and you'll have to remove that fitting in order to run the included ball lock. So, even if you really just want to run normal sankey taps, you can throw away the ball lock taps, buy sankey fittings for the air lines, and still be way ahead on price. I'm running 2 and 2 right now.

Now for a list of observations in no particular order:

The packaging of the kegerator is shockingly robust. It's in a really nice custom crate with metal blocks that hold the wheels in place. All the crating around the kegerator is sawn plywood and not just cheap wood. You're going to want a pry bar to get this thing apart, as each joint has 3 nails securing it. Very impressive.

The packaging of the rest of the stuff is kinda meh. You'll get a box with the tower in it, and another box with everything else. They will be cellophane-wrapped to the top of the kegerator, and all of that to the top of a shipping pallet. The two accessory boxes came pretty bashed up on mine, but there was no damage at all to the stuff in the boxes. They're mostly air inside the box, so they seem to crush easily on the corners.

Take a close look at the return policy. Everything has to be returned in the original containers and in new condition, and there's a restocking fee, and you pay shipping. As I noted above, the beer lines are set up with sankey-style fittings that are crimped on. You have to cut the lines to install the included ball-lock fittings, and doing so makes the item non-returnable according to the return policy. Same with the 4-way CO2 manifold, which comes with mounting hardware, but you have to drill some holes to mount it, again making the unit non-returnable. You need to make darn sure you are happy with the size of the unit and the noise level of the unit before you assemble it all, and if you're not happy with that, you're still looking at dropping a few hundred dollars to return it between freight fees and restocking fees. I don't think policy is non-competitive vs. other commercial kegerator suppliers, but remember this is not being sold by Amazon, so you should not expect Amazon's return policy.

My unit did not come with diamond plating for the floor. Instead, it came with a heavy rubbery plastic waffle mat. The listing very clearly specifies diamond plate, and it's in the photos, so I expected diamond plate. That being said, I think this mat might be better for my usage (which is at home, not commercial), as it seems to absorb shock quite well and may dampen some vibrations. I did not call to complain about it, but really if you're going to list diamond plate, you shouldn't swap that out for something else without any notice.

It took a friend and me about three hours to set it all up. Some of this was time wasted arguing about things like where to mount the gas manifold and which screws to use for the tower - the ones that came with the tower or the ones that came with the kegerator. But there are a lot of parts to assemble here with the four tap system. If I had to set up another identical one, I could do it in about an hour, I think.

There were some quality issues with the factory assembly.
- The door seal fell off the first time I opened the door after uncrating it. I apparently didn't get it back in quite right (you need to use a screwdriver or something to seat the seal into the track at the corner - you can't just press it in or it falls back out) because it came off again a couple weeks later, which ended up making the door not seal properly, running the compressor for about 12 hours straight and freezing all the beer before being discovered.
-The tower mount sleeve in the kegerator is two pieces, with the top piece keyed to the top of the kegerator, but the bottom piece just pressed in place, and the holes were not aligned between top and bottom preventing the bolts from going through. It's pressed in place quite tightly, so it took some time to determine it was not in fact glued in place and to get it loose to align the holes and reinstall.
-Two of the screws holding the faucet T-top to the tower were loose.

The unit is loud in a very weird way. The compressor itself isn't all that loud, and it doesn't run that often once you've reached a stable temperature with the kegs. The problem is the internal fan that runs 100% of the time circulating air in the kegerator. For whatever reason, that fan causes the entire unit to vibrate slightly - the door, the tower, the sides, the kegs - everything vibrates at the same low frequency. The low frequency vibration of the sheet metal sides casts out beams of low frequency hum that reminiscent of maybe 20 fluorescent tubes all humming together. By "beams" I mean this is highly directional where if you are about ten feet from the unit, you can stand in one spot and hear nothing, and then move 1 foot to the right, and be inundated with hum, and then move another foot and it goes away. If I press my hand firmly against the center of the side, I can significantly mute the noise. The manual says if the unit vibrates, make sure it is level. Leveling mine did nothing to dampen this. This is the only real drawback to this unit. It would likely not be noticeable in a commercial setting, but if like me, you set it up in the bar of your man cave, it is not ideal. You might want to consider a homeowner-grade kegerator, as they omit this fan completely (which has the drawback of not being able to chill the tower without adding a tower chiller with a small fan).

The installation instruction specify to make sure the air hose goes all the way up the tower, but the air hose is not actually long enough to go all the way up the tower, as far as I can tell. I was able to get mine about 1" short of all the way up prior to it pulling out at the other end. The tower stays nice and cold.

The tower is insulated, but the T-top faucet box is not. I don't know if that matters, but I found it interesting. There appears to be plenty of room in there to insulate the 3 non-faucet sides and the top with some rigid foam without blocking the tower inlet, and I may try that to see what happens, as I have a sheet of rigid foam lying around.

You'll see a lot of people online recommending 12 ft beer lines, and this comes with six. The six seems to work just fine for me without foaming. I'm running ~35 degrees, 12psi CO2. It pours fast and well on both a pale ale and a brown ale. Make sure you bleed the keg pressure down to your desired pressure when you first tap a new keg, as they can come in pretty high from the brewery and cause a lot of foaming.

The thermometer that comes mounted to the air box in the back is not super helpful. It seems to be strongly influenced by the evaporator temperature such that it'll drop 10-12 degrees whenever the compressor turns on. I'll probably move it more towards the front or get a digital one.

Though there is a shelf on the back to install the CO2 bottle, it barely has enough headroom for the bottle. The two-gauge regulator does not fit in the normal position (I think if you had a 1-gauge regulator it would fit fine). I had to cant mine forward about 45 degrees to clear the top, but then you have to rotate the bottle to clear the back, so the regulator sticks slightly into the keg space, and it's aimed down and to the right, which makes it tough to read. It's not easy to fit 4 kegs in there with the regulator jutting into the keg space like this. I note on one of the manufacturer's web pages it says you can do 4 with an external CO2 mounting kit, but the other pages do not mention this limitation. I can verify that you can fit 4 of the 1/6 barrel kegs in there with the CO2 bottle inside the kegerator, but it takes some careful packing, and you have to assure that none of the beer/air hoses are dangling down pinched between the kegs or it won't fit.

The back of the kegerator has four tapped holes for the external mounting kit which is available for around $25 if you call the seller. I ordered one, and it is very well made, but the bolt holes drilled in it did not match the holes on the back of the kegerator. They were the correct horizontal spacing, but too long vertically, so re-drilling was necessary to mount it.

Finally, these are the combinations of keg sizes you can fit inside:
- 4 x 1/6 barrel kegs - doesn't matter if they are commercial beer kegs or Cornelius kegs, they both fit
- 2 x 1/4 barrel slim (the "slim" ones are full 1/2 barrel height but narrow diameter)
- 1 x 1/4 barrel slim + 2 x 1/6 barrel
- 1 x 1/4 barrel short ("pony keg", which is full 1/2 barrel diameter, but only half height
- 1 x 1/2 barrel

Original review: The biggest issue I have with this counter top ice maker is size. It is not a small device at all. Other than that issue, and the amount of counter space that is needed for this item, I'd have to say I, and the rest of my family, really like this gadget -- the third in a line of similar gadgets. The first was, if my memory serves, an Emerson branded device that was obtained from a former partner of the A to Z online store where you are reading this review. That device is one that I purchased about 6 years ago. It lasted about 2.5 years and then unfortunately just refused to work any longer. Considering how dependent my spouse and I, and the others still living in the house with us (our next generation), were on the ice that the gadget made for us (we use it up about as quickly as the ice maker makes it), we were all very sad when that device gave up the ghost.

When that device died, it was replaced with a smaller cousin of this Igloo Counter Top Ice Maker (one of these: [[ASIN:B00FI4DBTU Igloo Portable Countertop Ice Maker]]). That ICE102 model (which oddly can't be found, at least not in the silver color, by searching for the model number as that search will turn up an RCA re-brand ([[ASIN:B00INXGA1O ICE102 Compact Ice Maker]]) of the same thing. You can find a Red color Igloo version in your search if you are lucky) recently started making awful noises as it was unable to move the tray/bucket that holds the water that is used to make the ice cubes and thereby also unable to drop and shovel the cubes into the tray that the cubes eventually get shoveled into. I heard it making the noise and did my best to clean it up and try to eek more life out of it, but at the same time stopped at my desk and hit the order button to get this replacement item ordered. My cleaning and efforts at making some progress in restoring that older model to some use did get it working for just long enough for this replacement to come in and get put to use. Actually, we had a few days of overlapped use of that ICE102 before it gave up the ghost again, this time with some metal shavings or mineral shavings that seemed to be coming from the areas where the gears are on the side of the cup/bucket/tray that holds the water that is used to make the ice. Yet again, I was able to do a bit more clean-up on the device and get it to function again, but at that point my spouse and I had already deployed this replacement into service.

I can compare this device to the other two mentioned Counter Top Ice Makers (the [[ASIN:B00FI4DBTU Igloo Portable Countertop Ice Maker - ICE102]] and [[ASIN:B00KTJ3MT8 Emerson Portable 26 lbs Ice Maker Refrigerator w/Ice Scoop & Electronic Controls]]) having used all three of them by now. The quick comparison would note that the ICE102 model works, but has a much smaller catch tray for the ice that it makes. With that smaller sized catch tray that model tends to fill the catch tray quickly and then stop making ice as it considers the device full and must wait until the sensor that gets blocked when the tray is too full is clear. A quick note about that sensor by the way, with the ICE102 model the sensor is an IR type that uses line of sight between two points on either side of the tray. That sensor can get confused easily if you have the ICE102 model sitting in heavy sunlight (we had that happen in our home). The over-making of ice may be part of what killed that device for our family.

The Emerson device that we originally used was useful enough until it died. It had a larger capacity catch tray, though by comparison, at least by my memory, it was probably still a little below what this ICE103 model can hold and produce.

Our family's biggest complaint/concern about this particular unit, once you get past the size of the thing, was the plastic that covered it during shipping. While it should peel away easily, it was apparently on the main case of the device before the top of the device was snapped on, therefore the plastic wrap doesn't peel away like it should from that area. Again, that is secondary to the issue of just how big this box is. It isn't huge, but it isn't small either. You will need some counter space for it, but if you've got the space and can dedicate it to this device you can look forward to producing a lot of ice over time.

Buyers and users will likely find that the results of the use of the cube size button on the front of this device are not what you'd expect. For the most part these units seem to have a single cube size most of the time, no matter what choice you selected. You may get a little variance in cube sizes, but don't expect much there.

I had previously noted, in a review of the earlier cousins of this device, that this device makes WET ICE. The ice that sits in the device will melt while it sits waiting to be used, or waiting to be transferred into a ice bucket (as an option). The ice melts and turns back into water that will again be made into ice cubes. I should also clarify and note that the ice that these devices make is typically not cubes, but instead cylindrical in nature. If you really want cubes, then look elsewhere, or get ice trays for your freezer and enjoy filling them regularly (as I do in my workplace, where I also want a lot of ice for my drinks).

One last note here: be prepared to clean these devices regularly. Depending on the quality of the water you feed it with (and note, the area that is shown on the side of the device that almost looks like it would be where you can connect a hose to fill the device with is not for filling, rather it is for draining water from the device when necessary) you'll need to clean it regularly. Vinegar and water will be your best option, though you'll then need to flush it with plain water multiple times to get the vinegar smell and taste out of the ice that will be made following that cleaning. Failing to clean it regularly will leave it getting nasty quickly (or at least it will likely do that). Brownish, murk and clouds of algae will invade and you really don't need that stuff in your ice or the water that will be used for making the ice. Using filtered water is highly recommended, as that would help keep down mineral buildup that you would otherwise experience.

I bought this refrigerator when our 20 year old Kenmore stopped making ice, which is a staple around our house. We bought the floor model, since the dealer did not have what I wanted in stock, and this was the only one I could bring home that day. I had to remove the doors to get it through the front door of the house. It is really big and heavy, and I am glad the doors can be removed with just a few screws and unplugging a couple of control wires. Connected the water line and reinstalled the doors with no problem. The water filter is easily accessable, and it's nice to know that we have filtered water for the ice and water. Now to the PROS and CONS of the appliance... It is bigger than the 22 Cu Ft that we had previously, with ample room for everything. I had to remove one of the clear front panels on the middle shelf on the right door to allow access to the shelf when I raised it enough to get a gallon of milk in the bottom right door shelf. The second pull out drawer is very nice for storing soda cans and yogurt. A big CON for me is the ice storage. Although the ice maker recovers pretty fast, and dumps about every 40 minutes, it does not hold very much ice. I find that after filling a few glasses (about 6), it runs out of ice. I need about double of what it will store in the bin. The in the door display is more of a novelty than a necessity. With the access to the internet on my iphone, I do not need the nutritional feature that it has. Another PRO of this unit is the metered water dispenser. When you want 8 ounces of water, it accurately dispenses 8 ounces, or what ever amount you want. I was impressed. The water is not as cold as our old fridge, so I guess it does not have the cold water storage that the Kenmore had. My guess is that it just chills what is in the filter. I also like the temp control. You can set separate temperatures for the freezer and fridge. I wish it had the actual temp display. It only tells you what the setpoint is, not what the actual temperature is. I put a thermometer inside and it was fairly close... within 2 degrees of what it was set for. Since this was the floor model, we got a good discount, and still have the warranty. We've only had it installed for 3 weeks, but I am pleased with it so far... except for the ice maker. All the models I looked at essentially had the same size ice makers. It's bigger than those whose icemakers were on the left door. They seemed too small for what I wanted. I hope this helps in making your choice. The only reason I did not give it 5 stars is because of the ice maker's limited storage capacity. Other than that, it's a great appliance.

*** Update... 11-05-11... I updated my rating to 5 stars. I took off the plastic paddle on the icemaker, which allows for more ice to be made. We have yet to run out of ice, even after several parties with iced drinks. If you happen to do this, just remember to dispense the ice from the storage bin to lower the lever, before removing the maker. My favorite feature is the measured water dispenser. I can fill my glass with ice, then select the amount of water, and leave it, because I know the water will stop when it measures what I want.

If you are replacing this part on your LG dishwasher like I did, you will likely need to replace the rubber seal that is probably worn out and allowing a small amount of water to leak onto the diverter motor causing its failure.  If you don't you will probably end up replacing the diverter motor again in the near future as it will also become corroded and fail like its predecessor.  The replacement seal I needed was part number 3920ED4009B, but obviously check to make sure your model needs the same replacement seal or you'll have a disassembled dishwasher in your kitchen for a few extra days.  It's a fairly easy repair, and you will need to replace the seal from inside your dishwasher's sump by removing the spray arms and sump cover.  While you have your dishwasher out, you probably should clean the floats in the clear compartments on the left side of the dishwasher as they are likely filled with crud and will end up malfunctioning.  You shouldn't have any problem finding repair videos for any of these parts

Installation of this new pump: My motor shaft was swelled so badly that I first thought the new pump had too small an opening for the shaft. After spending two years handwashing items The precedent has been set that basically anything is going to be much better. I was pretty impressed with the machine up front and just to address one issue with leaking. There is none if you connect and use it properly. If you read the manual it clearly states it’s an overflow safety valve that will pour onto the floor if you overload the machine. If it leaks you need to stop stuffing it. Also with the drain valve make sure you put the clamp on properly and it should never leak. That said I do think quality control is pretty low on this unit. Upon opening the box There was a loose screw laying at the bottom of the box. I can’t find any where it would’ve gone so it may just have been one that fell in the machine during production but still should’ve been removed on an inspection. The second thing it’s a bit annoying is that the display screen is not lined up with the window for the display so you can only see the top half of the numbers and have to lean over to really see behind the blocked portion. Not that big of a deal.Overall the construction is a little on the cheap side but for 200 bucks what do you expect. It’s all really flimsy plastic and unfortunately the biggest problem I’ve had so far is some serious offgassing. To the point where all the clothes kind of smells like chemical plastics/hot rubber. This may be why they tell you not to use hot water. I don’t think the plastics are rated for it. I try to always use cold water with just a little bit of warm so that the water is at least room temperature. The machine is working well and cleans clothing really well so that part is impressive. As others have mentioned the spinning cycle virtually dries anything that’s not absorbent to the point where you don’t even have to put it in the dryer. You can just hang things right up on the shelf and let them air dry for 10 minutes. The spinning is very impressive. However the rinsing is pretty disappointing. Sometimes with towels or cottons I’ll have to run the rinse cycle five or six times so that suds finally stop coming out of drain. Overall I’m fairly happy with it however the offgassing and the strange smell is really bad. I’m going to use it every day until the return window Is over to see if it gets better and if not sadly it’s going back. It’s just that offputting. Especially with kids clothing.

Item ships without replacement clips or thermal paste so have care when removing original damaged thermostat.

Take a couple pictures of the original thermostat before removing so you easily reassemble it correctly.

If searching youtube of replacement videos, all were wrong about the installation of the retaining clips. If you do remove them without documenting, the clips were factory installed in the one I repaired such that the ends of the clips projected into the center of the cavity where the thermostat goes and the spring "curve" in the clip faced outwards. In the example videos usually the instruction is to install the clip the other way around. You will know you have it right if the new thermostat is held centered in the cavity and the top of it projects 1/16 to 1/8th inch above the plastic. If you push down on the thermostat, it should go into the cavity and then return to being proud of the surface. This spring tension keeps it firmly against the side of the actual ice tray so it measures the temperature of the tray and not the air in the refrigerator.

The alumilastic paste is expensive. Likely you can recover the original paste from the old thermostat and where it squeezed out onto the ice tray. I had some left over CPU heatsink paste that I augmented the recovered paste with that seemed to work fine as a substitute.

After replacement, it will take several hours before it starts making ice. The ice tray has to reach 16 degrees F before it will harvest the cubes that were in the tray when the thermostat failed and then it will fill so give it over night before deciding that there's more wrong.

The most important thing that needs to be understood about this product is that it is an ice maker, not a mini ice freezer. It is designed to produce ice quickly and for that ice to be immediately used or moved to a freezer. It does not keep ice cool and instead collects the water from melting ice and runs in through another cycle to produce ice cubes again. If the ice sits too long, it begins to melt and then clump up, so you want to get it out quickly. Fortunately, the device has a loud alarm to signal that the ice level is at capacity, so you'll know. Changing cube sizes between small and large is just a matter of pressing a button.

This ice maker is great for event-type settings when you need a lot of ice and need fast cycles. It's very easy to lift out the ice basket, pour in more water, and let it keep producing ice. The first few cycles seemed to take longer, but it did seem to produce ice faster after that (I didn't time it, though). This is where that loud beep comes in handy. When you're done with it, you can simply pull the drain plug and let the remaining water drain out.

One big gripe of mine is that the drain plug is very small and difficult to grip, especially when it's wet. The last time I drained the water reservoir, I had to use pliers—which risks damaging the rubber plug (I ended up putting the ends of the pliers in a plastic Ziploc to minimize damage to the plug and not put a non-sanitized tool into a place that holds water for consumption).

If you're looking for an ice maker to remain constantly on, such as tucked behind the bar or in a camper for weekend trips, I wouldn't recommend this one. The constant cycle of "water-to-ice-to-water" can get annoying if you're not constantly moving fresh ice out of it—and that "ice is full" alert is really loud and annoying when you left the device plugged in overnight. If you want something for parties, cookouts, and things like that, it's a great product.

In the Wisconsin summer, the default setting of "Medium" causes the sensor to kick in on a humid summer day, and stay on until it times out, just to kick back in again. On the "High" setting, I have to run my shower for 5 minutes before it kicks in.

If you were a landlord thinking of installing this in a renter's bathroom to avoid issues with mold -- unfortunately the sensor can be turned off, and there's no way to disable this override. If you press the button to turn off the fan while it's running, it also disables the sensor, which won't turn back on again until you press the button to manually turn it on. There really needs to be a mode that sets the button to call for the fan on-demand, but that honors the sensor above all else.

I have an indoor orchid garden and my old hygrometer stopped working, so I ordered this one and another type/brand. I was interested in trying this product because the bluetooth feature sounded neat. As far as the hygrometer and thermometer part goes, it has great accuracy. If you are gardening indoors, this is a great tool to have. You may be surprised at the temps and humidity around your plants. If you have any orchids, exotics, etc., your plants might have special requirements and you can only assess the environment with proper tools like this one. For me personally, my garden environment dramatically changed in the past few weeks while I was without a thermometer/hygrometer. My garden room is getting more sun than before because of the change in the sun's position this time of year. Because of this, the temp has been higher than usual during the day but I didn't notice (or feel) it. Once I put this thermometer/hygrometer in there, I was shocked because it was at least 5 degrees higher than it should ever be and upon close inspection, I see that one of my exotic orchids is just starting to show signs of distress. I corrected the situation immediately with a thicker sun filter, increased air circulation and increased A/C. But without this tool, I didn't realize anything was wrong. I like that I can access the data with my phone and check-in on my plants.

If humidity is something you need more of, a simple spray bottle to mist a small indoor garden can go a long way for little cost. Mist your plants daily and use this hygrometer to see if you need more or less. I hope that helps...I have struggled with some of these things myself. Gardening is one of my passions, so the fact that you are reading this review means you care about your plants, too, so we have that in common. :)

This is a great tool for an indoor garden but keep in mind, you will need to keep it plugged in. The other hygrometer/thermometer is equally accurate but it's smaller and requires no plug. It does not have bluetooth capability but if that's not something you need, you can find a more simple hygrometer/thermometer for less. Overall, I'm happy with it and would recommend it to someone who wants the bluetooth feature. Good luck and happy gardening!

Drinking water has a maximum allowable concentration of 4 ppm of chlorine (standard drinking water is perfectly safe for humidifiers). If you are using reverse osmosis or distilled water in your humidifier, then all the chlorine has been removed. The manual was very clear on first steps: let the compressor fluids settle by standing upright for 24 hours, level it, start up empty to cool the box then fill up with drinks and cool. I did those things and the set temperature of 43 degrees (35 degrees is the minimum allowed) with about a 1/3 full of room temperature drinks was reached in about 2 hours. The glass shelves have holes in them to allow for circulation. The unit is very quiet; what I mostly hear is the fan and it is not loud. This unit replaces a 12 year old Marvel unit which was much louder. Shelves were arranged to accept upright 12 oz cans and small water bottles on the top shelf. I chose to lower the top tray to put in long neck glass beer bottles. Doing that still left a gap that permits 12 oz cans to be stored on their side on the shelf below it. Some reviewers complained about having to unscrew a holding nub to get the shelf out. You don't need those nubs if you don't want the shelves to slide out and not tip. When I moved the shelf, there was no hole to put the nub into so only fixed locations allow slide-out shelves. The bottom of the unit has grooves so that wine bottles can be placed there. Note though only Chardonnay type bottles will fit. The long neck Riesling bottles need to be placed on any of the other shelves. I picked up one of these ice makers because I was tired of messing with the ice cube trays that had taken over my freezer. We use a LOT of ice in the summer, and it was getting to the point where we were running out of fully frozen ice cube trays by mid-afternoon. I run the ice maker twice a week, bag the ice in 1 quart freezer bags, and pile them up on a shelf in the freezer. When I want ice, I thunk a bag on the counter to break it up, and fill a glass.

The machine *does* have a fan on the side to vent the hot air produced by the compressor, and it does make my kitchen a bit warmer--particularly when the temperature outside is in the 90s. However, it is not terribly noisy, and it doesn't create any unpleasant vibration on the countertop. It lets you choose from three sizes of ice--S,M,L. The size difference is actually in the thickness of the ice, which forms on condenser "fingers" in the top, back portion of the machine. The larger the size, the thicker the ice that's allowed to form on the fingers. The ice itself is not a cube, but a bullet-shaped tube of ice, like the bottom of a test-tube, with an opening on one end.

The small and medium sizes are a waste if you're pouring hot liquid onto them--they disappear immediately. The large size is the best if you need it to stand up to freshly-brewed tea and coffee. For beverages that are already cold, the smaller sizes seem to work well enough.

So far, I like the unit, I like the look of it on the counter (next to a black countertop convection oven), and I haven't run out of ice. :)

I've been cooking since I was about 10 years old and have experience cooking on gas cooktops, flat electronic cooktops and coiled electronic cooktops but had never tried out an induction cooktop such as this one. The size of this unit is large enough to handle all but the largest of pots and it is still small enough to be called portable. It has a nice, sleek look and is very easy to operate.

When I got the unit I plugged it in and was greeted by a non-stop beeping noise. It turns out this burner is smart enough to know when a compatible pot or pan is on top of it and if there is none the beeping alerts you to that fact. Only cookware that is induction capable will work so make sure that you have something made of cast iron or other ferromagnetic metal. Modern cookware will normally be marked with an induction symbol if it will work with devices such as this one.

The unit has ten settings, which acts pretty much the same as turning your old-fashioned burners up and down. This induction device heats up the cookware by using electromagnetic induction which means it is the pot or pan itself heating up and not the cooktop which heats up to transfer the heat.

If you're not used to cooking on an electric cooktop it may take you a little time to figure out which heat settings you should be using for various types of foods. The pans can get very hot very quickly at the top settings and I believe the product specs when they say they can heat a pan up to 460 degrees. The first thing I did after receiving this product was to put a cast iron skillet on top of it and make some bacon. The pan immediately heated up and I turned the power up to its maximum setting for a moment and quickly realized that was WAY too hot for cooking the bacon. I quickly turned it back down and luckily no bacon was burned!

The unit does have a fan inside which can be clearly heard when cooking, but nothing that would keep me from using it. The noise is no worse than a computer fan ramping up when the temperatures rise.

I can see where there might be some use for this device as an addition to a normal stovetop, especially during parties and family gatherings where there never seems to be enough burners for everything you need to cook. Where this device would truly shine is in dorm rooms or even to take along on a road trip to give yourself the option to make a meal in any hotel room. It would also be perfect for camping if you have a generator that can pump out the 1800 watts of power needed.

Overall this is a nice quality and easy to use cooktop that is small enough to be convenient and large enough to handle even large pots and pans. As long as you have a compatible pan, which are easy to find, you shouldn't have any issues using this device. A must have to the dorm room!

That said, the overall design sucks. Which WILL happen at some point seriously impeding the unit's ability too provide humidification. So if your unit runs constantly like mine, be prepared to replace the filter every say 4-6 weeks. If it had a frame you could flip it and get a bit more life from the unit since the top half stays pretty clean compared to the bottom which is submerged in water.

Watch the video review for this product. It's really quite helpful and will give you ideas on how you can get a system going that works for you. If you buy this, get a system you can live with. As much as I encourage looking at someone else's review, here's my 2 cents.

Key points:
*The hoses are short, particularly the drain hose. Where you use this has to be within several feet of an outlet, a couple feet of a water source and pretty much right next to where you want to drain it. You can get around the hose length by using a bucket to add water (fill the bucket in a sink or tub and pour water in - the machine is indifferent to how the water is added, since that's a manual process anyway - the hose is a suggestion, not a requirement) or drain into a bucket or tub. Using buckets involves lifting a couple gallons of water a few times during the process, so sinks and drains are far more convenient. If you have the included hose too taut, it's more likely to pull off of the faucet, and that means water all over the place. I end up putting it in front of my bathroom sink and drain it into the toilet, as the tub is just too far away from the sink to make it convenient otherwise.
*You need to put it on something. It uses gravity to drain and the drain hose is at the bottom. I use a side table purchased for $12. It's rated for 30 pounds, which technically this is going to exceed when in use, but the weight is evenly distributed and shouldn't cause even a cheap little table to collapse. Elevating this by too much might make it harder to use for shorter folks (might be hard to reach in to get things if it's on an actual counter), but leaving it really low could cause some back strain. Find a cost effective and comfortable height that fits YOU, and remember that you'll have to interact with it a few times per load.
*You may find it stretches some of your clothes out or causes some items to pill. Use laundry delicates bags. They sell them in various sizes, and you want to use one big enough to let the garment move around, or put a few articles in the same bag. If you use a spin dryer, you can put them in the dryer still in the bags or take them out.
*There's no magic rinse cycle or spin cycle like on full sized washing machines. You drain and refill or rinse separately (you can do a few loads of wash in the same water if you'd like to - I don't pay for water where I live and we're not in anything close to a drought, so I'm okay with using a little bit more detergent to use fresh water every time). I typically run with detergent for the full 15 minutes, drain completely, refill completely to rinse (I may let it sit in the rinse water for a few minutes or even run the machine for 5 minutes or so if I think the clothes are more likely to retain detergent), drain again, and then have a second rinse with fabric softener if I choose to use it, during which I run the machine for 3-5 minutes to make sure it's distributed evenly. After the final drain, I wring each item out and then finish off in a spin dryer then hang to dry for a few hours. I keep a cheap colander with the laundry stuff to use to hold items between rinsing and putting them in the spin dryer, and have also used it for rinsing items that I pulled out before I put the fabric softener in. It lets things drip dry a little bit, which helps prevent unbalanced loads in the spin dryer.
*Capacity is several small items, or one larger item with really small items. I've washed full sized sheets (flat in one load, fitted in another). Adult pants can be washed with other things, depending on size (I'm a ladies 12 and I can get some shirts in the same load). A bath towel is a large item. Socks and other things like that can always go in with a large item. You can fill as much as can move decently well in the water, with the water level about 2/3 up. If you fill it more, it might splash out the drain hose.

Laundry is more involved than tossing in the washer and then in the dryer, but it's more convenient for those of us who can't have full sized machines. It's not too loud, but it's not silent. The timer ticks, the motor isn't super loud, but you can certainly hear it, and the water sloshes around when it spins. It's probably comparable to the dishwasher in my apartment, maybe slightly less noisy (my dishwasher is loud, though). This may be TMI, but I use reusable menstrual pads and it got one of those completely clean (after a pre-rinse under running water), so it certainly cleans sufficiently. I'm not running to the bank to get several rolls of quarters and can do laundry when I feel like it, not when my neighbors don't feel like doing their laundry (or just leaving their laundry in the machines...).

This range is an amazing piece of technology. The level of control you have with the induction cooktop just blows away that of any other range you have ever used. Because you are not transferring heat from a burner to a pan, but are exciting the molecules of the pan directly through a magnetic field, you have instant and precise control over your cooking, and an unparalleled evenness of heat in your cookware. Gone are the days of moving pieces of food back and forth between the center and edges of the pan while sauteing. Every piece of food anywhere in the pan cooks just like every other. Everything about the induction cooktop is faster than you're used to. About the only time you'll set this on high is when you want to boil water, and you'll be amazed how quickly that happens... just over two minutes for a 3-qt sauce pan half full. It takes a bit of adjustment to get used to the different timing of things. I like how it boils more quickly, but it's changed all my timing of when to start water for potatoes or pasta. Where you may be used to putting a saute pan on medium high and giving it several minutes to be hot enough for water to 'dance', it will be about 30 seconds with this one, and it's easy to smoke your oil until you get used to using lower settings than you're used to. Once you get used to it, though, you'll love the level of control you have over your food. In fact, you have such fine control that you don't need a double-boiler for tasks like melting chocolate. This cooktop has such precise control that you can melt delicate foods in a single pan. Yes, you may have to retire a few old favorite pots and pans, but there are many high-quality multi-ply stainless steel products out there that will work brilliantly, as will traditional and enameled cast iron. I have had this range for three weeks and I already cannot imagine going back to a primitive electric or gas cooktop.

The oven in the range does a very nice job, though we're still getting used to how it varies from our old one. One thing to be aware of is that they turn a 'feature' on by default that lowers your temperature by 25 degrees when using convection without telling you that its doing it and without showing you the actual temperature in the oven. Personally, I think that's daft. Your oven should heat to the temperature that you set, and even if they think some people will like this, it should be off by default. They give you a way to turn this off so that your oven is accurate while convection cooking, but if your electricity is interrupted it loses that change and you'll have to remember to reset it. (A bit of non-volatile memory would have been nice for retaining your settings in a power outage.) Other than that little quibble, though, the oven couldn't be nicer. I love that it shows you the temperature while pre-heating, and the easy slide rack is fantastic for a heavy item that needs to be pulled out to check its temperature. It maintains a relatively even temperature and is extremely well-insulated. We haven't used the warming drawer yet, but I think it will come in handy at times.

That's pretty much what I have to say about operating the range, but there were some notable things about buying and installing this range that are worth commenting on for those who may buy online and/or install it themselves as we did. The range is very heavy, between 200 and 250 pounds, so you will want to take this into consideration when planning the installation (assuming you will do it yourself). You'll definitely need a hand truck to move it into the kitchen and you'll want to protect your floor from the feet when moving it into place. We set it on a piece of heavy material to slide it around to protect the hardwood floor and that worked well. Putting the plug on is easy, so don't let that dissuade you from installing it yourself. It comes with an anti-tip bracket that should be screwed into the wall or floor for one of the rear feet to slide into. This prevents the range from tipping forward accidentally, which would be pretty serious with something this heavy. At first, it looks like getting it all lined up will be a pain, but they have made it so that you just install the edge of the bracket exactly where the edge of the range goes and everything lines up. It turned out to be very simple, and is cheap protection for the type of accident it is trying to prevent. Leveling the range was a but fiddly, as it is with any range, but it wasn't hard if you remove the warming drawer first. Be sure to take the time to use a spirit level.

Most slide-in ranges won't directly replace a free-standing range, because they are less deep and require a piece of counter behind them. This range is the same depth as a free-standing range, which could be good or bad for you. If you already have a free-standing range, it's great because it is a direct replacement and it will fit. If you already have a slide-in range, check the installation guide before installing to be sure this will fit. It may not. I really enjoy having the controls on the front so I don't have to reach over hot pots and pans to adjust a control.

The oven vents heat, and some moisture, from a vent at the back, so be sure you have an appropriate backsplash behind the range. We put a stone backsplash behind our counters and thought about putting it behind the range. Instead, we ended up with a stainless steel backsplash directly behind the range and stone behind everything else. I'm glad we did that because we can see the moist condensation on the backsplash sometimes. Stone would not have been a good material for that.

Buying this range online was a bit of an adventure in itself. I saved several hundred dollars by doing that, but it wasn't without a certain amount of trouble and risk. There was a mix up between the seller (Amazon 3rd party seller) and the carrier, with the seller telling me it had shipped and the carrier telling me it hadn't. This lasted about a week and created some stress. Receiving an item from a freight carrier is quite different than receiving something shipped by UPS. The carrier called me to arrange a time, but there was confusion about exactly what service they were to provide. They started by telling me that they would bring it in the truck and that I would have to unload it. For extra money, they would lower it to the ground and for more extra, they would move the box inside. Be sure you get this worked out with your seller before you finalize your order. It's the seller that sets the terms of the delivery. Then, on the day of the delivery, the driver called to verify that he could get a tractor-trailer into and out of my street. (The answer was a definite 'no'.) Unfortunately, they assumed I knew it would arrive in a tractor-trailer and I assumed a company delivering an appliance to a home would use something the size of a furniture delivery truck. This had the potential to be a real problem, but luckily the driver was really great. I drove my garden trailer out to the truck and he came back with me and helped me get it in the garage. He didn't have to do that last part, though, so it could have been a very difficult time. The upshot is, if you buy this range online, be sure you consider all these issues and get them worked out before the delivery day. There were several times in this process during which I was wishing I'd paid the extra money and bought it locally, but it all worked out really well in the end, so now I'm pleased to have saved the money.

All in all, I couldn't be happier with this new range. I know that professional chefs love gas (and I did, too, before) but I don't care who you are. Once you've used an induction cooktop, you'll never go back to gas or electric again. It has all the instant control advantages of gas with the precision and consistency of digital controls and the ubiquity of electric. Combine that with a large, high-end convection oven, and you have an exceptional cooking appliance. I enthusiastically recommend this range.

I just bought these filters so more comments to come. I did however read several comments about these filters which I think I can help with.

1) They are "not NSF 372 certified" or "they are not NSF61 certified" and so went to look this up to understand it. Here is the actual certification definition:

"The METHOD: NSF 372 is NOT a standard. It is a method of measurement used to comply with the standard. Therefore, anything that has a full NSF 61 Certification has been certified to NSF 61 via the methods and values defined in NSF 372. "

This means that by the fact these are NSF 61 certified, they were certified (by law) using NSF 372 (which is NOT a certification by a method to achieve the NSF 61 certification). It seems everyone is confused, including the sellers.

2) Black soot coming out - You need to run several quarts of water through the newly installed filter to remove any loose carbon - that is the "black stuff". Drinking carbon soot will not harm you, but you want to wash it out so that the water looks clean. Just continue to fill a quart pitcher and dump the water until its completely clean water. This could also apply to the "water tastes funny" comment.

3) Did not reset the filter alert - All refrigerators I am familiar with require you rest the filter alarm manually. Usually there is a procedure explained in the owner's manual to rest it. The filter alarms I know of are just time based and do not really reflect any change in the water quality (there may be newer models that I am not familiar with that are exceptions).

I will return and write more once I have a chance to install and use one of these.

It seems like these pilot light/thermocouples last about 20 years. The first one went out and I called a technician because I had no idea what the problem was. Once he explained it, I happened to remember that conversation from 20 years ago and looked for the replacement. Of course, I found it on Amazon.

It's definitely one of the more expensive units, compared to other types of pilot light assemblies. Work slowly, take pictures and pay attention. There are plenty of YouTube videos, but if you haven't worked with natural gas or propane before, you may want to call a technician.

I have replaced these before on patio heaters, but my first time for a furnace. I was happy that the pilot flame came out nice and blue and was large enough to ignite the burners. This also gave me an opportunity to vacuum out 20 years of accumulated crud (always vacuum, never ever use any kind of blower unless you want a dust explosion).

Just make sure that you check any gas connections for leaks using a soapy solution, which will create bubbles if placed around the connections and if there is a leak. The smell test can work pretty effectively as well since the natural gas additive (also in propane) is designed to be picked up by the human nose at very small concentrations.

We live in Southern California, so our furnace doesn't get a tremendous amount of use. If your furnace gets fairly constant use during the winter, probably a good idea to have a technician check it out every couple of years.

The first time our pilot light assembly broke was in the middle of the winter. The second time was when I was relighting the pilot after having turned it off over the summer. I am debating Just leaving the pilot on over the summer. That's about five bucks a month and I just don't know how good the quality of this non-brand item is.

You should also check to make sure the safety feature works. With the pilot light off AND The entire component nice and cool, try running your heater. You should not hear or smell gas and most heaters have a safety feature where they will start running the fan if they detected an "on" Condition, but nothing from the thermocouple on the pilot light. I believe these are designed to fail in the "off" condition.

I was pleased that this pilot light assembly had the right orifice, fit perfectly and worked correctly both lighting the furnace and also as a safety shut off.

I'm disabled, and having to lug laundry to a laundry mat and pay for it has grown increasingly difficult, so I have looked into a portable washing machine. I wanted one with a dryer, or as much of a dryer it can be, and I love this thing. It can be kind of difficult to maneuver it around your house or apartment, and mine is very tiny, but not having to lug things downstairs outweighs the con of that.

Pros:
- It's portable! If you have the space, you can essentially place it anywhere that you have access to an outlet and a place to drain
- The dryer makes it pretty dry. I have a hanging rack, and my clothes dry pretty quickly. Pulling it out of the "dryer" side they're slightly damp, and they get way drier than I expected it to be.
- It came with instructions: I did read other reviews that it did not, and they didn't know how to use it. Mine actually came with instructions, and I believe it was a different model than shown.
- It's very quick - I am doing mini loads of laundry very quickly, and I am getting lots of laundry done in an hour compared to a big washer/dryer
- It saves you money in the long run - compared to paying for laundry, I am saving money and time (because time is money!) on 2+ hours of laundry at a laundry mat, and 5+ dollars on quarters in money.

Cons:
- Filling it up is a hassle. The tube they gave to fill it up doesn't attach to any faucet at all, and requires gravity to dump water into it. I unfortunately don't have a shower that has a detachable head, so I fill up a pot of warm water and dump it in. It takes a little bit more time to do this.
- No lint catcher - this model I got does not have a lint catcher, so I had to buy some portable ones to add to my washer side. It's not entirely a big deal for me, as reading old reviews the lint catcher didn't really work, but if you were looking for one, it doesn't have it.
- Draining water requires gravity. The way my bathroom is set up that trying to place it in the bathtub the cord to plug it into the outlet doesn't extend all the way, so I prop it up on something so it can drain. It can suck doing this because of that, there isn't a pump system so if you got a funky bathroom like I do, or just wanted it to pump water out itself, then this may be a con for you.
- It is too small to wash anything big like a comforter. This will fit a lot of things in it, but it won't fit a comforter.

Overall, I love this thing. Besides it being fascinating to watch and do, my clothes get clean and I love it. If you hate going to the laundry mat, are disabled, or want to save money and time, I would recommend this for you! It's great being able to do small loads of laundry throughout the week and not have to spend money on it, and unlike a laundry mat where I have to save a bunch of laundry to get more bang for my buck here, I can just pop in shirts, pants, underwear, etc. and get it clean for the next day!

This is one of my favorite serials ever. It’s sexy, sassy, funny and dark.

This serial belongs to the dark and brooding Sean Ferro. He’s the first Ferro I was introduced to, and he holds a piece of my heart. As the series start out, Sean is very mysterious, and to be honest – 15 volumes in (when I’m writing this review), he still is a bit of an enigma. There is still a lot to be learned. He’s a dark SOB, this one. He’s got his fetishes, but holy wow is he delicious. And scary. Seriously, I love him – but if I had known him IRL I would have been scared s***less, and kept my distance.

Then we have Avery. This girl’s got some spunk. I mean she has to, given that Sean is her love interest. She’s a struggling student when we first meet her, and when her best friend, Mel, realizes this, she reveals what her REAL job is. She’s a high dollar call girl. Ms. Black latches on to Avery immediately, and if Avery just takes one client, it could solve all her problems. She only has to say yes. Problem is she only wants one guy, Sean. Enter: a s***load of trouble.

“I’m rewarded, uh, I mean punished, with a slap to my backside.” - Avery

This is an erotic romance, and you can expect some mighty steamy scenes. Some of the volumes more so than others, because there is a hell of a lot going on in this series. The Arrangement, and Sean basically, was the catalyst for all the other books from this same world. Sean has made an appearance is in every spin-off so far. So this is obviously a great place to start if you are curious about H.M. Ward’s books. Just remember to start at the beginning. You would not understand half of what’s going on if you jumped into it halfway through.

It’s important to note that this is a fan driven series. Essentially that means that as long as the fans want more, there will be more. And I honestly can’t picture the day we won’t want more. So if that is not for you, I recommend you go pick up something else, because this story has been going on for a good while now, and I certainly hope it will go on for a long time to come – as long as Holly wants it to.

Another important note is that these are split up in volumes, and each one end on a cliffhanger (Holly is the queen of cliffhangers). It’s nerve-wracking every time. And it is one of the tings that keep it just as exciting as it was in the beginning. As well as the fact that they’re always fast paced, and it never gets boring. Each volume starts off exactly where the last one left off. I always like to re-read the latest volume before the next one releases because you really get thrown right back into the action without any recaps. It really is kind of built like a TV-show, which is so awesome, because something like that is currently in the works! *fangirls* Just Imagine seeing THE Sean Ferro on screen…

I used these as replacement parts for my Whirlpool dishwasher. After a little more than a year of use, the hub for one of the wheels broke, so we had to be really careful when sliding the upper rack in and out, to avoid having it slip out of the wheel, causing the rack to fall. A few weeks later, the corresponding hub on a wheel on the other side broke, so I finally bought these parts.

I was able to replace both sides within about 10 minutes. No directions are included, but it was pretty easy to figure out how the whole thing comes apart and goes back together. The only tricky part was figuring out how to gently disassemble the height adjuster enclosure on each side so that I could remove this part--it comes apart at the bottom with a little gentle pressure from a screwdriver. There are three other brackets on each side that need to come off, but when you look at them it's pretty obvious how they come off. Just do one side at a time so you can refer to the other side for how everything fits back together.

I was cautious, and so I was able to avoid breaking other parts. There are larger kits on Amazon that include the other plastic brackets and so forth, but if the problem is simply that the hub of a wheel is broken, these parts are all you need. Durability remains to be seen...I'm hoping these will last longer than the originals. It's sad how poorly made appliances are nowadays--a dishwasher should last for more than a year before you have to start replacing things.

I've been on a quest to find the perfect reusable Keurig filter. I'm happy to say this one is tied for the best I've found. One nitpick is that you have to align this filter to get it to go into the Keurig. This isn't a big deal, but is slightly annoying.

A more serious problem is that this isn't the easiest filter to clean. Because there is relatively little mesh siding, I've found that rinsing it out takes more work. I usually have to bang the used grounds out, whereas in other filters with more mesh siding I can spray enough water to loosen and remove the old grounds.

I've never had issues with grounds ending up in the coffee.

Ultimately, this filter is tied for best out of the ones I've tried. It brews a great cup of coffee every time, even if it requires a few more seconds to clean each time.

My Samsung refrigerator works great except for one design flaw - ice build up beneath the vegetable bin due to the evaporator drain freezing shut. The refrigerator has a small clip that attaches to the heating element and hangs down into the drain that is supposed to keep the water in the drain from freezing. However, it is insufficient to prevent the freezing, and when the drain is frozen shut the water then drains to the bottom of the frig below the vegetable bin and freezes and eventually makes it very difficult to open the bin.

There are YouTube videos that show how to remove the back panel inside of the frig to replace the clip with the BlueStars clip. The clip has a larger surface area that make contact with the heating element and also hangs lower into the drain. I used a hair dryer for a while to melt the ice buildup in the drain, but the plastic frig interior gets very hot and I was afraid it would start melting the plastic if I continued. The drain remained frozen further down. So I began pouring hot water down the drain, then used an ear irrigation syringe to suction out the cooled water. Repeated this operation several times and eventually the drain opened.

I only gave 4 stars in my review because the clip did not 'fit perfect' as advertised, in my Samsung refrigerator. It was too long and too wide to fit in the drain. So I trimmed it down with a wire snips and on a grinding wheel to get it to fit.

Seems crazy that you should have to do this to fix what appears to be a widespread design flaw, but if you are looking to get the dang drain to stop freezing shut, this clip will work (maybe with a little modification).

My husband and I have discussed a large ice machine purchase since we do host a couple of large events each year and ice is always the thing we need more of, but just can't stomach the cost of one.

A friend told me about these and I decided to give it a try, I'd return it if it was junk.

It is NOT junk. It does make the first ice cubes in a matter of several minutes and those first cubes are a bit soft, but all of the ones after that are perfect. I do wish that the ice collection tray was larger, but it would necessitate a larger machine, hence trying to find a place to put it. This sat on my kitchen counter while I had a houseful on New Year's eve and bothered no one.

Cons- Because the ice catch tray is much smaller than the water it holds, you need to be around to empty it when full. If it gets full, nothing happens, but as an energy saver, it stops running the freezing amount of coolant/compressor, so your ice can start to get watery and stick together when refrozen in your storage freezer.

When I researched this item, the biggest complaint that I saw was people complaining about it being loud. That I guess is a matter of perspective...
Do you hear the ice drop into the plastic tray sitting over a large container of water? Yes, but I hear my fridge ice maker dump if it's not full.
Do you hear the compressor run while it's making ice? YES, I turned it off at bedtime, but as I said, a houseful of company and music playing, we didn't hear it. The reality is this~ Having one of these is the equivalent of having a freezer on your kitchen counter. If the noise bothers you, then you could set it on a porch, in a laundry room, garage, whatever works, but it is certainly quieter than my chest freezer. A freezer, as this is, has a compressor. When you're paying for the convenience of something roughly the size of an overgrown toaster that has a compressor, it's going to make noise.

I have wanted an ice machine forever. I'm so over filling ice trays and refilling them. So I was super excited when this came.

It's pretty easy to set up. The directions state it's important to leave the machine unplugged with the lid open for 24 hours after setting it up. I imagine this has something to do with the coolant and it getting displaced from shipping/jostling. It's important to have it in a spot with sufficient clearance around it because it throws off some heat when in use. Plan on this taking up a fair amount of real estate on your countertop.

The instructions are mostly clear and helpful. It is a bit confusing as to what type of water to use. In one place it says to use spring water and another to use mineral water. I generally use distilled water in my appliances (like my humidifier, coffee maker, etc) to prevent mineral build up and mold/bacteria growth. I feel like that would be best for this ice maker as well but after emailing the seller, they specifically said to use mineral water and not distilled. Where I live, finding bottled water that is specifically mineral water is impossible. Spring water would have to do. So that is what I settled on using. I'm guessing there is something within the sensory mechanics of this machine that requires a certain density or reading of the water to determine when the water level is too low. I'm no scientist or engineer but I did see something like that mentioned on Google. It would be helpful if the instructions clarified the issue of what type of water to use if it is integral to the machine's function.

So, with that issue settled, I wanted to make ice. It's super easy. Lift up the basket. Fill to water line. Replace basket. Close like. Press the power button.

I timed how long it took to freeze one set of ice cubes. It was in the range of 9 to 10 minutes. The machine holds about half of a gallon of water. To use up all that water in one go, I think it took a couple of hours. So, if you don't want to waste water or babysit the ice machine for that long, I'd add less water. Of course, you do not have to baby sit the machine but your ice will not stay frozen if you leave it there for long. The machine is insulated but not refrigerated in any way so it doesn't keep your ice frozen in the basket. If you don't want wet ice, you need to be on top of emptying the basket fairly often and putting it in the freezer. For my first time, I put it in a gallon freezer ziploc bag. Some pieces did freeze together from being a bit wet but a good crack on the counter split them up.

So far, everything was going pretty much as expected. But when it stopped due to the water level being low, I was unprepared for it. There was probably a quarter inch or so of water left in the bottom. I knew there was a way to drain it but the plug is under the machine and would require tilting it up to get to it and having something under it to catch the water. I was not in the mood to do all that but I knew leaving water sitting in it couldn't be good for it. So I ended up trying to scoop the water out which was not effective since it was so shallow. I settled for the truly scientific solution of putting a towel in it to soak it all up then left the lid open for it to air out. Not the best solution but for the time being it worked.

I should mention the noise level as it has come up in other reviews. This machine is not silent. It's noticeable. It sounds a lot like my microwave when it's running. I have a cheap microwave so it's not very silent either. The volume of the noise it makes doesn't really bother me but I could see it being distracting if it were in close proximity to where you're having a get together.

So, I think it could use some improvements but for a basic level ice maker, I think it does its job splendidly. I really wish it didn't leave water leftover when it is done. I do not want to have to mess with that drain each and every time. I will have to find a work around. Having it be refrigerated so the ice doesn't melt would be awesome but, that is reserved for ice makers that are at a higher price point.

This filter is excellent. It seems like a simple device, but there are many manufacturers who can't get this right. A few of the key things to look for are:
1) Does it fit properly?
2) Does it filter out the grinds well?
3) Is it easy to clean?
4) Is it durable?

This filter works very well in all of these points.
1) It fits into my older (original) Keurig model perfectly.
2) I use fine grinds and these even filter those grounds very well.
3) The most important part is how easy is it to clean it out afterwards. It's horrible to have old coffee grounds stuck inside the filter; and that's where this filter excels. It is well designed with no areas that trap or catch the old grounds, so when you dump it the old coffee grounds come out easily. A quick rinse is all that's ever needed to get it completely clean.
4) It also appears to be very durable and well made. Many other ones I've used in the past fail if there's even a small amount of coffee ground on the rim, and the plastic gets old after a while. This one is pretty heavy duty -- wipe the rim of course, but it doesn't seem like it will bother this filter at all. I expect these to last a very long time.

BOTTOM LINE:
This is a well made filter that allows good water flow through the grounds, keeps even the fine grinds of coffee from getting into your cup, is durable and easy to clean. Don't worry about purchasing this product, it's a good one.

First some background: After doing a significant amount of research, it seems that most hoods are a 1 dollar per CFM, regardless of other features. The CFM rating of over-the-range microwaves is a complete joke, as even a 100 CFM dedicated range hood will out-do a "300 CFM" microwave. The bigger brothers of this unit, the 330 and 430 have a lot of reported circuit board issues. I had a 200 CFM hood in a previous home and it worked well until doing cooking that generates a lot of smoke, like blackening or skillet searing meat.

With all of that, in mind I knew I wanted at least a 300 CFM hood with good lighting. This fits the bill perfectly, it clears smoke and odor beautifully so long as I open a window somewhere for it to draw air from. The lighting is very bright, the transitions are nice but just icing. It doesn't come down or stick out too far, and looks attractive enough. Clean up is also much easier than other hoods I've had. Quite happy with the my purchase.

A note about installation, it requires sealing several spots on the unit with foil tape, so make sure you have some. It will maximize airflow and prevent whistling noises. You will also need two people, it is far too awkward to install solo.
