5-year PREFACE:
In January of 2020, I will pass the 5 years of usage point. This Wonderwash is still one of the greatest purchases I have ever made. If you read past the preface, you get the entire story. I wrote my first review after 1 month followed by an Addendum after 1 year. I thought I should come back to give this update... I'm still cranking & my clothes need less detergent to get clean. At some point, between 1 & 5 years, my rinse water started running clear after the detergent removed the dirt. I don't ever need to wash twice now; nor do I need to soak as much. I generally do let the detergent & softener rest for about 10 minutes then crank for 1 more minute. However, I'm no longer dealing with old stains & buildup so my clothes are cleaner. Bonus: they look better too... like new again. I love my Wonderwash!!!

ONE MONTH REVIEW:
Stains are fading! I've been using it for approximately 1 month now and I've noticed the stains in my dishcloths and cloth napkins are fading away! My clothes seemed to be looking better but I thought it was my imagination until I noticed & watched those specific stains. I guess it's the smaller loads or something? Whatever! It works better than the standard washer I was using... And it's Eco-friendly! Win-win!
If you were wondering about ease of use... Be sure to measure the water, per the instructions, and away you go. I do switch arms to keep the workout balanced... Generally, 2-3 loads each day I do laundry; alternating arms by day, not load. Once you get it going it's 100% aerobic...but EASY! The water gets flowing & it is almost self-propelled; if you feel like you are struggling you have too much water or clothing... Or you didn't get it going fast enough, crank faster. Once you get the speed right, the water seems to do most of the work. Just remember not to smash the clothes in too tight and you should be fine. [When you drain the water, if the clothes fill more than half of the washer... you got too many clothes in there!]
As for drying, I use the Nina Spin Dryer - also from The Laundry Alternative. They are a perfect match. By the time I finish another load in the Wonder Washer, letting it drain for a while between cycles, the prior load is almost done hang-drying. I let the rinse drain until the first load dries, then I spin dry and hang. It makes the process almost relaxing. A friend stopped by while I was washing & was amazed that things hang dry as fast as his big electric dryer can dry things. He was also amazed at how much fit inside the washer...looks can deceive.

ADDENDUM:
Now that I have used the washer for a year, let me just say that my clothes like the gentle treatment! Stains don't last, fabrics have smoothed out, and the things I have purchased since buying it still look like new... it's like a front-load washer only MORE gentle!
I see that they have updated the lid, which I think is a great idea. The first time my daughter used mine she didn't get it closed all the way cuz my old style lid requires many turns to tighten/seal it... she spilled water everywhere. But just once!
I have oiled it once but it is squeaking here & there so I will probably have to oil it again soon... making oiling necessary about twice a year. I haven't had to replace any parts but they are all available from The Laundry Alternative. It was super easy to put together [when it arrived] and replacing parts that break instead of buying an entire washer is another bonus.
I have to admit, I do 3 cycles most of the time. I do the detergent cycle, a white vinegar cycle, and end with a softener cycle. I crank each cycle for the 2 minutes they recommend for washing. I count 120 cranks; as the cranks take about 1 second each. That's 6 minutes of cranking per load. [Super dirty stuff gets extra rinse water thrown in WHILE DRAINING & comes out clean.] I also alternate forward & backward cranking, not just left & right arms, & my arms look GREAT! Just thought I would throw that in.
I should add that I am enjoying the exercise factor. It has gotten so easy to crank that I love doing laundry! I also find that the rest of my body benefits from the isometric exercise; holding the rest of my body still while cranking has toned me from head to toe...And my clothes look great on my toned self; more bonuses!!!
One year later, still cranking & loving it!!! ^_^

It's been a few weeks of laundry and the bearings are working great. My wife said it's the quietest the washer has been for years. I went to a tractor supply and got a large 8 inch long bolt threaded all the way up with a couple nuts and several large washers that matched the size of the bearings. I then got a few steel light box covers with the center hole knocked out as the counter pressure to the bearing. Cost me under $10. The washers with the large bolt behind them applied the pressure to remove and replace the bearings. This works in getting both bearings almost out. There is about a centimeter of compression left that you will use a hammer and socket wrench extension to knock it out the rest of the way. I will say that I bent several washers in the amount of pressure needed to pop these free. You will need a long breaker bar and wrench. I cleaned everything up and applied some lithium grease. I used the old bearings to help seat the new ones as they were the exact size. I used the same bolt with washers to draw pressure in as to seat the bearings back in the aluminum tube. The difficult part was keeping a sleeve in place to hold the spacer that sits between the two bearings. Several videos on you tube show how to do this but didn't really provide a good inexpensive tool. hope this helps others.

Have a vacation place where the fridge doesn't have an ice maker. For years we lived with the pain of ice trays. So figured we'd give this unit a try. It is really simple to use - you lift out the basket which catches the ice, and fill the reservoir with water - up to the point where the plastic level changes. Put the basket back it, and turn it on.

You have two choices of ice size - I chose large, which is about the size of a large finger tip. It would take about 12 minutes to make a batch of ice, and will continue until the ice basket is full or it runs out of water. If either of these occurs, it will light an indicator.

The ice is hollow in the center and damp when made. This is because it works by creating a dam which it fills with water and then lowers the refrigerated "fingers" into the water which the ice forms on. When the time is up, the remaining water goes back into the reservoir, and the cubes drop into the basket.

The unit itself is not refrigerated. It is insulated and stays cool while making ice because of the refrigerated fingers. But the ice will melt with the water going back into the reservoir if you don't take it out.

Because the cubes are damp, if you move them to your freezer, they will freeze to each other. We would fill 1 gallon freezer ziplock bags with the ice. When we wanted ice we would bang the bag onto the counter top to separate the cubes.

How well did this work? We never ran out of ice while our place had 12 people with the outside temperatures in the 90s with 90% humidity. It can make over 20lbs a day. We would run as needed to keep about 4 of the gallon bags full (probably 10lbs)

You can hear the fan if you are near it. You can hear the water pump and the dumping of the ice too. So it is not silent. We did not mind. It became a running joke for someone to say - "ice is ready" when we would hear it dump another load.

It does come with a little plastic ice scoop which you can use to scoop the ice out the basket if you want to fill a glass directly. Also, if you like to chew ice (sorry ADA) by being hollow in the middle they crunch pretty easily.

According to Fellow, the "Go" was produced after the Prismo, so they do not suggest using it with a Go. AND YOU SHOULDN'T if you don't want to put in a slight amount of elbow grease. However, considering Fellow has not produced one to fit a Go yet in the past 2 years or so, I thought I'd do a little experiment.

Trial and error was how I gauged how much to sand the underside of all 4 tabs around the outside of the Prismo (see my pictures of the finished sanding alongside my Go). All I used was a regular old emery board that had the grain of a finer sandpaper. The process took maybe 15 minutes of sanding and checking and sanding and checking before I was satisfied that it fit snugly enough and didn't take all of my strength to tighten into place on my Go. I'm confident anyone could do this project - you don't need to be crafty in any way.

Also in my images, you'll see that even with the additional height of the Prismo in comparison to the original paper filter attachment that came with the AeroPress Go, the red cap still fits over the cup with everything neatly packed inside. So you can still travel with it all bundled together and be assured that the pieces won't scatter on the road.

Bottom Line: As long as you don't mind it looking a little scuffed up, sanding the underside of those 4 tabs should do the trick.

I hope I remember to update later if it worked or not and I hope this helps anyone on the fence about trying it out with their AeroPress Go.

When you’re washer agitator starts slipping and makes that awful grinding sound, time to replace the “dogs”. Easily done with plenty of videos on you tube to guide you if you are unfamiliar with replacing dogs. The whole job takes twenty minutes if you’re slow. All you need is a ratchet with an extension rod 12 inch will do and a 9/16 socket. Socket size can vary from machine to machine. Remove top cover (pops off with a screw driver. There’s a notch under the cover to put the screwdriver in. ) use socket wrench to remove bolt holding agitator. Remove agitator with a good pull. You will see the dogs in the agitator, just pull dog assembly out of agitator. Replace dogs with new ones. Make sure dogs face in the right direction (easily seen which way they go). Reassemble and replace the agitator in machine. Replace and tighten bolt. Done. You can test your job by just taking your hand and twisting the agitator. It should go in one direction only. Very easy job.

This makes ice, just as the listing says it does. Put water in, ice comes out. But...

My refrigerator's built-in ice maker died, and I needed a replacement for morning iced coffee. That's my main use - not soft drinks or ice water. Does this make ice? Yes, it makes thumb-sized hollow ice bullets. BUT. There's no freezer/storage ability in the unit. I knew this going in, so that's not a surprise. But, it's important. This makes ice very quickly, and will keep making ice. As it makes new ice, it tips the cubes into a basket. New cubes come in, and the "old" ice in the basket melts. The melting starts immediately - the water drips through the basket into the water bin and gets pumped back through to make more ice. There's nothing keeping the ice cold, except the machine tipping new ice into the basket. The warmer the ambient temperature of the room, the faster it melts. Still, that's not news.

Here's the thing. If you think you're going to wake up in the morning to a basket of hard frozen ice, sufficient for your 30 oz travel tumbler of ice coffee, that's not really going to happen. There will be a bin of ice, maybe 5 inches deep. The bullets on top are brand new and solid. The ones on the bottom are on their way back to water. And they're hollow bullets - that means there's less actual ice than the room they take up in your glass. They have a lot of surface area and are not super hard, so they melt QUICKLY if you pour hot water over them. You may need to rethink your recipe - let the coffee cool before you pour it over ice, or go with a cold brew.

My method with ice from the refrigerator's ice maker is to brew highly concentrated hot coffee (Aeropress) and pour it over a full travel tumbler of ice. Like magic some of the ice melts to make the coffee the perfect strength. The rest of the ice stays unmelted for hours in the tumbler to keep the coffee cold for a while. NOT happening with this ice maker. Nope. Not even close.

The bullets are not as hard as the ice from the refrigerator ice maker. It melts faster. Even filling up the travel tumbler with ice, the ice is nearly gone (and the coffee not chilled) within seconds of my pouring the hot coffee over it. AND, there's no more ice in the basket because I used it all in the 30 oz tumbler.

My initial thought was to use an Alexa-compatible smart plug to go on at 4 in the morning, make a full bin of ice, and then shut off when I left for work. Then the machine wouldn't be making ice all day while I was gone. Nope. Not workable. In order for the machine to turn on after the power is off (or the smart plug turns on), one must push the ON button. Unless I was going to get up at 4 to hit the button and go back to bed, my hopes for an Alexa-controlled ice maker were dashed.

Next idea? This one actually worked, but it's not really simplifying my life. After work I start the ice maker. As it pops ice into the bin, I tip the bin into a container and put it in the freezer. Over the next couple of hours, I keep tipping more ice into the container. Then I just turn off the ice maker (or let Alexa do it). The next morning, I have a full bin of ice in the freezer (more than a single bin from the countertop machine), fully frozen (not as soft as what came directly out of the machine). Since the bullets in the machine are in a perpetual cycle of freeze/thaw, the bullets in the container may need to be broken apart some. The bullets are wet when I put them in the container, so they stick together when fully frozen.

Make my 30 oz travel tumbler of iced coffee, enjoy it in the car on the way to work. Come home, and repeat the "make ice before bedtime" routine so there's enough for the next morning's coffee.

Not a perfect solution, and not one that I'm willing to continue indefinitely. I have already scoped out the available room in the freezer to just use stacking ice cube trays until I can replace the broken part on the refrigerator ice maker.

As for noise, yes, I can hear it in the living room (about 25 feet from the machine). Is it loud? Not particularly, but I can hear the clatter of ice dropping into the basket. If I had this on all night and my bedroom were near the kitchen, I would probably hear it. A light sleeper could awaken from the clatter. The compressor runs constantly when the machine is on, blowing hot air out the side. If that were going all day, it would be fighting the a/c in the kitchen, for sure. The compressor makes a sound like a small fan, which may or may not bother some people.

I waited for about 1 1/2 years before reviewing this product. When I bought the product there were a bunch of negative reviews that it didn't last long and I didn't want to spend 350 dollars on something that only lasted a few months. I believe I know why other units didn't last which I will go over after the review of the product.
Pros:
* Great Ice
* Easy to fill
* Ice keeps for a while and remakes as the ice melts
Cons:
* MUST clean regularly
* Constantly adding water (daily 1-2 times a day with a family of 4), side tank would probably help
* Takes up a lot of counter space
* Can be loud at times, mostly when it gets low on water. Hasn't been a huge issue honestly.
* In the morning, the ice is half melted, I am not really sure why the low ice sensor never seems to kick on and it really hasn't been an issue, but it is strange :)
Warnings:
* If your bin is full of ice and the water bin is full and you lose power, unit gets turned off or unplugged, etc...) when the ice melts the water will overflow. Was almost an issue for me, when the unit accidently got turned off.

So is the unit worth it? I totally love it and don't regret the purchase, currently the only ice my family uses comes from that machine (even though we have 2 other ice makers in the refrigerator). Refilling the water can be a pain, but it doesn't take long and I hate cleaning the unit, but once again totally worth it for the nugget ice.

On to the reliability problem. I really think many of the issues have stemmed from 2 different things on the machine. First, you must clean this unit or it will get a mold|mildew issue which can clog the pumps and burn them out (this includes cleaning the air intakes). Second, I have noticed that the low water sensor on my unit doesn't always work as quickly as I think it should. This causes the pump to pull in air which could burn out the pump. I believe if you address these 2 issues you should have no problem with your unit.

I follow this regime for my unit:
1. I use distilled water (I notice the drastically cuts down on scale and mold issues between cleanings), if out I will use regular tap, but I preffer the distilled water.
2. I only clean out my unit every 3-4 weeks (it calls for every week) or if I see scale or any other issue start to pop up. (Regular tap water, I needed to clean about every week)
3. I use diluted vinegar to clean, run it through 2-3 clean cycles, then use diluted bleach water run it through 2-3 clean cycles, then run clean water through the unit a couple of times, draining each time. Then I throw out the first small batch of ice.
4. I keep my ice maker running all the time, but I make sure to regularly add water to the unit so it doesn't get low on water.

I think my cleaning step might be overkill, but it is pretty easy, I just move it next to the sink, and then let the hoses in the sink and uncork them to drain between cleanings. Totally worth the price and upkeep if you like nugget ice.

My dishwasher (Kenmore 587.15263900) stopped draining and was pooling water at the bottom. I flushed the drain line and ran a few cycles with vinegar to clean it out. I even pulled all the parts in the bottom and washed them by hand. After all that it still wouldn't drain so the only thing left was to replace the pump.

I got this pump in a day via Amazon Prime. My old pump lasted 8 years. Hopefully this will last at least a few years before I have to replace it again or get a new dishwasher.

I started by shutting off and disconnecting the water line and drain hose that led to the dishwasher under my sink, and shutting off the breaker to the dishwasher as a precaution. I then removed screws from two L-Brackets attached at the top of the dishwasher above the door to the bottom of the countertop. This enabled me to pull the dishwasher from under the counter. The only minor hiccup I had was that the wiring from the wall to the dishwasher was not long enough and only allowed me to pull it a little more than half way from the beneath the counter. Ideally you want to pull it all the way out and pivot tip it sideways for easiest access to the pump below.

There are two wires inserted with plugs into the pump that I removed by gently pulling them out. I then placed a towel beneath the pump in anticipation of it releasing some water when I removed it. There were 3 torx-20 screws removed from the face of the pump which allowed it to easily be removed by hand.

After removing the old one, I replaced it with the new one and installed everything back the way it was. I ran a test cycle and checked it when it completed. No more pool of water at the bottom of my dishwasher. Success!

I've never used a device like this before, but decided I needed one to operate/control a secondary heater for my inflatable spa, that only heats the water to a max of 104. 104 is nice, but the max temp typically drops a few degrees once the spa is uncovered and the jets turned on, so I wanted a way to get my "start temp" up a few degrees, and keep it there each time I open up the spa and get into it. The heater I chose is a 1500W submersible model (at 110/120V household current, that's a draw of about 12.5 amps). Saw all the reviews from guys who complained that their Inkbird promptly died under this kind of load, but the device IS "rated" to safely carry a load of up to 15A. I've now used it a little with the spa and secondary heater, and so far, it's working as advertised.
If you've never used a device like this, trying to figure out how to program and use it from the instruction manual is hopeless. The manual is like trying to read hieroglyphics. Even a few YouTube videos I found featured guys whose descriptions of how the thing works made it sound like you're operating a nuclear reactor. Once you find the right video (as I did after three tries), you'll finally see that setting this thing up and running it is VERY easy.
One probe/input monitors heat, which is controlled from the "Work 1" outlet. The second probe/input monitors cold, which is controlled from the "Work 2" outlet. When the Work 1 outlet is on, the Work 2 outlet is off, and vice versa. You can't program both outlets to work at the same time ... they toggle back/forth, so in my application, I only need/use the "Work 1" outlet.
Once the unit is plugged in, and a temperature probe is plugged into the input jack that corresponds to the Work 1 outlet, the unit immediately starts showing the ambient temperature sensed by the probe ... that's the top number on the display. The bottom number is your maximum heat setting, and it's very simple to set. When the temperature of the probe reaches your max setting, the Work 1 outlet is turned off. You can then set any differential you want between your max setting and the point you want the Work 1 outlet (e.g., heater) to come back on. It will then remain on until your target temp is reached again. The Work 2 outlet/probe works the same way, except you're setting it for cooling instead of heating. So, with this one controller, you can control both heating and cooling from one power source, as long as your heating and cooling devices never have to be on at the same time.
This thing has other features, but I'll leave discussion of those to people with greater experience/needs than me. Just wanted to say I'm very pleased with the way this thing is working for me so far, no thanks to the instruction manual supplied with the unit. Only time will tell how long that continues.

I've recently switched to more regular coffee drinking in the mornings, and traditional single-use K-Cups can get expensive over time. Decided to give these reusable and refillable cups a try. For the price of a mere dozen or so disposable K-Cup, you receive a set of 4 of these stainless steel beauties.

The complete set contents include the 4 cup, lids for each, instructions, and a rubberized (possibly silicon) finger cover for safely extracting the cup from your coffee machine after brewing. You simply fill the cups 1/4 to 2/3 full (per the instructions) with coffee grounds, press the lid firmly into place, and insert the cup into your coffee maker with the orange indicators facing left and right, and the indicator arrow facing you. Make your brewing size selection and off you go.

As for the brewing experience, I noticed a couple of things. Firstly, if did get a couple more coffee grounds in my mug than with a traditional K-Cup. However, they were so few and so tiny, it was no issue at all. The second observation, was that the water flowed through the reusable cup much more quickly than usual. After extracting and opening the cup, it appeared that the water pressure had pushed the grounds up higher in the cup, against the lid, suggesting that only a portion of the grounds got properly saturated. These factors resulted in a slightly weaker/paler cup of coffee than I'd expected. I'd suggest getting a darker roast than usual if you intend to switch completely to these reusable cups.

That said, the coffee was still quite tasty. Then comes the cleaning part. Despite the inclusion of the finger guards in the box, they were unneeded. Just a few moments after the coffee machine completed it's cycle, the cup was cool enough to handle with my bare fingers. You simply remove the cup from the machine, pop off the lid, and dump the used grounds. Most of the grounds came out easily with a shake over the garbage, but some clung persistently to the sides of the cup. Running a spoon around the interior took care of most of that. Then a quick rinse in the sink, and you're all done. Admittedly, the ground from the lid and sides of the cup rinsed out quite easily, but a couple of grounds would remain stuck in the bottom. A few extra passes with the facet (in sprayer mode) dislodged them in short order.

While I like having the extra cups included in this package, they are so easily cleaned that I can't imagine needing more than the one unless I needed to make several cups of coffee or difference cups of coffee at once.

At the end of the day, I think this is a great product for both the environment and your wallet, though depending on the type of coffee you like, you may wish to make changes.

An appliance repair man wanted $150 to replace our broken icemaker. It worked when it felt like it, and water leaked from both ends when it did. On a whim, I ordered this piece. Make sure you put your ENTIRE model number. We have a Whirlpool, and the model number on the door was different from the model number listed on the right side wall of the fridge. The assembly comes with several different wiring arrangements. What I did was leave the original wiring, unplug the wire that came with the assembly and plug the old wiring into the new assembly. I did this because I knew the old unit was producing ice, so there was no electrical reason why the old wiring wouldn't work. If that ever became the case, I still have the wires that came with the assembly and can switch them out if necessary.

All you need is a ratchet that fits the existing screws on the old unit. Truthfully, if you don't know what you're doing (like me) I watched a few YouTube videos on how the install the unit. It's really simple. UPPLUG THE FRIDGE!!!! If you can't get back there, flip the circuit breaker. Unscrew the bottom screw (watch out you don't drop it... it's hard to find In a freezer full of food (did you think I dropped it???? You're right if you did). There are two screws on top... just loosen them and the unit can be lifted off those screws. You'll see on the bottom a a little square with a lever that you can push with a screw driver and that will release the wire plug that goes to the wall of the freezer. Remove the old unit, plug the plug into the new unit, set it in place over the 2 top screw, insert the bottom screw and you're good to go.

Here's where I freaked out... It didn't make ice for two days, but I read that the unit has to reach a certain temperature to produce ice, so I let it go another day, and then back to YouTube... Why is my new icemaker not making ice? So here's where the Freak started... I needed to "jumpstart" the motor. You take a wire with two bare ends (make sure it's insulated... wrap some black tape around it, or a piece of rubber, and insert the ends into these tiny holes marked T and H on the front of the unit. I cut an old plug from a radio that didn't work, scraped the plastic of the two end twisted them. I wasn't sure if I was going to set the house on fire or electrocute myself, but neither happened... The dial started to turn and I heard water fill the tray. YAY!!!!! It's working fine now, and I have a full ice bin. Took about 2 days, but I'm so happy not to have to buy bags of ice anymore... been doing that for a year.

This is our second Acme Miami dryer booster. When we installed our first one ten years ago, we were overjoyed to discover that we no longer took over an hour for dryer loads. I’m convinced that the booster paid for itself in energy savings with much shorter drying times. Not to mention less wear and tear on the dryer itself. Our dryer vent run is over 30 feet long with 3 90-degree bends from dryer to outlet. Every foot of vent pipe length and every bend adds more resistance to air flow. This dryer booster helps your dryer to do its job more efficiently.

Installation is not difficult but does require maybe a square foot of floor space between the dryer and vent connection because the booster sits on the floor. Installation also requires making a pencil-size hole in the vent hose coming out of the dryer to allow use of the air-pressure tube that automatically turns the booster on when the dryer starts and off when the dryer stops. I wrapped the vent hose with a band of duct tape, made a small hole through the tape and hose with a sharp pointed tool, inserted the air pressure tube and sealed around it with more duct tape. The previous installation worked flawlessly for ten years, and the new unit is working perfectly as well. Our original unit was still working when we replaced it, but it had developed a loud motor bearing noise that was annoying and probably a sign that the booster was nearing the end of its service life.

I do love MOST things about this washer. I previously had a Kenmore Elite Calypso Top Loading HE for 12 years. I wanted to get back to an agitator/fill-with-water type washer because I didn't feel my clothes were getting as clean. Odd thing about this Speed Queen though, is in the User's Manual, it directs you to use a low-sudsing HE detergent (see picture!) Of course I read this after I'd gone out just to buy regular detergent and used it in the four loads I've done so far with fine results. I even ran an extra rinse cycle on this last load just to see if there was any remaining soap, but none of note. I will try it with the HE detergent that I have on hand to see if it still cleans well.

Pros for this washer:
- Will fill to the top on Extra Large setting.
- The lid does not lock. You can open the lid at any time during the entire wash/rinse/spin cycle.
- Very short wash times.
- CLEAN laundry! Can actually smell the clean. Didn't notice the absence of that clean smell until I got it back with this washer.
- End of wash signal.
- Delayed start for up to 24 hours (haven't used this yet but looking forward to setting for early morning so laundry doesn't sit wet overnight.)
- Extended, 5 year warranty on parts and labor comes with the washer. I've read that some people say you're paying for it in the cost of the washer, as the price used to be $300 less than current selling price.
- Can set up to 9 different Favorite settings.
- Different wash cycles have different spin speeds (e.g. delicate spins slower than permanent press).

Cons for this washer:
- The most annoying thing is that this washer will not fill, agitate or spin when lid is open. I can understand agitate and spin, but fill? Directions tell you to pour detergent in bottom of washer, then add clothes, THEN close the lid to add the water. That means some clothes are just sitting right on top of non-diluted detergent. This is a very annoying feature, and I would love to figure out how to override for at least the fill time. I even watched a video on YouTube before I bought, which showed a guy doing a load with the lid open. He doesn't state he's tweaked it in any way. He is using the AWNE82, and I have the AWNE92, but I can't imagine that Speed Queen changed that feature between their two electronic models.
***EDITED: I used the instructions and photos I found on the discussion forum of www.automaticwasher.org to bypass this feature - easy to do and works great now!. (http://www.automaticwasher.org/cgi-bin/TD/TD-VIEWTHREAD.cgi?39369) I'm leaving this as a CON, however, because of the need to bypass it.***
- Size of tub is only 3.3 cubic ft. - however, I still was able to fit one queen sheet set and one twin sheet set and 5 bath towels in one load.
- When delivered, the tub had a black film on it. You can't see it with the naked eye, but rub a white towel in the tub and you'll see it. I had read about this and was prepared, but it did take two no-clothes wash cycles, one rubdown with Goo Gone and FOUR rubdowns with Windex and a white towel before it was all cleaned off.
- The only cycle for NORMAL is combined with the ECO setting, which starts with warm, then switches to cold water, regardless of your settings. Also, the directions say to not use the fabric softener dispenser on the ECO setting. This is annoying. So, instead I will set up a Favorite for my "normal".

I've only had this machine for one day, so these are all initial impressions. I will update if anything of note happens. Even though it looks like I've listed many cons, these are minor, and overall I'm very pleased with the machine. One thing I realized, however, is if you don't use HE detergent, it may become hard to find regular detergent in the stores! Also, at the time of this writing, there were three pictures on Amazon for this unit. The main picture it is showing is NOT the AWNE92 with 9 cycle settings. It is showing the AWNE82 with 3 settings. I've attached a picture of my AWNE92 panel.
***EDIT: Update 1/2016 - still loving this machine, definitely worth the money!

If you are here, you probably already have a top loading washer that will not rinse and spin. Chances are it is the lid switch. It is an easy repair, and this washer lid switch is a great replacement part. I have a Kenmore Series 80 washing machine, model # 110.20802990. I removed the broken switch and it is part number 3949238. These Kenmore washing machines are made by Whirlpool.

This is a really easy repair, you only need a phillips head screwdriver for the 2 screws that hold the switch and the 2 screws that hold the control panel. Then you need a small socket, nut driver or wrench for the green/ground wire. For a few great and helpful videos google "replacing lid switch kenmore series 80 washer" it will result in YouTube videos that will walk you through the repair.

Don't lose the 2 screws that mount the switch to the washing machine or the nut that holds the green wire. The switch does not come with any screws.

I Searched the web for this part and most sites charged $25 or more. I bought this on Amazon, and it was from Seneca River Trading, and it only cost $8 DELIVERED! This is a warning to those installing this product or others kits like it. It comes with a wire harness with attached spade clips, a Bi-Metal thermal fuse, and screw terminal block for ease of installation. I followed the installation instructions and disconnected power to the appliance, cut off the factory installed spade connectors, stripped back the wires and inserted them into the terminal block and tightened the terminal screws as tight as possible.
After two years the heater element failed causing an over current condition on the circuit, because of a high resistance (poor mechanical connection) on the terminal block the wiring overheated burning the wire and melting a hole in the internal chassis (see picture). This may have been caused by corrosion of the copper conductors due to moist conditions in the dishwasher. The Bi-Metal fuse was supposed to fail to prevent over heating of wiring. It did not fail causing a potential fire hazard.
I recommend that if you are going to install this product, discard the terminal block and use silicone filled heat shrink crimp terminals and a crimp tool available at most hardware stores to attach the wires. Then use a lighter or heat gun to shrink the insulation around the connector and wires to seal out any moisture. Crimp connections are low impedance and will not heat up like screw terminals.

I purchased this ice maker over two years ago and for two years it worked amazingly well. It makes wonderful ice. Small, cylindrical, crunchy, perfectly sized and ideal for drinks. We LOVE this ice maker and used it every day. We always used purified RO/DI water and it never gave us problems until recently. After years of reliable service it started making horrible screeching noises. If you read other reviews, you'll see that this is a common problem. Some people encounter it sooner than others, I suspect this has to do with whether you use purified water or not. Although it still made fine ice, the noise was so loud you could hear it across the house.

I tried to clean it with vinegar many times and overnight per the instructions and while it helped for a few days, the squealing noises always returned. It was incredibly frustrating. I was ready to give up on the ice maker when I decided to try one last ditch effort and take it apart to fix it. It's now been several days and the ice maker is working good as new. I wanted to share the steps I took to fix it in case it helps others.

I wouldn't attempt this unless you're somewhat handy. Be sure to set aside all of your screws and keep track of where they go. There are several different types of screws that go into different places and you will forget which ones go where if you don't keep them organized.

Repair Instructions:

1) Use pliers to remove the black rubber plugs at the top of the ice maker. You'll find screws underneath. Unscrew and remove the top. Disconnect the wire connector so you can put aside the top.
2) Unscrew and remove the metal plate on the rear of the unit.
3) Unscrew and remove the sheet metal casing that covers the front and sides of the unit.
4) Disconnect the two wires across the top to give you space to work.
5) Unscrew and remove the black plastic cover and styrofoam insulator that covers the center metal cylinder.
6) With everything opened up and looking at the front of the unit, you will see a white water reservoir on the right side and the metal ice 'screw' cylinder in the center.
7) Unscrew the screws holding the white reservoir. You will need to shift this aside in order to access the metal cylinder. While you're at it, you should clean the reservoir because there will certainly be some dirt/dust in this container.
8) Use a socket wrench or pliers to remove the hex bolts at the top of the metal cylinder.
9) Pull off the metal top of the cylinder. You will find a heavy screw drive shaft in the center and a white plastic sleeve. Pull the screw drive and white sleeve out.
10) Using a paper towel, long nose pliers and q tips, thoroughly clean the center cavity of the metal cylinder.
11) Thoroughly clean the metal screw drive and the white plastic sleeve.
12) Using plumbers silicone grease, lubricate the whole screw drive. I used a thin layer on any surface that touched another surface. This included the bottom, the sharp spiral edge of the drive itself and the top of the drive that fits into the plastic sleeve.
13) Reassemble the metal cylinder, screw the hex bolts back in, etc.
14) While you have the unit open, use an air canister to blow all the dust out of the unit. Be careful with the radiator fins on the side as they are very delicate.
15) Reverse all the steps that you took to take the unit apart and put it back together. Remember to reconnect the 3 wires that you disconnected.
16) Run the ice maker on clean cycle a couple times.
17) I made a full bucket of ice then threw it out to start clean. I used the ice from the second batch forward.

This whole process took me about an hour, but it absolutely worked and the machine is working good as new. The photos I included will show you the silicone grease I used. The silicone is used for faucets and is food safe. If I didn't love this machine so much, I would not have gone through this much trouble to try to get it fixed. Hopefully others find this helpful!

The smaller board has the optic emitter which tends to go bad.

It’s easy to unscrew and disconnect the board. Reconnecting the board is not easy because the cord is short. I needed a long flathead screwdriver to force the connector to snap in. You can shock yourself if you directly touch the board when it’s connected to the fridge and the power is on.

After replacing the smaller optic board the red light turned steady red when depressing the left door switch which is what you want. I didn’t need to replace the larger board. When I closed the door I could hear the fridge turning on the water and got ice 3 hours later.

I've bought two sets of these so far, they're reasonably consistent in regards to the reported values. And they're comparable to DHT22's sold by others. Which is good because I use a number of these throughout my home. And the readings are consistent between individual sensors and the reported values are also consistent within a reasonable range.

The supply voltage is crucial to these sensors regardless of the vendor. The part (DHT22/AM2302 w/o a board) is spec'd 3.2 or 3.3 to 5 volts. If you are running one of these from a ESP-12E or other MCU with an integrated 3.3v regulator then chances are it will work without issue. And at 5v they'll work without any problems. However, I'm running them from an ESP-01 and external LM1117 regulator board where the regulator is an SMT part. There I've found that the regulators can be off and supply a voltage as low as 3.0 volts. NOTE: The ESP-01 supply voltage is spec'd at 2.7 to 3.6v or 3.7v, depending on the information source.

When the supply voltage is at 3.2 or lower the device will not report correctly. Depending on the exact supply voltage the device may either not work at all or intermittently report "NaN" when using the Arduino library.

The solution I found for my devices (ESP-01 + LM1117 SMT) was to supply the DHT22 with 5v and use a BSS138 circuit to handle the 3.3v VS 5v sides of the circuit. This has worked extremely well and a "test" device has been running 24/7 with the modified circuit for 3 months without any reading errors. Before that the error rate was about 20 to 50%.

Bottom line, this is an excellent sensor for most hobbyist applications. It has the required resistor & capacitor already on-board and the connecting wires are a nice addition. However, for my application I would have preferred male/female wires instead of female/female.

I purchased this unit for two main reasons. One, I liked that it offered a separate section for beverages and another for wine. Second, and probably most important, it did not cost $2,000 like many similar units I found in local appliance stores. Now that I have been using it for a little over a month I will say that I am pleased with the purchase.

The combo unit is perfect for us. I find that the unit is able to maintain two different temperatures for each section easily. The temperature read outs are easy to see and adjust. The only draw back is that the placement of the shelves in the beverage side is not optimal for the beverage sizes you normally find in the US. For example, typical American beer bottles do not fit the unit right out of the box. However I did find that half liter bottles of water and smaller bottles had no problem. I did read that other customers had removed the rack support and modified it to support larger items. What I wound up doing is removing one shelf, which was a fairly easy thing to do if you follow the directions provided. Even with the shelf removed, I was amazed at how much the unit could hold. The shelves are fairly deep and this provides great capacity. The wine side required no adjustment and it was able to store all sorts of different bottles and shapes with little problem.

The unit is quiet in its operation. It is not whisper quiet, yet we do not hear it when it is running in other areas of the house. I would say it produces slightly more noise that our full size refrigerator but nothing objectionable. I was also impressed that the unit came with a five year warranty on the motor and compressor. Finally, it was easy to install under our cabinet and its appearance is quite pleasant. Overall I am very happy with the unit so far and would recommend it to others.

I drink cold brew coffee everyday so I make it in large batches to save. As far as the filtering goes this system did a great job of eliminating the fine particles from the coffee beans leaving a very clear final cold brew solution. I didn’t really notice much of a difference in the filtering when not using it so that’s what I’m doing.

If you’re looking for a quality system to make large batches of cold brew coffee, this system works great. I would recommend based on the quality of construction, ease of use, and ability to filter the coffee beans and strain quickly.

I bought my first washer-dryer pair in 1977 as a kid in college--a GE set in avocado, no less Great set. Over the next 20 years, in various homes, I had 3 GE sets. These were the excellent Filter-Flo machines first introduced in 1957, refined and improved over the years. Then, in 2000, I discovered that GE had brought out a newer line with cheapened controls and flimsy construction. From 2000 to 2017 I owned 2 front loaders. While they washed well and efficiently, they both eventually blew that front bearing that costs well over $500 to repair. Also--I live alone and don't generate but about 2-3 loads weekly at most.

When this last front loader just blew its bearing I decided to look around and was quite disappointed in what I saw. Mostly front loaders from Korea at the big-box stores, with lots of electronic toys on them (even wi-fi!) but no real improvements in durability. Fortunately, my city still has a traditional appliance dealer and he carries Speed Queen. After looking at their front loaders I decided to go back to the traditional top loader for durability and simplicity. Actually, the electronic control panel model of this same washer was only $20 more and with a longer warranty, but I decided to stick with this. My last front loader gave me hell for a few years with electronic control glitches. It was under maintenance but that doesn't wash the clothes!

I'm quite pleased with this machine. In order to satisfy the government, it does have a normal-ECO cycle on it that limits the water and the hot water temp. Fortunately, there is also a 'normal' cycle that gives traditional deep-water wash and rinse, and hot at the temp I choose. It is not loud, but definitely not completely silent as my front-loaders were. I like the idea of energy and water savings, but I use so little extra I don't feel bad about it. I'm really loving the fact that I can open the lid and add items while it washes; I used to be really bad about wanting to add something on the front loaders and I couldn't. I will say that I find the clothes marginally wetter at the end of the wash because the spin speed is slower than my front loaders, but not disturbingly so.

I learned that this, the last 'knob' machine by Speed Queen, is being discontinued at the end of 2017. Why? Well, our government is once again meddling with our washers. Apparently, according to SQ, it wasn't possible to satisfy them with a mechanical timer. Of course, the same excellent machine will be offered with their electronic board--and it's commercial grade--but obviously there will be changes, not necessarily for the better. Those of us with newer dishwashers know how the government regulations have messed them up.

I'd recommend this machine highly, but if you want complete control over your washing, you'd better buy before 2018.

I’ve wanted an ice machine for a long time and was thrilled to have the opportunity to test this one out. As far as I’m concerned, there’s usually not enough ice in the ice box (sorry, “freezer”). Other people in the house like to empty out the ice trays and not refill them.

So, even though this unit takes up a sizeable amount of countertop space, I’m glad to use it to remedy this problem. I didn’t know what to expect, and as a first-timer, here’s some things I ran into.

-The unit needs to stand upright for 4-6 hours before you even start looking at it.

-The unit requires a cleaning cycle before you start using it. The manufacturer recommends this Nu-calgon nickle safe descaler/cleaner product. So, if you know you’re a rule follower, order a bottle of this stuff along with the unit! I couldn’t wait, so I ran it through the cleaning cycle with a white vinegar/water solution.

-The unit requires running through at least 4 dumps of ice cubes (dump these out) before you should start getting usable ice.

Sheesh!

-Once the ice is made, it is not kept cold, and immediately begins to melt. However, the water reservoir is directly below the ice bin, so when it melts, it melts back into the source water, to again be made into ice.

-The product is advertised as giving you ice in 6-8 minutes. This is roughly true, but it gives you a handful of cubes. It then produces another handful of cubes every 8 minutes or so. So, it takes quite awhile before you have an ice-bucket full of ice for your mixed-drink party.

-I should clarify: They’re not “cubes”, they are kind of nubbed, rounded missile-shaped with a big hole in the bottom/flat side. They are opaque, whitish, and not clear.

-Operation and use is easy. On-off and select your cube size (small/large, although they’re not that different from each other). Another setting to run the cleaning cycle. A red light that notifies you if the basket is full or if the water is too low.

-It makes some weird noises, which you need to get used to.

-To drain the excess water after your ice-making session, there is a little rubbery plug underneath the unit. Unplug and let it drain into a cup or pan, etc. One time I put water in the reservoir without having re-attached the plug and had quite a watery surprise on my legs and feet! In the initial ownership of this item, I’m most worried about this little plug and even littler strap that attaches the plug to the unit… how long can that thing possibly last?

I must admit, I was disappointed the ice isn’t kept cold. I guess you have to get up into the $500 machines for that extra feature. But, you figure out how to deal with it, it’s not a deal-breaker. I transfer the ice into the freezer, or directly into drinks.

The most pleasant surprise, however, is that once these ice nubs are in your drink for 5-10 minutes, they become really soft, unlike my regular freezer ice, which gets smaller as it melts, obviously, but stays hard and crunchy. This ice actually gets chewy and kind of soft, which is wonderful news for my teeth and jaw.

Oh, and there’s a little ice scoop included as well.

It's advertised as "compact and portable". The measurements are 16.42 x 12.28 x 15.28 inches, which I guess I wouldn't consider "compact", so measure that out first before you decide if you have room.

If you have the counter space, and the need for such a unit, or know someone that would love it as a gift, I have no trouble recommending this ice machine.

Background: Single guy living in 1960's condo with no washer/dryer hookups. Laundry in the basement (3 toploaders, 3 dryers, 36 unit building).
I got tired of having to tapdance around other people and have had some clothes ruined with bleach stains from communal washers. Got tired of going up and down the elevator and setting timers for wash and dry cycles. Got tired of large folding chore from letting laundry pile up.

So I gave this a shot. This definitely cleans clothes well, and quickly. My 'light' loads wash for 4-5 minutes and my heavier jeans and towels, I wash for about 5-7 minutes; I rinse for about 3 minutes; then spin for 2-3 minutes. At an average of 10-15 minutes per load, it is easy to get through a week's worth of laundry while doing other activities. TIP: I fill this with a bucket rather than the included hose. The hose works well. but it does not fit on my sink faucet. You can save LOTS of time by filling your bucket during each cycle. So fill your bucket, wash, and while washing, fill your bucket for rinse; while rinsing, fill your bucket for next load. This REALLY speeds things up.

I am not a country boy or a smelly single guy -- I am not a metro, but my Mom, so many years ago, was a clean freak. Clothing isn't clean to me if it smells at all. AT ALL. It isn't clean unless the rinse water has the merest tinge of blue fabric softener, no brown or gray from dirt. So, I am not one to reuse wash water, and I do not. That said, a 5 minute wash REALLY gets clothes clean. To each their own, but I am particular about clean clothes, and this machine does the job.

Like most men, I overload washers constantly. You cannot overload this guy or the clothes will not spin to clean. Be patient, and remember that you are not sitting at a laundromat or a dank basement. :)

For a load, I use less than a tablespoon of Tide powder, less than a table spoon of fabric softener, and then add a bit more fabric softener in the Rinse, just a touch. There are a few bubbles in the wash drain cycle and Rinse water is clean. This is the correct amount to use. If your water is foamy like crazy, you're using too much product. For lightly soiled items, you can load and wash. For dirtier or thicker stuff, I let it soak in the soapy water for 5 or 10 minutes. For whites that aren't so white, I have used OxyClean in a bucket, allowed my whites to soak for an hour, then wash them and they came out 'okay'.

If you use bleach with this machine, make sure to RINSE TWICE. This should get rid of enough of the bleach to keep subsequent loads safe from bleach stains.

Clothes come out of the spin cycle more dry than they do out of a commercial washer, and I hang dry everything.

I have done 6 loads and am still working out my "system" but filling buckets during wash and rinse cycles is really where its at. It really speeds up the entire process, and I LOVE being able to work or watch TV or clean the kitchen or whatever while the wash is getting done. The smaller loads encourage me to do a load or three whenever I have time, and the clothes are clean and fresh. I own two drying racks in case I ever get behind, but so far, I've only needed one.

My only concern is that even after the machine has run a full Drain cycle, there is still water in the bottom of the machine -- not the bottom of the tub -- the bottom of the machine. I have yet to devise a solution for this. So far, I have just picked the machine up , turned it upside down, etc. This is not going to be a solution for many people who use this machine. The concern here is that the rinse water, which should be pretty clean, is just hanging out in the dark recesses of the machine. Storing the machine with the doors open is a good idea to avoid mildew.

Has anyone else noticed that there is still water sloshing around in the machine? How do you handle it?

All in all, for around $200 with shipping, the machine is good looking, well built, light, and allows condo and apartment dwellers and older folks who cannot go up and down stairs so well, as well as summer home/cabin by the lake dwellers, etc., to have a great wash option that is quick, easy, works great and is convenient. It was worth the money to me.

EDIT: I am 6" and a big guy and I can fit a fair of jeans and several shirts in one load. I can fit 2 regular towels and lots of kitchen and hand towels in one load. I can fit maybe 5 pairs of boxers and 5 pairs of socks and a T shirt or two in one load. If you have oversized towels, or beach towels, you'll have to wash one at a time with one or two smaller items.

You can wash slightly more than you can spin dry at a time -- but the spine drying LITERALLY takes between 30 seconds and 2 minutes. For example, I washed a thermal hoodie, XL, with rubber liner (for extreme cold and wind), and several other items. When the wash and rinse was done, I put JUST the hoodie in the spinner and ran it for about 30 seconds, and it came out VERY dry. Then, I spun the rest of the stuff for a minute or so. The wash and rinse cycle is long, but even with a few seconds of spinning, the water is mostly out of the clothing. Spinning longer is a waste of time and electricity. That spinner is efficient.

I'm surprised to see so many negative reviews for this product. This is my second 2.0 model and I had one of the original Opal machines before that. I never had any issues with them. The complaints seem to boil down to 2 topics primarily, people that apparently receive non-functional machines and people that complain about the noise, price, and size of the ice maker.

I've had no functional issues with any of my 3 machines but with Amazon's excellent return/exchange program and GE's excellent customer service (used it a couple of times for other appliances and it was quick and easy), those that may get a DOA machine should be easily able to get it resolved.

This ice machine is definitely for ice enthusiasts that crave that soft, chewy, amazing pellet ice that some restaurants use. This machine is a game changer as there are very few options for making it at home. If you're not dedicated to having nugget ice at home then you probably won't see the value in this machine. Just get a regular cube ice machine that will be quieter, smaller, and cheaper. If you love nugget ice, you'll love this.

The magic of nugget ice is that it's compressed as its frozen to give it that magical texture. That's also why it's noisier than regular ice makers as it has to run the compressor to freeze the ice, the water pump, the part that compresses the ice, and the part that cuts the ice as it comes out into little pieces. It's really a pretty marvelous piece of engineering.

In particular this 2.0 version offers several improvements over the original Opal. It's quieter, has a better ice box design that allows you to open the bin and it sits open at the perfect angle to scoop out of with no need to hold it with one of your hands like the old one. It also is "smart" and can connect to WiFi and GE's app to let you control the machine. I don't find it hugely useful but it's there if you want to use it. I really wish they'd add the ability to schedule the light inside that lights up the ice bin. It would be nice to have it turn off at night to extend the life of the LED.

Anyway, my family loves nugget ice and love this machine. I highly recommend it if you love nugget ice!

With such a relatively small basket it is kinda hard to load it incorrectly. I think this may be due to the lack of the traditional agitator that reduces load size in full size machine. The sink faucet adapter that is included might have some issues with your faucet. They incude a rubber washer that is necessary with most water hoses. Your faucet probably has one as well. When you try and install this with the included washer as well as the one in your faucet you might run into an issue. If it won't screw on simply remove your faucet's rubber washer and install the new washer in its place. Removing the quick connect adapter may make installation of the sink adapter easier. About the only thing I do not like about this washer is its communication skills. Sure, it can complain with beeps if it has an issue but you've no clue how long until the next cycle. You can time each cycle so you will know but it would be nice for the machine to have that info ready. By the by if you have an issue with adding softener you can set a separate timer or purchase detergent with softener included.

July 2016 update: After using the Panda for a few months, below are some updated observations.

Filling: Purchasing a diverter with hose and hand-held shower head helped quite a bit. Unfortunately, though, the hose (which appears to be pretty standard in length) is just baaaaarely long enough to reach the washer's tub, even with the Panda right up against the bathtub. This forces me to have to stand with one foot in the bathtub to make it work. Climbing in and out of the bathtub repeatedly is not my idea of convenience. I know it's not the Panda's fault that the hose isn't long enough...I mention it because it demonstrates how much finagling needs to be done to successfully use this machine.

Drainage: Like another reviewer suggested, I took to elevating the Panda by placing it on top of a plastic tub right in the bathtub. This helps employ gravity to drain and also helps with filling the washer's tub by getting it closer to the filling source, but it's a pain in the neck having to lug the machine up and down like that. With this arrangement, I can't leave it unattended at all for fear of it shimmying itself off its temporary pedestal during operation. It's a labor-intensive, hands-on way to wash. Yes, it's an improvement over washing by hand, but not vastly so.

Washing: I find that this machine is hard on clothes. I've only been washing and rinsing for 1 minute each, respectively.

I find myself not using the Panda very much. Really, only for "emergency" mid-week loads. Knowing what I know now, I think I would have been better off buying separate counter-top washer and spinner units. They would do basically the same thing but be much easier to maneuver and store.

April 2016: This is the first of a multi-part review.

My previous machine was a Haier (http://www.amazon.com/Haier-HLP21N-Pulsator-1-Cubic-Foot-Portable/dp/B002UYSHMM?ie=UTF8&ref_=cm_cr-mr-title) that lasted 6 years. I wrote a review/update each of those years and will do the same with this machine.

Tonight I tried it out for the first time and below are my impressions.

Drain set-up: I had a bit of a challenge with the drain hose at first. I tried hooking it over the edge of the bathtub then over the edge of the sink, but the narrow u-shaped hook didn't fit. In my case it definitely had to be placed over the toilet edge. Once I hooked it there and closed the seat and lid, I finally felt confident to leave it semi-unattended during the drain cycle.

Intake set-up: The intake hose seems like it might only work with a standard kitchen faucet. In my very average builder-grade bathroom, it wasn't ideal. I had to stand there and manually shove the nozzle onto the faucet and clutch it while a bunch of water uselessly flowed over my hand and into the sink. Filling the machine took longer than I would have liked. Unless you plan to use this with a fairly small faucet head, you should think about finding another way to fill the wash tub. Personally, I'm following the advice of the top reviewer and buying a diverter and hand-held shower head; if not for that, a bucket would be preferable for a bathroom set-up.

Detergent: Wow...you really only need like a teaspoon of regular detergent, if even that. This machine really suds things up. I'm going to buy HE detergent in the hopes of cutting down on the rinse process.

Noise level: Impressively low! The videos make the machine sound much louder than it actually is (no fault of the videographers). In particular, if you properly balance the spinner, it will practically hum.

Overall time: The agitate and spin cycles are vigorous enough that only a few minutes each is required.

Spin-dry feature: Clothes come out drier than any other machine I've ever used.

Drainage: This is the only real complaint I have thus far. The drain motor isn't strong enough to completely empty the machine. At one point I had to move the hose around to sort of prime it. At another point, I lost my ever-loving mind and actually sucked on the end of the tube, which worked but OMG don't do it. In the end - in order to thoroughly drain the entire machine - I had to raise it and use gravity before tucking it away into the closet. But, this is a small complaint in light of the bigger picture (price, convenience, etc.).

So far so good! Updates to follow.

My old machine delivered HOT WATER so that's no different on this one, but it sounds like most new machines 'water down' the hot water. That's dumb.

This machine just won't go out of BALANCE! I love this about my washer. My old one could, at times, act like a bucking bronco. This one has never so much as moved a tiny bit across the floor. And I've washed some pretty big loads including comforters.

I don't like the AGITATOR. My old one would take the clothes down into the machine very quickly. I have to wait on this one longer and combined with the stupid way you can't lift the top without it stopping, it just makes for more time fidgeting around with doing the wash. I wish it pulled the clothes in better, but I can live with how it works and I suppose it is easier on the clothes this way. Still....

We did have a REPAIR person come out once. This was pretty early on. I had washed a crocheted blanket and I am theorizing that it ended up being very heavy with water (or it got caught somehow, although there was no evidence of this). I would recommend this washer to anyone who is not overly concerned about the noise level (and maybe mine, for some reason, is just louder than other reviewers' machines). I don't consider the problem with the rinse cycle as anything to worry about. I think it might be 'user error'.

I have been running my unit for 9 days at the highest fan speed (maximum humidification). Prior to purchasing this unit I had other humidifiers in the house so the carpets and furniture shouldn’t have to absorb too much humidity from the Venta. It just does not seem to be doing much to raise the humidity in the house. The readout on the Venta shows that it is seeing 45% relative humidity in the air. However, 2 other (accurate) humidity gauges 15-feet and 28-feet away never seem to get above 40% at best. I do not expect the humidity being pumped into the air to reach my back bedrooms, but the humidity gauges I mentioned are in an area with an open floor plan and the Venta is centrally located there. The area mentioned is around 900 to 1000 sq-ft with 10-foot ceilings. The (up to) 1600 sq-ft (or so) rating seems wildly inflated. Probably based on a sealed test lab with 8-foot ceilings I would guess. I had an evaporative unit from another manufacturer rated for 600 sq-ft that performed at a level equal to this Venta, at 1/10th the price. I just got tired of constantly refilling that small tank and mixing caustic chemicals into the water with every refill, so I bought this Venta as a “step-up”. I bought in to the positive reviews here, but (belatedly) checking with Fakespot produced a review quality grade of “F”. In addition, the water tank cap gasket isn’t thick enough on my unit. I have to tighten the cap down way too much to get it to seal properly without leaking. Then it is a bear to get back off when it is time to refill. On the plus side the controls are well designed, the unit is quiet on the lower speed settings, and the roll-out water tank and drawer makes refilling painless. While I expected more from the LW60T, purchasing the next higher capacity Venta airwasher model is not in the cards at nearly twice the price. I will give the LW60T another week or so to see if things turn around. It is putting 4 gallons a day into the air. That has to be going somewhere.

Rev. 01/19/2020
The Venta is helping keep the humidity in my house above 40% ... most of the time. While the optimistic coverage rating (earning it 3-stars) of this unit was determined in a lab setting/tight room with 8-foot ceilings, my house has 10-foot ceilings and is not as “tight” as their lab. There may be more effective and less expensive ways to ensure a comfortable humidity level throughout the whole house, but it is hard to beat the convenience of the device. Just make sure to rinse/wash out the water tank and tray and disks every week or two. In my case, a lot of crud was being pulled out of the air and being deposited in the bottom of the tray. That is a good thing.

Rev. 01/20/2020

I contacted Venta-USA about the failure. After some back and forth they sent me a replacement LW60. Within hours the replacement unit started producing a periodic clicking or chattering noise. While that noise was present the disk stack (that provides the humidification) stopped turning. This was the same noise my first unit made before it failed completely. We all know that ice trays are punishment from god for the sins of your past lives. Fridge ice isn't much better, because it is, unlike how ice is supposed to be, white. What the heck, man?!?!?!?! Ice is supposed to be clear; I don't need a visual reminder of the mineral content of my H2O every time I try to take a sip.

Bag ice from the store? Yeah, that's fine, if you make a special run to get it, drive home immediately, bash it against a concrete wall, then enjoy grabbing it by the handful every time you pour a glass of sarsparilla or whiskey or whisky or bourbon. Then you get to suffer through the snowy last quarter or the bag, dump out wet plastic, and start the whole process all over again. And hobos pee in those ice coolers. Better than the other options, for sure, but still sub-optimal.

What we really want is Sonic ice, or at least as close as we can get.

That's exactly what you get from this marvelous machine: tiny, chewable chunks of ice at your command.

You can absolutely get a glass of ice five minutes after you turn it on, and in way less than an hour, you've got plenty for some serious highball abuse. Just fill the front-loading reservoir (or hook it up to a water source; haven't done that yet, but it looks pretty straight forward), put the bin in, and press the button. It even shuts off when full, and you can set it to either fill constantly or on command. It also has a self-cleaning function, though you should drain it out every week. Couldn't be simpler. Oh, and it includes a perfectly sized scoop and a tray to catch the drips.

My only complaint is that the machine doesn't cool the ice it makes, relying on the ice to cool itself. This'll work for about a day, but if you leave it overnight, it'll be empty by the morning. So, grab a bucket and stick the excess in the freezer, or just let it melt and reuse the melt water for the next batch, as the ice bin drains right into the reservoir and it takes less time to start it up than it takes to run a coffee pod.

I absolutely love this thing. It doesn't take up a ton of space, looks great on the counter, and, come to think of it, wouldn't look at all bad on the table next to my bed. I have had this little gem for a little over six months. I moved into a mid-rise apartment that has three washing machines per floor and with over 25 apartments per floor, it can be difficult to get laundry done in the PM hours after work. Also, I don't enjoy taking my dirty clothes outside my apartment. I looked at this machine for a long time before I made the purchase. It's a good little washer but it is quite temperamental.

1. Don't expect to use the large/heavy setting without problems. Often it will just shut itself off right before it needs to spin to remove the water. I don't do it often but I have washed a queen sized fleece blanket in this machine and occasionally it will just shut off for no apparent reason. This only happens when I use the heavy setting when the water is filled as high as the machine allows. For the most part, I only use the normal or quick cycles and I haven't had any problems with it shutting off midway.

2. This machine frequently becomes unbalanced and will shake, rattle and roll during the spin cycle. The way the clothing is agitated causes the fabric to knot up in the machine. This happens a lot with knits, sheets, cotton towels and denim. It can get a little loud so if you have neighbors, it can be a problem. I don't do laundry after 9pm for this reason. Usually you can fix the problem by shifting the clothing but occasionally it just won't be quiet. If it's severely unbalance, the machine will shut itself off.

3. My recommendation is to do small loads. I only fill it up loosely with clothes to about halfway. I also suggest batching your clothes by fabric type. Since the machine unbalances frequently, the machine seems to work better when the fabric type is similar.

4. Don't expect super stain removal. If you have stains, be sure to pre-treat before washing. Using the normal wash, you wash once and then rinse once. There aren't extra water changes during the wash like in a regular machine. I find that if something is really dirty, pre-treat and in some cases wash more than once. And, use a good quality HE liquid laundry detergent. I use Tide, Clorox 2 and Downy with great results. I tried a cheaper brand (Purex) and it did not clean my clothes at all.

5. Don't forget to switch the water over to cold when you use the fabric softener. Since the machine hooks up to the sink, whatever temperature you start off with is the one you'll finish with if you don't adjust it during the wash. I usually wash in warm and then switch it to cold as soon as the fill is finished (the first water fill on then normal or quick cycle) so I don't forget.

6. If washing towels, don't wash more than two bath towels at a time. The machine just isn't equipped to do heavy loads, like towels. If you want to wash sheets - queen or king sized, only wash one at a time. The machine isn't big enough and it will knot up like crazy. If your sheets are particularly heavy the machine with either shut off or unbalance. I wash queen 800 thread count cotton sheets with no major problems other than the knotting up issue.

7. Get yourself a really good lint brush. You'll need both the tape and the brush kind. This machine does nothing to remove lint. I have long hair and I also have two long haired cats, so everything comes out clean but with cat fur and my hair all over it. Anything very linty will also require some extra maintenance after washing.

8. I did not get the dryer that matches this machine because it has to be vented outside. I got two large folding drying racks from Ikea for under $25 each. You can set them up side by side to drape a queen or king sized sheet over it to dry and they hold a ton of clothes. In a pinch when I need something dried quickly, I'll set up a fan to blow it dry.

Overall this is a great little machine, despite the minor issues above. It has more than paid for itself over the last six months just in the amount of laundry I do. I probably do about 4 or 5 loads per week for one person. The machine is small enough to keep in my tiny kitchen and with the wheels, it's easy to roll it out of the way when necessary. I'm hoping this last for the next two years when I am ready to purchase a home (with laundry in unit!!). So far I cannot complain too much about this machine. Yes, it has issues but it certainly beats spending money on laundry and hauling dirty clothes up and down the halls.

I'm sure the remarkably bad experience I had with my former dishwasher, a Whirlpool Gold® GU2800XTV, has a direct bearing on my enthusiasm for this Bosch dishwasher. That Whirlpool dishwasher was without a doubt the most troublesome appliance I have ever owned over a span of 60+ years. Fortunately I purchased the extended warranty but even the Whirlpool warranty company eventually wrote the GU2800XTV off as a lemon.

This Bosch, on the other hand, has done everything asked of it in a marvelously competent manner. I'll agree that dish placement is different from other dishwashers I've owned and I'm still going through a learning curve but I've managed to successfully load everything to this point with increasing speed as I learn how to organize the dishes we normally use.

Page 7 of the owner's manual offers four different loading patterns for the top rack and four more for the bottom rack. With that many suggested alternatives and a little creativity one should be able to develop one or more loading patterns that will work for your family.

With my Whirlpool I had a constant problem with wet dishes at the completion of the cycle even when their "Hi-temp" wash setting and "Heated Dry" were both engaged. In order to test the Bosch I used the "Auto Wash" setting but did not engage the "Sanitize" option. I have been delighted to discover the dishes, including plastic cups, come out dry and need no additional drying before replacing in the cabinets. We no longer need the dish towel when unloading the dishwasher which was an absolute necessity with the Whirlpool.

Although we have no way of objectively measuring it, my wife and I both agree the dishes are coming out with a shiny sparkle they most assuredly did not have with the Whirlpool.

I had the dishwasher installed by a professional and the installation went smoothly and very fast. There have been no problems with the dishwasher and it has consistently done an outstanding job. While it is very quiet, the Whirlpool was, perhaps, a little quieter but that is the only good thing I can say about the Whirlpool; it washed poorly and dried poorly very quietly.

I tried to follow all of the setup instructions that came on the extra sheet "Getting started with your new dishwasher." This is a loose sheet but has some important information on it, be careful it doesn't get thrown away during unpacking.

On page 9 of the manual it is pointed out the Bosch uses less water than most and therefore needs less detergent. The detergent cup is measured and has lines at 1, 2, or 3 tablespoons. On page 10 we are told that 1 tablespoon will clean most loads and that is what we have done with excellent results.

Since we do not wash our silverware in the dishwasher we have removed the basket. On page 8 of the manual detailed instructions are given on placement otions for the basket and the loading pattern for silverware placement in the basket.

The top rack is adjustable and can be moved up or down to accommodate larger items in the top or bottom rack. The top rack can also be completely removed. Some of the other Bosch models come with a sprinkler head for washing really tall items. This arrangement permits complete removal of the top rack and the insertion of a plastic sprinkler head that enables the user to wash really tall items that would sit on the bottom rack. The sprinkler head does, however, fit on this machine as well and can be ordered as part number 5600-037-096 (PP-TV20).

After three years of failure in trying to get the Whirlpool to do the job it was supposed to do you can imagine my joy in finding a machine that does the job vastly better right out of the box. I recommend this machine highly. For the record, a noted consumer reporting agency also classified this model as a "Best Buy."
