I see a lot of positive reviews, so i hope this more moderate one makes it into the review page. The hood looks nice. But here are some things to provoke second thoughts. The rated capacity is 500 cfm. In our town, a hood over 400 cfm requires make-up air to avoid sucking furnace flue gases into the HVAC system. There is no way to control a motorized damper to let in outside air. (in our previous home, our 600 cfm Broan controlled such a damper so that when the hood was on, there was air sucked in from the outside. Keep a window slightly open when Cosmo is on) . The lights are an annoying blue-white. Can be replaced by warm-white corn-row led bulbs. At full blast, the suction is only modest. Watching the rise of smoke - not all gets sucked into the hood. It's very noisy. If mounting to the cabinet above accessing the bolts at the rear is difficult. Make sure the cabinet is properly mounted and can support the weight of the hood (58 lbs). Finally, if you are cooking, and standing next to the stove, the remote adds no benefit. Not clear to me why you would walk away from the stove while the pan is hot enough to make smoke. One last thought - the factory- installed 1 watt bulbs cast a blue light that is weak and very unappealing color. So, you can easily replace them with bipin 7 watt led bulbs such as
Amazon Basics 50W Equivalent, 3000K White, Dimmable, 10,000 Hour Lifetime, MR16 (GU10). These 7watt bulbs or similar are much brighter, and a pleasing color. The manual for the hood says these should be replaced from the inside - by removing the grease filters. Almost impossible. But can be removed from beneath. Turn counter clockwise to drop them. A small flashlight placed behind the grease filter illuminates the lamp socket to make it easier to line up the pins of the replacement. I used a piece of sticky tape to grab the front of the old bulb so I could turn it - there is nothing to grab onto.

Update:
Ok, so I have had this machine for a couple weeks now, and I love it! It has been awesome to have an extra dryer for a change!

Some quick background, our house has a normal laundry set, one washer and one dryer, on the main floor, and in the basement I have a Panda washer. I primarily use this washer when I have delicates or small loads that I need done. (Small note, you can buy a small washing machine cheaper then getting the mini one that goes under a full size washer.) I'll also use it if a load is specific, ie: needs to soak, covered with mud, color treatment, ect...

Anyways, due to having this, I always have extra laundry that needs to dry. I was using a drying rack but it only had so much space, and being in the basement, was often time consuming due to being fairly cool.
Needless to say this dryer has helped substantially! It is also currently winter so it is nice to have a little extra heat to go inside the house. The exhaust from the machine is pretty well filtered, with little lint. It is also not super warm like a normal dryer, so don't worry. To be sure, as I am currently venting it inside, i made a filter out of some cheap furnace filters, to help safe guard against any stray lint.

Overall the dryer works very well, and I have had some time to test each mode. The best one for daily use for me is Auto. Everything except the manual settings use the sensor to help dry. I feel like when using the normal, heavy duty, delicates, or towels, that it does not read the sensor long anough. This often results in things still being fairly damp. This is not an issue though honestly, when I use Auto, it works perfectly! Drying clothes well, and not over drying them. Manual mode works well too, just set your heat and time. If I use manual mode I just keep it on hot, unless im just refreshing some clothes or have something truly delicate, then I'll use warm. Being 120 volt, it does not get as hot as a normal dryer. However, I look at this as an added feature, as drying times do not seem to be bad. They might be a little longer, but not by much. But due to being a lower temp, your clothes should last longer as they are subjected to much less high heat, this should also produce less lint.

Overall, I highly recommend this to anyone looking to upgrade from a drying rack! It has been great so far! The only thing I would to say if you buy this, is double check your size requirements! This unit is bigger than I expected, but is not an issue for me. If you have very specific size requirements, I would potentially get the small version of the same unit.

Our 15 year old LG DLG5966W gas dryer had been making squeaking noises on start up, sometimes continuing to squeak while running so it was time to either call the repair man or give it go myself. A quick search and I found this kit that had everything needed, along with a great YouTube video by PartSelect with a guy named Steve that walked through most of what I needed to do. Tools I used for this job were:

1. A decent cordless drill https://amzn.to/3ZdVBvn
2. A set of metric box end ratcheting wrenches https://amzn.to/3IMt8r8
3. A magnetic mat to hold/sort screws as removed https://amzn.to/3IN37b2
4. A vacuum or hand vac https://amzn.to/3lWjHfN

Once I got the dryer apart (labeling and placing on the magnetic mat as I go) and lifted out the drum, I could see that the right rear roller wheel was not turning at all! It had a flat spot on it from the drum rubbing against it. What Steve didn't go into in the video I mention is how to remove and replace the complete roller wheel assemblies, which requires an extra couple steps and is why you'll need the wrenches I mentioned above. The front roller wheels are easy to access and replace, however the back roller wheels will need you to remove the inside back panel by taking out (6?) screws holding it in place from the back of the dryer. Once those screws were out, I just needed to gently tilt forward and lift out the shroud, being careful to decouple from the heat pipe, in order to remove and replace the back roller wheel assemblies with a couple of the wrenches.

While you're in there, vacuum out the lint - I had to empty my hand vac a couple times due to how much there was. I also removed a bunch of hair that had wrapped around the motor shaft.

The kit came with a new belt, belt tensioner, and spring. My belt was frayed in a couple places, so really glad the kit had a new one in it.

I cleaned all the dust and lint off of the drum, and put it all back together. I am happy to report, the dryer is running like new again! It's so quiet that we have to go in the laundry room to see if it's still running.

Hoping these parts last another 15 years. 90 minutes and about $30 - it was well worth it! Anybody with even a little mechanical ability can do this job. Go for it!

Update after 1 month:

Belt started slipping after a week or so, could have been installer error as the belt was out of the motor pulley and was just on the smooth shaft. Belt was frayed and grooves were smooth on much of it. I'll take the blame on that one, but put on an "OEM" replacement belt, ensuring to have it properly seated in the pulley before closing things up. I also notices a little wear on the front wheels, some fragments coming off the sides. Time will tell if that will turn in to a long term problem.

Another tip - wear gloves when disassembling - both times in taking off the bulkhead, I cut my hand on a sharp edge. Not a problem assembling, just in trying to wrestle the bulkhead out of its retaining clips and lift it out is when I got nicked.

After that, all the grounds were caught by the mesh filter.  However, in using the steel mesh with the paper filter, I noticed some very fine sludge on the paper that had passed through the mesh. After plugging my model number into a google search it led me here to Amazon. I did a quick search for the part number and Amazon was the cheapest by a narrow margin.

Install is tedious and requires removing the dishwasher from the cabinet it's housed in, removing a side plate, removing the control board, and removing a protective plate at the bottom of the dishwasher.

Caution: Make sure you turn off the water supply beforehand or you're gonna have a bad time. Flip the breaker as well because you'll need to remove the electrical supply to the washer before removing the protective bottom plate. All-in-all it was a 30 minute job that saved me from buying a new dishwasher.

I had a rather loud "clunk" sound every time I opened the right side (fridge) door for some time.  I bought this to fix it.  Ok, so like many items the You Tube video on this I found was very helpful.  That said, this was a fair bit harder tearout and installation that I expected and needed several items not everyone will have laying around.  As the video(s) show, you need to block the underside of the fridge door.  I thought I could use a 1 ton floor jack but its lowest point was too high.  Like the video, I had some 2x4 and 1x4 pieces lying around so I stacked a few of those until I got a good fit.  This is likely the most crucial aspect.  Next you will need a small ratchet with a small extension and an 8mm socket for best results.  The lower "L" hinge is easy; 2 8mm bolts loosened and then remove.  My plastic/rubber "cam" was not damaged but only loose.  Still, I decided to change it all out.  Remove the bolt and install new cam on metal hinge.  Set parts aisde.  Here is where things get fun.  The two 8mm bolts on the upper hinge are from the bottom up, meaning you CANNOT SEE THEM as you are trying to work on them.  I have a small telescoping mirror that you can likely find on Amazon.  This little mirror, a flashlight, and a helper, were critical to getting the upper hinge removed and re-installed.  Nothing fancy, just loosen the bolts (with very small heads and which are prone to slip).  Right one was for the cam, left one for the outer plate that holds it in.  Once out you will see that the metal "pin" on hinge fits into the plastic "boot" that is part of the cam (shaped kind of like an "L") that goes on top.  There is also a mesh shim that seems to go between those pieces (but the instructions seemed pretty poor on this point.  Reinstall the black plate (left) bolt first and then the L boot cam as the bolts are short and don't want to get a "bite" in the threads very easily.  Total operation took about 20 minutes and now the door works fine.  Note that the package was broken open on delivery so some of my hardware was missing.  I just re-used the old stuff.  In short, vs. factory price ($8 for just the boot) this kit is a bargain and the operation/hassle worth the effort if your fridge is like mine.  Note also that my exact model (Maytag MSD2500VES00) was not listed on the chart but the parts worked fine.

Like many others, I found that this scoop held too much coffee and actually over-filled the pods. I couldn’t just scoop and dump. I had to scoop, then shake some out. Sometimes still too much, sometimes not enough . . . well, you get the idea. I decided to see if I could modify the scoop so that I would get the perfect amount every time. My solution was to take a small, plastic, screw-on lid from a bottle (I think it was a bottle of steak sauce), invert it and put it in the bottom of the scoop. After a bit of trial and error, trimming the edge of the bottle cap, I got it down to a size that would displace just the right amount of ground coffee. Then I super-glued the cap into the bottom of the scoop and — woo hoo! — a quick and easy scoop, dump, tamp down, and brew. This little modification turned an okay item into one of my favorite kitchen gadgets!

I ordered the Sentern portable ice maker after a lot of consideration and reading many product reviews. Some were cheaper and more in the price range I wanted, however I also wanted one that produced ice that didn't melt quickly and produced ice quickly. This ice maker is fantastic, actually the production is faster than I use (I cut off the unit until I'm ready for more), the ice cubes are just the right size to fit in stacked 2x3 rows of ice for my water tumbler and the ice stays ice and cubes don't melt quickly. LOVE this machine, very happy with all it does. It has an automatic shut off when ice tray is full, shuts off if the water level is low, is very quiet, cubes, although coming out in full sheets or half sheets are very easily broken apart by hand. The only time the sheets are frozen too thick to easily break apart is when the ice tray is full and the sheet in the form can't empty and more ice forms on top. In that case, which is rare for me, I turnoff the machine, let the ice in the form melt a little and soon it falls into the tray. I LOVE this machine! I use only filtered water in it, use it every day, most of the day, use ice for my filtered drinking water (I don't like the taste of treated county water or room temperature water), and put cubes in my ice cooler.

My research showed the round bullet ice melts relatively fast, not so these cubes. I drink from my insulated water tumbler all day; I fill it with cubes and water in the morning, refresh the cubes about once during the day and still have cubes in the tumbler by evening. So far so good with this unit, it is worth the price. I'm very satisfied, no complaints on speed of making ice or having the ice expended in the tray in sheets or half sheets--no problem at all, the cubes are easy to break apart by hand. It's compact, fits easily on the end of my kitchen counter and underneath my top cabinets. Water reservoir is filled from the top, controls are on the front and let you know if the water level is low. Very nice machine.

This one broke about a year later. There is a trick to fixing it if you have the tools and some superglue not perfect but it works.

The trick would be to create a cavity or multiple cavities after the handle breaks at the top. and insert some rods. you can go to home depot or get them on here. They are metal threaded rods but very thin. You make some holes in the plastic on both sides of the break. shove some super glue into the holes and shove the proper-sized threaded rod into them this will give them strength at the point of the break. Then place some super glue at both ends of the break and push them together. The threaded rods 1mm size will likely work the thinner the better but you don't want too thin. A regular wire could also work but scuff up the surface or brade a couple of strands first as this gives the wire adhesion. The threaded rod type will hold in the superglue as the superglue will form around the threads and grip the rods better.

Don't...
buy a Bosch induction cooktop until Bosch explains the conditions that cause the cooktop to automatically shut off at some arbitrary time during use. This applies to the 500-series, 800-series and Flexinduction models. I discovered this can happen while reading manuals during my web research on induction cooktops.

Here are the respective web pages and page numbers advising of this stipulation in each model's "Use and Care" manual:

500-series:
[...]
(page 14)

800-series:
[...]
(page 16)

Flexinduction:
[...]
(page 15)

I called Bosch Customer Support 5 times over a two-week period and each time talked to a different rep including a Support Supervisor on my last call. I asked for an explanation about the specific circumstances under which the cooktop would shut off. I cited several examples of cooking situations where one would not want the cooktop to "just turn off" on its own. On my last 4 conversations with Bosch support reps, I was told they would research the issue and "get back to me with an answer".

Well, they didn't get back to me, and I still don't have an answer. The support people don't know, and further, they told me they don't communicate with Bosch engineering (who certainly would know the answer). How strange is that? But I was copied on an email from a Bosch Senior Support Representative to "an unknown at Bosch". The email contained the following exact wording from one of the manuals:
"Automatic time limitation:
If the element is used for prolonged periods of time without changes in the settings being made, the automatic time limitation function is triggered. The element stops heating. "F8" and the residual heat indicator "H/h" flash alternately in the display. The indicator goes out when any symbol is pressed. The element can now be reset. When the automatic time limitation is activated depends on the selected heat level (from 1 to 10 hours)."

The email also briefly revealed that "a customer" (me) wanted to know the conditions that can cause the cooktop to shut off, but didn't offer any relevant explanations. Whatsoever! I was told by a couple of support reps that the cooktop turns off for "safety reasons" but no other details were offered. Safety reasons? Really? Does that mean the cooktops are nearing a dangerous state? Are these Bosch cooktops the only cooktops ever made that turn off "for safety reasons" Maybe, but if so, I'm not aware of any others.

I hope I am not alone in thinking Bosch needs to inform prospective customers exactly what conditions can trigger these (expensive) cooktops to shut off? Or better yet, just make a cooktop that doesn't arbitrarily turn off.

Bottom line is, buy one of these Bosch cooktops only if you are willing to risk it automatically turning off sometime between "1 and 10 hours". Or, if you'd be content to just stand watch over it to be sure it stays on while you're cooking a corned-beef for 4-5 hours.

Bosch engineers take notice!

We remodeled our kitchen in Feb 2012 and bought over 5K worth of SS appliances (and 5-year warranties) from Brandsmart in Deerfield Beach,Fl including this lovely-looking Whirlpool-Gold stainless-steel French Door Bottom Freezer refrigerator. Just 6 months later the plastic CENTER SUPPORT SNAPPED IN THE FRONT to cause the 2 vegetable/fruit bins it supported to 'fall' and become cockeyed (dropping inward, toward the center next to each other); this made the veggie bins hard to pull out and made the bottom DELI bin impossible to pull out (since the 2 veggie bins above it were now sitting upon the DELI bin below them).

There was no problem with Whirlpool Customer Service to send out a new plastic center support REPLACEMENT part since this was well within the 1-year warranty period from the Manufacturer (and the Brandsmart 5-year warranty period). Installing this part was easy and at first we chocked this up to 'infant mortality' where a somewhat defective piece of plastic had gone bad...(but we were WRONG!)...I say this because just 6 months after installing the REPLACEMENT part from Whirlpool, the same thing happened again...the same plastic center support SNAPPED IN THE FRONT to cause the 2 vegetable/fruit bins it supported to 'fall' and become cockeyed (dropping toward the center, and making the DELI drawer impossible to open).

Examination of the failing part shows a very weak engineering design concept in my opinion...that a 1/8-inch-thick piece of plastic that's about 1-inch wide,front to back could support the contents of not one, but TWO Vegetable/Fruit bins. Everyone knows that apples, oranges, pears, lettuce, lemons, and nearly every kind of fruit or vegetable has some WEIGHT that must be supported, and in this case the weight of a normal amount of veggies and fruits will cause the breaking failure of the plastic center support over time (6-months in my case). I have never owned a refrigerator with such a flimsy support system for the vegetable drawers or had to 'estimate' how many pieces of fruit or vegetables I could safely ADD to the two bins to avoid this CENTER SUPPORT SNAPPING failure due to their weight. So now I have an expensive piece of stainless-steel fridge that looks great on the outside but is very poorly designed inside with respect to the CENTER PLASTIC SUPPORT that really 'CAN'T SUPPORT' much weight in the vegetable/fruit bins at all.

To make matters worse when I called up Brandsmart Warranty services for a new veggie-bins center support the girl I spoke with told me "THIS ISN'T SUPPORTED BY YOUR WARRANTY TERMS AND CONDITIONS"- and that they would only support "ELECTRICAL AND MECHANICAL FAILURES of the fridge". When I questioned why a SNAPPING PIECE OF PLASIC THAT SUPPORTS TWO VEGETABLE/FRUIT BINS didn't fall into the MECHANICAL FAILURE category, she still denied my logic; when I asked to speak with a supervisor a man got on the phone and backed up the poor girl that first answered the phone... so I told the super I'd find a new place to shop the next time, and would never buy another Brandsmart Appliance or Warranty again! I reminded him that when I bought the FIVE-YEAR WARRANTIES for all my new kitchen appliances in January, 2012 the salesman told me they would cover "ANYTHING THAT WENT WRONG" with them...the Warranty Supervisor told me that I was "misinformed" and that I should have read the terms and conditions before purchasing the warranties. I told him that I'd believed their salesman to be an honest guy and there was no mention about 'not replacing broken plastic parts' within the appliances when he sold me the warranties. So much for Brandsmart Warranties!

The good news is that I was able to buy a replacement plastic center support part from a local appliance parts store for under $20 that included a "free replacement of the part for LIFE". I installed the new part and will now hope this replacement part will last more than the 6-month lives of the first two that broke! Honestly WHIRLPOOL, did you ever TEST for the breaking weight of this extremely flimsy plastic center support for your two vegetable/fruit bins before releasing this refrigerator for sale? In my opinion the only thing that will permanently repair this engineering flaw is a center support part manufactured from metal instead of the plastic part supplied. For this reason only I'm giving this refrigerator a '2-star rating' as the rest of it has been working fine so far. (knock on wood!!!)

My four year old Kenmore Elite dishwasher was getting louder and louder. After looking online I read that there was a design flaw in a faulty seal that allowed water to rust one of the motor bearings, and that the bearing would need to be replaced. I purchased the replacement bearing, but procrastinated in installing it. Finally at about five years the motor gave out all together. I watched a YouTube video that showed me that I could remove the motor from the inside, without totally uninstalling the dishwasher. I followed the directions, uninstalling the motor and immediately two things were apparent. First, not only was the bearing disintegrated away to nothing, but the shaft it installed on was also severely rusted and would require a LOT of work before I could get the new bearing on. Secondly I had failed to buy a replacement seal kit, so even if I was able to get the new bearing on the same thing would probably happen again. At this point I decided I was better off to order a whole new motor assembly. I found that there was a new replacement part number for the motor which I ordered at about 5:00PM to be overnighted to me. The following day the motor arrived at 11:30AM, and by 12:10PM I had it re-installed, the dishwasher reassembled, and was running a test load of dishes. I had forgotten how quiet this dishwasher could be. I had to check to make sure that it was running. One thing I noticed is that the probable reason the replacement part number changed is the new motor has a redesigned triple seal as opposed to the original single seal. Hopefully this improvement will lead to more than four more years of continued use. The dishwasher now seems to work as well as the day we bought it.

Just want to add that now almost three years later this motor is still running great and quiet!

My clothes dryer was not drying the clothes properly thus indicating that it broken and need to be fixed. I check and see that the average cost to have an appliance repairman to come out and repair it would be $250. At that price, I decided to fix it myself.

I heard that the most common cause is the valve coil going bad so I check the cost of a valve coil. It ranges from $15-$30. I thought that is not too expensive just to buy a new one and replace it. When I actually talk to a supplier, the cost turns out to be $100 because my dryer is a very old model.

At that price I decided that I better diagnosis first before spending $100. After taking the dryer apart and testing the flame sensor, I notice that the flame sensor did not shows any continuity. The Multimeter shows OL(Open Line), thus showing the there is no current flowing through the flame sensor while connected.

I decide to replace the bad flame sensor first before spending $100 for a valve coil. Ebay had one for $16 and I order it. After sometime, I finally receiving it and replace the flame sensor on my dryer. Now my dryer works perfectly.

I decided to check on Amazon to see if they have this item and they had it for $14.5 and it qualify for prime 2 days free shipping. I could have order it from Amazon and get it in 2 days for free with my Prime Amazon membership, thus would have been able to use my dryer in 2 days instead of having to wait for a long period before receiving the flame sensor from an Ebay vendor, resulting in not being able to use my clothes dryer for quite awhile.

Again I should have check on Amazon before looking elsewhere. But who would have thought that Amazon would have a flame sensor for a clothes dryer.

The liquid water reservoir sits under a plastic basket that holds the newly frozen ice so that as the liquid cools over time, the 'ice-time' drops a bit lower than the time to 'first ice'.

The only problem I see is that the contraption has lousy insulation and that problem, coupled with the big and relatively warm liquid reservoir underneath the ice keeps the ice is a state of permanent slow melting. Futile that is UNLESS you use the ice first---and THAT is obviously the point. For most purposes this will deserve its great reviews. For the price, it is a great deal.

As many others have stated, the fan works well, but the mounting process was less than perfect. I'm an avid DIY'er and this project took longer than it should have. The biggest problem for me was the mounting system. It was not easy to hold the fan in place and mark the screw holes on the fan housing for pilot holes. Not to mention it's terribly uncomfortable sending screws into your brand new fan. I used the appropriate length, included screws, but had the same problem many others had where the screw hit the fan blades on the inside when I turned it on. Mine only did it for a few seconds then stopped. Hopefully it didn't break the fan blades, but I haven't pulled it apart to check yet. Which leads me to my next point. Cleaning this thing every 6 months as recommended is going to be murder. I am going to have to rethink the surrounding duct work because it would be terribly difficult to unhook the two connections and clean this fan. I tried the rigid/flexible 4" duct work with a hose clamp, but the male connections on the fan are a fair amount smaller than the hose and the clamp cut the hose because I had to cinch it down so far. You also need hard pipe within two feet or so because you have to install the pressure switch hose into a hard duct.

All that said, the thing is up and working now. It turned our long dryer run into a working vent again. After I moved our dryer and the duct work was an equivalent of 40+ feet, the output outside at the vent was abysmal. After installing this fan, the dryer vent output was like we only had a 10ft run again. So after making it through the rather complex installation, it works well.

I purchased this washer dryer on Sep29, 2012, so I have been using it for over 1 year now, and feel ready to write a review of it, after using just about all of its functions, and learning about all the pros and cons...

First let's start with the pros:

1. Size was indeed the motivating factor for us to purchase this unit. It is very compact, so much so, that we have it in our pantry. I love the space it now frees up for us.
2. It actually does a half way decent cleaning job. Just based on cleaning alone, I would give it a 4 star, but read on...
3. If it's not spinning, it is pretty quiet. I usually don't know if it is running or not (but it runs all day in our house, everyday)
4. Our electric bill has lowered BUT ONLY IF YOU DON'T USE THE DRYER SETTING!
5. Fairly easy to maintain, as the error codes are easily looked up on the net, and then troubleshooting isn't bad. I have a ton of experience fixing appliances though. You will mostly be emptying the filter, checking water pressure (if you need to turn off the water to your house for something, and release pressure in the lines, this will not work until the lines are repressurized, which takes a few minutes)

Now the negatives, which I think are at about the same level as the pros:
1. This thing, in my house (2 adults, one 2 year old), runs ALL DAY, ALL NIGHT, EVERYDAY. That's right, all day all night everyday like I said. We are not filthy people, but we use rags instead of paper towels, and we cannot keep up with the amount of laundry we produce. The load size is to blame, but we knew that going into the purchase. It's not a deal breaker, but we just had no idea how much laundry we were going to do...
2. Our bills lowered, yes that is true, but we don't use the dryer function. Our bill actually went up when we used the function for whatever reason. I personally don't think the dryer function works worth a crap! We live in an environment where we can just hang our clothes and let them dry in a few hours, pretty much exactly what you're getting with this little unit. If your relative humidity is around 15-30%, you are wasting time and money drying it in this machine. I don't know how this works in Europe, but this does not dry our clothes (most likely because we overload it in an effort to keep on top of our laundry). This is our biggest disappointment with the machine overall. It adds a huge step to our already busy day, which is hanging our rags and clothes after a wash. I am used to it now, but at first we were very disappointed. I just hang the clothes whenever I have a free moment now (which is rare with a 2 year old).
3. If you use the dryer function, your electricity bill will not go down, and might go up. Depending on how much laundry you do, you will be using this drying function all the time since it takes hours to get your clothes to the point where they are still damp. If you live alone in an apartment or something, this may be exactly what you are looking for, but for even 2 people, it is just not enough for drying. Washing function is fine, but the loads are too small, which leads us to have this thing running all the time. This translates to a HIGHER utility bill when running all the time with the drying function.
4. The spin cycle: Jeez, this thing gets going at like 1000 rpm's if I remember correctly. It shakes our whole house! It is scary enough that my two year old runs away from it when it gets going. Luckily, that only lasts for a few minutes, but leveling the unit only helps for a few days before it starts shaking again. It's not enough for me to worry about it, but man, this thing can wake up the neighbors. I actually don't mind it, because I know my clothes will dry quicker this way, but my wife wants me to include this in my review.
5. Frequent emptying of the filter. Yea, this thing needs maintenance. I have had to empty the filter 3 times in one year so far, but also, have had to clean the inside free of detergent, as it just builds up in the loading tray for some reason. I think a slightly more powerful jet spray can clear out this area better, but some vinegar in the tray cleans it out fairly well. Its a huge pain when your laundry is done, and you open the tray to see maybe 25% of the detergent made it to the clothes (maybe that is better for my body, who knows). It happens somewhat frequently, and we stopped buying detergent and made our own, which works better (much more finely ground).

Overall, I would not recommend this to a family of any size. Really, think about what you are getting yourself into here. Do you want to do laundry all the time? If I knew this beforehand, I probably would not have purchased this unit. But I am trying to be as fair as possible in my review, and for a young couple, or a single individual, this would be a dream machine, as long as you are willing to maintain it (clean out the machine, and empty the filter), which can get tricky sometimes, as the drain is at the very bottom of the unit, making it very difficult to not spill water everywhere when emptying it (who designed this thing?)). It has saved us money in utility bills ONLY IF YOU DO NOT USE THE DRYING FUNCTION. That's important, because there are all these reviews touting this thing's energy efficiency... Well you could get similar results using just a regular washing machine without a dryer. The estimated cost of ownership sticker on the top of the machine indicates that we will spend $15/year to operate it... WHAT??? How in the world is this number calculated? We spend that much in water costs alone PER MONTH to keep it running. Obviously the dryer function is not included in this cost, but our water is cheap where we live, and I definitely uses more than $15 per year! I have absolutely no idea where that number comes from. I am also aware that it is based on usage and utility costs, but even with the most conservative estimates for these variables, there is absolutely no way that a small family will be spending any less on this unit, than they would with another, due mostly to the low washing capacity, necessitating the need to do laundry all the time.

So in summation, I have learned to accept this thing after 1 year, and give it 3 stars, or 2.5 stars. I am used to hanging laundry, and it never really takes more than 5 minutes, but this thing runs constantly in the background of my house. I personally don't think it is worth $800, and you could buy a cheapo washing machine from a big box store for 1/4 of the price, and get the same exact results in both washing ability and utility costs, but a much more dramatic increase in the size of your loads, leading to less laundry going on. My wife agrees with everything I've just said! Good luck, and don't let my review dissuade you from your purchase, just know what you're getting into!

This product has really upped my Aeropress game! I've tried many "espresso-like" coffeemakers and own several, including a Nespresso and a Moka Pot, and this little gizmo makes the best version so far (wish I could afford that Breville espresso-maker with the built-in grinder, but alas, it's about 30 times the price). For a LOT less money, the expresso that is pushed out through the little hole is deeply rich, has a little crema, and the amount can be varied with changes in bean/water ratio much easier than capsules.
The key is finding the correct grind - too fine and nothing will come out without a LOT of force; too coarse and it's just too easy to push down, not giving the right amount of pressure to create that rich dark elixir. On my Baratza Encore, it's between 7-10 depending on the beans (without the Prismo I grind at 14 for a perfect cup of strong coffee).
One caveat, which they mention in the literature about it - though it is often depicted over a glass mug, make sure that the glass is thick enough to withstand the amount of force needed to push the plunger down; not borosilicate glass, most likely. I haven't tried with my borosilicate mug, but I can imagine it shattering all over the kitchen.
Also, for those using the Aeropress in the "upside-down" position (which I do), you would NOT do that with the Prismo attached; the liquid is trapped until you put the plunger into it and so can be set up right on the counter and filled with water, thus allowing you to heat your cup or mug with hot water to prep it.

The two ovens are both usable. The wide coursing of the heating elements produced uniform heat in both, even when placing a baking sheet on the bottom rack position. But for this price, you darn well should get a few extra inches of heating rod. That said, the fancy extra features have turned me off. 1) The control buttons. There is an array of 9 and an array of four buttons for the upper oven on the left, and a symmetrical array of 4 and 9 for the lower oven on the right. The arrays of 4 are identical; that's good. But in the larger 9-button arrays, only the warm button is in the same place on the two arrays. The buttons you will typically use (bake button, oven light button, broil, etc) are in different places on the two arrays, and so even once you are familiar with the oven, you will be hunting and pecking. 2) The manual. It reads like a computer software manual ("for the pizza feature, select the pizza button"). It does not explain why you would want to select a "pizza feature" instead of just using "bake". Is it hotter? - No, the max temp is still 550F. What's the difference between the separate settings for fresh pizza or frozen? The manual says that "1" is for fresh, "2" is for frozen. Well, that certainly explains it to full intellectual satisfaction. Moving on to the slow cook settings; neither the manual nor the oven display reveals the temperature, but you are asked to select among four types of food and two heat levels. I used a calibrated oven and a long temperature probe to measure the temperature of 4 quarts of water, heating in a 5.5 qt ceramic slow-cook covered pot. When set to "stew" and "Lo" and "7 hr cook time", the water reached 202F by 2 hrs, full simmer of 207F at 2.5 hr, 203 F at 3 hrs, and then dropped slowly, dropping below 200F by 3.5 hr. I don't know of a cook , hoping to retain nutrients and proper food texture by a low temp slow-cooking method, who would choose to nearly boil the stew for over an hour. Using 2 quarts caused hours of frank boiling. When I tried the "beef" and "Hi" setting on 4 quarts of water, it reached 209F by 2 hr and dropped to 200F only by 3.5 hr. Any beef would be cardboard texture by then. Moving on to the "roast convection", this has nothing to do with roasting (which involves an oiled food in a uniform very hot oven). Instead, the top heating element comes on, which if not used very briefly, will char the topmost part of your otherwise evenly browned food. It is best used when one wants a broiled effect, but desires to keep the door closed. As long as GE won't engage the consumer by providing a mechanistic explanation of its dozens of settings, I would plan on using the ovens only in broil, bake, and convection modes.

I'm pretty happy with this. It'll go down to 36 degrees which is all you need for some nice cold drinks - for the sake of comparison a full-size fridge only goes down to 34 and most people keep them at around 37. I haven't tested out the stated capacity, but it certainly holds more than I've put in there too date. It's fairly quiet - you actually don't hear the compressor at all. It's the fan that makes a little white noise - but it's nothing that will bother you in a quiet room. The shelves can be adjusted or removed to suit your needs, and they have a stop. So you can pull them out to get at stuff in the back, without accidentally going too far. I also have a NewAir wine fridge that's been going strong for 5 years, so they are reliable. My complaints are few: The LED lighting is not great - it sits at the top and the bottom is pretty dark. A white interior instead of black would have helped with that. Also, the door will not close by itself. It has been left open a crack many times because people are used to regular refrigerators where the heavy door tends to close and seal itself when pushed. This won't. Some competing models have open door alarms. That would have been appreciated here.

Is this as good as a Marvel or a Summit? No. Those are American made units with commercial grade build quality that cost well over $1k. This is made in China, clearly intended for causal home use, and the components are decent, but not the highest quality out there. It's good for what you pay - but you get what you pay for.

Pros: Front exhaust, huge capacity, quiet, adjustable and removable shelves, lock for the door, door is reversible.
Cons: Wire shelves are flimsy, the lighting is inadequate so the black interior is too dark, no door open alarm.
Conclusion: Highly recommended.

So after not having a dish washer for almost 2 years I finally decided to pull the trigger and buy this dishwasher. It had good reviews and was within my price range.
THE INSTALL:
The way my kitchen is set up is not conventional so I could not use the provided hoses. I'm sure they work fine if you need to use them. So in my townhouse the washing machine hook ups are next to the kitchen sink but the counter space for the dishwasher is too far for the hoses to hook up to the sink. So after spending an hour at the hardware store searching for connectors that fit the other end of the drain line I found a solution. I used a 1/2 inch od compression to 5/8 fitting then put a clear silicone hose on the end with a clamp for the drain line. For the inlet it takes standard 3/4 washing machine hoses so I bought braided lines and a t fitting in order to hook up both the washing machine and dishwasher to the cold water connection. Side note: The provided instructions mislabeled the inlet and drain lines. The bigger line is your inlet and the smaller is the outlet. Anyways after all of that I was able to finally do a load of dishes.

LOADING AND OPERATION :
Loading is straight forward the instructions give you a basic guide on how to place the dishes. I didn't have alot so it was pretty easy. The operation is pretty simple. You hit a button and select the mode. I selected normal wash. The machine is not super loud and gets the dishes clean. It is perfect for two people as long as you pre rinse your dishes.

Now for the negative.... there is a substantial dent on the corner from shipping despite the ample packaging. I was tempted to ship it back but honestly I needed a diswasher that works and weighed the cons of trying to ship it back.

I will update the review after I have had a chance to use it more.

This is a really basic stove, which is what I like. I actually had a nearly identical model in white, but it was from the year 2000 and really in bad shape. Our house has the old-school 32" cutout, so this was my only option (until we remodel in the future) besided the ceramic/glass top one. Installation was ridiculously easy, just lift the old one out, drop this one in, connect the wires. There are wire spring hold downs included to keep it snug.
The burners are standard for this type of stove. The small ones are 1250 watts, the big ones are 2100. I think they perform just fine; I'm not in cooking race, and I don't pay attention to any extra time it takes (extra 30 seconds or whatever) to boil water or heat a pan. Now if you need more heat, the common replacement elements available at most home improvement stores are 1500 watts and 2600 watts.
Quality is on par with an inexpensive simple stove. The knobs are plastic, but thick and easy to grasp. They turn smoothly and have a nice 'snap' when they are rotated to the Off position. Heat control is good, I went through about 20 steps of the knob and every position gave me slightly more heat, so I'm not sure what the complaints are about. One minor gripe is that the Off position is at 9 o'clock, not 12 o'clock like you find on most stoves. But you get used to it.
The top is real stainless steel, not painted, not coated. Other reviewers who said it was just a "stainless steel finish" are just wrong, or blind. The drip pans are the typical chrome plated steel, and of course they will eventually rust, that's why they are removable. The markings on the control panel are simply silk screened, and if you scrub them they will come off. You can scour the top if needed, but of course it will scratch.
I'm not sure what all the "thin metal" complaints are about. This is a low-end stove, and of course it's going to be sheet metal. When mounted properly, it does not sag. I've put 4 normal sized pots of food on the burners, and there is no significant bending. You can get out your micrometer and measure the deflection, but it's not much; anything will bend with weight applied. The metal on this stove is the same thickness as the one it replaced with a manufacture date of 2000.
The burners all sit flat, as do the drip pans. The top itself is flat. Again, I'm not sure what people are doing, but the stove itself is fine. And of course you have to know how to install the burners, seat them all the way, or they will stick up. And you have to know how to adjust the sockets so the burners sit flat.
In short, it's a good low end stove, very functional, and about the only choice for this oddball size cutout.

I've been using this washer for about two months now and it's still going strong, the manual is VERY inadequate in explaining how to use the washer, and there's a few extra things you should know:

HOW TO USE
1. Make sure the middle switch is set to STANDARD or SOFT before adding water via the hose
2. Attach the hose and add med-hot water and detergent (about half what you'd usually use)
3. Add dirty clothes, you can do about half of a normal load (or about 6-8 pairs of jeans) make sure you don't overfill.
4. Wash with detergent for about 10-15 mins, then switch the middle switch to DRAIN the detergent water.
5. Switch back to STANDARD and refill with regular water
6. Wash 5-10 minutes, and then switch back to DRAIN.
7. The spinner can only handle 2-3 pieces of clothing OR one pair of jeans at a time, but only needs about 2-3 minutes of spinning to get most of the water out. DO NOT OVERLOAD THE SPINNER or it will make bad noises

THINGS TO KNOW:

- The hose will NOT work with a regular W/D hookup, and I highly recommend only using warm/mildly hot water otherwise the hose will crack if the water is too hot
- It gets things just as clean as a regular washer, however I've found a lot of my clothes have gotten stretched out and won't shrink back to size because there's no heating element to the spinner.
- Make sure the washer is on a FLAT surface, otherwise the spinner will make an awful clunking noise.

I think that's about it, overall worth the price, I've included a picture of our setup. We're lucky enough to have one sink faucet that the hose fits in perfectly, and then we use the large clear bin to drain the water and dump into the sink.

I like the concept of this item. I bought it to use to clean dog towels, blankets, and smaller beds that I didn't want to put in my washing machine either due to hair on them or they occasionally get peed on or thrown up on. I use it out in the yard so all the hair and dirt can just go in the grass or in the bathtub with some panty hose over the spout to keep dog hair from going down the drain. I've found it useful as a 'pre-wash' to get these items decent enough to put in my washing machine, but not as a sole washing device. Issues I found are listed below:

1) It's a lot smaller than I thought it would be. I can fit one small dog bed or a couple of average sized towels. If using for clothes I could probably fit a couple shirts or a pair of jeans, but not much more.
2) It really needs a lid. There's no way to use this without splashing water all over yourself and the floor. I definitely would NOT recommend using it with bleach. A solid lid across the top would have made this a much better item. I had to put my rain boots on because even pumping it up and down gently I still got water splashing over the edge onto my shoes. If I put in less water, it didn't fill the little clothes basket to the top so the top wasn't getting cleaned.
3) The plug on the bottom needs a quick open/close button or some other type of valve. You open and close it multiple times during the wash cycle and that means bending over and twisting it quite a bit. It also would be nice if the cap was attached with a string or something. I had trouble finding a place to sit it while the tub was draining (it takes a little while to drain) and was worried I'd lose it.
4) The end stage where you put the items in the bottom of the main tub and squish the water out with the smaller tub doesn't work that well due to the holes in the smaller tub - the excess water just goes up into the small tub and then falls back on the items being washed when you raise the small tub. I ended up hanging items over the fence for a few hours until they drip dried enough to bring into the house.
5) It didn't get my dog items very clean. It did get off most of the hair and larger debris but even with extra soak time and adding a second pumping up and down wash cycle I could see still stains and surface dirt (although much reduced). It did get it to a point where I was okay with putting it my regular washing machine but I wouldn't use it as a sole washing cycle. It probably works fine for regular clothes to just remove odors and stuff, but not for soiled items.
6) I had to do 2 or 3 rinse cycles to really get all the soap out.

I will continue to use this because I really don't want dirty dog items directly in my washing machine, and it's much better than putting those items in the utility sink or just hosing them off, but it isn't quite the miracle device I was hoping for.

We have had the PHS930SLSS GE Profile induction range about 6 months, and are generally very pleased with it. We finally took the plunge into induction cooking, and don't regret it a bit--much happier with it than with the glass top range it replaced.

Of course, you need induction-ready pans, but one thing we didn't realize is that all induction-ready pans are not alike! We noticed that some pans-usually lighter ones--heated up a lot faster than others, so I did a little experiment and found that to boil 16 oz of water took between 1.5 and 4.5 minutes. The fastest times were pricey, quality stainless-clad pans and the slowest were light, inexpensive pans from that Swedish household goods superstore. They work, but just are not as efficient or responsive. I'm assuming that it has to do with the amount of iron or steel in the bottom of the pan.

Here are the Pros for this range:
--Easy to clean top. Because it doesn't get nearly as hot as a radiant glass-top range, all that scraping and scrubbing is gone! Ten times easier to clean than any other range we've owned.
--Stylish, modern design. It's a beautiful appliance.
--Interface of the control panel is excellent. Very intuitive and quick and easy to set.
--Good convection oven. The temperature differential (called "Auto Conversion" in the manual) between convection (usually 25° lower than non-convection) can be adjusted or eliminated. I turned off the Auto Conversion and the baking times are more realistic. Baking is even, and preheating is not terribly fast but not a problem either.
--The Warming Zone, the middle back "burner," works well. It is thermal, not induction.
--Proofing feature of the oven is handy for bread making.
--The oven probe works well on cooking meats and is easy to set up.
--Visibility into the oven is good.
--Range has internet connectivity, but we do not see a need to turn the oven on or off and set the temperature remotely. A solution looking for a problem. Also, GE asks for a lot of personal information to use the app.

Cons:
--The beeps of the timer and oven preheat are way too soft. Even set at the loudest setting, they can be inaudible.
--The broiler requires that the oven door be closed. Many cooks like to have the door open a bit to broil.
--The glass control panel gets messy because of splatter, and must be turned off in order to wipe it clean...otherwise, the cleaning cloth activates the various controls. Not a big issue, but an inconvenience.
--The oven light stays on forever. I much prefer a time-out on the light after an adjustable time so you don't find the light on the next morning.
--The "soft close" drawer under the oven required some adjustment when we got the range, and it only works when the drawer is within an inch of closing. Just as easy to close it all the way yourself.
--Very few accessories are available. GE only offers broiler pans and more wire oven racks. I would love to see optional deluxe oven racks that have drawer-slide mechanisms which pull all the way out without tilting and maybe spilling oven contents. Many higher-end ranges have these, and I would like GE to offer these as an optional accessory.
--There is a slight hotspot in the middle of each induction burner. This may be the case with all induction ranges, but the evenness of the cooking area could be better. This is mitigated by a quality pan which evens out the heat across the surface of the pan.
--No printed manual. Come on, GE...this kind of money for an appliance and no printed manual?

Even with these cons, it's the best range we've ever owned.

I bought this motor to replace the one in my dryer that died. Well, I’m pretty sure that the motor itself is still fine (as I kept it) but it was really the motor’s centrifugal switch that had died on me, and try as I might, I couldn’t find just a replacement switch. I’m guessing that either a surge or lightning (which would still technically qualify as a surge) ran in on it and completely arc welded the dead switch. The physical motor swap was quite easy, but when it came time to connect the wiring, everything was completely different. To make matters even worse, there was nothing else in the box I received besides the motor (and switch attached to it obviously). I had to do a lot of digging and finally discovered that several other buyers had posted the information I needed to rewire the switch into my dryer. The new switch has a few male spade connectors that are 1/8” as opposed to the typical 1/4” ones so I had to buy a bag of the 1/8” female spades and wait for them to be delivered before I could finish the installation. I saw where a few of them were supposed to be included with the motor, but I’m guessing that they were attached to the instruction sheet that wasn’t in the box. If you are replacing the motor yourself, take the time to ensure that you are connecting the right wire to the right terminal. The terminal numbers are molded in the plastic switch housing and are therefore the same color and somewhat hard to read, and that is made even harder to read because when the motor is installed in the dryer, they are facing the back of the dark dryer interior. Also, there are some terminal numbers that do not have a corresponding terminal connection, just an empty space. The numbering method of the terminals are not sequential either as #1 and #2 are the first and last posts on the switch with all the other numbers in between them. Connecting  a wire to the wrong terminal is fairly easy to do judging by the questions asked in the Q&A section and I myself had also mistakenly connected one of them incorrectly. Thankfully however installing a new dryer motor isn’t a frequent occurrence and all in all, I believe that this motor should last a good while.

At some point I think Vornado changed the manufacturer or material for the wicks and they stopped working as they should.  They would not wick water at all or for only a short time.  Most of the issues with this type humidifier can be traced to the water quality.  I use water which goes thru a softener, than an filter/RO unit to remove impurities.  This is about the best water quality you can get in your home.  With these wicks I found them to be slightly oversized 1" wider, compared to the originals.  At first I thought this to be a problem but than realized the opening for air to come thru the wicks is trapezoidal in size, wider at the top by 1" than the bottom. and these wicks did a better job of filing that space.  If you don't have all the air going thru the wick it really is not efficient and produces less humidified air.  These wicks work much better than all the others I have tried.  I also clean the wicks every three weeks and interior surfaces with a bleach/water solution to cut down the bacteria growth.  About 1/2 cup bleach in a gallon of water in a small 12"x10"x 4" plastic pan.  Soak for an hour and rinse until the smell of bleach is minimal.  I find the water from the wicks can be squeezed out with out damaging the wicks as other reviewers seem to have an issue with.  I also use the same bleach/water mixture to clean the humidifier pan and the water jugs.  This process with these wicks has given me better results with this humidifier.

I used this to replace a bad switch in an electric range in an apartment.  If you need to know how to replace look on YouTube.  With electric coil type ranges when the surface burner stops heating it is either the breaker (electricity to range), the heating coil (most common), the connector, or the infinite switch.  I had one tenant who placed very heavy cast iron pots on the burners and that would push the coils down until the connector broke.  Then the coil and the infinite switch would go.  Moral to the story, use pots that are appropriate for your cook top.  If the infinite switch / connector / coil burn out several times in short order, that is a good indication that something is destroying them and it is not the components in and of them selves failing.  5 stars for functionality (minus 1 star as I always think I am gouged on price for appliance parts).

This oven is just bad, and horrible customer support makes the experience of owning it even worse. It was the most expensive appliance I purchased when I redid my kitchen two years ago. Most expensive by a fair penny. I expected to enjoy its high end features, despite not using the oven more than a few times per month.

After the 3rd time I used the meat probe (just over a year after buying the oven), the plastic insulation split where it attaches to the probe, completely exposing the wires inside. As an electrical engineer, I have always taken care not to flex wires in ways that strain them, and this probe was no exception. It was just poorly made with no strain relief, and I suspect that material and dimensions are under-designed for their function. After a painfully long process of reaching the right person and explaining that a premium brand like Electrolux can't possibly expect a probe to fail after 3 uses, the representative finally agreed to provide a replacement rather than charging me the ridiculous amount that I have since blocked from my memory. However, they would not just ship me the probe. They insisted on having a service technician come out to inspect the broken probe and give me a replacement. I offered to send them the defective probe for them to inspect before sending the replacement, but they declined. Hence, I was forced to miss a morning of work and Electrolux was forced to pay a third party service provider to visit my home. Poor economics on both sides of the equation.

Then, yesterday, I was cleaning the oven. It's now a bit over 2 years old, and I was running the self-clean for the 2nd time ever. About 1.5 hours into the cycle, I heard a big bang. The middle pane of glass in the oven door had shattered. When I called Electrolux, the representative explained that the glass exploded because the temperature got too hot for the glass. I explained that, since Electrolux designed the self-cleaning process (and doesn't enable users to set self-clean temperatures) and since Electrolux specifies the glass used in the oven door, the problem she described sounds like a design flaw on the part of Electrolux. The outcome of a lengthy call (with a little discussion interspersed with longer times on hold), Electrolux agreed to give me the $258 piece of replacement glass at no cost, but they will not provide a new door and they will not cover the cost of the service call to have a technician disassemble the door to replace the glass.

I have gone back and done some searches on shattering glass in Electrolux ovens. This is not an uncommon phenomenon. Given the marginal increase in cost to use a more robust piece of glass inside the door, it is unconsionable that Electrolux has chosen to let even a small % of it's customers be exposed to this problem. I was cutting up pineapple with a very sharp knife when the big 'bang' occurred. I jumped, and easily could have cut myself. Beyond that, I have read about peope whose exploded glass was not contained within the door and could have caused other injury. For a product in this price range, it is absurd that the manufacturer does not spend a few more dollars (or SEK) on materials and add few more dollars (or SEK) to the price and just insure that its customers will not be exposed to this problem.

I hope to be able to get the door repaired without some of the onerous delays I've read that other people experienced, and I hope to get many more years of use from this oven. However, I do not intend to ever run the self-clean again, and certainly do not expect to ever purchase another Electroux product.

There are no instructions inside the box on how to put the screen in properly, but it isn't hard to figure out.
The bird screen is a piece of galvanized 1/4" mesh builder's cloth. That's fine, it's sturdy and won't rust. On the top it is held in place by friction behind the top bend of the mouth of the vent cap. On the bottom the screen is folded into a flat S shape, and one of the hollows of that S fits over a small metal flange that is attached to the bottom of the mouth of the cap. 3 press joins (like rivets only without the rivets) hold it in place. My flange piece was in the bottom of the box. It did not stay in place firmly. So I took a tiny amount of JB Weld, aligned the press join spots, and glued it in place. Held it down with 3 small C clamps until things dried. As the damper flap end is very close to this join, I put a length of duct tape behind the flange prior to gluing it, and then removed that after the glue was dry. Thus there is no rim of extra glue on the inside of the bottom of the mouth, where it could interfere with the flap closing cleanly. It was a very simple fix, but if Famco had done a couple spot welds instead of press joins, this never would have been necessary. So now the screen is on securely, and eventually the vent cap will be installed by my contractor.

[[VIDEOID:4c8bfc24d9992585746260ee6bdb38c9]] Pros:
- Well laid out display that can be configured to display most of the temperature information anyone would desire.
- Additional weather related information is also displayed that most casual weather observers would want to know (barometric pressure, phase of the moon, etc.)
- Access to simple functions is straightforward.
- Provides alarms based on time, temperature, humidity, dew point, (and on WS-11 barometric pressure.)
- Most data sources can be calibrated.
- Once calibrated, sensors are accurate within Ambient Weather specifications.
- The back-light changes color to reflect either the indoor or outdoor temperature if desired.

Cons:
- Console displays a lot of information and is a bit busy. It is difficult to view for those with vision impairments.
- The graph function is limited by the resolution of the LCD display.
- Accessing some of the more advanced features isn't particularly intuitive, so that infrequent use will probably require consulting the manual.
- The alarm functionality only applies to the first external temperature and humidity probe.
- The WS-110 is limited in the sort of information in can provide by the nature of the sensors it uses. It is a very capable device for monitoring temperature data, but could be a disappointment if the owner has more general weather interests.

I received a pre-production version of the Ambient Weather WS-110 to review and test. Actually, I first received a WS-11, however unfortunately the console was not working. Such failures are to be expected in the development process and Ambient Weather sent me a replacement console by second-day air. That is certainly commendable customer service.

This reviews includes a video that contains 2 photographs and 4 video clips of the WS-110 in various modes of operation. Because it was impractical to eliminate the background noise, the video is silent. Practically speaking all that is missing is the audible confirmation of the button presses.

If you are interested in either the WS-11 or WS-110 I urge you to download a copy of the documentation so that you can go though the available features. At the time of this review, the documentation wasn't on the Amazon product listing, but you can download it from the Ambient weather website.

WS-11 documentation:
http://site.ambientweatherstore.com/Manuals/ws11.pdf

WS-110 documentation:
http://site.ambientweatherstore.com/Manuals/ws110.pdf

Where appropriate, the review video includes a citation to the manual section for the feature that is being demonstrated.

Even if the packaging was also pre-production, Ambient Weather had already come up with an eco-friendly design that used mostly cardboard and had an absolute minimal about of plastic to product the fragile electronics. Included in the video is a photo of the packaging. Setting up the WS-110 is straightforward if you follow the manual instructions. One thing to keep in mind is that this device requires 4 AA batteries for the console and 2 AAA batteries for the remote temperature and humidity sensor. Batteries are not included in either unit.

The WS-110 and WS-11 are very similar. The main difference is that the WS-11 includes a forecast based on barometric pressure and allows for alarms based on barometric pressure. If you are interested in this model, keep in mind that barometric pressure is a limited mechanism to forecast the weather and can be particularly unreliable in areas like California. If you really are interested in getting a warning of possible severe weather, you would be far better served by purchasing a weather radio that can receive alerts from the National Weather Service such as the Ambient Weather [[ASIN:B00EYI8GTQ Ambient Weather WR-091 Rechargeable Emergency Pocket AM/FM/WB Weather Alert Radio with Digital Tuner, Flashlight, Headphone Jack, AC Adaptor]]. Such alerts are generated by professional weather forecasters with access to much more data than barometric pressure alone.

The WS-110 omits the barometric pressure alarms and forecast icon and instead has an indication of the phase of the moon. This might be a better chose especially if you are in a part of the world were barometric pressure is a poor predictor of the weather.

Both the WS-110 and WS-11 come with a F007TH wireless thermo-hygrometer. A photograph of this device is included in the video. Either console can display data from up to 8 devices like this. You can mix and match the following devices: the Ambient Weather F007TH thermo-hygrometer, the F007PF floating pool and spa thermometer, the F007T temperature sensor, and the F007TP temperature probe. We already have in operation a F007TH wireless thermo-hygrometer from an WS-07 console, so I configured the new F007TH with the second device ID. As designed, the WS-110 found both probes and started displaying their data. As you can see in the first clip on the video, a very pleasant way to keep an eye on your environment to have the console in so called "scroll" mode which has it display all external probes one after the other in 5 second intervals. The ability of having 8 temperature probes opens up a wide range of potential applications. I intend to put the second thermo-hygrometer in the attic to monitor the effectiveness of attic fans. If you are interested in improving your energy efficiency, this is a way to monitor temperatures in multiple locations.

I compared the accuracy of the instruments against our Davis Vantage Pro-2 weather station and the indoor and out temperatures were accurate to the specifications of the devices. I also made some tests to confirm the range of the remote sensor. Taking the F007TH to the far end of the yard, over 200 feet, did not cause the signal to be lost. I then placed the F007TH inside the steel glove compartment of our 1965 Buick wagon that was in the garage. The heavy steel construction of a 50 year old example of Detroit muscle did not block the signal. So for most uses, you should be able to place a remote sensor a any desired location. One thing to keep in mind though is that the number of wireless devices is constantly multiplying. Most homes nowadays have Wi-Fi, wireless phones, and perhaps wireless music relay devices. You may have some problems with interference between the all the wireless devices in your home. These Ambient Weather devices use the 433 MHz band.

Both the WS-11 and WS-110 have a very elaborate system of adjusting back-lighting based on the temperature. It attempts to emulate our own intuitions of which colors would correspond to different temperatures. I suppose some people will find this feature really cool, but honestly it feels a bit silly to me. In order to experience this feature you need to look at the console and course you could just as easily read the temperature value to a tenth of a degree. However, if you find this feature appealing it is designed with care and can be customized to the point that you can have the colors progress in a range suitable for your climate. If you are a pragmatist like me, you can select a single color and that is probably preferable for ease of reading.

One of the features of both the WS-11 and WS-110 that is of limited value is the graphing feature. There simply isn't enough resolution in the LCD display to make much sense of the graph. The third clip on the video cycles through the available graphs. This is rather commonplace as many weather station consoles suffer from the same limitation. The only station I'm aware of that has high resolution graphs on the console is the [[ASIN:B00O9ZR6K4 Ambient Weather WS-1200-IP OBSERVER Solar Powered Wireless Internet Remote Monitoring Weather Station]].

If there is a feature that stands out on both the WS-11 and WS-110 it is the ability to set an alarm based on temperature or humidity. There is some limitations on this, you can only use the first external sensor for alarms. Still, this opens up many uses, especially for improving your energy efficiency. For example you might use such alarms to be more systematic about using room air conditioners or space heaters. You can also set alarms based on time, humidity, dew point, and on the WS-11: barometric pressure. The alarm is loud enough to be heard in a room and adjacent rooms. However, you might not hear it if you are too far away, so it won't serve as a "whole house notification." Should you miss an alarm, there is an icon on the console indicating that an alarm has gone off.

The alarm feature is as good an example to point out the general downside of this type of electronic device. There are only 4 push-buttons to access every feature and the user-interface is terse and arbitrary. For example, there is not a consistent button to confirm a selection nor is there any uniform way to exit a mode. On a device with so much capability, the setup mode is a long sequence of options. The second clip in the video cycles through all the configuration options. In the case of the alarm setup mode, you can either wait 30 seconds and it will automatically return to the normal running mode, or if you want to immediately return to the running mode, you'll have to cycle through all the possible parameters that can be alarmed in order to get out. Some attempt has been made to reuse buttons in an intuitive way, but these 4 buttons are seriously overloaded with functionality. Basically you'll have to either memorize an operation or go back to the manual. The vast majority of electronic devices have user-interfaces with a few overloaded buttons, so it is hardly a surprise. Nonetheless following the status quo is a burden on WS-11 and WS-110 users, and the awkward user-inferface may discourage you from getting the most value from either the WS-11 or WS-110.

In summary, the WS-11 and WS-110 are definitely niche products. They should be purchased because you really want the particular collection of features they have. Ambient Weather alone has a wide line up of similar devices, so you should make your selection based on your true needs and interests. If your main goal is simply monitoring temperature, the [[ASIN:B00BWUOVE8 Ambient Weather WS-07 Big Digit 8-Channel Wireless Thermo-Hygrometer]] is simple and easy to read. If you desire having the highs and lows displayed, then the [[ASIN:B00EW463SS Ambient Weather WS-08-X2 Wireless Indoor/Outdoor 8-Channel Thermo-Hygrometer with Daily Min/Max Display with Two Remote Sensors]] might serve your needs. If you desire additional meteorological data like barometric pressure and forecasts based on pressure, perhaps you should consider the [[ASIN:B003OSSH9G Ambient Weather WS-1171A Wireless Advanced Weather Station with Temperature, Dew Point, Barometer and Humidity]]. If you have a greater interest in astronomical matters, perhaps the [[ASIN:B00BQFWYF2 Ambient Weather WS-1173A Wireless Advanced Weather Station with Temperature, Dew Point and Barometer]] would be a better match. If you are really interested in monitoring your overall weather conditions, perhaps you spend a little more and get a complete weather station like the [[ASIN:B003OSJ08S Ambient Weather WS-2080 Wireless Home Weather Station]]. For that extra cost you get an automated rain gauge, anemometer, and the potential to connect your station to your computer if your interests further grow. For a modest additional investment, you would end up with a complete weather condition monitoring system that is expandable. Nonetheless, the WS-11 and WS-110 do have their place. Either model could be extremely helpful in making your living space more comfortable while lowering your energy costs.

There are many things a Bertazzoni is not: it is not a Viking or a Wolf, and it does not approach their price tags. Nor is it a Blue-Star, with four jet-engines where burners should be. If you need 22k BTU burners, this is not the stove for you.

This is what the Bertazonni is: a fully-mechanical, all steel gas range with attractive Italian styling, a convection oven, and a storage compartment that can double as a warming cupboard given that the main oven flame is a couple of inches away. There is no control panel to go wonky in this range. There is no "Chicken Nuggets" button. No power? No problem. You can light the burners with a match; the gas line is kept open with a thermocouple, which means that if the flame goes out for any reason (even if the power is out!), the gas will immediately shut off. Yes, the mechanical nature of the thermocouple means that lighting a burner takes a few more seconds worth of attention than stoves you may be used to-- you have to hold the knob in to keep the gas going until the flame heats the thermocouple enough to keep the line open.

The top is all stainless-steel, with sturdy continuous grates. The steel cleans up incredibly easily with a damp microfiber towel. The flame is closer to the pots than on american stoves, so despite the top burner rating of 15,000 BTU, much less heat is lost than on a comparable GE or Frigidaire. The gas is remarkably easy to control, and the stove holds a simmer exceedingly well. One thing I love about the Pro versus the Master are the knobs; yes, they are more stylish, but the fact of the matter is that it is very easy to tell from *across the room* if someone has left a burner on. With more than one person in a household, this can happen more often than one might expect. The reassurance to be able to glance up and easily tell that all the burners are off is really wonderful.

Unlike the higher-end stoves, it is possible to pair this stove with a recirculating hood; you do not need an outside vent, make-up air, or remote fans, which is handy for those of us trying to remodel kitchens in old city buildings. The oven compartment is not as capacious as a GE or Blue-Star. I've not run into any problems due to this, but as with any kitchen remodel you should assess what your specific cooking needs are before evaluating ranges. OTOH, if you're going for looks, well- it's a very pretty range. We also happen to enjoy cooking on it very much.

Washing -

My 16 year old fridge started to drip water out of the dispenser after filling a glass. A quick second tap on the dispenser paddle would stop the drip. I ruled out air in the line and decided to replace the valve. The moment I unbolted the old valve drips started leaking from the connections (yikes!) so I'm glad it wasn't leaking when installed previously. I guess the seals were worn out too! I installed this new one in a matter of seconds:
1) Turn off water to fridge (if you can't, just remove the filter and it stops water flow as well since water line hits the filter before the valve).
2) Unplug fridge power.
3) Remove the back bottom panel and unbolt the water valve from the fridge.
4) Use a 3/8" wrench flat against the white connectors (around the water tube) to push in on the white connectors to release the old tubes.
5) Use a 1/2" wrench to loosen and remove the incoming water line.
6) Unplug the power cables.
7) Plug in the new power cables, push in the new water lines fully, tighten on the supply line, and bolt it all back together!
8) Plug in fridge, turn on water, test for leaks... bleed the air out of the line.

I had to replace my filter too as the water was coming out super slow with air in the lines. I used the bypass cap that came with the fridge to remove the filter from the line and bleed it of all the air... then put in a new filter as it was time anyway. Now it is fast and functional with zero leaks.

ONE caveat and I hope this stops with time... as air leaves the ice maker line... but the ice maker water fill is screechy/loud!
