I've read about as many reviews on the Cabrio line that I could, and still went ahead with buying one myself (WTW5700XW3), plus the matching Cabrio dryer. Instead of just being a cheerleader or basher...I'd like to just dive in and list some observations about what I see when I wash clothes in my Cabrio and then contrast it with what I read in all the negative reviews. You can be the judge on what you think.

First off, this Cabrio doesn't just shut off in the middle of a load. It actually pauses to let gravity drain the load for a minute or two and also does water level checks. Yes, it sounds like the washer just died; falling completely silent. Yes, your traditional washer doesn't do this. Yes, there seems to be a lot more logic in this machine making decisions for you along the way to optimize the washing process. In the end....it will continue on just fine, if you let it...

In the beginning cycle where it does the sensor stage to determine the load, you would think the sensor stage is done after a few brief spins with no water. I thought the same, but the sensor cycle is a little longer. The washer runs for a couple minutes with just a little water added, but it's STILL part of the sensing cycle (note the light hasn't changed to the wash cycle yet). The clothes are actually absorbing the first dump of water as the machine tosses them around. The washer will pause again and then add additional water after it has checked how much the clothes have absorbed. Of course, the water level will never be above the clothes like a traditional washer, since the clothes need to press against the bottom washer plate to be moved around. This is also the part that most are getting hung up on, or can't accept. If you watch closely between the clothes, you will see a level of water under the clothes. The clothes will churn out, under (into the water/detergent brine mix), and the back up the center.

The clothes actually do move throughout the washer from center to outside in a donut fashion, it's just in slow motion. If you are used to a traditional washers, where the clothes slush around gallons of water in a fairly fast pattern, then you will need to re-adjust your brain for how this HE process works......and yes.....it does work!

Now for big sheets/towels/blankets/etc.. the "bulky" setting is the one you want. It'll use much more water, but it will also allow the large items to churn in the wash cycle correctly. Using the Bulky cycle is next to worthless for regular loads, because the wash plate at the bottom will not come in contact with the clothes and move them correctly. It's tempting to set all your regular loads to Bulky to satisfy your old cravings for gallons of water sloshing around, but that is not how an HE washer works. Do that, and you will be frustrated (hence the gobs of negative reviews).

My favorite cycles are "quick wash" and "normal". Quick wash is really useful if you just have lightly soiled clothes. Let's say something like the clothes wore to an office, verses construction work. The cycle is pretty much identical to the Normal cycle, but runs about a one half hour only. The Normal cycle handles most everything else, plus whites. The washer has a whites setting, but then it burns hot water and runs a longer than normal cycle. If your whites are in hurting condition, then by all means go for the whites setting. For me, my whites are not in that much of a need for aggressive cleaning.

I have thrown just about every type of clothes at this washer (work, play, blankets, towels, sheets, etc...) and it has performed flawlessly. The clothes are clean! The water usage is low. The washer is reliable with no baby-sitting/re-balancing of the cycles required so far. Since my model of Cabrio (5700) has the glass lid, I can see the clothes churn several times down and around the drum; coming back up the center every 2-3 minutes. All clothes are cycling through the water/detergent brine several times. I have seen nothing that is left bobbing on top totally dry at the end of the cycle, like some other comments have said. Dryer time is also reduced significantly because the washer does such an excellent job on the spin cycle to remove most of the water from the clothes. The clothes come out of my dryer with no wrinkles. I can understand what folks are seeing when they take the clothes damp, to almost dry, out of the HE washer. The clothes will dry just fine in the dryer with the wrinkles gone. Again, folks with traditional washers might be used to their clothes being a lot wetter coming out of the washer; but I never found that to be a feature/benefit.

In conclusion, I don't fault the consumer as much as the companies that have designed these HE washers. They have obviously dropped the ball on educating the public about what really is going on with these machines. Just saying they use less water, and the water line will be below your clothes doesn't cut it. You make a new technology HE washer, and then the consumer sees it stop at times for minutes thinking it died, then not explaining the details of the cycles and what it's accomplishing (sensor technology? tell the consumer more about how it does this and the fill lines, the flow of the clothes, etc...), and then these companies just tell you it makes different sounds you not used to and all is fine??? ....well....to me this paradigm shift is like we're going from horse-n-buggy technology to gas powered automobile technology with these HE washers .....and the folks using them are still looking for the ropes to giddy-up.

I would highly recommend this HE washer to anyone that wants to significantly reduce their water consumption and have clean clothes. My water costs were high. This HE Cabrio washer put a significant dent in the water consumption. Now, if you can't get your head around what's going on inside these HE washers and agree with how they work, then stick with what you know. Buy a traditional washing machine that fills the bucket full of gallons of water, and be at ease with your decision. As for me, I look forward to doing laundry every time with my Cabrio, and the savings it brings.

I have a GE Cafe fridge...french door, bottom freezer type, model# CFSP5RKBD SS.

There was a car accident recently that took out a transformer, or whatever, and the power at my house had some spikes, then eventually was shut down by the power company so they could assess the damage. After the power came on, the fridge was completely dead; no compressor running, no fan, no lights, no display...nothing.

After poking around and reading online, it seemed like a 95% chance it was the main control board. Found this on Amazon and purchased. While waiting for the item to arrive, I cleaned the fridge out well and got everything ready for the board swap. The new board came, I swapped it in, plugged power back in and nothing. Bummed out, I swapped the old board back in and prepped the new board to get returned to amazon. In one last ditch research effort, I saw a guy online who said that you could try unhooking the left door's wiring harness and sometimes that can fix it (it didn't for him). I unhooked the harness to the left door and replugged it back in, and the fridge came alive after 30 sec or so with the old board...it ran for a few minutes and then died again. At this point, I reconnected the new board and plugged in the fridge, unhooked and reconnected the left door's wiring harness and presto, it came back on and has been running normally for two days or so.

So, don't freak out if your refrigerator doesn't magically/instantly come on after the board swap...you may need to "reset" the harness located at the top of the hinge cover on the left door.

Sooo... either this thing is defective out of the bag, or it is not the right one/size for our compressor. But we will never know because it's a big secret how many horsepower refrigerator compressors are. Now I get to go buy an OEM new start capacitor for $40.

My main gripes about the dishwasher:
We intermittently received the OE error that corresponded to dishwasher not emptying water. After lots of troubleshooting I discovered the problem was with gunk getting stuck on a float that detects the water level in the tub. The dishwasher was draining fine but the float was not moving giving a wrong reading to the computer. The fix requires that you disassemble the plastic levels on the left side of the unit and clean them well.
We had an incident were significant amount of water started dripping from the dryer vent on the door. Looked online for help and identified the issue as having a clogged drain hose on the drying sistem. I fixed the issue by blowing an air can through the hose. A ball of paper gunk came out (I guess we washed something with the labels on).
The mounting brackets are flimsy and I have had to replace them because they failed (bended and cracked) with regular use. I finally decided to reinforce them with a thin metal plate.
The washing racks are severely corroded after 6 years of use. The corners and other parts are just falling apart.

These are all issues that I would consider unacceptable for a $500 dishwasher with 6 years of use. Based on my bad experience with my cooking range (bad knobs) and the issues with the dishwasher I will not buy LG appliances again.

I live alone in a converted attic apartment. Its odd shape and quirky features make it awesome, but I don't have access to the main house's laundry room. Instead of fighting with the landlord to honor his advertised promises, I decided to get my own washer, with the added bonus that I'll never have to run (or trip) up & down outdoor stairs to wash my stupid clothes in the dead of winter (and Wisconsin winters are coooold). Also, I layer my clothes (i.e. a camisole under a t-shirt) so I can wear the outer clothing more than once between washings, reducing how often I need to do laundry. I read through many - possibly hundreds of - reviews before choosing this machine (the 45L option). I wanted a separate extractor so that, if the extractor broke, I could still wash my clothes. (I wouldn't have to send the whole machine in for servicing. I'm ok with wringing out things by hand for a few days while a new extractor comes in the mail - thank you Amazon Prime!) If I had more laundry, I might have chosen an automatic machine, but I think this style, akin to the old wringer-washers, cleans clothes better. Anyhoo, on to the machine!

1) One person mentioned that 3 minutes is enough to wash her clothes. Ditto - the agitator can be pretty rough on your clothes so you don't want to go much longer than that.
2) Someone mentioned that the agitator is very strong and can damage your clothing. Like another reviewer mentioned, put delicates in a *strong* mesh bag to protect them. From my own experience, put enough water in the machine so that the clothes move freely (fill 'er up!). Don't add too many clothes. The agitator should swish the water, not your clothes.
3) Many people mentioned problems from using too much soap. I'm using liquid detergent that works in both regular & HE machines. I started out using the tablespoon of soap that one person recommended. I didn't get any suds. I added half a capful the next time I washed. There were suds in the first load but they were gone after I ran the second load through the same water. With both amounts of soap, my clothes came out clean (one wash & two rinses) and not soapy but smelling like... oxyclean. I hate that smell, so I think I'll try other detergents. I'll also try adding a few drops of essential oil or something to the last rinse, but not fabric softener, which doesn't rinse out well according to other reviewers.
4) The mouth of the drain hose needs to be higher than the water level in the machine. I took the drain hose extension from my extractor and attached it to the washer's drain hose so that I could completely fill the machine without any drips or splashes from the drain hose (which others complained about). I also place the machine in my bathtub before filling it to contain any splashes, to give the waste water a place to drain, and to keep my floor dry when I'm shifting around my dripping-wet laundry.
5) Filling the machine can be a pain. If you have a spigot, you can slide the fill hose on & let 'er rip. If, like most of us, you don't have a spigot, you have a few options. If you can get the aerator off the sink faucet (which I can't), you could get a screw-on spigot attachment at a hardware store for less than $2. You could also get a nut that would let you thread the hose through, seating the rubber part into the nut to create a seal, and then screw the nut on to the faucet. If you have a hand-held shower head, put it in the washer to fill it or take off the shower head & just connect the shower hose to the washer's fill hose. A water pitcher & some elbow grease also work well. I had some 1/2" hose left over from my shower repair debacle... I mean, project... which fits over the machine's inlet tube and inside the provided fill tube, effectively giving me an 8' longer reach. So, with the machine in the bathtub, I hold the rubber end of the fill tube against the sink faucet with one hand, pinch the connection between the hoses with the other hand, and silently swear while the machine fills (because I get bored easily & occasionally spray myself when adjusting my grip on the faucet). I'll eventually get fed up with this & find a better way to fill the machine - one that doesn't require me to stand there the entire time.
6) As many have mentioned, this is a more work-intensive way to wash clothes. However, I think they get MUCH cleaner. I actually grew up with a wringer-washer, so I'm familiar with this style of laundering - and prefer it! I fill the machine & wash 3-4 loads in the same water, piling each washed load in the bathtub (or in a laundry basket, which I don't have) while the next load runs. I put in the most important stuff first (underthings), then shirts, then jeans, then towels. I drain & refill the machine two or three times - once for each rinse, and the clothes share rinse water, too. (You could use 2-3 tubs/basins/sinks full of water to dip-rinse instead.) I lightly squeeze the dirty water out of the clothes, back into the washer, as I pull them out. When I pull the first set of clothes out of the last rinse, I start running them through my extractor. It takes some shuffling, but it's at least as quick as an automatic washer and your clothes end up cleaner.
7) I was worried about the size of the machine - I didn't want to spend a month laundering each article of clothing separately! That's not an issue. I can fit 2-3 pairs of jeans (size 10), or 7ish shirts (size large), or lots of underthings, or 2-3 regular towels, or one "bath sheet" (~3x bigger than a towel and a true joy to wrap around and around and around myself), or one set of queen-size sheets (minus the pillow cases), etc. I figure that one (heavy) load in a full-sized washer = 4 (light) loads in this washer and it takes less than an hour (unless I get distracted by something shiny) from first filling the machine to hanging my clothes up to dry (about the same as an automatic washer).

A family member in another household was ready to get rid of a fridge that was less than 5 years old because the doors would shift open when they were closed.

The problem was the family had done something to break one of the door "closing cam" catch latches off and while doing so, also broke the "hinge" for the part off of the gasket retainer ( ASIN B00AH5Z7GA ).

The french doors are designed with a closing cam on each door. As you close the doors, you are compressing the air inside of fridge ever so slightly, and that air wants to escape, pushing out on the doors ever so slightly. When everything is in place and not broken, the cams interact with catch inside of the top of the fridge, allowing the doors to push open just a hair and then close back, equalize the pressure but keeping the doors closed and sealed. When the cam is missing, there's nothing to pull the doors back to the closed position, resulting in one or both doors opening itself just a hair and if you don't notice it and close it all the way, you end up loosing the fridge's cold air.

I ordered new closing cam latches for both sides and the replacement gasket retainer mentioned above from amazon and looked at few repair videos online. (ASIN B00AFSMXHK, ASIN B00AFSMY24, ASIN B00AH5Z7GA ) ***Important note - the closing cams and related parts are side specific, so make sure you are getting the correct one if you are only getting one side***

Less than 20 minutes worth of work and I had both the closing cam and gasket retainer replaced.

If you don't have a full stove, you MUST get this. It heats up a lot faster than you're expecting though, so beware. No joke, if you set something in it, turn it on, and expect it to take a few minutes like you're used to, and leave to do something else like chop something up, your pan will overheat and smoke. It's faster than a gas burner even. The power of this thing makes it feasible to actually cook using a standard 120v outlet, without a huge 220v outlet. Get rid of your potable electric coil burner (unless you still need it for non-magnetic pots you have). The portable electric coils are severely underpowered, never get hot enough, and take forever to get hot at all. This unit works more efficiently and heats up much hotter and faster. Aluminum and stainless steel, however, are not going to work with it. It's also difficult to control the temperature so you have to use it for a while to get used to it's quirks. It cycles on and off like an oven, rather than a traditional stove-top that stays at a constant level of on. I'd give it a better rating but I hear they now make ones that let you pick the temperature rather than a 0-10 setting like this one, which would eliminate the learning curve. How much can you shove in here? Something like;
4 pairs of fabric pants
2/3 pairs jeans
10 tank tops/light t-shirts (girls)
6 heavier t-shirts (boys)
2 regular bath towels
1 beach towel
one set (fitted AND flat) full size sheets
one queen size sheet (fitted OR flat) at a time

With all of these, you could throw in a couple washcloths as well.

Spin cycle:
You will only be able to fit half or even one third of the clothes that fit in the washer into the spin dryer. Not much of an issue as the spin dryer takes very little time. You will not be able to use the spin dryer for beach towels or queen sheets. It's too much weight for it to spin properly, even if you try wringing out a lot of the water by hand first. The spin dryer shakes a little bit at the beginning, but should even out pretty quickly. If the load is "unbalanced", it will get worse after those few seconds instead of getting better. It is very obvious when that happens, and you should stop it and try to redistribute or put less things in. If the load is balanced, the machine won't shake, but it will still move slowly across the floor. Mine is trapped inside my bathtub, but even then, don't leave it alone while you are spin drying until you've done it a bunch of times. And like I said, spin drying takes very little time, so not a big deal. This will not get your clothes completely dry, but it will make them take much less time than stringing them up on the line when they are soaking wet.

How I use my washer: I put it in the bathtub. It is the first time I wish I had a curtain instead of sliding glass doors. I am not entirely sure how one would use this washer without putting it in the bathtub (or I GUESS on a counter, but if you want to run it on a counter you'd better hold on to it the whole time the spin cycle is on) because the drain hose is too short to reach over the tub from outside. Also, the hose provided to connect to a faucet for incoming water does not work for my faucets. Well, because it's in the bathtub already because of the drainage tube, I just use my detachable shower head. That is my saving grace. If I didn't have that, I probably would be much more upset with these tube issues, but using the showerhead is working for me. Especially since apparently my boyfriend used a metric sh*t ton of soap when he does laundry (we don't live together but sometimes our laundry gets mixed up), so every time I get to one of our shirts that he has washed recently, it seems like there is soap for days. You really find out how much laundry soap you've been wasting in regular machines when you can see the water before it drains away. I've had to rinse some of these shirts seven or eight times in the beginning (and he wonders why he gets a heat rash when he sweats in long-sleeves, well, that might be your answer). I can use the showerhead to give the clothes an extra bit of rinse, so for now I don't mind so much that the tubes are ineffective. I might tinker around with them later.

Overall, I am very pleased with this machine as I HATE going to the laundromat. I will still need to go there for larger blankets or if I get back from a trip and have a lot of laundry to do, as this is more for keeping up with one person (two people is pushing it) wearing a normal amount of clothes, not for doing ten loads in a day. The load sizes are small and you have to be more involved in the process with this machine as apposed to an actual washing machine. You have to come back and set up the rinse and spin cycles yourself, then go hang them to finish drying. I did a lot of laundry with this when it first arrived, and if I had that much laundry today I would just go back to the laundromat.

If it fits your circumstances like it fits mine, it's fantastic. But don't think it can do as much as a regular washing machine.

Over time, the plastic hinge wears down and lid breaks free but I would expect that of anything plastic going through dishwasher over 200 times. Thought of switching to metal ones with a hinge but I think those would be too hot to touch and remove from brewer right after use. We often do one cup right after another so that is important to us.

Other notable point. These fit into the holder of our direct-plumbed Keurig K150p. As with all other pods we've tried, the K150 doesn't officially support reusable pods so one will typically experience clear water escaping from the top of the lid and dripping or streaming out the bottom side of the Keurig head making a mess and watering down one's coffee. I took care of this by adding an additional rubber gasket up underneath Keurig's gasket surrounding the needle/puncture element. My gasket was about 1/8 to 5/32 thick and offered some slight give/compression as it appeared to be rubber. Works great - no leaks using either these reusable pods or regular pods - and it doesn't come in contact with the coffee as it is parked up behind Keurig's installed gasket. Just slide Keurig's off, slide yours on, then slide Keurig's gasket back on over it. If the added gasket is too thick, you'll crush open the top of the disposable pods and coffee will leak everywhere. If too thin, you won't have a seal against the reusable pods and coffee will again leak everywhere. So get a small assortment at the hardware store (very cheap) and do some trial and error if you must.

It occurs to me that Keurig could have easily designed the unit to accept reusable pods but made a decision not to support them in a commercial brewer for reasons I can only speculate. They told me over the phone that reusable pods just are supported in these "commercial" units. Nor is there a consumer-grade direct-plumbed model in their lineup. Go figure.

This hose from LG was the original part. Water line runs from the water valve to the water filter assembly. Took 10 minutes to replace using the following steps:
1. Turn the power off to the unit.
2. Pull the unit out.
3. Shut the water off.
4. Remove the lower access cover.
5. Take the valve off the unit.
6. With the valve removed there is a clip that is under the ring that goes around the tube. Remove the horseshoe clip. Push in on the ring that goes around the tube toward the water valve and pull the tube out at the same time.
7. Go to the front of the unit and remove 1 screw at the front of the water filter housing.
8. Once removed, slide the water filter head forward.
9. Disconnect the small tube with the elbow on the back of the refrigerator.
10. Take the tubing out of the clips on the back of the refrigerator.
11. Once this is done you will be able to take the entire water filter head out.
12. This will allow you to be able to access the compression fitting on the back of the filter head to remove the tube like the one on the water valve.
13. You will then reinstall in reverse. Hint: Make sure that you push the tubing back into the fittings all the way.

PROS:
Looks good and will squeeze into most apartment or condo closets.
Has large timer display that counts down time left on cycle.
Uh - hmmm, that's about it for pros.

CONS:
Clothes will be damp at best for most loads. If you remove the clothes immediately while piping hot, the steam will dissipate and sheets or similar weighted items will dry if spread out. (I use a fan directed at the damp items to help finish off the drying process.) It is almost impossible to dry sweaters, towels and jeans. So, if you live in a climate where heavier clothes are the norm, you may want to take this into consideration.

Users will do better if they understand that you cannot employ the regular load washer/dryer mentality when using this machine. Mix the weight and size of the items - one sheet, two pillow cases, two bath towels and face cloths mixed in with a few gym socks or underwear.

It takes forever and a day to wash/dry one load. I've found that setting the cycle to wash and then opening the door even for a few minutes, THEN going back and starting the dry cycle cuts down the dry time considerably. Of course, this defeats the purpose of setting and forgetting a load to wash/dry un-tendered; but if you are a busy granny-nanny like me, it cuts down on hours of dry time. Plus, it's only an extra step and you still don't have to haul the load from the washer to the dryer in the process.

If you don't crack the door and let the moisture dissipate between loads, you may get this awful stench that is best remedied with a quick Chlorox rinse.

Lint accumulates around the rubber door seal and may re-deposit on the next load if not wiped down.

Our machine is less than two years old and has broken down completely once and at times will just shut down due to an uneven load, even with two equally weighted sheets. We will also get an arbitrary error message that can only be remedied by unplugging the machine or resetting the circuit.

The Range is very well made, is solid stainless steel on all sides & top, has heavy cast iron grates, heavy thick stainless oven racks.
4 excellent burners that are the exact ones used by Wolf, made in Germany and 15,000BTU each and all 4 are the same which I required.
I cant stand stoves that have 4 different burners, one big powerful burner one or two medium and then one tiny almost useless burner for just simmering.
That is just a total waste of a stove top to me.

I much prefer 4 really nice powerful burners where all 4 also become very low simmer burners, MUCH better configuration.
The burners are spaced enough apart to be able to use 4 large pots/pans at the same time.

Like ALL stainless it is rather easily scratched but other than that it is easy to keep clean and except for a couple tiny scratches still looks like brand new after a year of constant use 3X a day, 7 days a week.

Prior to buying ours last March this one review right here on Amazon was the one and only bad review I had ever found for this stove, and as you can tell has NOTHING to do with the stove itself but is a shipping problem.
Have since seen 2 others both complaining about the enamel on the inside of oven chipping badly. Both were the DRGB model and seemed like it was probably a bad batch of enamel.
Have only seen 2 reviews about that so must not have been wide spread problem.

The other review here from August 17th sounds as though they don't even own the stove just regurgitating something they have heard, which I have heard the same thing. But all they say is that it "can rust & spot", but apparently either they don't really own the stove or it hasn't rusted or spotted they just suspect it "might".

Not exactly sure how much difference it really makes between 304 to 430 stainless on a stove that is an indoor range and not some outdoor BBQ sitting in the elements. 430 stainless is only slightly less stain/rust resistant and I think the only molecular difference is 430 does not have the 8% Nickle that 304 does.
Technically the best stainless would be 316 stainless which virtually no one uses except for BBQs made for marine environments.

Anyway, we are very happy with the stove so far, cooks great, looks great and didn't cost an arm and a leg. We bought ours for $1799.00 total cost shipping included. A Kenmore we were looking at cost more and the NXR is easily 10X the stove that Kenmore would have been.

The Infrared broiler works very well, oven works great, knobs are nice, the door is heavy duty and even after having the oven on at over 400 degrees for hours the door is only just warm to the touch.

For the price there is NOTHING that beats a 30" NXR for value, not even close.
Can you get stoves just as nice? Yep, but you will pay dearly for it.
Only other stoves that are as good and even better in some respects than the NXR start at least $1000 more.

Blue Stars are decent, although I see a lot of complaints about them, Capital Culinarian is very good but both of those will cost considerably more.

All you need to do is connect one end of the tube to the syringe, and submerge the other end of the tube in a cup of very warm water. Draw the water into the tube by pulling the plunger toward you. I spent a little over an hour cleaning a 4" clogged vent about 16' long through 2 bends in the pipe.
The process went something like this:
- Put 4 rod sections together on the brush head.
- Work through what you can easily (turning forward only on the drill).
- Remove the brush (turning forward only on the drill).
- Shop vac out what you can reach.
- Put your brush back in (turning forward only on the drill).
- Add 2 rod sections.
Repeat the process... take the brush out, shop vac what you can reach, put the brush back in for more, add 2 sections, and repeat until you get to the end.

Take your time, always turn the rod forward, and it will work.

Our house is now 64 years old. When built, the builder installed the GE low-voltage relay-switched system for lights and some outlets. Over the years, renovations meant some lighting was changed to direct AC power switching. However, many of the lights remained on the GE relay-switched system. There are some real advantages to this system - particularly if you want multi-way switching; the ability to turn lights on or off (or outlets, for that matter) from multiple locations. The relays are latching so once energized by the wall switch, they do not draw power to stay in the on- or off-state. We have two of the original multi-room switches that use a rotary knob to select which room or lights you want to turn on or off. A very early implementation of what is now part of a "smart home" system. In fact, current versions of this system enable control over a wired or wireless network and some third-party vendors make add-on electronics to let you control things from a mobile phone or tablet. These systems can then be integrated into a "smart home" system. My only complaint is that it can be very difficult to replace defective relays (they do fail after years - some of the relays in our system are original, so they've been in operation for 60 years) as the mounting brackets had holes for the relays in front and back rows. Without removing the relays in the "front" row from those holes, it can be nearly impossible to replace a relay in the back row. I just had to do this. I did not have to disconnect any of the relays in front, but I did struggle to get them out of their bracket holes. The newer systems have a single row of holes as far I can see on the current Web pages that describe the various systems. The other problem was that manipulating the replacement relay into the back row resulted in one of the control wires breaking off it's soldered connection. Fortunately, I was able to reach that connection with my soldering iron and solder it back in place. A better connection system for the control wires would be a good idea for GE.  They did replace the bare wire ends on the control wires with a push-on connector, so if you have the newer mounting boxes, they will simply plug in. But a connector on the relay body itself for the control wires would avoid the problem of bending the control wires around so much to get the relay in place if you are replacing a relay in an older system.

2/14/14 UPDATE -- It's still workin' like new!

APPLIANCE:
Kenmore 500 top loading washer

PROBLEM:
Washer suddenly would no longer spin during rinse and spin cycles. Therefore, clothes would be soaking wet at the end of a wash, and would not be ready for the dryer.

TROUBLESHOOTING:
We believed it was not a motor failure, since I could hear the motor trying to turn the tub. Googled the symptoms and found out clutch failure was a common issue with the Kenmore 500 top loaders. Ordered this replacement part on Amazon (~$8.95 plus expedited shipping; total still was under $18). Received it in 2-3 days.

INSTALLATION:
I should point out there are many helpful videos on youtube.com now for appliance repair. Watch more than one since they are not guaranteed to be accurate. I found at least two that showed how to take apart a washer similar to ours. They also showed how to put a new clutch in.

TOOLS USED:
channel-lock pliers to remove supply lines
pail to catch water from the supply lines that you are going to disconnect
several dry towels
flat tipped screw driver to remove top control panel and clips
3/8" drive ratchet
6" ratchet extension
7/16" socket to remove agitator bolt
1/2" socket to remove motor bolts
pliers (normal slip-joint type) to remove hose clamps if desired
needle-nose pliers to remove clips
nut driver set (optional but very convenient)

RESULTS:
Our washer now works like new.

COMMENTARY:
I could see how worn our old one was when I took it out. These clutches are somewhat under-built for the job; basically the design is like a drum brake, but the pads are not very substantial. The new one is similar to the old one, so it may wear out again someday. However, this part fixed our problem immediately, so if it does break again I know I could probably swap in another one in about an hour.

Changing humidifier wicks (for "evaporative" type humidifiers) is a necessary evil and recurring annual expense. It's necessary because after a few short weeks, the hardness in your water will be left behind as a precipitate in the wicks, turning them hard. Also, bacteria and mold/mildew can begin to build up, causing an off-smell and discoloration. These things will occur no matter which brand of wick you buy, so the only essential criteria that matter with regards to buying wicks is:

* Do they fit your make/model of humidifer ?
* Do they have a good evaporation rate throughout their lifespan ?
* Do they maintain their physical integrity (i.e., not fall apart) ?
* Are they a decent value, compared to similar brands ?

In my case, the answer for this brand appears to YES on all 4 counts. Previously, I'd always bought Holmes HWF-100's, but as of this writing these are less expensive. This package includes 6 filters (3 pairs), which in my region is enough to last me one winter season (just over 1 month per pair).

Recommended.

p.s. Terminology nit: amazon, and various vendors and reviewers frequently (and erroneously) refer to these as "filters". They are, in fact, "wicks". Any filtration that occurs happens indirectly, as a result of the wicking and evaporative process.

HOW I USE MY AEROPRESS
When I bought my Aeropress Go, I wrongly assumed that the smallest size this company would go was the standard 16oz mug. I hated the suggested brewing methods because they either wasted coffee or brewed too weak because I had to add more water to get a full cup.

That said, I use mine like a hybrid between a pour-over and a French press. I add my grounds and water, stir, then continue to top it off as it slowly drips in. Most of the time, the flow rate slows so I press it, then have to retract the plunger back to finish adding all the water (*see note about finicky paper below).

FINE SIZE
❌ This is a very minor grip, but I think it matters to many users. You apply LESS pressure to plunge this than paper, perhaps that affects the flavor a bit?

ULTRA-FINE SIZE
❌ Plunging this was hard. I started to question if I was going to break something. It worked, but I prefer the other size, given my brew technique.

TAKEAWAYS
❌ The edges are sharp. Be careful. Comes with a felt bag for protection.
❌ The plate gets hot, but still must be removed after brewing.
❌ This makes cleanup a lil more tricky, but not a deal breaker.
✔️ Flows like paper would.
✔️ Oils make it through. Paper extracts some of the best parts of coffee in my opinion, this doesn't.
❌ Sludge can make it through. This makes it more like a French press with the sediment at the bottom.
✔️ Paper is wasteful. This obviously fixes that.
✔️ Paper is finicky. The stiff plate doesn't flex like paper sometimes does if you need to, say, retract the plunger.

If you have never tried an induction burner, I would suggest that you do. I first used one over 15 years ago and it caused me to buy a full-sized induction stove. That stove lasted 10 years until one of its circuit boards blew and they were no longer making a replacement. I then bought a second induction stove. BTW, I also use a portable induction burner in my campervan which I run off of a solar generator and solar panels. In that situation, I'm using the power of the sun to cook my food!

Why do I love induction? First, there is no flame or exposed element. Second, induction uses magnetic waves to directly heat the pot so controlling heat is as quick as using gas. Since the pot is heated directly you can regulate (turn up and down) the heat as quickly as using a gas range. Lastly, the surface of the "burner" cools down much quicker as any warmth is secondary from the hot pot that is sitting on it. By the way, Induction cookers are the most energy-efficient of all cooktops.

How about this little burner? In many ways, it is similar to other burners in this price range. In several significant ways, it is better than many in this price range.

How is it similar to other sub-one hundred dollar burners?
-Fan noise is loud and very similar to other tabletop induction burners that I have used.
-Controls are similar. You can control temp, time, or power level. I only use power level as using it is very similar to using a regular stove.
-Size of the magnetic field is relatively small (see my flour on the bottom the pot photo). I have tested a number of these burners and they all have a relatively small "hot area." This has never been a problem when I cook, but I'm a simple cook. When camping I make foods like eggs, grilled cheese sandwiches, pancakes, and canned soup. For these items, I have not noticed a problem with significant uneven heat. However, if you are a gourmet cook you may want to invest in a more expensive burner that has a larger magnet.

How is this burner better than similarly priced burners that I have tried?

Style- This burner has a little style to it. The one that I'm currently using in my camper is a pretty ugly basic rectangle.

Power- I have tested several of these burners that claim to be 1500-1800 watts and the ones that I tested were all only around 1000 watts when at full power. This includes the one that I use in my camper. I measured this unit at close to 1700 watts, which means that water will boil faster on this unit than on some similarly priced ones.

Power control-Most units control the level of power by cycling on and off. On my camper unit levels 1-3 cycle 400 watts on and off and on levels 4-9 (it has 9 levels) it cycles 1000 watts (despite saying it is 1800 watts).
This unit actually controls the power in incremental steps, so when it says that it is set on level three which is 600 watts it is actually using 600 watts. This won't be very important for most, but it is important enough for me that I'm considering changing out my current burner for this one. Since my camper uses a solar generator it is much easier for me to manage my power if I know that a unit is using 600 watts consistently rather than 1000 watts intermittently.

The bottom line is that this unit is consistent with other units at this price point when it comes to fan noise and small heating circles. However, it is significantly better than some 1800-watt units as it actually delivers almost 1800 watts (1700 watts) and it controls its power by using lower power levels rather than turning on and off a higher power level.

I’m so happy that I purchased this. I have a condition EDS that makes my joints dislocate easily and getting to the laundry mat and carrying a heavy laundry bag can be difficult. Now to be honest this takes some practice to get the hang of it. But it’s well worth it. Clothes come out so dry that it takes maybe 30 minutes to finish fully drying all my clothes on my drying rack  with a big box fan blowing on the clothes. This little spin dryer has handled heavy sweaters, blankets, sheets, towels, pants etc. If it fits it can handle it..I found that the lightest clothes need to go on the bottom of the spin dryer and heavier clothes need to go on top. Then I give the clothes in the spin dryer a little shove to squish them down. If I don’t the whole thing shakes a little. I’ve found hacks that really help make it work perfectly every single time even on fluffy queen size blankets, big heavy sweaters, jeans etc. When doing fluffy blankets clean a heavy bath towel along with soft fluffy blanket. Set fluffy blanket in spin dryer first and then set bath towel on top of blanket inside the spin dryer and push it all down then close lid and turn on.. Pushing down gentle or hard on the clothes doesn’t seem to matter as long as they are pushed down. If you just toss them in the dryer can’t seem to balance correctly.  I really shove the clothes in and fill it to the top with no issues. I saw  many comments about it in the reviews saying that the shaking and bouncing was awful  and it will if you treat it like a normal dryer and the clothes are rung out and tossed in first. It shakes. A lot. I found tossing in soaking wet clothes works best and shoving the clothes down as flat as you can once in the spin dryer and making sure heaviest clothes are on top works best.. The I turn on and hold top of spin dryer down until I’m sure it won’t bounce, ten seconds tops.  If it does spin I rearrange the clothes slightly give a shove and try again. It rarely happens though if done correctly. Then I just wait for all the water to come out. If you can place it in a tub or over a drain it is easier because you don’t have to keep emptying a bucket but my small bucket fills twice max per load.I do keep two big square plastic dollar store buckets on hand. See photo. Because it will fill fast and you’ll need to pull it out to dump and place another under it while you do so. I stop my spin dryer when the water bucket fills half full. Wait a minute for water to slow. Dump bucket and then re start. This works best for me. The spin dryer has never taken more than two minutes to fully spin dry my clothes. It’s super energy efficient. Using it every other day my electric bill went up ten  dollars but I was also running Christmas lights every day at the same time. So I’m guessing that the spin dryer might cost five dollars a month to run. I personally love it but if you don’t have patience on trial and error and just want something that works perfect no matter what you do this probably isn’t going to be for you. Unless my machine isn’t normal and it came slightly broken or something it does seem to take a little practice. Hope this helps and if you do decide to purchase I hope you love it as much as I love mine.

For what it is, it works well - so the 5 stars. This would be great in your personal 'bar' for IMMEDIATE usage but is not really going to work as a IceMaker you can use for even a 12 hour period.
First it is not insulated (as it states in the instructions) and will NOT hold the ice (frozen) for ANY length of time.
Second, the Ice it creates has a lot of AIR which makes it freeze fast, but the physical quantity of 'frozen water' is not that much. This makes ANY style of this type of ice melt fast.
Third, when the water runs out, the unit shuts down. Meaning the bin of Ice will melt faster.
Let's say you were to leave it running 'unattended' expecting to have a bin full of ice a couple hours later: What would actually happen is it would make the first "ice" pretty quick and it starts to melt some. Ice would continue to be made and melt slightly until it ran out of water. At that point the Freezer shuts down,it warms up and the ice in the bin melts faster & faster. This thawed water will fall into the WATER RESERVOIR until it all melted and you would find it with no Ice, full of water and saying it needs water -OR- might restart and refreeze the thawed water, over & over again.
Also, the ice is really only good straight up; i.e. crushing or chipping would be marginal due to the air content.
LAST, I bought it to use in a true (commercial) ice shaver for a quickie snow cone without using every cube in the freezer and not having to wait or keep my freezer full of extra Ice Cubes. The "ICE" this unit creates will NOT work with a "Shaver" due to the AIR CONTENT.

The swap was successful for me but any contemplating the swap should do their own research and determine if  this would be safe for them in their application. Remember "TRUST BUT VERIFY" before attempting the swap. I am not advocating in any way. Your safety is your responsibility. Pictures attached show the model I received and how I wired my Maytag DE 712 to the W 10410892. The ground wire was attached to the clearly labeled ground on the motor switch. After reading many reviews, I decided to try these for my home Bunn Thermo Fresh, as it is so difficult to find the Bunn filters! Anyway, I received them and began to experiment with methods I'd read in the reviews, as yes, they ARE larger than the regular ones you buy. Placing the filter in the holder and then dampening it around the edges under a bare trickle of water from the sink works great, but I wanted a way to make it fit quickly and without any fuss--and I definitely was NOT going to take the scissors and trim them! No way--too much trouble. So, I kept experimenting with the filters and have found that the fastest and easiest way to make them work is to place the paper filter into the filter holder, and with your fingers on the inside of the holder against the paper filter, press the filter against the edge and 'scoot' it down towards the bottom. Do this all the way around (it only takes a few seconds) and you will see that the bottom of the filter has 'risen' a bit and has several little 'folds'--and that is fine! The coffee grounds will settle beneath those folds and the water will flow freely through them. It just so happens that the grinder bowl of the nifty little Epica coffee grinder I also bought on Amazon fits PERFECTLY down into the filter holder and after I grind my coffee, I invert it into the filter and it also helps to press the filter down deep into into the bottom edges. The greatest thing about these filters (other than the obvious one: the price) is that you will no longer have grounds in your coffee!!! These come all the way up to the top of the holder (unless you press it way down, further than you need to). I've had a problem from the beginning with the force of the water spraying coffee grounds over the top of the filter and then having them in the bottom of my cup! Yuk! I called Bunn and they sent me a special flow adapter that was supposed to rectify the problem--but it really didn't. I ended up just putting the original one back on and learning to live with it. This, however, has solved that problem. I am beyond 'tickled' with these filters!!!!

The original RLY02807 purchased five years ago was "Made in Slovakia" and I have included a pic that shows where the board appears to have suffered a burnout. This new replacement RLY02807 indicates it was "Made in Mexico" and works as expected. The design of the newer version is slightly different and hopefully an improvement.

I want to love this thing, but I've got a couple of complints that could be fixed with a little re-engineering.

First off, these are solid plastic bottoms. The other guys have mesh screening. This doesn't allow the coffee to flow through all the grounds. There's a few centimeters or so of a "bucket" at the bottom of the pod that basically just get wet without any flow through. I don't feel like I'm getting my money's worth, or strength, with this design.

Next is cleanup. The grounds left in the bottom just stick there. You've got to bang the crap out of them to get them loose, but even then it takes some water pressure and grounds going down the drain.

This could likely be fixed or at least a big improvement by adding a mesh screen to the bottom. Water will pass through all the grounds on the way to your cup, and then you can backwash the filter better to clean it up. They likely wouldn't stick as bad with a little air flow at the bottom.

Toying with the idea of drilling some tiny holes into it to get a little improvement.

Overall, decent product for a fair price. I'd definitely go 5 stars if they add a screen to the bottom of it.

If you're interested to hear how this compares to several other solutions I've tried, here goes – but the short answer is that this is my top-rated option for 4 or so decently-sized (not strict 8-oz) cups of coffee.

For mornings where it's just us, we used to be big on the AeroPress, and while I still love AeroPress coffee, the fact is I don't love to super-heat plastic. Now, we only take the AeroPress on motorcycle trips where space is a premium.

For larger groups, I recently bought both the Moccamaster KBT 741 and the Cuisinart PurePrecision Pour-Over coffeemaker (an electric "pour-over" simulator). Both of these machines are fantastic for larger groups; the flavor is unusually good for electric machines. Both have their drawbacks. The Moccamaster sprinkler feature is less than impressive and I find the coffee tastes better if I stir the grounds as the water begins to pour over it.

The Cuisinart can scald the flavor of the coffee if it's not removed from the burner, and I'd prefer a stainless carafe.

Both of these larger-capacity coffeemakers don't brew great coffee in small batches (2-3 cups). To get the same boldness of flavor for smaller batches, you have to use way too much coffee, because the water runs through the grounds too fast.

Enter this wonderful contraption. I love it so much I have bought two, so I can bring one into work where Keurig is the name of the game (I hate Keurig pods and the mediocrity they rode in on!). Whether you're brewing enough for one mug or four (that's about the max, and even that is a stretch), you get the same strength, providing your coffee-to-water proportion stays consistent. In fact, because you're pouring it yourself, you can gauge the color of the brew and it's easy enough to see when the brew is weakening and it's time to stop pouring.

I held out for a few months with my old electric kettle, trying to clumsily pour spirals and spilling on the counters with metronomic regularity. But I recommend taking the whole plunge and getting the gooseneck kettle, too. Pour-over is a lifestyle, my friends! There's a less-expensive but well-reviewed one on Amazon that works great, and I'm sort of enjoying the slow, attentive pour-over process; there's something a little bit Zen about it. You can kind of fix your focus on these slow, controlled spirals while you collect yourself in the morning, and with a cup of perfect coffee at the end, it's a hell of a lot more productive than pushing around sand with a tiny rake like those desktop zen gardens.

We bought this machine and it's matching dryer from Lowes for $1200 including setup, delivery, haul away, plugs, hoses and tax, We've only owned it for a week so I'm initially giving it 4 stars because I don't have any comment on it's long term reliability. I don't write many reviews but when I see all of the negative comments posted here about a machine that has gotten very good reviews elsewhere I feel forced to add my comments. We have done about 10 loads in this machine ranging from heavy bedding to everyday whites and colors. The machine is installed in a first floor laundry room on a vinyl covered floor. The drum was checked for level prior to using the first time. These machines replaced a failing 9 year old Whirlpool Duet front loader pair. We have observed the following:
1. The machine does not go out of balance during cycles, and is in fact quieter and vibrates less than the Duet.
2. Clothes do not remain stuck in position during wash cycles. They move.
3. Bleach placed into the dispenser does not leak out onto clothes before the machine is started.
4. Both machines are very quiet.
5. Both machines do their job well. The auto moisture sensor in the dryer is the best we have ever seen in a dryer.
6. It does use more water than the top loading Duet but not much.
7. You do not have to load the machine any special way. The manual says to put larger heavy objects on the bottom and we do. We spread clothes evenly in the tub and it washes perfectly fine that way.

I questioned the installer about vibration problems and he said that he had seen an occasional problem with machines placed on hard (concrete) floors and not leveled properly.

I will withhold the 5th star pending a longer observation period but these machines so far are quiet, efficient, easy to use, and well built.

Frankly, I am shocked at all the negative reviews for a paper coffee filter. I don't know how everyone else uses these but I have a couple reusable K-Cup housings with gold filters.

The gold filters let too much of the fine ground coffee through along with the oils and acids associated with brewing coffee with hot water. The result is coffee that doesn't really taste all that great and has a fine dusting of coffee grit at the bottom of every cup.

To fix this I started cutting my own filters out of a paper towel and found I could press them into the gold screen basket with a cough syrup measuring cup (the little cup that comes on top of the cough syrup bottle). That fixed the problem but added significant time to making my morning coffee so I started looking for a suitable replacement for the paper towel solution.

I found these SimpleCup filters rather quickly on Amazon and have never used anything else. I have never had any sort of issue with them other than a couple deformed filters. Since I was already familiar with using the cough syrup cup to press a filter into the cup, this wasn't much of an issue.

For at least the last 6 years I have been using this solution without any kind of paper filter failure. I have to assume the reviews of those having filter blowouts must be using some kind of cup that has no support (no gold screen basket) and expect the wet paper to hold back the pressure a single cup coffee maker generates against the coffee all by itself. My suggestion would be to look into a different replaceable K-Cup setup that works without filters; then add the filter to it.

This is an Aprilaire humidifier panel. If you have an Aprilaire humidifier that it fits you'll want to buy one to replace the old one at least once a year. Other than that, there's not much to these. They're a big mass of glued-up material that holds water.

Replacing this part is fairly easy. On mine, you press a lever on the bottom of the unit near the furnace and lift the cover off. Set that aside and you will be looking at the old panel inside a snap-together frame. The frame comes apart by just prying it in the right direction. Didn't take much. The previous owner hadn't cleaned mine in years, so I soaked mine in vinegar for a while to clean up the scale. Snap the new panel into the frame, put the bottom into the unit and push the top into place. It's just friction-fit in there. Put the outside cover back on by getting the top slots into place and snapping the bottom in and you're good to go for another year.

We had our contractor install this hood a couple of years ago when we remodeled our kitchen in 2011. We wanted something reasonably attractive, that didn't call attention to itself, that fit in our kitchen. On aesthetics, this hood was fine. Not an award winner, certainly, but quite acceptable and better tha most every other choice in its price category. We had installed a more expensive brand, imported, in another house, that we liked a lot, and in retrospect,we wish we had paid the extra amount to duplicate that earlier hood in this house, as this Broan has been a pain to live with. Two major functional problems with the design make it a hood that I would avoid.

1. It has some kind of sensor (heat? steam?) that automatically turns it on, at its special super-high and thus super-noisy speed, when you do something like boil pasta. Not immediately, but only after your pot has been boiling a bit, about the time the pasta is done and you're getting ready to sit down to dinner. Once it goes on this way, it cannot be turned off--there is no switch to turn it off. We couldn't believe this, assumed there must be a switch we couldn't find that was too obvious to mention in the manual, which didn't mention any, and so we finally called the local dealer for help. He confirmed there was no way to turn off this super loud fan once it turned on. That meant that every time we made pasta, we had to eat dinner to the accompaniment of a jet engine sound at our kitchen table. I finally installed my own switch in the electric line that feeds the hood, which is obviously hard wired and does not normally have a switch. Not something you would expect to have to do.

2. After about a year or so, we had to replace the light bulbs. That's perfectly reasonable. But the problem is that the normal pressure one must apply when screwing a bulb into the socket easily knocks the socket off its footing inside the hood. The bulbs then flop around and frequently the lights don't work. I had to take the hood apart to fix this (and that was feasible only because I had previously installed the switch, see number 1, and so could turn off all power going into the hood). Once apart, the problem was obvious: the sockets are themselves connected to the internal structure via a couple of flimsy clips that are clearly inadequate. You push on the bulb as you screw it in, and you knock the socket out of its footing inside the hood.

Both these design flaws are so obvious it's hard to imagine how any competent designer could have produced this product. I would stay away from this.

UPDATE: Just visited a friend who has the same hood--and who experienced precisely the same problem that we had with the bulb socket on the right side coming off.
UPDATE 2 (April 2014): Now both bulb sockets, right and left, come off, and somehow this happens over time in normal use, not just if you are replacing the bulb. Each time this happens, I have to spend a tedious and unpleasant half hour taking the hood apart (after cutting off electricity to it) to put the sockets back in place. I would not trust any positive review of this hood unless it is from someone who has owned it a couple of years--long enough to have had this flaw appear.

Marvelous! We've tried/tested several different devices for indoor-outdoor temperature & humidity (see my other reviews) and this one stands out among them for its features, especially ease of use, ease of viewing, and having the right info in the right place.

THE PLUSSES

It's easy to read from a distance; it properly puts temperature first, then humidity; includes a barometer-- and a graph of pressure for the past 24 hours, so you can see if weather is getting fairer or not; and has a Moon phase display which is great for those who enjoy stargazing.

You can also cycle the 24-hour graph through for indoor-outdoor temperature and humidity, too,

We got this one because it has humidity "calibration"-- you can alter the display +- a certain amount. However, we've found both temp and humidity quite accurate. That was gauged by comparing it to a set of regular thermometers and other gauges-- and to itself! You put the sensor next to the device indoors and see if the indoor-outdoor readings match.

The backlit colors are great, too; giving one a feel for the outside temperature by color code.

One big plus-- this operates off both electricity and battery. Best to leave it plugged in. The cord is long enough to put it on a table.

A PRO AND A CON

Now, the display is BRIGHT! That's great for seeing and reading it but, at night, the light is almost blindingly bright-- so much so that you'll think someone has left a light on in the room it's in! OK, no problem, as the top button can be pressed to turn off the light, then in the morning, you can turn it on again.

A NEGATIVE

However, pressing that top button takes a fair amount of pressure and you have to hold it down for a couple of seconds to turn the display on more than momentarily. This worked fine for us-- until this morning, when the kickstand broke off and the device slid off the table and crashed to the floor! Turns out that the kickstand is attached to the back only with two tiny plastic pieces that are easily broken off!

It's a real shame as it means the unit can no longer be propped up on its own for viewing! (We had a spare, inexpensive plastic mini-easel that works, though it looks poor aesthetically.)

The moral of this story is to use 2 hands to turn on the backlight-- one, to hold the unit and the other to press the top button. Otherwise, the pressure is transmitted directly to the kickstand and it will eventually break off, as it did to us.

In any event, other than that, it is a good product and now occupies the central place in our corral of indoor-outdoor devices!
EXCELLENT PRODUCT

I have a whirlpool dishwasher, model wdt730pahz. It has one serious flaw, and that is that there are 4 plastic clips securing each of the wheels of the top rack. A rack that gets quite a bit of use and movement and stress. These fragile plastic clips have broken one by one over the past 2 years since we bought the dishwasher brand new, and last week one wheel completely lost the post holding the wheel on!

After reading many reviews, and seeing that most part suppliers would only sell the full assembly that attaches to the upper rack, and this assembly STILL uses the 4 plastic clips, I figured it was worth the risk to try for a cheaper fix and this single, improved part.

The first 2 photos show the old, broken clips next to the wheel connected instead with a screw and washer. Already this seems like a vastly sturdier way to attach the track wheels.

A couple reviews for my particular model of dishwasher stated that these new wheels did not fit the track (too large), so they replaced them with their old wheels or shaved some plastic off them to make them fit. However, mine fit fine. I don’t know if they’ve changed the product, but you can see from my third photo that the new wheels are actually very slightly smaller than the original. I’ve saved my original wheels… just in case. But installed the piece with the new wheels still in place.

Installation was a little tricky. I think a video would have helped, but I managed to tinker around and figure out disassembly and reassembly one side at a time.

During assembly, I found one defect with the product: a rectangular hole, which is cut out so that another plastic piece can clip it to the rack, was not fully cut out. You can see in the 4th photo how some edges remained, so the clip wouldn’t sit flush inside as it was supposed to. Once I figured this out, all it took was a pocket knife to shave off these rough edges. This was surprisingly easy, which makes me a little concerned about the strength and quality of the plastic, so I will be keeping a close eye on it and updating my review if I notice any cracks or breaks in it over the next year of use.

Either way, once I shaved out that bit of plastic, the clip fit in perfectly. This seems like a strange oversight, since it’s such an important hole. Keep an eye out for that if you purchase this.

Once fully installed, the rack is a bit stickier to adjust up and down. I’m not sure if this compares to the old piece when the dishwasher was brand new, but it does feel like a tighter fit and takes more muscle to move it up and down. Maybe it’ll loosen up over time, maybe it won’t. I’ll keep an eye on this as well.

Overall and so far, I’m impressed and pleased that my fix ended up only around $17 instead of $60+!

- You can CALIBRATE the room temp +/- 5° easy as pie.

- Has a default cooling on/off deadband of 1.2° with option for 1.7°

The TINY click-click when it calls for heat/cool is typical of a stat using actual RELAYs on board which is a proven durable means of switching the furnace/ac lines. Its not annoying to me at all.

I was a little worried after reading a few reviews about the flavor being weak or grounds in the bottom of the cup. Here's what I learned. If coffee grounds are too big, the water runs through quickly and the coffee flavor is weak. Since I enjoy stronger coffee, I saturate the grounds and let steep and "bloom" for 30 seconds before slowly adding water around the edges of the filter. Water poured into the center it tends to go through more quickly, making weaker coffee. I noticed baristas pour slowly when they do a pour over.

For me, the key was getting the right size grounds. Since I like strong coffee, I use a finer grind which means I do have a tiny bit of grounds in the bottom of the cup. But since the coffee tastes great, I don't mind. After having 2 french coffee presses crack (took ten years) and then using a pour through with filters where the bottom of the filters would open up, causing a huge amount of grounds to go into the cup, I tried a brass and plastic model. But it was difficult to clean and I didn't like using something where the hot water would contact the plastic.

So this is perfect for me, easy to clean, and well-designed for one cup of coffee. Love there isn't plastic. But most important, the coffee tastes great. If your coffee is too weak, add more. I found with the larger grounds, I had to use 3 heaping teaspoons. The larger grounds had very little sediment but the taste for me was bland.

I recently received a Keurig K10 and a box of 18 single use K-cups of coffee as a gift. The single use K-cups worked fine, just like a TV commercial.....but these reusable cups...not so much.

As a number of other folks rating this product 1 or 2 stars have commented, not all the hot water is making it into the reusable cup and water is bypassing it (and the coffee grounds) and dripping into my wide mouth coffee mug resulting in a weak mug of coffee. I can see a thin and weak colored stream of coffee exiting the funnel tip with clear water dripping out on both sides of the housing.

The filters seem fine and I have not had any tear. The lid of the cup fits very loosely without the filter but sees to fit fine with the filter and with the filter filled with coffee grounds. I use a standard sized coffee scoop to add a single scoop of coffee grounds to the filter in the reusable cup, leaving it loose and not tamping down the grounds.

The cup fits fine in the housing BUT I have had to gently force the handle down a number of times since the fit of the puncturing "spike" is not perfectly aligned with the hole in the lid. (Of note, the cross section of the spike is not circular whereas the hole in the lid is...think of a rectangular tab trying to fit into a round hole). UPDATE: while explaining and demonstrating the situation to my wife, as I lowered the handle I had to use more force than before to close the housing. When I raised the handle to open the housing, the lid of the reusable cup was GONE! Where was it? It was impaled on the spike and had been lifted up along with the upper housing. Sigh....two stars drops to one star (and the only time I've ever wanted to give a product ZERO stars).

After looking at the whole setup, in addition to the poor fit of the spike into the lid I suspect the main cause is the reusable cup is not tall enough and that the rather beefy flexible seal around the base of the spike is not tight enough against the top of the lid allowing the pressure of the pump to force some hot water (1/3 to 1/2 on my machine) to "blow out" and spill over the sides of the reusable cup and not adding to the brewing process.

I don't see any way to easily correct this situation so I deem this product, at least in my machine, a FAIL.

There are a lot of features that I like and some not. Although the construction quality is decent, I didn't expect so much "chrome-colored" plastic. I expected some metal in a Cuisinart product. The K-cup holder system doesn't swing down like the Kuerig-branded models I've had. The Kuerig models are deigned with a cantilevered holder so that when you open the holder lever, the holder compartment flips down about 30 degrees to provide nice angle to insert the K-cup. Not so with this one. The holder is at a fixed angle, so that inserting and removing K-cups is a bit more cumbersome. Althtough I like that there is an included DYI single serve filter (in a cool little hide-a-way compartment), I expected it to be a refillable K-cup holder. But it's a complete replacement of the holder and a separate open filter cup. I don't like having to switch back and forth between the two "systems" to use K-cups and using my own grounds. I like that there are 5 cup sizes. Although there are separate buttons for "Brew", "Hot Water", and "Rinse", there isn't much functional difference between them. If you only want hot water or want to rinse the system, you still have to open and close the K-cup lid to "reset" the "Brew", "Hot Water", or "Rinse" buttons to use them. There is NO difference between "Brew" and "Hot Water" as far as I can tell. The serving size is the same, the water temp is the same, and the water is dispensed through the same spout. So, if you wanted Hot Water and you have an old K-cup still in the K-cup holder, you're going to get diluted coffee instead. So Cuisinart! What's the point of the separate buttons? The "Rinse" button seems to dispense about half the water volume, but is otherwise the same. My final complaint is that although, unlike the Kuerig models I've had, you can select water temperature (seems like a good feature), even the "X-Hot" isn't all that hot. The optimum coffee brewing temp is supposed to be 190 F (I forget where I read that), even the hottest temp is cooler than that.
So, I generally like this K-cup maker, it could be better.

Just got this after a long wait.  Turned it in and can only get it to make a small handful of cubes (about 1/4 cup) then it automatically goes into defrosting mode and melts all ice in bin! Fan is loudish, runs constantly when it is making ice. As expected. This is how compressors work. When they are making ice, the fan runs. Problem was, as others have noted, the lid is just plastic resting on the plastic storage bin so there is no seal of lid to bin, therefore the ice inside slowly melts down and drips back into the reservoir which then clears the "full" beam which triggers the machine to make new ice. So, even if you are not using any ice from the bin, the machine kicks in and makes a new set of cubes about every 30 minutes to replace the ice inside that has melted. I tried to add a simple rubber gasket to fix the issue, but could never get a good enough seal. Partly because the lid is so light it doesn't have enough weight to make a seal, but also because the curved nature of the lid design made a perfect seal impossible.

I finally folded up a heavy towel and draped it over the top of the whole machine so the lid is covered, and this solved the issue. Now the ice inside does not melt away while just sitting there. My wife hates that we have to leave a towel on top of it to make it not run all day and night, but that is what she gets for buying the 100$ ice maker.

So the question you have is: does this motor work? Yes, it works fine. I replaced the motor in my dryer fairly quickly, and we can now do our laundry again. So for usability and quality, I'm giving this high marks.

But installation really should be done by a professional, or at least a skilled amateur. The issue is the safety switch.

In the dryer, there's a spring tensioner with a pulley that keeps the belt tight and which also has a safety switch that shuts the motor off if the belt breaks. This keeps the motor from turning with no load (which will eventually overheat the motor and will probably damage your clothing.)

To solve that, you have to pull off the wire that goes to the safety switch on the motor and run the wire through the switch attached to the tension pulley. The thing the instructions don't explain well is how to do this - and the little bit of wire included with the motor is not right for the job, making things more confusing.

What you have to do is just connect the safety switch on the motor and the tension arm switch on the dryer in series: you do this by unplugging the wire connected to the overload switch and running it to one side of the tension arm switch. Connect a jumper wire from the other side of that switch to the overload switch on the motor.

Your old motor probably has a couple of loose wires dangling from the harness: you can use those, along with the Male-To-Male jumper that came with your replacement motor. If one of the jumper wires doesn't fit the terminals on the Male-Male jumper, you can cut your original jumper and use the bare wire and wire nut that came with the motor.

Rather than use the wire nut, I elected to do a solder splice and cover that with shrink tubing. That made a nice, clean splice that looks like a factory job.

You actually *can* install this motor without using the cutoff switch on the tension pulley, but it's probably not entirely safe to do so. If you don't feel comfortable making wiring modifications to your dyer, then it's probably worth calling repair man or looking up a video on replacing the motor.

UPDATE after almost a week:
Bumped up to 3 stars from 2 because, well, it does actually make ice. Here are my observations after some use.
1) It does make good ice slightly faster than the GE/FirstBuild Opal
2) It is LOUDER than the GE/FirstBuild Opal
3) The top-load design is tall, but superior to the GE/FirstBuild Opal in my opinion because the GE/FirstBuild Opal we owned always tended to leak out the front. Their solution was risers that tilted the device, but that had issues, too. If you let the Opal run all day, it would condense and leak out the front. When we had the GE/FirstBuild Opal, we had to keep a water tray under it at all times. The NewAir is MUCH better in that regard.
4) The NewAir has a superior water reservoir compared to the GE/FirstBuild Opal. NOTE that I'm not consider the extra tank available on the Opal. (I didn't own that.) Filling the water reservoir on this machine will produce several cycles of ice.
5) The user interface on this device is, at best, simple. Once it "detects" full (and I'm dubious it's actually detecting anything), the only way to make more ice is to power cycle the machine. That's right. You have to push the button to turn it off and then push the button to turn it back on. You cannot interrupt an ice cycle. Once you've pushed the button to make it start, push it again all you want but it will not stop. You have to unplug the machine. Why would you want to stop an ice cycle? Because it's so loud that you want to eat in peace. The Opal included a bluetooth interface, scheduling, etc. that was great.

Overall, I like this machine because it's solid and makes ice. But receiving a machine that leaked water all over my counter, the sound when it operates, and the not-quite-there user interface really detract from what could be a great ice maker.

What would I change? The price. I think a lower price point would be more appropriate for this machine's lack of sophistication. It makes ice, but it doesn't do so in a $500 way. They're trying to compete with Opal at $500, but that machine is much more elegant. They need to compete on price to be compelling.

UPDATE after over a month: (went up to 4 stars)
OK, I've come to really like this machine. Yes, it's loud. Yes, the user interface is quirky/unpolished, but it does crank out the ice. And it's very easy to maintain. It also seems easy to work on if the need should ever arise. Everything in the machine is designed to be accessible, easy to replace, etc. (Although, replacement parts haven't shown up on their site yet.) Regardless, with some adaptation on our part, it seems like a great machine. I think the problem is that I expected it to just quietly sit there full of ice. It doesn't. It runs one cycle at a time. Once it's full, you have to recycle it, etc. (Like I said, quirky.) The trick is knowing such things and adapting. Now, we normally make ice in the morning and just store it in an insulated ice bucket for use throughout the day. Not perfect, but good. (And, again, it seems mechanically simple and solid.)
