The inside of our Samsung fridge has been leaking icy water into the space under the deli tray for at least 2 years. We kept tongs and a face cloth next to the fridge (how attractive), used several times a day to mop up the water, or it would freeze and prevent the deli tray from opening. Recently, I went to pop out a shelf and it seemed to be stuck. Upon closer inspection, I saw ICE had formed in all of the shelf-holding slots. Very quickly, it got worse. Now there was ice protruding from all around the edges of the cover panel at the back, inside wall of the fridge. Then this plastic cover panel began to bulge out with more and more ice building up behind it. The last straw was when it became so cold from all of this ice that it started freezing my produce.  -And as a side note, this was not the only problem. When we pulled out the fridge, there was a dripping ice formation on the back, right under the connection box for the water filter/ice maker. We never connected the fridge to a water line, so there was no reason whatsoever for any water to exit that area, except that it was coming through from the mess under the deli tray inside the fridge. We came to find that this dripping water had begun to rot the plywood under the flooring.-  Anyway, I started looking at new fridges. My husband started looking on YouTube.  Everyone was using this little gadget.  A few bucks compared to about $3000 for a new fridge. We decided to try it. The process was not easy. Even with an oscillating heat fan running inside, it took a day to thaw enough ice to pry the panel off. And it was still ice packed in behind. That was the VERY hard part.  My husband removed the old drain clip and I put on this new one -  in about a minute.  At first, we had a small amount of water reappear in the deli tray and drip from the back. Must have been residual, as it stopped after two days. It has been a couple of months now, and we have no leaking water - inside or out - and zero ice inside the fridge. We couldn’t be happier! This little gadget bought me the time I need so that I can wait for my kitchen remodel to buy a new fridge - which will NOT be a Samsung.

My first review for the Kalita paper (with Kalita dripper) was not very happy. Overall I thought it too small to make a big mug of coffee efficiently, and I ended up with coffee that was not sufficiently hot or strong. To get stronger coffee, I ground more coffee beans than usual, and used up my expensive beans much faster. I tried using 2 or 3 Kalita filters to slow the brewing time, but additional Kalita filters revealed an unacceptable paper taste.

However, I love the pretty, glass Kalita dripper, so I experimented and FOUND A SOLUTION to balance prep time, heat loss, and coffee strength. I made two mugs of coffee, using same freshly ground beans and mugs and 205 degree water. Only the filters were different. I carefully squished a [[ASIN:B00WA6TGDE Melitta Cone Coffee Filters Natural Brown #4 (100 Count (Pack Of 3))]] into the Kalita dripper. It fit perfectly in contact with both sides and bottom. After prewarming with 205 degree water, I added freshly ground whole beans (using Peet's Sulawesi for those who want details) and poured the first water, also @205, watching the coffee bloom. (I love that moment.) After a minute, I slowly poured hot water through the grounds. The water did NOT rush through the Melitta as it did with the Kalita filter. It took its mellow time, and resulted in a PERFECT and still HOT mug of coffee. I give the Kalita dripper a 5 now, and the Kalita filters a 1. Hope this experiment helps other perfectionist coffee drinkers!

I already had the original broken coupling out and both the transmission and motor shafts cleaned up. I tried both halves of the new coupling on both shaft ends and in either case I could only get either one on about .125 even with light tapping. I did not want get the couplings stuck on the shafts so I pried them off. There were drag marks on the flats so I set to work with a small fine cut file. File a little off both sides of the flat, test fit, file again, test fit again, etc. until I had a snug fit and each half of the coupling shouldered out on a shaft end. I pried the couplings off, applied a very thin coat of white grease and put everything back together. The grease is not necessary but just a precaution to prevent the metal bushing from seizing the shaft.

I did not consider the "filing to fit" to be an "extra effort" since the fit was already very close. Due to normal manufacturing tolerances on the coupling and shaft it is better to have to remove a bit of material to insure a snug fit than risk a loose fit.

IMO If you want to insure a snug fit and eliminate any chance you may have to file a off a bit of material, I recommend you get one of the OEM couplings without a metal bushing. The plastic will deform to fit the shaft as you tap it on.

The connector on the filter is made out of really crappy plastic. It bends and leaves you unable to replace the filter as it leaves the internal "nubs" mis-aligned.

If you are unable to put in your new filter, it's likely because the part in the refridgerator is not turned all the way. Fear not! it's an easy fix. Depending on the LG model, the little nubs should be at 12' o clock and 6' o clock, or 3' o clock and 9' o clock position.

To fix the issue:
1. Take the old filter, file off the knobs (see image)
2. Look into the hole that the filter goes in. You will see two little nubs. Likely just off of the 12-6 or 3-9 position. Take note of the direction they need to turn to go back to 12-6 or 3-9 (depending on fridge model). It should only be a bit off.
3. Insert the modified filter into the fridge, as if you are putting in a new filter. Push it in all the way, and slowly turn just a little bit in the direction needed to get the internal nubs back to 12-6 or 3-9
4. Pull the filter out, look into the hole, and check if the nubs are at 12-6 or 3-9. If they are not, repeat step 3.

5. Try installing the new filter, if it goe sin, great! if not, repeat steps 3 & 4.

6. Save the modified filter so you can fix your filter nubs in the future if needed.

Purchased the refrigerator (Whirlpool Model GI6FDRXXY04) in 2012 from a local scratch and dent store. Various parts have failed throughout the years and it was now time to replace the ice maker. A big thank you to my deceased father for all those years of making me "hold the light", it seems that time was worth while after all. The replacement part came quickly and though I initially thought it was dirty or used, it seems that the grease is simply lubricant. Without any instructions I availed myself of the University of YouTube. The original support clamps are no longer in use for this model as it appears there was a manufacturing change at some point and the supports have been replaced with an under carriage that is not documented or videoed anywhere that I could find. Three bolts later I was at least able to loosen the original part and wiggle it out of a resting position. The new one easily connected to my existing electrical harness so the two that came with the replacement were not needed. A couple of more wiggles to get the new part in and we were off to the races. The key part here is to get the intake funnel (the part that transfers the water from the refrigerator into the ice maker) aligned without having the shutoff arm come out. In my case I'm pretty sure I only got it "close enough". Return the three support bolts to the under carriage assembly and turn the refrigerator back on. About 6 hours later I heard a sound I had not heard in a year. The whole family looked up in amazement as we realized the house was not being broken into, our first produced ice in a year had finally come!
A side note, this refrigerator also had a bad water inlet (part Whirlpool W10498990 Water Inlet) which I had replaced previously. In my case the ice maker had stopped a year ago followed by the water dispenser six months ago. Although, replacing the water inlet did not fix the ice maker directly, I am pretty sure that this was an indirect cause of the ice maker failing.
One thing is for sure, Whirlpool makes you a more educated home repairman. Thank you for that and thanks Dad for always insisting on fixing our own things rather than calling out the experts. I may not have appreciated it at the time but I understand now...and insist my own son holds the light. Guess I've leveled up.

The part that tells the humidity level is a bit iffy in lower humidities. My house got very dry last winter, and I bought these as well as a humidifier. After about 10 minutes of turning them on, three of the four synchronized enough that they were within 2 degrees and 5% humidity difference from one another. That's what the manufacturer states is the range they might vary at (if you need something more accurate, you also need something more powerful and thus more expensive). The fourth one, although it's temperature was within the 2 degrees, it's humidity reading was always 10% or more lower than the others. Now, we're talking less than 20% humidity max. Over time, I noticed as the house got less dry (from running my humidifier) that the 4th one now varied between 7 and 10%. I figured I had just got a fluke, and put it in a room I didn't care so much what the humidity was. Well, this summer as the humidity has increased to above 50%, I noticed that its humidity indicator had "caught up" with the others. So these are less accurate at lower humidities, although that is consistent with my understanding of how these things work.

I do wish they came with a light, maybe something like what watches have, where you push a button and the screen glows. That's definitely not a big deal; it's just that sometimes when I would wake in the night, I would want to check the temperature or humidity levels.

Overall, these were a good purchase.

I am surprised by the negative reviews here. I have owned this dryer for over a year and my experience has been very positive. Coming from a conventional, vented gas dryer, I expected long, slow drying times but did not get this at all. We changed from large, conventional washer and dryer to the European-sized models so we don't cram every possible piece of dirty clothes into one load. I typically run 4-5 smaller loads per week: dark, light, white, towels and jeans, and dress shirts. This dryer does a great job of drying all these clothes types, especially if you take advantage of the special settings. For me, the key is to remove clothes immediately at the end of the cycle. This is true of all dryers, IMO, but especially with this one. It *does* leave a small amount of residual moisture in the clothing, depending on setting. If you pull clothes out while they're warm, then fold or hang immediately, almost all the wrinkles disappear without ironing.

If I have one complaint, it's that the dryer only rotates one direction. This means very large items (california king sheets, for instance) can get tangled and not dry evenly.

There is one MAJOR advantage to this dryer. Living in a drought-prone area, I put the drain hose into a bucket and recover one to two gallons of water from each load that I use to irrigate my garden. Clean clothes, happy tomatoes. What's not to love?

After a careful review of the wide array of countertop oven-gap fillers, this thoughtfully but simply designed product seemed the best for my situation (and I suspect for any situation). I don't usually get enthusiastic about simple products, but this one deserves praise. Its form, fit, & function make it a piece of intelligent design. Clearly, the inventor and fabricator thought about the problem and followed the KISS principle.

Our new stove top stands about a half-inch above the countertops to the left and right. So, none of the silicon "T" section products would have fit without awkwardly lapping up over the edge of the stove. (Plus, these are wide and unattractive.). This product is crafted from durable, cleanable stainless steel. Each filler lies flat (almost flush) against the countertop and the stove edge, and together they look as if they are part of the stove top, not like something awkwardly grafted on. The adjustable springs make installation very easy (the ease of installation in the video on Amazon is completely accurate) -- and if, need be, the fillers can be removed if the stove has to be moved for repair or for cleaning. The footing under my stove was uneven and the top needed to be leveled. So one of the stove-to-countertop gaps was very narrow; and I was unsure how the filler strip would fit. But with the most minimal manipulation, the filler strip fit right in. The result is perfectly symmetrical, and both right and left gaps are invisible.

Yes, this product costs a bit more, but it's well worth it -- especially when you consider what stoves and countertops cost to make them look good. You can buy this product with confidence.

Replacing the evaporator motor in a refrigerator is ABSOLUTELY a DIY job. It's also a BIG job and an hours-long commitment. Plan on two hours minimum.

The reviews here and elsewhere complain that this part does not include a new thermistor or grommet. These people are idiots. The OEM part WR60X10185 does NOT come with a new thermistor or new grommet! This part ONLY includes the evaporator motor, four hard-wired conductors (wires), and a 6-pin male Molex connector, of which four pins are filled--the other two are for the thermistor pins which you must insert manually. ANY instance of a WR60X10185 that includes the thermistor and grommet should be considered used or held suspect!

Some reviewers also mention that the thermistor wires must be cut to complete this repair. These people are idiots. No wires must be cut for this repair! The correct repair procedure for the evaporator motor replacement is as follows:

The thermistor shares the 6-pin Molex connector with the evaporator motor (the former uses two pins; the latter uses four). The thermistor AND evaporator motor wires, six total, pass thru the grommet together. After accessing the fan shroud/motor mount assembly, disconnect the 6-pin Molex connector serving the thermistor and evaporator motor and remove the entire assembly from the freezer compartment. With a paper-clip, small jewelers screwdriver, or (best) a Molex pin removal tool, push the two pins serving the thermistor from the old Molex connector. Remove the grommet from its slot in the assembly. Carefully cut the grommet along ONE seam and pull all six wires from the now-slotted grommet. Transfer the fan and spacer from the old evaporator motor to the new. Remove the old evaporator motor from its mount and install the new motor. Separate the grommet and press the four evaporator motor wires in--be careful to match the grommet orientation as before. Separate the grommet and press the two thermistor wires in, then press the grommet into its slot in the assembly. Press both thermistor pins into the open holes in the Molex connector--pin placement is not important--then reconnect the Molex connector to the harness. Reinstall the assembly into the freezer compartment.

The tamper needs to be metal or hard plastic, something that will firmly pack a coffee in place. I modified the tamp procedure and was able to get a good crema and the coffee tasted good.

As I was a barista for many years there are many things you need to consider when you’re making good espresso. These things include the age and quality of the coffee, the tamp, and the grind. Fresh roasted beans will need to be a little less finer with a little less tamp where as older beans that has been open for some time or preground will need a finer grind and a hard tamp. The trick is to get the grind and tamp down in order to make a good espresso with a nice crema. It will take patience and trial and error to get this down and the more you do it the more you’ll get used to it. With the kit I received, the tamper/scoop didn’t work but I was able to scoop the coffee and press it on the edge of the container and then I tamped with my finger to get it packed. My 1st cup came out pretty good. I will be ordering a metal tamp right now😉.

Making good espresso is a skill and it will take some time to perfect. Remember each time you buy new beans you will have to adjust your method as you will also have to adjust as the beans get older and dryer.

I bought this hood here at Amazon and installed it last week.

Today I was in a local Best Buy and noticed they had an appliance section with high end equipment. (First time I've been in a Best Buy in maybe ten years; is it an illustration of Amazon dot com's success?) I saw about a dozen range hoods made by Viking, Thermador and Vent-a-Hood, and though I was no longer in the market, I was curious how my hood compared with the big dogs.

Bottom line up front: the Cavaliere has the same, often better, quality for half or less the cost.

Some of the most expensive hoods used the same type filter system, where you grasp the bottom of the filter to extract it from the hood in order to put it in the dish washer. The Cavaliere, in fact, has larger handles, easier to grasp.

A few of the hoods had their filters off, giving me a chance to look underneath at the fans. Some hoods had only one (!?) fan. Even the hoods with two fans, those fans didn't look as large or rugged as the fans in the Cavaliere.

Most of the hoods had controls in front (like the Cavaliere), but some had them underneath the hood. That seems a sure way to get covered with steam and grease, and is why I didn't buy a Broan at Lowes.

The only way I saw that some of the big-dog hoods were better than the Cavaliere is that their controls were push button. Want to turn the lights on or off? Push a button. Want to decrease the fan speed? Push a button. Want a higher speed? Push a different button. And so on.

I like this method. Switches are easy and inexpensive to replace, plus there's not a lot about switches that can break.

Which leads me to my main concern with the Cavaliere: it's that while the Cavaliere uses more elegant controls than switches -- simply tap a screen -- the controls need an electronic circuit board to make them work.

In other words, everything -- on/off, lights, fan speeds, timer, clock -- goes through the circuit board. If the board goes out, so does the hood.

In fact, that's what happened to me, and is instructive in this review.

I installed the hood with the help of a pro. The hood weighs about 60 pounds, too much for my wife to hold while I'm drilling screws into the underside of the cabinet. When we then tested the hood, the fans worked but the lights wouldn't turn on, neither by using the hood's control panel nor by using the remote control. (Yes, we also get a neat little remote.)

I emailed tech support and got a reply the same day. (Big points there.) The email gave me a phone number to call. I then talked with a tech in Support, describing the situation. To be sure I had all the parts needed to fix the problem, the tech sent me a new circuit board, a new control panel, and two cable assemblies. (More points.)

Long story short, the new circuit board fixed the problem. (Still more points.)

However, replacing a circuit board in this hood is not at all like replacing a circuit board in a desktop computer. It's not a case of dropping it into a connector. Almost ten wires have to be attached to the board, and the location of the board is awkward to access. I was an electronic maintenance tech in the Army many years ago, but someone without experience with wires and circuit boards in tight places will probably find themselves in the deep end of the pool.

I don't know what Cavaliere would have done if I couldn't have fixed the hood. I'm not sure if they have techs to send to our homes. It may not even be something they can do.

So let me summarize:
1. The hood's quality and appearance are first rate and impressive. Thick stainless steel, solidly put together, 900 CFM, quiet (even quieter than the 200 CFM hood it replaced), halogen lights easy to remove and replace (unlike other hoods, according to reviews here at Amazon).

2. Tech support is excellent, responsive to both email and telephone.

3. The price is many hundreds of dollars less than other more famous brands.

4. However, repairs - even warranty repairs - are done by the homeowner. (If I'm wrong on this, am hoping someone from Cavaliere will correct me.) That's the nature of buying something online and not from a local retailer, so it's not the fault of Cavaliere. We pay much less for the hood in return for taking on some risk if the hood needs repair.

My wife, a great and enthusiastic cook, loves this hood. She had misgivings about our spending so much money for a brand we'd never heard of and from an online retailer. (By the way, the shipping box is excellent. No worries in that area.) Now she thinks I'm a very smart fellow (finally, after 45 years).

If the hood continues to work, it will be one of the best purchases I've ever made. If it doesn't, I'm not sure where I'll find someone to fix it.

19 June 2017, an update a couple years later. Everything is still running perfectly. Once or twice a year the fan and lights turn on by themselves. Has never happened in the middle of the night, when it would wake us up. Am pretty sure something is sending an erroneous signal to the hood, but as infrequently as it happens, I haven't yet seen a pattern. I have a plastic dishwasher, so instead of the magnet I have been using the self adhesive velcro. Unfortunately, the velcro is attached to a cardboard piece very poorly attached behind the magnet. This is an exact replacement. Thus, it will fail again if you use it to pause the dryer. My dryer would not tumble, so I removed the top (two screws) and the front (two more screws) and swung the front to the left side. Using a VOM, I checked the continuity of the door switch. It was intermittent, but mostly not working. So I replaced it. Still the motor would not start. So I tested every other part that was possibly failing--except the controller. Everything else was working. It had to be the controller--or more specifically the motor relay. A new controller fixed the dryer.

Actually, the new controller, which fits many different models, made the dryer work better.

I analyzed the old door switch and failed relay. What I found was that using the door to pause the dryer caused arcing in the door switch after a thousand or two pauses, the switch contacts were burned off on the motor side (the other side turns the interior light on and off.). Interestingly, the motor relay had the same problem. Interesting that they failed simultaneously.

The new controller board, however, changes the way the door switch functions by not permitting the door switch to turn on the motor back on. One must press the start/pause button on the controller. This prevents the door switch from arcing. The controller also seems to have other improvements, doing a better job of controlling the heater coils and determining how long the drying cycles will take to complete. But note, the initial time on the first run will be very long. The controller learns as it goes. After 30 or so loads the time is rather accurate.

We bought a Keurig from Costco a few months ago which came with Keurig's My K-Cup reusable filter. Using that filter was a bit of a hassle since you have to pop out the normal K-cup holder from the machine and replace it with the new My K-Cup assembly. If you like to switch back and forth between brewing your own grind and using K-cups, this quickly becomes a chore since you have keep swapping the two different assemblies. The ekoBrew fits into the standard K-cup assembly which removes the need to keep swapping things out.

Capacity - both the My K-Cup and ekoBrew hold about the same amount of coffee.

Coffee taste - I did the "used K-cup hack" on the My K-Cup - where you trim a used K-cup and put it in the My K-Cup to help increase the brewing time. I think the My K-Cup with this change brews a slightly stronger cup of coffee than the ekoBrew does. It's not a huge difference though and only noticable to me in back to back tasting.

"Mud" - The ekoBrew does seem to result in slightly more very fine grinds ending up in the bottom of your cup. It doesn't bother me personally.

Cleaning - I think the ekoBrew rinses out more easily than the My K-Cup, mostly thanks to the mesh bottom (the bottom of the My K-Cup filter is solid plastic).

Overall, I think the ekoBrew definitely wins out and is cheaper to boot (assuming you buy the My K-Cup separately that is).

Whats good:
1) great price given the size. Most refrigerators of this price range barely hold enough for one. This one can get our family of 5 through for a week and a half room wise.
2) It works great. It does exactly what it should and keeps everything cold- do not set it to the coldest, thats overkill especially on the bottom half.
3) I love that they did not try to change up which end was the frozen food. It is extremely awkward and can lead to back problems if the frozen stuff (which is always heavier) is on the bottom. This design keeps the freezer on top which prevents the physical strain.
4) the shelves are easily shifted to fit everything where you want it. No more trying to decide which shelf can fit what- prefer drinks up top? set the shelves appropriately. Prefer them mid or bottom? adjust how you will.

Downside:
1) the freezer is a little small. That said, I still like the fact that even the freezer has a shelf that can be adjusted- no more having to pull everything out to get the thing buried in the back!
2) I thought this fridge was larger than it actually was, but that was my fault for miscalculating. So not really the company at fault- just a note to those buying to make sure they properly measure things.
3) It was a little slow to cool down. I don't know if this is typical of all new fridges, but I was glad I had not purchased anything that needed to stay frozen or I would have been in trouble.

Over all, once this is set up and has had about 5 or 6 hours to reach its normal running temps, this fridge is great for the price. If you do not absolutely have to have enough food to feed an army at all times, this is a much better deal than spending over a grand on a bigger fridge- or 700 on a fridge that belongs in a hotel room.

An installation tip... The nylon triangles that act as wheel retainers are tough to remove. Because the wheels come with new ones, I simply cut the outermost old ones off, cleaned and lubed the axle/shaft, slid the new wheel on and pushed on a new retainer. (I left the old backmost retainers in place because it would have been difficult to slide a replacement retainers past the front retainer groove on the shaft.)

The dryer is SO much quieter now, I'm wishing I'd done this much sooner. As for longevity, these appear to be softer rubber than the originals, but I'd happily do this every few years to keep this good old dryer running quietly.

I have an older LG washer that was getting loud when I’m the spin cycle. The last time I took the washer apart for a repair, I recall seeing these dampers and googled if they go bad. Sure enough, they do and you will typically see an oily residue come out of them when they are no longer effective. The other thing that shows the dampers are not working is when you push the washer tub and it bounces freely instead of feeling some resistance. Think of it as blown shocks on a car.

Installing these is a process, the top, front and rear panels need to come off. All edges of washers sheet metal are sharp and if you don’t wear gloves you will get cut. Removing the plastic pins that hold these dampers in place is also a pain but easier if you use a socket over the pointy part of the pin. This depresses the tab while you pull from the other side. I would recommend finding some YouTube videos of this repair as a reference.

If you do plan to take on this repair, unplug the electrical and let it sit for a while to dissipate any energy in the motherboard and be mindful of any water lines. I did my install with the water lines still connected with no issues. Wear gloves, get a good headlight to see into the washer, take photos of where all the screws and pieces go and work slow. Replace one damper out at a time to help support the tub.

Once you remove the old dampers that are leaking oil, you will be able to cycle them up and down about an inch with no resistance, that is a sign and reason why the washer was so loud.

Don’t know the longevity of these new dampers but the first few wash cycles have been drastically quieter then before replacing these dampers.

We ran a load of towels through the normal way using soap and hot water.

I purchased a box of filters specifically made for reusable pods and tried that. Using the filters eliminated the sediment and the coffee was clear. I fill with medium ground coffee (that I had on hand), leaving about 1/4" space at the top, close and press firmly to seal the lid all around. Maybe halfway through the brewing process coffee starts dribbling at the front edge as well as the stream going into the cup. I just position my mug to catch both. Clean-up is easy, just remove the filter with the coffee grounds over the trash can and tap the lid on the side of the trash can to remove grounds stuck on the inside of the lid. Then rinse thoroughly and air dry. Yes, the actual K Cups are more convenient and don't leak or dribble and you toss the whole thing, but for the price difference it's really not that big of a deal. I've been using an almond nut milk bag for the last two years. Filtering is a pain and I found I needed to filter twice after using the nut milk bag. I purchased this organic cotton cold brew coffee bag and it works pretty good, but not completely sludge free. Here's how it went down: I used 12oz of Peet's Major Dickson's blend whole beans. I use a burr grinder and had it set on the coarsest grind. Placed the ground coffee in the bag and cinched it up tight. Placed in a gallon container and filled with cold filtered water and sat on the counter for 24 hours. When it was finished, I noticed a small layer of sludge on the bottom of the container. I took out the filter bag and gently squeezed the bag, then dumped the grounds. Mind you, not near as much sludge when using the nut bag. I only had to filter it one time to get it perfect. This is an amended review: the EZ-Cup holder and filter combo really does work very well. The holder is the size and shape of a K-Cup, with a lid that snaps on. You put coffee grounds or tea leaves in a filter that's also shaped like a K-Cup and has a flap on top. This is essentially what a K-Cup is.

Something I didn't know when I first used it: if your Keurig produces higher pressure than normal, the filter could tear and deposit coffee grinds or tea leaves in your cup. If that happens, use two filters for added strength. (They're inexpensive, so it's no big deal.) The company's president told me that in the next few weeks, they will have filters that are twice as strong, so it won't be necessary to double up.

You should also grind the coffee very fine -- one notch coarser than espresso, on the commercial grinder at the store. This is the grind used in K-Cups and is different from what's used in the My K-Cup re-usable assembly made by Keurig (the wire basket of the MKC will get clogged with a fine ground).

I find the EZ-Cup to be a much better product than the MKC for two reasons: it fits the standard holder, so you don't have to keep swapping them out (I was afraid of breaking the small tabs on the holder), and you don't have to clean a basket full of compacted waste. Just pop out the used filter and toss it in the trash or compost bin. The filter package seems to be made of PET plastic, so that gets recycled with bottles.

I received one of these items with my Keurig machine which I purchased elsewhere about 2 years ago. It was an excellent addition to the coffee maker, as I soon realized that purchasing K-cups would get expensive. With the My K-cup item, I get the benefit of the single-serve coffee maker (1 cup of fresh, fast hot coffee without wasting any), and still have the freedom to choose any type of coffee I want. Some people have mentioned having problems with this item, but I have found most problems can be avoided by doing the following:

1)Do not pack the coffee tightly into the cup, or try to fill it completely to the top. A little space is needed at the top, to avoid ending up with a sludgy mess.
2)Make sure the plastic portion, the rim of the cup, and the outside of the cup is free of any coffee that may have spilled over.
3)Make sure the needle part is clean, as residue can affect the dispensing of the coffee (but this is true with the K-cups as well).

I love my Keurig machine but I’m not so happy using the wasteful and environmentally unfriendly k-cups. I had been using a refillable pod that is much bigger than this one and which required the user to take out the K-cup holder insert that has the needle in it (see photo for comparisons of old one and this new one). It was a pain. So I decided to find one that would fit in the machine exactly like a k-cup does. This one will now be the only one I use, and here’s why:

This pod is the exact same size as a k-cup so you can pop it in your machine without any modifications to your Keurig machine.

It is so simple to use, just fill, set the lid on top and use exactly as you would a K-cup. My old one was basically a big case for a reusable filter so it had more pieces and required more cleaning. This one is simple and sleek.

Cleaning is so easy! Let it cool and then tap out the used grounds into the trash and wash the pod.

K-cups are expensive! This will save you a lot of money if you are like me and you drink a lot of coffee. You get two pods and I feel the price is good considering how much it will save you long term.

A few notes to keep in mind. There are no instructions. Sounds like a weird complaint, after all it is a self explanatory type of device. However the product description on Amazon shows that it must be placed into the coffee machine with the arrows facing up and down and the rectangles to the side. Honestly I don’t think it matters how it goes in, but if those instructions are in the product description they should also come printed with the item either on the packaging or on an instruction sheet.

Also, being stainless steel, it gets hot! My old one was plastic and I could remove it immediately and clean it. You can not do that with this pod unless you use something to grab it with because it is hot! You will probably want to give it a little while to cool before touching it.

Overall I am extremely pleased with this, a definite upgrade from my previous one!

I had my ice maker in my Frigidaire stop working about a year ago. I did some basic troubleshooting and did not have time to fix; because...life. When I finally came up for air and did more research on the issue, I found out (as you all probably already know), that a common problem with the factory units is that a little heater coil (yes a heater coil in an ice maker) fails. After discovering the issue, I ran across this exact replacement here at Amazon. I ordered it, it arrived, and I removed the old one and installed this new one.

I unplugged the old ice maker from the freezer. There are two 1/4 inch screws that have to be removed from where the old unit is mounted into my freezer. Back the screws out *almost* all the way. I then removed the old ice maker, installed the new one, tightened the screws, and plugged this bad boy in. 1 hour later, I heard this noise. A noise that I had not heard in quite some time. It was the glorious noise of ice being dispensed into a long- empty ice tray! Woohoo! It is the simple things in life that you take for granted. Note* i did not have to turn off the water to the freezer at all to change the ice maker out. This is just my experience, but I recommend that you refer to the install instructions and follow them carefully. I am a reasonably handy person and this was an easy replacement after I figured out that I needed a 1/4 inch socket on the end of a drive handle. One like this: https://www.amazon.com/GreatNeck-ND72-Professional-Driver-7-Piece/dp/B004FEJEZO/ref=sr_1_11?keywords=1%2F4+socket+driver+handle+sae&qid=1554991866&s=gateway&sr=8-11.

We've had ours for over a year and learned some things about it.

It makes nugget ice! Lots of nugget ice! Crunchy nugget ice!

It requires regular routine maintenance. This is not a maintenance free appliance.
You MUST use filtered water. Good filtered water.
You MUST clean it with bleach once a week. (Bacteria)
You MUST clean it with vinegar once a month. (Mineral buildup)
You will see nasty stuff grow if you don't. You will not like it and it will break down if you don't maintain the machine. Of course, this is true for its larger Scotsman and Hoshizaki cousins as well.
After about 6 months, you'll want to blow it out with compressed air (low psi) or canned air to get all the dust bunnies out. (See below)

it's loud. It's has an AC compressor in it. It has fans running. Find a place in your kitchen away from the living room or better, put it in room away from the living area.

It needs a lot of space. It needs really good airflow to keep it running smoothly. We keep about 4" of space on both side of the vents free and clear so that airflow is optimum. It's obvious when it isn't because ice production is significantly reduced. After time, dust buildup will also cause ice production to slow down and it will need to be vacuumed/blown out. It doesn't have to be opened, just use a tool to clean from the vent areas.

All in all, this is a wonderful and amazing home appliance. We will always want one in our house from now on!

Prepare yourself for a fair bit of cardboard when unpacking this. The first thing you will notice is that the machine is white, not silver - that's because it's covered in an awful lot of plastic film that you will have to carefully peel off. This is a major nuisance and may have you cussing.

Once you've got your machine unwrapped and positioned on the counter top close to the sink it's time to give it a thorough clean. You would hope that wouldn't be neccessary with a new appliance but, trust me, it really is. Peel off the tape securing the front of the lid, open it (it's hinged at the top) and un-tape the basket and scoop so you can give them a thorough wash.

You will need to wash out the machine thoroughly because the insides will have dirt from manufacturing. To do this, take off the water lid at the top and fill the tank with warm water. You can also pour water in to the ice receptacle at the front. You might want to use a drop of dish soap. Give it a good scrub with a cloth or a brush. On the front, dont forget to wipe the whole mechanism including the plastic tube, lip, and even the metal tray. When you're happy that it's clean you will need to empty out the water - tip the rear in to the sink and open up the little plastic tap at the back. Watch out for the clear plastic cap _inside_ the tap - this is super important to stop it leaking when in use. If you used dish soap give it another couple of thorough rinses.

Hopefully this will have taken about a hour since you started, so the coolant will have settled and you can get going.

It's now time to plug it in. You'll notice this isn't the quietest appliance in the kitchen. I find it on par with my dishwasher.

Fill the tank with some cold water (I find it holds about half a gallon) and let it run. Throw out all the ice it generates from this - you may spot more dirt or white powder. You might want to give it another wipe.

The first thing you will notice is that you aren't actually getting ice *cubes*. I would best describe them as thin three-sided ice sheets. They are clear, but I find they dissolve super fast in room temperature drinks. Not at all what I was expecting, and a bit disapointing given the premium price.

The machine will keep on making ice as long as it has water (either in the tank, or in the resevoir from melted ice) and isn't full. The way it decides whether it is full or not is based on whether the previous block of ice fell in to the tray, and this is not always super accurate. Sometimes the ice just doesnt fall properly and gets stuck on the sensor flap.

Occasionally the machine will say it's out of water when it isn't. If this happens, try tilting it backwards to drain some of the resevoir water in to the mechanism. If this doesn't work, switch it off and on again. If it still doesn't, drain it and start again.

Generally feels like a pretty poor build quality and I don't hold out a lot of hope for a long and productive life.

Well, I wanted an ice maker because our fridge ice maker is psycho. It works when it wants to. I searched high and low for the best one. I wanted a stand up style and was considering the GE model because it supposedly made sonic ice. It was also expensive to me. I kept searching and stumbled on to this machine. It makes nuggets ice as well. There were no reviews on this model but I decided to take a chance.

When it arrived, it was well packaged. My husband put it on the counter for me. It’s not extremely heavy but has some weight to it. There were no dings or scratches. I like how it looks on the counter. It doesn’t take up much space. Just remember to sit the machine upright for 24 hours before plugging it in. I almost missed this warning on the machine.

I used a white distilled vinegar and water solution for the initial wash cycle and plain water for the subsequent 2. We have hard water in S. Florida so I decided to use the water from fridge dispenser because it’s filtered. There is an option to attach the machine to water line but I can’t filter that water. I will clean with a descaling solution once a week to avoid any build up.

The initial cleaning was easy and the drain tubes, on the back, are long enough for me. I simply added water and pressed the CLEAN button. Buttons are soft press and not an issue. I used a large mixing bowl to collect the water. Works perfect. Just be sure to have the bowl ready as soon as you uncap the tubes. If not, you will have a mess. I can purchase extensions for the tubes but not necessary for me. The machine was not loud. It makes a slight humming sound. Nothing that would bother me.

After cleaning, I filled with water and started making ice. I will say it’s neat. When the ice maker is filling ice making section, water streams from the top of the machine back into the reservoir. Still not a loud process. Sounds like running water when you’re close to it. About 10 minutes later the first nuggets start to drop. In about an hour, we had a full basket of ice. I was able to collect 4 baskets of ice (each basket almost filled a gallon ziplock bag) in about 4 to 5 hours. I think I could have made more ice if I was watching the machine to remove ice and add water timely.

The machine shuts off when the basket is full. If the water level is low, the add water light would come on. This light only came on when I removed one basket of ice. I usually added water after each ice dump and filled to the max line. In that instance, i added water but I didn’t fill to the line.

ICE ICE BABY!!! Now, the ice is nugget style and resembles sonic ice. However, it does not have the consistency of sonic ice until it softens up. So, if you leave it in the basket and use it from there, it’s softer. If you remove right after making it’s harder but still good ice. Of course when you freeze it, it’s going to stick together but we just dropped the bag on the counter to break it up and it was fine. Still nugget but harder. The taste was good and the ice was clear. It didn’t change the drink taste and everyone wanted some. It’s not a restaurant machine. So, I didn’t expect the ice to be just like hospital or Sonic ice. Those machines have the perfect temperature to not over-freeze and store the ice. This machine does not. If you want the ice to soften up, leave it in the basket, place it in a Yeti, or a styrofoam cup.

It’s also easy to store when not in use. I simply drained the water, dried the machine/basket, and pushed it to the side on my counter. I center it when in use for proper ventilation. I will say that I have a great replica of a nugget ice maker. The machine is relatively quiet and gets the job done. I’m glad I purchased this machine. Let’s see how long it lasts.

I got these because I just can't see using the plastic single use pods or even the reusable pods that require disposable stickers, plus I want to be able to use coffee from a local roaster. I've been fiddling with these for over a month now & can report these DO work, mostly, with a couple of issues.

First, as noted by many other reviewers, you cannot put enough grounds in, even if you "tamp" a very very fine grind. Tamping in as much of a very fine grind as the pod will hold results in somewhere between zero to a teaspoon of espresso and it makes it VERY difficult to open the Nespresso machine to drop out the used pod. Using slightly less of a pretty fine grind that is still very firmly tamped will result in a bit over a tablespoon of passable espresso, with a bit of crema. If you have two or three of the pods ready to go you can run them all through, one right after the other & get a single shot. If you use less grounds or don't tamp as firmly or use a courser grind, you can get more coffee out from a single pod, but it will be like "regular" coffee & NOT espresso.

Second, the rubber gaskets that sit directly under the lip of the pod have a very annoying tendency to come off IN the Nespresso machine, which requires you to retrieve them carefully from where the pods sit during the "brewing" process. So far, I've been able to put them back on & keep using the pods; but, since they are necessarily fairly thin, I don't have high expectations for their longevity.

So, all things considered, fiddly as they are to work with, I still find them worth using over single use pods on those days I'm not going to my local coffee house. But I'll also keep searching for something that works better.

First off, Altura's customer service is fantastic! When I wrote to them for advice on which of their 3 products (Mesh, Disc or Ultra) would best suit my needs, they sent me a free sample of other two so I could try all three out! And so I did...the verdict: while all three are high-quality products with a lot of thought invested in their design, the Disc wins out in my experience. It's more durable and easier to maintain than the Ultra while maintaining the same functionality. The Ultra can occasionally buckle under pressure if not fitted perfectly right whereas the Disc is rigid and fits perfectly every time. The Mesh works a lot like the Disc but has a thicker frame around the mesh that does not fit easily into the filter cap of the Aeropress and could damage it over the long term. I found that all three products performed about just as well with different grind sizes, with the Ultra and Disc working better with finer grounds. All in all, any of these three are a significant improvement over the paper micro filters that come with the Aeropress because they allow a good portion of the oils through whereas the paper filters trap most of the oils and result in a rather sterile tasting "clean" brew - I certain prefer my coffee extract with its natural oils!

After purchasing the smaller reusable stainless steel capsule for expresso brewing in my Nespresso machine and having been satisfied I hurried to order the larger size capsule to regular cup size (aprox 8 oz.) to expand our capacity and save money. Although the unit appears to share the same design of the original, I have been experiencing difficulty with brewing using this model. Slow brewing rate ( dripping and straining) and inferior cup of coffee. I ran the capsule empty and it seemed to flow well. I then emptied one of my original Nespresso capsules into the stainless reusable capsule and it brewed in a similar fashion as the original capsule. This leads me to believe I need to try and experimenting with my grind settings. I use a Cuisinart coffee grinder that allows me to adjust my settings to from powder to coarse. I am presently experimenting with different grind settings to find what works best with the new capsule. I will try and post a follow up and share what I have learned.
Follow Up... I have continued experimenting with the stainless steel coffee capsule with positive results. As I grind my own coffee i sm setting a grind size slightly larger than the grind that comes in the nesspresso capsules. I also don't scoop the coffee form the container and pack it in the capsule using the weighted tamping tool. I have had more success by gently pouring the coffee grounds into the capsule and just tapping the capsule to settle the grounds without packing. If I get grounds on the threads I wet my fingers and run them along the threads to clean them of grind or powder. Once I start screwing on the top if it appears to be difficult to tighten I just place the capsule under a bit of running water at a 45 degree angle to clean out any residue to secure the top to the capsule gasket making it water tight and ready for brewing. I know it has not been as easy as advertised but I do enjoy being able to select different coffee types and brands and the outcome is a smooth cup of coffee that is worth the process. Especially if you enjoy coffee. I use original capsules and the reusable ones as well. Original works best but reusable is a close second.Happy Brewing!

I ordered these many times over the years, and there had never been an issue. I made the mistake of going on Amazon's auto-purchase system, which led me to keep the filter on the shelf for some time before use, making a refund request impossible. I actually thought the refrigerator had a major malfunction--shortly after installing the filter, not only did the water stop flowing, but the refrigerator made loud banging and whirring noises. I called an appliance repair person. He identified that the filter had frozen, warmed it up and reinstalled it, water was flowing again. Charged me about $100. Within two hours, the problem was back. At least I now knew that the water filter was the problem. Searching the internet, I found this was a known problem with some of the recently sold filters of this type--their casings are apparently the wrong size (counterfeit?). Following a "tip," I folded some paper towels and taped them to the filter before reinstalling, leading to a tighter seal. That worked, but just for a day or two. I went though months of having this problem the water would stop/noise start, I'd remove the filter and reinstall it, it worked again for a short while. I finally gave up, threw out the offending filter and installed another that was on my shelf from the (now cancelled) Amazon subscription. That one worked, no problem. But this was a big pain, I'll buy direct from the manufacturer in the future.

Added info, 5/22: I made the mistake of ordering another of these from Amazon. Same problem--the fit is slightly off, so the soon the fridge starts up with a grinding/hammering noise, etc. This time, I was able to return it and reordered direct from the manufacture. So far no problems with the manufacturer-direct filters. This is a small sample size (two defective units), but I will not again order these from Amazon, and I hope Amazon will take a close look into their source for these filters, which may be different from the bona fide units.

I had a terrible experience using the Bosch dishwasher.
I bought the Bosch dishwater SHEM3AY55N/28 in January 2022. The drain has always been problematic (error code E24). I installed the dishwasher with the drain hose connecting to an air gap, then to the disposal – a standard connection setting. At the beginning the drain cycles may succeed 50% of chances but now down to 10% chance.
Recently I called Bosch customer service. The tech came my house and verified the problem. He said Bosch dishwashers always have problems to drain water completely if the hose is connected to an air gap. He suggested to connect to the disposal directly. He said even an expensive model has the same problem since all Bosch dishwasher uses the same pump, which is not powerful enough. The following is his comment on the service report:
“Client had error code of e24, when I arrived I found in the unit so I had some water and initially tested the drain cycle ensure enough it was draining very slowly. I did not find an installation issue everything was good including the loop for the drain hose. After tracing down where the congestion was, found that the unit drain fine with disconnected from the air gap even though the air gap had no debris inside, advised client that the drain cycle and pump were not designed for a run that long, he should disconnect from the air gap and go straight into garbage disposal as the unit has no issue pumping water out that way”.
So, it is a design issue. How can you have a dishwasher not able to drain through an air gap. No where of the machine’s user manual mentioned it should not be connected to the air gap. I called customer again and try to find a resolution. They do not want to help. The supervisor (Chris) said “it is your installation issue”, shamelessly.
I am going to connect the drain hose directly to the disposal and see if it drains properly and if it leads to backflow (since not using air gap). I will keep you updated.

I have been a big fan of pour-over coffee for years now, and I own another pour-over with a small water reservoir, but it is made of plastic. Plastic with hot water (no matter how safe they say it is) in my daily consumption rubs me the wrong way, so I went about looking for an alternative and found this stainless steel pour-over.
Immediately upon opening the box, I loved the aesthetic. It looks rustic and reminds me of something I'd find in an antique store. It isn't the heaviest duty, but it doesn't feel like I'm going to dent or bend it without actually trying. It isn't as convenient as my plastic version, but there is no plastic to come in contact with hot liquids with this one which makes me a lot happier. I like that the filter basket is entirely removable and can be used in other vessels. I haven't tried making cold brew coffee with it yet, but I'm sure it will work wonderfully. I like that there is no need for a paper filter with this one. I hate having to waste a paper filter for every cup of coffee with my other pour-over, and this one seems like it will keep filtering for a long time. A bonus feature of not having to use paper filters is retaining your coffee oils in your finished cup rather than having the paper absorb some of them. I would argue that this pour-over makes a better-tasting cup of coffee than one which uses a paper filter. It's easy enough to clean as long as you take care of it immediately. I wouldn't let the grounds sit in the filter basket too long after making your cup or you may end up with a slight mess to clean up. The only con I see with this pour-over, which is remedied by design, is the sharpness of the edge of the filter basket holder. It comes covered with a silicone ring, so you'd never notice until you take it off. If you care to, you can take a fine metal file to it and take the roughness off rather easily, but it isn't necessary.
Overall, I really like this pour-over. It is functional, made of safe materials, and it even looks nice in my kitchen. If you are a bit of a coffee snob like I am, you won't be disappointed by the fantastic cup of coffee you will get out of this.

I bought this style thermostat specifically for use with a 30-40 gal ZooMed heating pad. So far I’ve had it for 3-4 months and it’s worked flawlessly.

The length of the wire connecting the thermostat probe to the unit is ample enough to submerge the probe into the substrate a few mils above the center of the heating mat (to get an accurate read of the temperature of the substrate) then run the probe data line to a corner of the tank and up the corner out of the tank, keeping it very hidden, my tank is 40Gal too and it runs from basically the center so no issue really.

The display text is large and concise, it reads the current temp and the set temp, wether the heating or cooling element is on or off. Programming the unit is fairly intuitive, as it has an alarm (never tested that), heat and cooling settings and the temperature setting. Heating turns power to the outlet on the unit on while the probe reads a temp lower than the desired temp and Cooling turns the outlet on when the temp is above the desired temp. It’s accurate to an integer number of degrees (Fahrenheit or Celsius, you can switch between the two seamlessly) and the display is backlit very well, in fact it’s so bright that at night you may have to cover it because it will act as a mini night light.

So far the only downside I’ve encountered is that it won’t directly support multiple heating or cooling devices a once, only having one power outlet. However this can be partially rectified by plugging in a surge protector strip and then plugging in either heating or cooling devices only into the strip. Be warned though the total power consumption of all the connected devices, in this manner, in watts, cannot exceed the maximum power rating for the Zoo-med digital thermostat. In fact just Incase of a surge you probably should leave a 15-25% space for power draw so you don’t fry the thermostat. Also don’t do this if you’re not a professional.

My oven recently stopped working. I tested the resistance of the bake igniter and it was measuring as an open circuit (infinite resistance). I also realized the igniter in my oven is the same for bake and broil, so I swapped the two igniters around and then bake worked, but not broil. I was a bit concerned since I couldn't find a direct replacement for DG94-01441A (the part number on my old igniter from a Samsung NX60T8511 range), but for $25 I took the risk. This igniter is a plug and play replacement for the original, no splicing or coercion needed. I measured the resistance of this igniter and it measured ~175 ohms, versus ~110 ohms of the remaining original working igniter. As a result it takes almost twice as long to light the gas (higher resistance means lower current means longer to heat the igniter element sufficiently). I can live with this small drawback though and for $25 I can't complain about the value at all.

This item is great for when you need extra ice or if you don't have a built-in ice maker in your freezer. It is true to its word and can make 9 cubes in 6-8 minutes. Although if you want the large size cubes it takes a little longer. This is a closed system that does not require tying into a water line. You manually add the water to the reservoir (just like a coffee maker). Due to the design any water not used for each round of ice falls back into the reservoir. The unit is insulated but it is not designed to store ice long term, so you will want to use the ice right away or transfer the ice to your freezer or a cooler when the basket gets full. However, if the ice melts the water simply falls back into the reservoir so the chance of a mess or wasted water is small. Connecting the unit to the Govee app is surprisingly easy. I was very impressed with that as I have suffered through many products/apps that are a nightmare to connect. This is truly a feature that they nailed. Why does an ice maker need to be connected to the internet? Well it doesn't, necessarily. But if it is connected, you can control device settings from your phone, and also you will get a push notification on your phone if the ice maker runs out of water or if the basket is full. The ice maker will beep if those things happen, but having the app is great for when you are out of earshot of the ice maker. The unit does create noise, but it is equivalent to the noise of a small refrigerator. This is expected since it uses similar technology. I can't speak to the longevity/durability of the ice maker as I have only had it a few weeks, but I will update this if there any issues.

Awesome Product. I bought this to replace a 10 year old igniter for my ge profile oven. My oven was not able to reach cooking temp and sometimes I would wait for an hour just to reach 350. After looking online for tips on what might be wrong, I found several youtube videos of other ge ovens that use this part number. To replace the bake igniter for a ge profile with a warming drawer, these are the steps:
1. Turn off gas and unplug the oven.
2. Take out racks from main oven.
3. Remove the oven bottom panel by unscrewing the screws located at the back of the bottom panel. Lift from the rear and slide back. Then remove it.
4. Remove the warming drawer by sliding it out and depressing the clips.
5. There is a panel at the back of the warming drawer compartment that says "front" on it. Remove two screws at the top and pull the panel out.
6. The igniter wires connect right under the igniter through a hole so you need to pull the wires out to access the connector clip. Disconnect the clip.
7. In the main oven compartment, the igniter is fastened with two small bolts. Remove the bolts taking care not to drop them (as I did - doh) and pull the igniter wire out that you previously disconnected.
8. Connect the replacement igniter taking care not to drop it or touch the ceramic thingy. Tighten the screws and connect the spring clip to the clip in the warming drawer compartment.
9. Feed the plastic wiring clip back through the hole and put the panel (with the word "front" on it.)
10. Install the warming drawer door back on.
11. Re install the oven compartment bottom panel, install the racks and connect the gas and power.
12. You are done.
Previously, I would turn the oven on and the temp would increment like once every 60 seconds or so taking forever to reach the proper temp. Now, it started right up and was at temp in about 5 minutes.
The igniter was the exact same part as my old igniter and even contains two ceramic wire nuts which I did not need

After doing extensive research on numerous undercounter icemakers, I went with the EdgeStar. All brands had the same pros and cons for the most part. Being a plumbing contractor myself and having installed TONS of icemaker kits, I did not use the plastic tubing that came with the kit because the compression fittings often leak and the chance of kinking whenever the unit is moved it always a worry. Installed a copper tubing line with an external single stage water filter. Haven't noticed any loud compressor noises as stated by other reviewers yet but I will say that purchasing the extended warranty is a must.

I would definitely recommend this to anyone but stress that you spend the extra time and money in installing it properly. Install it level and on a solid surface because I've notice what other confuse for loud compressor noises might just be vibration. Install an external filter to protect the internal coil of your icemaker from clogs or sediment build up. Definitely go with copper tubing to ensure more solid compression connections and please leave slack. Lastly, try not to completely enclose this icemaker where it barely gets fresh air. Coming from a contractors perspective, don't choose vanity over utility unless money is no object to you.

Good Shopping and hope this review helps you decide when shopping.

Now the bad.

As mentioned on other sites the ice maker is loud. Loud enough that we can hear it from our bedroom with the door closed at night. Our bedroom is across the house 3 rooms away. At first it was alarming since we were not used to the noise but we have gotten used to it.

Ice maker comes unseated and won’t produce ice. Opening the door and reseating it solves this.

Ice get stuck in the shoot and backs up. You have to open the door and poke at the ice while depressing the ice lever to clear it. Invariably whatever glass you have is not large enough and the ice spills all over the floor.

Items fall behind the freezer trays and can hold the freezer door open. We found our freezer half thawed and have covered in ice when this happened. Apparently the door alarm does not work for the freezer door, or not when it is only slightly ajar.

Problems we have had with the fridge in the first year.

Two of the door bins have broken and fallen off – leaving our 29 cf fridge with 26 cf of usable space. The bottom trays from the right and left doors are broken and the upper right tray is showing signs of failing. The plastic that holds the bin on the door is thin and brittle. Cracks form which cause the shelf to fail. A gallon of milk and some salad dressing bottles prove enough weight to cause the failure. The french design of the fridge is such that the only place you can put milk and other taller items such as a pitcher of juice or 2 liter bottle of Coke is the door. The thin plastic of the bins in my opinion is a design flaw and will not hold the weight causing the bin fail and fall off the door. It is common enough that they sell replacement bins on Amazon.

The bar seal on the left door is malfunctioning. When you close the right door 1st the bar on the left door hits the right door when closing. At some point something will break entirely.

The right vegetable draw gets stuck open. It appears to get wedged due to the rollers getting out of the runner. You have to use a combination of force and wigging to get it closed.

Samsung customer support was neither sympathetic nor helpful. They told me my fridge was out of warranty based on the SN despite having been purchased 10 months ago. The Samsung Execute Response Team told me if I found my receipt they could help me. We do not have the receipt and the store we purchased it from has closed.

At 51 yrs old this was the most expensive, largest, and I had hoped the nicest fridge I have owned. Unfortunately much to my disappointment it has been one of the worst appliance purchases I have made. The design which causes failure of the door bins and other issues, whether and inconvenience or complete failure of the fridge to operate at intended is unacceptable for an appliance of this class.

If you decide to purchase I would suggest you get an extended warranty, keep your receipt handy, and cross your fingers.

Best of luck to you.

All of the YouTube videos I watched on the subject have you replacing it from inside the oven. You could start that way to see how much give you have on the two wires, but the comments "Don't let the wires 'fall back' into the insulation" requires a better explanation. The fact is that those wires are attached to the original element from the back and *then* cable-tied in the back. I found that I couldn't get enough wire out to attach, and eventually one did 'fall back' in the insulation. But I discovered that my range pulls out very easily and it took about a minute to take the metal covering off. From this vantage point, you can go ahead and screw in the new element inside, and attach the wires with ease. For mine, I clipped off a cable tie to give me more wire to work with, and then secured with a new cable tie once the wires were attached. Bottom line: don't spend more than a minute trying to attach the wires from the front .. just go ahead and accept that it is much easier from the back.

I spent a lot of time on-line and looking in stores, closely examining the reviews. My daughter gave me a used Nespresso machine (190), which works very well. I have been happy with this, but I also LOVE the blend that Peet's uses for their cappuccinos'. Even though very strong, it is not bitter but has a "chocolate" after-taste which is great. I have not found a Nespresso capsule blend that tastes like the Peets. So I was looking for a "new" machine that would allow me to use the Peet's blend at home, or while traveling.

So I purchased this Aero Press. I didn't want to spend a fortune on a huge machine either. Many people have a "full-kitchen" and don't want to add a large number of expensive, space consuming appliances to what they already have. Here is my review:

Pros:

1. The Aero-press definitely makes a lovely coffee, especially for cappuccino. If you want to you can add hot water to it for a fine Americano Blend. It still tastes great. The coffee tastes as good as it does at Peets, even though there is no "crema." I cannot tell the difference in the taste between Aero-made and at Peet's Coffee house.
2. This unit is portable, small and you can carry it anywhere, using it in hotel rooms if you wish
3. It is very, very easy and quick to wash, and you can clean it in two seconds in a hotel sink on-the-go
4. It weighs virtually nothing and you can fit it into your suitcase or carry-on.
5. Ejecting the plug of coffee grounds is NOT a messy process and you can do it on the go at a hotel room without splattering it on your clothes or the sink.
6. It is NOT necessary to jam the plunger all the way to the bottom of the cylinder in order to express all of the water through the grounds. Attempting to do this may make a mess and require a lot of pressing. Just press it until you no longer can, and wait.The water will go through the grounds without all that much "force." If you make more than one serving, just wait slightly longer. The water will eventually go through.
7. Stirring thoroughly is a must. You must use the long stirring rod provided. A spoon will not do it. Unless you stir it thoroughly the coffee serving will not turn out right. You cannot "blame" the device if you don't follow the directions.
8. The wider mouth attachment helps keep the coffee from "dripping" all over the table. Use it. Same with the hot water pour.
9. The little attachment with the opening on the side is used for "stabilizing" small coffee "shot glasses" so that the device will not slip out and make a mess when you use the press. If you use a regular coffee cup it is not necessary. You just put the "shot glass" into the holder.
10. Some people have tried to press the plunger all the way in without waiting, causing a mess if the plunger slips and the entire device goes all over the place. THAT is not necessary. Just be patient and allow the coffee to express through the grounds. That is part of using this machine properly.
11. This device is very inexpensive and will stand up to lots of use, unless you "crush" it while traveling.

Cons:

1. Keeping the coffee serve hot is definitely a challenge. This is especially true if you want to put a foam on the top of your soy/regular milk cappuccino.
2. It is necessary to use a micro-wave on the serving AFTER it is prepared if you want it really hot. I have found that this works well, even though nothing is said about it in the directions. Ordinarily you might expect the micro-waving of the serving to ruin it. That does not happen.
3. Even with "setting everything up" and super-heating the water, it just takes TIME to make a serving. During that time, the serving will cool. If you are like me and really want very hot coffee, you must use a microwave to re-heat it after you are finished. The serving still tastes great after that.
4. Don't expect this process to be as "quick" and easy as if a barista makes it for you. You have to do it yourself. You must "fust" around in order to use it. However, it is vastly cheaper. Some people like to manipulate devices like a toy, which this very much is.
5. Unless you also have a micro-wave in your hotel room, your coffee will turn out cooler than you like it, even though it still tastes great. Alternatively, you can just drink it black. If you do that, it will remain hotter, because you consume it immediately.
6. It is unrealistic to expect to be able to "travel" with a large cappuccino maker in your suitcase. Even if you travel with one that uses a hot plate or open flame to heat, you have to find a hot plate in a hotel room.

I would be curious to hear your replies to my rating. I did not give it 5 stars due to the basic design of the device. But that said, it produces a wonderful serving of coffee that is indistinguishable from a barista-prepared "dose." If blind-folded, I would NOT be able to tell the difference. I admit that I prefer my serving to be extremely hot. Many people cannot drink it that way, but I can and prefer it.

This product was supposed to take advantage of using less water and at the same time be a top-loading washer. Front loading washers use gravity to assist in washing and circulating the water through the clothing. The engineers of this product "hoped" that their use of a small center "agitator" would "swish" the soapy water through the clothing, and also allow the clothes basket to "wobble" thereby assisting in water movement.

Nice try.

It didn't work. No even close. The water is engineered not to even cover the clothes. The clothing sits in a basket of barely moving water, and only the bottom of the clothing gets wet. They tried to mask this defect by an extreme spin cycle, which squeezed every last bit of water out of the clothing. Most of the very long process is spinning.

It is true that the clothing comes out very well spun, but still dirty. According to Whirlpool, you are not supposed to wash sheets at the same time as other clothing. That is correct. If you try, the sheets gather up the clothing into a snug cocoon, and the agitator batters the cocoon on the side of the agitator for 50 minutes. When it starts to spin, as you guessed, it is an unbalanced load, and must be dissected apart.

If you try to wash a comforter or blanket, they will sit, not even covered with water, almost unmoving in the tub. You might just as well put your laundry into a large tub in the back yard and just let it sit. Oh yes, and don't cover it with water, either. On the plus side, it uses very little water. But it doesn't wash your clothes either.

Obviously I don't like this machine. I kept it a week and paid a restocking fee of 90 dollars (gladly) to get rid of it. I am still buying a Whirlpool front loader. I guess I am crazy, but it is labeled a "Maytag."

I guess you could say that this was a disaster. I wish I had read more reviews before I bought it. Don't buy this machine, unless you just want to soak your unmoving clothes in a tub of water that doesn't even cover a half of it. If it were possible to not give this even one star, I would do it.

I have used dozens of these in my Sears 11-gallon Wicking Humidifier, in a few years. The interlaced wire-frame allows the "filter" to remain upright.

For those who wish theirs lasted longer, I can offer my observations from a farm. Two of my several 120#+ working dogs come into the house. There is a lot of residual dust in the air despite frequent vacuuming.

I bought some material at walmart. It's a very fine material often used in collars on shirts. Then I got some "sticky-putty' stuff at a hobby shop and stuck the material to the outside of the Humidifier. Generally the inbound air sucks the cloth against the device. The Tacky-tape helps hold it also.

The effect is that, when the outer cloth is rinsed by hand in the sink daily, that the filter inside the humidifier lasts a bit longer. I tried the Bestair "filter" with an outer layer of cloth (much the same material as I used too) . However, frankly, it lasted 4 days. Though I can't say if it was a dirtier time due to 3 degree outside temperatures and thus drier inside ... hence mire available dust.

Also, consider the amount of very fine sediment in your water. We're on a well. I tried a simple 'Brita' as a test and have to opinion that filling the Sears Humidifier with totally filtered water extends the longevity. I am also using Bestair's Pink stuff water treatment, about 3 or 4 caps-full daily .. this helped improve longevity.

I have noticed that in winters where I had very few nights where one or two working stock dogs "over-nighted" that the Bestair humidifer filter lasted into the "several weeks" category.

The upshot is that the "Sears Kenmore Humidifier Wick Filter Replacement,42-14906" does a very good job and is well worth the price.
