I think that a lot of these reviews are from people who have never had a portable washer before and they give this machine high praise because of the relief it gave them from having to go the laundromat. Another thing is that many of the reviews state they've had the machine for a day or a couple of days or a week, so durability cannot be properly evaluated. I've only had it for a week myself, so can't speak to durability yet either. I'll update the review when it breaks. I will instead address performance and features (or lack thereof). My review will be from a little different perspective because I've had an Edgestar washer/dryer front load combo for 4 years, before buying this machine. I have something to compare it to, so I have a different perspective of features and performance than people who went straight from the laundromat to this machine. The reason I had to replace my Edgestar with this is because the pump started making a whining sound after 4 years of use (and I bought it used) and it sounded like a helicopter in the spin cycle. I didn't want to spend 1000 dollars or more on a comparable LG or the like, so I bought this Haier and the companion dryer. I bought them online from a local big box retailer and did the site to store option.

The reason I need a portable washer is because I live in an apartment without hook ups, and even though I live right across from the laundry room, the machines there are always broken and the wait for the 1 that works half way is horrendous.

My first word of caution is that you really need to make sure you have someone who has a truck to help you get the machine home. I thought it would fit in my 2 door Accord because it is so small, but it is double boxed and the boxes are huge. You've been warned :o)

I like the way it looks, but there are some important features that it lacks and they aren't clearly stated anywhere. The first thing it lacks is a water heater. My old one had a water heater built in, but with this Haier, the temperature must be controlled at the faucet. It does not mention this anywhere in the awful manual. The manual not only lacks details, but is poorly written with grammar and spelling mistakes. Another thing it lacks is a detergent dispenser. You have to add the detergents directly to the tub. It also lacks a count down timer, so you have no clue how much longer the cycle is going to last. That truly sucks! It also lacks a manual dial timer... the controls are electronic which makes advancing a cycle manually virtually impossible. If you want to skip to a rinse or change a setting in the middle of a wash, or add a second rinse (because the machine only does one rinse the normal and quick cycles and there is no option for a second rinse), you have to completely turn the machine off and then back on and press the same button multiple times to get what you want. There is no delay start option. There is no way to turn off the annoying beep. There is no hook for the hoses, but there is one for the cord.

The manual doesn't state how tight to screw the screw the wheels on, so when I attached them, I screwed them on as tight as I could get them. It was too tight and they wouldn't swivel. So, when I tried to roll the machine over an area rug, each half of two of the casters fell off. I had to flip the machine over and reassemble the casters and loosen all of them. Do not tighten them all the way.

This machine doesn't clean as well as a front loader would, but that is to be expected with a top loader. Front loaders have extremely long cycle times and a different wash action, and they just clean better. I had a shirt with ranch dressing on it and I had to wash it 4 times and pre-treat the stain with a Fels-naptha laundry bar and a half bottle of Zout to get the stain out with this machine. I could have washed it once in my old Edgestar and it would have come out fine after the first try (of course it had a 3 hour wash time, this one is only 20 minutes).

This Haier also has some pretty fascinating quirks. I was washing and I wanted to pause the machine to let the load soak, so I pressed pause. The machine stopped and I waited about an hour for the clothes to soak. Then I pressed the play/start button again. The machine washed for a bit and then stopped, beeped, and turned off to indicate that the cycle was done. The tub was still full of soapy water, and the machine should have gone through with finishing the wash and doing a rinse and spin, but it did not. It becomes unbalanced very easily, so know that before buying. When mine becomes unbalanced, it does not do the perpetual rinse and spin as the other reviews and manual indicate. It just stops everything and the rinse light continues to flash. I take out some of the clothes (and I do not over fill the machine ever), and then have to turn the machine off and then back on and start all over. Very annoying.

Another thing that you need to be aware of is that wall of the tub is ribbed, so buttons make an awful noise as the scrape against it. So does the Downy Ball, and you will need one because again, this machine lacks a dispenser and does not tell you when the rinse cycle is going to begin. I don't know about you, but I don't like to baby sit my washer... I like to let it work while I do other things. This one is not hands off.

The water inlet hose enters the machine on the top. Not only does that get in the way of the lid opening (depending on how you have it situated), but also looks bad. The other thing is that the cord comes out of the machine at the bottom right below the inlet hose, so if you have a leak there, it will drip right on the hose. Might be fun if you have a date over and want some sparks, but otherwise, that probably wasn't the best place for that.

The spin cycle is quiet, so that is a good thing! It doesn't get the clothes as dry as my previous front loader did, but it works pretty well. It spins for a few seconds, then stops to drain the water, and repeats that process until the final spin. The wash cycle is pretty quiet too, and the loudest thing this machine does (except for filling) is beep to let you know the cycle is finished (whether it's really finished, or it just got tired and decided to take a coffee break in the middle of a cycle).

The capacity is greater than I expected it to be (while still smaller than my old machine). I washed 1 queen sized sheet and 2 pillow cases and it did fine. I can also do a pair of khakis and a few polo shirts with several pairs of socks and underwear. If I were doing towels, I would put no more than 2 in this machine.

I know it sounds like I hate this machine, but really I don't. I've just noticed some quirks, and perhaps I was a little spoiled by my previous laundry processor because it was more fully featured. It also cost triple what that one did when it was new, so I may well be comparing apples to oranges. For the price, this is a decent little machine if it holds up.

Our house was built with the Dryer on the inside wall of the house so the only way to vent it was through the roof. It has worked for years but was not efficient. I pulled the hose out from the roof and let it blow into the attic. BIG MISTAKE. Not only did it put sticky dryer lint on everything stored in the attic but all the damp air caused mold to grow. I decided that the only way was to install a booster fan. My biggest problem was the central heat and air ducts ran right over the area I needed to mount the booster fan so I had to build a stand for it. I decided to add a lint trap even though I was over 15 foot from the dryer to the booster fan hoping this would keep some of the extra lint out of the booster fan. First off the booster fan is good and sturdy but you will have to do some work to install it. You must install the rubber grommets in the provided plate. I found the metal mounting plate to be light weight but strong enough to support the fan. The nice thing about the light weight support plate it lets you bend it to conform to the round bottom of the fan that you must drill holes in for the screws. Yes it is kind of hard to start drilling holes in a new fan but no two installations are the same. I installed a electric outlet in the attic and put a cord on the new fan in case I have to remove it for some reason. With the lint trap in line there should be very little lint getting into the motor but lint can get into anything. When I compare the quality of the booster fan with the quality of the lint trap I am happy with the booster fan. The lint trap is another story. There are about 3 or 4 different lint traps sold on Amazon but after reading the reviews they are all made of the same poor quality. After you purchase the lint trap go the the hardware store and get some heavy duty weather stripping. You will have to stick one strip in the bottom of the lint trap from corner to corner (see pictures) in the same direction the screen runs to seal the built in screen to the bottom of the lint trap housing. Once you put the weather stripping in the bottom you must put more weather stripping around the top to close the gap that was caused by the weather stripping at the bottom. I put weather stripping around all of the removable top (see pictures) were it meets the main box. This will give you a better seal and should stop most of the lint from escaping. I then temporally clamped the top to the bottom so the edged of the box will make some groves in the weather stripping on the top cover. I found for me the semi ridged pipe works better than the real soft pipe. You can take advantage of the 90 degree pipe adapters available. When using the booster fan you use up to 60 foot of pipe and 6 elbows.
UPDATE on the lint trap. I added the lint trap because I thought it was a good idea but I didn't really need it because I was more than the 15 foot they say you need from the dryer to the booster fan. I am so glad I added the lint trap. We always clean the lint filter on the dryer after each use, no exceptions. After only 4 loads of clothes the screen on the lint trap was full of lint. Part of this was caused because I moved the original pipe around and knocked some of the lint that was stuck to the sides of the old pipe loose. The booster fan with the amount of air it moves cleaned out the full 20 foot of existing pipe that comes from the ground floor to the attic. I will be checking the lint trap in the attic more often then I thought I would have to. Sure glad I made it easy to get to.

First thing I want to point out is the other reviews on this item that talk about TDS. First and foremost you are not buying this filter to remove TDS (Total Dissolved Solids) you need a RO/RODI (Reverse osmosis) filter unit in order to remove TDS. At the most this filter is a sediment filter (removes undissolved solids) to a point and then uses a carbon block to remove other chemicals from the water (ex: Chlorine, smells, taste, etc.) Overall just makes the water a bit healthier and cleaner with a “better” taste apposed to tap. Also helps prevent larger particles from building up in the fridge without removing 100% of everything in the water. Again research RODI units if you want 100% “clean, 0 TDS” water.

Other then that it does have a good taste to the water.
My biggest complaint is the cost. On average they last 6 months at $50 not on sale that’s approx $8.35 a month excluding tax. For a water filter. Just got this range at the end of Feb 11, and it took a couple weeks to get it installed in the house. The impact this range has had over our stock Whirlpool flat top electrical range I bought with the house almost two years ago, was significant. My wife was won over by the "Bread Proofing" function and a couple visits to local stores for comparisons to other models under consideration (GE, SAMSUNG, LG, BOSCH). Anyway, the ease of cooking with this range is much greater than we would have imagined in a couple short months. A few pros, two small cons, and a small warning are all I have to say about this excellent range.

Pros:

1) Easy to clean up. However if you let any food items get on the recessed cook top surface below the grill, your cleanup will be that much harder. Seems obvious, but I have a teenager in the house. The oven surface is also easy to keep up on.

2) Easy glide racks. I slowly worked on the wife for two years about easy glide racks being a major selling point. Every day use has made my case for this seemingly minor feature by significant labor saving feature.

3) Wave touch controls. My wife who does all the baking in the house loves these more than she ever would have realized until she sat down and read the instruction manual. Staged baking programming has made her a believer.

4) Gas cooking. I've never liked electrical coils, and using the range top has made cooking enjoyable if not fun.

5) Looks great with the understated control panel idle and when it is being used. All cooking information is visible and easy to comprehend.

6) Internal lighting with the shiny blue interior helps you see everything. The old Whirlpool had an internal light that made me feel I was looking down a mile deep shaft with a match trying to squint just a couple more photons of reception out of it.

7) No failures, no glitches, and no problems whatsoever to date. Build quality is high and I have yet to see a single operating issue and neither has my wife. I also didn't buy an extended warranty after looking up consumer complaints against the warrantor for the vendor I selected. I expect in one year and a day (after the manufacturers warranty expires) I'll see my first glitch.

8)Bread proofing function. This is what got my wife on board initially. She is a pretty good baker, but proofing the bread in our previous range was a lot of effort for her. This simple function has made it easier for her. Not one loaf has fallen since she started using it.

9) Precision control on burners. I am very impressed with how the burners are responsive and precise. Going from full flame to the lowest setting keeps food warm while you finish up other food items is simple. I have had no issues with our burners to date.

10) The oven comes with convection but my wife hasn't really used it a lot yet. The regular oven setting cooking results have been more even and come out cooked more thoroughly compared to our previous electric range.

Cons

1) Price, this nearly killed the deal. If I hadn't gotten shipping and installation with no sales taxes online, a local buy would have cost us well over $2600.

2) The recessed cook top scratches somewhat easily, so don't use metal based scrubbers.

Warning: If you leave a burner on simmer, it can be difficult to see in a well lit kitchen. It gets pretty low.

In short, this range has been one of the best deals I have ever gotten and I couldn't be happier with my purchase. I would highly recommend it.

This is a nice small stove with 4 burners. It comes ready to install in a countertop including a board with a template to use for cutting the proper size hole. It also comes with 4 feet so that it can be used on a solid surface. This is how we use ours – in our outdoor kitchen. It comes configured for natural gas but can be converted to propane with the included nozzles. It also comes with a pressure regulator for natural gas if that’s the fuel source you are using.

The branding is screen printed on the stainless-steel surface and ours was smudged when we opened it. This isn’t a big deal for us because we’re using it in an outdoor covered kitchen, but it wouldn’t look aesthetically pleasing in a home kitchen. The labelling of the burners front to back on each side is also backwards, so make sure you’re turning on the correct burner.

It comes with cast iron grates and a special holder for one burner that will support a wok. We use ours for canning and the large burners are sufficient for big 23 qt pots. The burners have electronic ignition and require a 110V regular outlet for power.

This is a really nice small gas cooktop. It comes with feet so if you want to use it on a tabletop or counter you can, you just have to have a fuel source. It uses either natural gas or propane. It comes with 2 sets of orifices – one for each type of gas, (see picture). The natural gas orifices are installed at the factory. You can change to propane if that’s what you need to use. If using the cooktop as a portable gas range with a propane tank, you will need to obtain the proper hose and regulator to fit your desired propane tank.

It can also be permanently installed in a countertop. A template is included in the box and it comes with all of the accessories for permanent installation. The power cord is for the electric ignition. The knobs have a push to turn mechanism that activates the electric ignition as soon as you push down on the knob.

The main body is made from stainless steel, the burners are aluminum, and the burner tops and grate are cast iron. The rating for the burners is 9500 BTU for the big burner and 6000 BTU for the small burner for natural gas. The BTUs will be higher for propane, so adjust your cooking temperatures and time accordingly.

We bought this washer and its matching dryer in December of 2012. I immediately loved them as they are such an enormous upgrade to the terrible, cheap top loaders I was using before. The sanitize and steam settings are fantastic for a family with three children and a husband who sometimes forgets to switch the laundry before going to bed.

The unit is also pretty quiet, it doesn't rattle or make any annoying noises like I've read about in other product reviews for other machines. I especially like the "singing" alarms which are a far cry from the noxious buzzer sound I'm used to hearing.

All that being said, I give this machine a 3 star rating because of one very odd problem : the lettering wipes off when one tries to clean it after the control panel has had fabric softener or detergent dripped on it. I discovered this when I tried to clean some Downy off of it, using a plain white washcloth dampened with water. Some light researching yielded many complaints about this issue, and I'm concerned Samsung will not be able to do anything so I'll have to use my extended warranty where I bought it to get a new washer (which seems silly). Apparently they didn't bother to put a clear coat over the lettering on the washers so exposure to certain chemicals -- particularly the ones used to clean laundry -- will cause the markings to wipe away. This wouldn't be so terrible if the control dial and buttons didn't add up to 20+ individual words and setting combinations. If they expect me to happily print off a picture of what it looked like "before", just so I can use the darn thing properly, they're wrong.

I will try to come back with an update on how my email to Samsung turns out. If they actually have a solution that doesn't involve putting another of the same in my house (with the same problem), I will bump this up to a 4 star but leave the warning. No one should have to worry about their machine being ruined by a liquid that is used *in* the product on a near-daily basis. And doing returns/exchanges is always a pain I like to avoid.

UPDATE, 1/16/14 : As of today, they continued to blame the control panel wiping off on me and refuse to admit fault. One rep did say they would pay for it, then the next guy who spoke to me after I emailed my model number decided they wouldn't do it after all. I saw another reviewer say going on Facebook and Twitter helped, so I will be trying that and come back with another update. Highly recommend getting a clearcoat if you buy any of their products and promptly treat the control panels as Google searches found problems with Samsung dishwasher and refrigerator panel lettering wiping away with water as well.

Apparently at one point a previous owner thought having an electric dryer was a good idea, and somewhere along the way switched back over to a natural gas dryer which left this plug active but unused. My plug was also in a weird spot, not where the current dryer is now (which made using the required ground pin interesting) There is a regular 110/115volt outlet there for the washer and dryer so I just ignored this 220/230volt plug for a while.

Then one day I decided to check with a multimeter to see if it was active and sure enough it was, but I didn't really have a use for a 220/230 volt outlet in that location. I wondered if there was a cool splitter to use each of the 110/115 legs that make up the 220/230 volt outlet as separate regular 110/115 volt outlets. This was one of the very few solutions I found that met my criteria. For example I really wanted one that had TWO outlets, one from each hot leg of the plug to spread the load out and fully utilize the potential of that unused plug. The other adapters I found online simply used one of the hot legs from the 220/230 outlet and didn't use the other at all, which wastes half of the potential throughput which seemed silly.

The ground plug requirement was an interesting situation since this outlet was not near any other regular outlets, so I couldn't just plug the ground pin into a grounded outlet. That alone was a strange requirement, like if I have a grounded outlet close by to use for that ground pin.. why would I want/need this adapter in most cases? Thankfully the instructions show alternatives to ground it like hooking it to a pipe or something else. I wedged it between a gap in my metal heating/cooling ducts for a solid connection. I know that the ducts are metal all the way to the actual forced air unit 20ish feet away and that the ducts are connected to the heater unit which has a grounded chassis. That way it has as real ground, or at least as real of a ground as I can get. Not the best or most professional looking, but I think it should work well long term. Using a cheap outlet tester both of the outlets from the splitter say they are "normal" and don't complain about an open ground or anything so no issues there.

We enjoyed our LG fridge for about six months. Then, the never-ending battle began.

First, we heard a knocking sound. After answering the door to no one for the tenth time, we realized it was the fridge. I Googled. I read the manual. I scratched my head. “Unplug it,” everything more-or-less told me. Great; restart it. Hold down CTRL+ALT+DELETE at the same time. Got it.

I left it unplugged for the recommended four hours. Then I powered it back up and the knocking immediately commenced. A few days later, we got the IF error code.

Error code? A refrigerator has an error code? Seriously. This was too complicated already. Once again, I turned to Google, the manual, and my scalp. “ I called the store. After all, they had strongarmed us into a warranty I didn’t want, and I’m so glad they did.

So the repairman came out. He told me that these fridges were notorious for breaking down. Then he proceeded to show me how to repair it myself because, “This isn’t the first time and it won’t be the last.”

We took the entire freezer apart to get to the ice blower fan, essentially. It gets frozen solid. Every three months like clockwork.

Was it manageable? Yeah. First world problems and all that. But then other stuff started going down:

-The large mechanism that slides into some other cheap, plastic part did something stupid, so the door wouldn’t always close. So guests would shut our fridge but not shut our fridge, which resulted in …
-A ripped rubber door seal.
-No matter what temp the fridge was set at, food sitting directly on the glass shelves or in two of the three produce drawers would freeze. And we’re not talking about some delightful icy crunch. Entire pieces of fruit, meat, even cheese would freeze solid. Did you know cheese could turn into ice? It can. We cannot store food in half of our fridge. (However, I lined all of the shelves in newspaper, which seems to have helped. Plus, I can now read about the local elections from a year ago every morning while I get the orange juice.)
-The freezer fan clogs with ice so often, I have to mention it …
-… twice.
-The water dispensing button is starting to stick.
-The ice dispenser clogs on a daily basis. We keep a knife honer nearby to stab into the bin. I repeat, this happens daily.
-It gets fingerprinted to he77. I know this is a hazard of being an appliance in a home where the occupants have hands. But I hate this thing and now I’m just searching for more to add to the list.
-The water valve that connects the water line to the fridge wore out. So now we don’t even get water or ice until I replace it.
-And now the ice maker is broken. That's a $120 part.

We have a second fridge in our house. We got it for free from an apartment complex that was throwing them away. We keep it in the garage as a beer fridge. Dudes, this fridge (I don’t even know the brand) is probably 20 years old (at least), is ugly as sin, and is chugging away like we do on beer.

The thing I didn't like about this item was that the plastic coating on the gas line is very thin and the plastic coating is easily breached - just carefully pulling the line thru a hole in my wooden cabinet was enough to scrape off some of the coating to show the metal underneath.  In my application, the gas line is not going to be bumped into or moved once installed.  But in many applications that isn't true, and the plastic coating on this gas line doesn't appear to be anywhere near as thick and durable as that on three other gas lines I have here at the house.  I'd rate this item 5 stars if it had a better plastic coating, but with the very thin coating I'm stretching to rate it 3 stars and I wouldn't buy it for any application where the gas line will be bumped or abraded in any way after installation.

This washer does not have a Torque Load sensor on either the washing motor nor the dryer motor.

This reusable coffee filter is a very good fit in the basket of my old Jet-O-Matic Model 10 ten-cup percolator (see the customer images).

Paper filters do not work very well in percolators, usually folding over during the percolating process and allowing grinds into the basket, thus into the coffee. At times I've made coffee without a filter, because it tastes good (paper filters trap some of the flavorful oils, preventing them from being in the coffee), but some of the grounds get through the small holes in the basket and into the coffee, and those grounds upset my stomach. This reusable filter is a perfect solution in my case. No, it isn't very big, but I rarely make more than two cups of coffee at a time anyway, and it is plenty big enough for that (it looks like you could make at least six cups of coffee in it; more or less depending on how strong you make it). Also, if it were much bigger, it wouldn't fit in my percolator's relatively small basket to begin with. This filter is the same height as my basket, and about a half inch smaller in diameter at the top (my basket tapers a bit to a smaller diameter at the bottom, so the half inch of "breathing room" is a good thing); it almost looks like it was made specifically for a Jet-O-Matic.

My washer was out of balance. I opened it up and found there were only two of these springs in use. I searched the inside of the washer cabinet for broken springs.
It turns out that the machines come with only two for some reason even though therr are mounts for four.
I replaced the two I had and added two more for a total of four.
You have to remove the top ring around the tub by unsnapping it from the plastic outer tub. This will allow you to hook the spring on. The other end has to be slipped over the suspension rods which means disconnecting them to do so. Make sure you spray some white lithium grease onto the sliding faces of the plastic bushings for the suspension rods.
Also look for the technicians manual that is likely in a zip lock bag glued to the inside of the cabinet. In there is instructions for activating the calibration mode for some washers. It says it's necessary after any suspension work.
In the end I replaced the suspension rods and the four springs that this review is for. About a hours work with a 1/4" nut driver and a short flat blade screwdriver.

My front loading Frigidaire washer developed mold after several years of use, primarily because I didn't leave the door open for a day or two to dry out as recommended - my bad. I have an excellent mold killer developed after Katrina called MoldStat that can penetrate nearly anything (bleach can't kill mold in wood), but even that stuff could not get mold out of the rubber gasket. Last week after finding another buildup of mold due to debris clogging the drain ports in the gasket, I decided to replace it. I used to be an engineer, very mechanically inclined, but this job nearly got the best of me!

Big Mistake: I tried to replace the gasket without taking the top and front panels off after reading here that it could be done - it was a nightmare trying to get the lip of the new gasket over the metal flange inside the washer. After fighting it for an hour, I gave up, exhausted, with bloody hands and bruises.

My suggestions from experience:

1. After you tilt the washer to get to the bottom screws, leave it up on a couple scraps of 2 x 4's, makes everything easier to get to.

2. Remove the top and front panels! Gives you much better access to the gasket flange. Have a few scraps of lumber ready for when you remove the front panel - there is an electrical connector that will prevent you from setting the front panel on the ground with it tilted - carefully snip the tip of the wire tie holding the wire harness to the back of the front panel -it sticks out through the flange of the panel (do not attempt to snip it where it wraps around the wires!), then set the panel off to the side on the lumber.

3.Do not use dishwasher soap to lube the flange or gasket - made it so slippery I couldn't get a good grip on anything. I rinsed off the soap, dried out the gasket, then sprayed a garage door lube inside the gasket, let it dry overnight - provided lube inside the gasket without being slippery to the hands. Any sort of spray-on dry lubricant should work.

4. Reinstalling the inner spring that holds the gasket to the inner flange was beyond miserable - the two spacers that came with the gasket were too large, couldn't jam them in place to hold the spring at 12:00. Instead, I got some scrap wood ~ 3/8" thick, and used a C-clamp to hold the first piece of wood and spring in place at 12:00. Worked my way down both sides using additional pieces of wood and clamps until I got the spring to 7:00 and 2:00, at which point the clamps were preventing the spring from stretching any further, so I removed all the blocks/clamps except for the two at 7:00 and 2:00, then got the rest of the spring in place - was a huge struggle though - had to use every ounce of strength I had to stretch that sucker far enough and roll it over the flange. For some reason at this point the spacers actually fit, used them to slowly get the last bit of the spring installed a few inches at a time.

5. While it's apart, take the time to thoroughly clean the inside of the washer where the detergent/bleach dispenser resides, use cleaner of choice and an old toothbrush - found mold in there too - then reassemble/reinstall the panels. Use a wire tie on the right side wire harness you clipped off in step #2 to hold it in place and prevent it from rubbing on the panel.

BTW, this Frigidaire gasket ($81) is identical to another one sold here under the Kenmore brand for $71, which is the one I bought - part number is the same - "Kenmore Sears Washer Front Load Door Rubber seal gasket 134515300-KE". Gave it 5 stars because the product is fine, although the instructions leave a lot to be desired.

It's a bit expensive, and it may look like Venta's just trying to sell you a questionable extra, but don't try to run your Venta Airwasher without it. It acts as a wetting agent, among its other more subtle effects, to utilize the full area of the machine's rotating plates. Without it, water will only appear on the plates in droplets. The smaller area of exposed water surface will result in much lower evaporation efficiency and disappointing humidifier performance. That will contribute to scale accumulation on the plates and inside surface of the tank, as well, further reducing the machine's efficiency and leading eventually to a difficult cleaning process.
I'm less certain about the need for Venta's cleaning solution, also expensive. I pretreat the water I put in the Venta to zero ppm dissolved solids (see my review of the ZeroWater ZP-010 10 Cup Pitcher), thereby eliminating scale accumulation. Apart from that, others have reported being able to clean their Airwashers with simple vinegar, which is a mild acid that dissolves scale. It may just be slower than the proprietary cleaning solution.

This filter is NOT worth the price asked. I ordered a replacement, and after installing it I dissected the original filter that came with our fridge. The attached images show how the filter is constructed. It is a simple activated charcoal cylinder with some very basic o-ring sealing, worth probably around $10 max. I estimate that about 65-85% of the cost of the filter is just profit.

Many companies play the same kind of pricing games for ongoing items, but I think it's deceptive, dishonest, and creates poor incentives for properly maintaining the appliance (which they probably want so they don't have to honor warranty claims). I despise these kinds of business practices, and refuse to cooperate.

Additionally, the 6 month replacement period is ridiculous unless your water supply is exceptionally contaminated. We are on well water and the only thing which needs to be removed is sediment (which is taken care of by a different filter system). The filter I dissected was used for 22 months, and based on what I found within I will now only be replacing the filter every 5 years or so.

Maybe others are happy to pay out the nose for very basic filtration, but I am not.

This is a great fix if your frost free freezer starts freezing up. We were seeing a fair amount of ice build up in the bottom of our freezer. We have a Kenmore Elite side by side that is about 10-12 years old. The first step was to manually defrost the freezer. We used a hair dryer to defrost the ice that had built up in the drain hole. Then we attached this heat probe to the defroster. Be careful! The defroster is made of glass or some other fairly easily broken material. I used a similarly sized screw driver or piece of metal to shape the round end of the probe to approximately the right size. Then I slid the round end over the defroster and directed the other end of the probe into the drain hole. I didn't even screw it on. There's a lot to like about these reusable, bring-your-own-coffee K-Cup compatible pods: work perfectly in my Keureg 2.0 machine, steel mesh basket (long lasting), exterior body made of material which transfers heat slowly (fewer burned fingers when impatiently removing a recently-brewed pod), good water dispersal (extracts from all coffee in the pod), and can even make a slightly stronger cup of coffee than the Keureg default. Bring-your-own-coffee is generally much, much less expensive per serving than unitized K-Cups. Reusable pods allow use of a Keureg brewer without the environmental hazard of single-use K-Cup waste.

In my brewer, there's only one correct orientation when inserting these pods into the brewer. The hinge connecting the pod's body and lid must be at the 12 o'clock position -- that'll safely guide the pod's spike receptacle over the brewer's pod spike, and it'll position the lid of the pod to be correctly read by 2.0 brewers.

With so much to like and to minimize environmental footprint, I want to reuse these pods many, many times. The challenge here is the previously mentioned hinge. It's made of plastic. It has to flex -- open and close -- at least once with every use. And the hinge arrives already exhibiting material fatigue. These pods are reusable, yes, and appear economical although they may be less durable than one might prefer.

The main seal/gasket always collects water after each wash, and if left there, it causes the gasket to stay wet and then mildew can form. Once the mildew appears then the washer will start to smell, and when the washer smells, your clothes smell. YUCK!

Not the same as the OEM filter. Here's why:

The water flows through this filter much faster than the OEM filter. Faster flow means less filtration. I could be a geek and sacrifice one by cutting it open along with the OEM one, but I'm not that much of a geek. I'm confident that if I did, I'd see a smaller carbon block inside.
I had to lower the flow rate with the small in-line water spigot that feeds the fridge from it's connection under the sink. With slower flow, the water is in contact with the filter longer and more stuff is absorbed by the carbon. Also, if you shove a lot of water through the filter quickly, you're also shoving contaminants through it as well. Faster is not better.

I remember when this fridge was new and I started drinking the filtered water that came out of it, just how pure and clean the flavor was- it was shocking how good it was. I hoped for the same experience when I changed the filter to this aftermarket one, but I did not experience it. It tastes cleaner than unfiltered tap water, but not as clean as the OEM filter.
There is about a $10 difference between the cost of the OEM Samsung filter and this one, over a 6 month period that amount is negligible, to get cleaner tasting water. After these filters are used up, I'll go back to the OEM ones.

Installation: Simple. The igniter has no harness attached to it, just the wires. The wires have little barbs at the end so that once you know which harness to use, you just push in the wires into the correct harness.

I removed all shelves, covers and oven door. Unscrewed the old igniter. Gently pulled up the cabling and luckily had enough slack that I could pull the connector up into the oven body and removed the old harness.
I then identified the correct harness and which wire goes into which harness slot and pushed in. I gently pulled on the wiring to make sure it was not loose. Then I reattached the connector to the new harness and gently pushed the wiring down. Reattached the igniter to the oven. Used the extra cladding to cover the hole I made by pulling the wire up and reattached the oven door. I then turned the oven back and saw the igniter glowing and igniting the gas. Turned off the oven and put everything back into place.

Durability: TBD

The key is to only use a table spoon of soap and you absolutely have to use a bit of fabric softener. Also do two rinse cycles. So do a cycle(I do 6 minutes) with a small amount of soap and softener, drain, spin out, do a 2nd cycle with a teensy bit of softener, drain, spin and then a final cycle with just water. Spin, hang, and youll have dry, clean clothes in the morning. Too much soap and no extra rinse and you will end up with very stiff clothes. I paid ~$1000 for my Kenmore 106.51132 210 side-by-side refrigerator/freezer in July 2016. The freezer light (what this part replaces) went out shortly after the 13-month warranty expired, so I didn't bother to get it fixed. Then a few weeks ago both fridge lights quit out a the same time. Sears/Kenmore wanted $99 for someone to come over just to take a look at it, and then labor and parts to repair would be on top of that. A quick search for part costs showed the main fridge light WPW10515058 (replacing W10515058) would be $185.90 MSRP and the freezer light WPW10515057 (replacing W10515057) would be $100.00. DIY sites also indicated two things: (1) The secondary fridge light (also WPW10515057) would likely resume functioning after replacing the main fridge light, and (2) The brightness of the main fridge light may depend on the freezer light working properly. Both of these turned out to be true.

I verified it was easy to remove both lights, and then ordered the Icetech W10515058 and Icetech W10515058 replacement (this part). Per their direction, I flipped off the fridge breaker (easier than unplugging it), extracted the old one using a flathead screwdriver, disconnected the wires, reconnected them to the new part, and installed it. Turning back on the breaker, the secondary fridge light worked perfectly, and the main fridge light worked at about 80% brightness, which is probably all I was getting out of the original part.

Then I repeated the process with the Icetech W10515057 replacement (this part), which also worked properly, and the fridge light replacement now works at 100% brightness.

I figure going with this solution saved me about $300 in parts and labor for both lights, plus the satisfaction of doing it myself.

The product arrived on time and packaged in a clear bag with instructions clearly written on it. At the time they arrived I had just replaced my Keurig filter, so I didn’t use them right away. Today I replaced it. I followed the soaking and rinsing instructions on the bag and which are the same as the OEM instructions. When I began soaking the filter I also pushed the filter under the water manually for a few seconds to insure the filter was completely soaked. I noted air bubbles escaping from the larger side of the filter, which is the bottom when installed. One of the negative remarks I read mention a clogging of the filter. The trapped air bubbles were probably the culprit clogging the intake manifold. So I suggest pushing the filter under water to insure the filter is fully soaked and any air bubbles allowed to escape. I always use filtered water in my Keurig either from the refrigerator or our Brita. As I always do, I ran 2 hot water cycles through our Keurig after installing a new filter. This operation cleans out any debris and allows me the check the water clarity. I read in another review about cloudy grayish colored water. The first hot water cycle produced a few bits of debris and the second was absolutely clear.
So in conclusion, the K&J filters perform just as well as the OEM Keurig filters at a fraction of the cost. Problems with the product posted by others were found to probably be a failure on their part to follow procedural details recommended by Keurig and K&J.

This is the updated, post-recall part for many LG refrigerators with the "frozen fan" error codes. Came with the ice maker door circulation fan but lacked the freezer circulation fan. Easy enough to harvest the old one and install on this panel. The recall update consists of an added electrical connection to a defroster coil on the ice maker circulation fan. It is a bit of a kludge by LG...the additional wire installs on the left side (facing the fridge) but is too short making the install a PITA. Install Instructions:

Remove the old panel (lots of YouTube for this). Pull from the top.
You'll likely need to use a hair dryer to remove a mountain of ice.
Disconnect the wires from the right side connectors.
Swap the fan from the original panel if needed.
Disconnect the yellow connector from the left side.
Connect the new purple defrost wire to the left side connector (where the yellow one went)
Connect the old yellow connector to the secondary connector on the purple wire. PITA ... hard to see but you can do it.
Reconnect right side connectors.
The freezer circulation fan won't start until the coils are cold so don't freak out.

I was hearing this terrible grinding noise from my LG WM0642HW washing machine.  It started intermittently, but over time it got louder and then the  drum stopped spinning.  Did some research, downloaded the service manual, and took the back panel off.  Turns out the bolt got loose over time and the metal teeth of the inner gear striped the plastic teeth of the outer one, which in the middle of the rotor.  Replacing it was very easy.  Loosen the bolt and pull the old rotor assembly straight back. Then push the new rotor assembly in, spin a bit to line up the gears and push it all the way in, tighten the bolt, and put the back cover on.  It was one of the easiest repairs I've done.  Now the washer runs very quietly and the drum spins as it should.

After about 15 years or so of having our whirlpool top loader with agitator, it finally started showing signs that it was giving up. So over the past several months or so I have been researching washing machines. One thing that I notice about most people who own a "HE" top load washing machine is either the thing breaks A LOT or people hate it because it doesn't seem to clean clothes that well. So, I also decided to research front loaders..............and unfortunately, you get a similar bleak picture regarding front loading machines. You hear about error codes where the washing machine will no longer work and needs service, part failures, etc. What the heck happened to a simple old school washing machine? Well the one company that seems to sell them is Speed Queen. It seems like everyone loves their Speed Queen's reliability and ability to clean clothes quickly and efficiently. I do admit that the price tag on the Speed Queen's can make you squirm in your chair and make you have 2nd thoughts about purchasing this machine when Whirlpool and some other manufacturers still make an old school washer. So what prompted me to purchase Speed Queen vs other brands? Simple. Look at the way they are built and check out their standard warranty on Speed Queen's website! Now granted........I have only had my Speed Queen for about a week but I have already done about 15-20 loads of laundry since it was delivered. Keep in mind that there is some residual black residue inside the washer. I simply filled the tub with hot water and detergent and ran 2 full cycles. That seemed to eliminate a good majority of it instead of having to scrub the heck out of the washer. After the 2 initial cycles, I then added rags and towels to a 3rd cycle and found that there was still a little bit of the black residue inside. However, the washing of the rags and crappy towels removed whatever remaining black residue was in the tub. So no scrubbing of the tub for me. Let the machine do it for you. Yes this machine is a little noisy but if it means my clothes are being washed properly and not in 6 inches of water like the HE machines I'll take it! On a heavy duty cycle with extra large load, heavy soil, and adding the 2nd rinse option takes the washer about 40-45 minutes from start to finish. So far, I'm very pleased with it. I'll update later down the road if I notice anything.

***UPDATE***
I've had my Speed Queen for almost a year and it's still running like champ with no isses! I'm very pleased with my washing machine. This machine can see upwards of 20 loads of laundry at any given time within a span of 2 days. I would have kicked myself in the ass if I would have bought an "HE" machine. Best "old school" washing machine that I have seen or used so far. Love it!

I concluded that I probably did not have enough solar panels to keep my 24 volt battery fully charged and added another 124 watts of solar panels, making a total of 424 watts in panel output. I used a credit card to pop it up at first, but eventually just made slits in the suction cups so they didn't work anymore, but still gripped because they're soft rubber. That worked just fine. No need for sticking them so hard to anything. Ever.

-My first machine was defective. I heard a "squealing" sound. It was air escaping because the bottom piece had not been properly glued on. It eventually popped off, but they sent a new machine immediately, so it must have been a dud.

-For some reason, I found this thing laborious. Put clothes in. Add water from bucket since it doesn't line up under the faucet/it gets really heavy when it fills halfway. Lid on. Turn a lot of times. Lid off. Drain. Add water to rinse. Lid on. Turn a lot of times. Lid off. Drain. Squeeze clothes out to hang (before I got the little dryer...which is amazing). It felt like it took forever and my back hurt from being bent over it constantly.

-It's literally held together with a few plastic clips and a metal clip on either side. That's it. It gets pretty heavy when it's full of water and clothes and cannot take any serious movement any way or another before those little clips start popping out. I recommend gluing them in if you aren't going to be taking it apart for any reason.

Anyway, like I said, I used this for about a month before switching to another product which did the washing for me and didn't quite as much babysitting. It clearly works for some people, but I don't have time for all that.

I moved into an apartment without a washer or dryer in July and immediately started looking for alternatives that I could keep at home. The Wonderwash looked like the best option. It is small but, for a single guy, it is more than enough. It runs a load relatively quickly and the barrel can be filled almost to the brim with satisfactory results. I add cloths, soap, and then water to the top of the cloths (usually about 3/4 full) and spin for about 5 minutes. Then I drain the soapy water and replace it with fresh water for a rinse for another 5 minutes. After this I wring out the cloths and hang them to dry on my indoor rack over a mat that catches dripping water. By the next day, the cloths will be dry, provided the house is kept at about 70 degrees Fahrenheit. I do a lot of very dirty work (wildlife biology) that involves hiking through swamp water, mud, and dust. I have found that the Wonderwash is not sufficient to clean mud-caked pants in a single wash. However, if I clean the bulk of the mud off my pants before placing them in the wash, they come out fine. Also, it is made of plastic (not the most environmentally-conscience substance) which, after several months of use, is showing signs of cracking around areas of strain (near the suction feet, mostly). Besides those two complaints, I have very much appreciated this good alternative to the laundromat. The Wonderwash is an affordable, quality product for anyone looking to keep their electricity bill down.

If you're like me, and you are incubating eggs for the first time, you need some pretty clear instructions. The instructions written in the manual are unclear and obviously not written with English as the primary language. The sentences are chopped and look like someone was writing in shorthand and the manual was directly copied as their shorthand. So, it takes a little bit of research before you can actually set it up and start.
Things you want to understand: This model doesn't have the wire in the hub that needs to be connected. It's out of the box, plug-in power cords, and ready to go type set up. You need to add water, but it doesn't tell you how much. Your best bet is to wait until it's warm to add your water and add slowly until it reads your desired humidity range. It does not tell you what your ranges for temperature or humidity need to be on the initial set-up page, you have to look further back in the 6-page pamphlet that counts for a manual. My husband had to search the micro-text for the information because my neurodivergent brain was looking where you would logically find it, in the set up prehatch stages.
I just set it up today, starting with 20 eggs (it will hold 56). Here's hoping we interpreted everything correctly. I will have another review in 21 days when we should actually have chicks.

Edit: UPDATE.
The only 2 problems I have with this model is that you have to remove the turning pieces to safely hatch chicks, the lid deforms a bit from the heat and won't meet the edges completely (masking tape helped keep the heat and humidity at level days 20-23), and when eggs are placed on the mesh grid for hatching so the chicks don't get heads or feet stuck in the egg turner it rolls them around and doesn't have a guarded edge to keep chicks from falling through. Lost one chick because she fell through the side to the bottom and drowned because she got stuck headfirst in the spacing. After that, I removed chicks before they dried completely and placed them under a heat lamp because it just isn't safe with them toddling around that edge.

I have owned some version of a countertop ice maker for about the last five years. Doesn’t matter the brand, and doesn’t matter the size...most if them work I’m the same manner. As ice cubes are made, they are held in a basket above the cold water. If they are not used, they eventually begin to melt, the water will drain into the reservoir, and new ice will be made. The unit itself is NOT a freezer, so keep that in mind if you consider ordering ANY portable ice maker. My story has been the same...the ice maker arrives, it supplies enough ice for about one person to be satisfied with. Hot summers become more difficult for the machine to keep up with demand, and frequently the lid is opened only to find a disappointing amount of ice has been made. Add another person to the mix, and it is impossible for the machine to keep up. UNTIL NOW...This machine is AMAZING (and it is quite a bit larger than most of the units I have owned). Well that extra size appears to pay off greatly...more than adequate ice in the morning (when the ice is softest due to non-use melting), and a full ice basket all day and evening long. The basket is larger and therefore holds more ice...more than enough for 2 people to use all day long. It is with hesitation that I used to open the lid in the morning  (expecting to just see bits of ice in basket), and am now almost overjoyed when I see a full basket of ice staring back at me. If you have had bad luck with an ice maker of an sort, you know what I am talking about,  I am THRILLED with this machine. However....these machines do not last forever, so I would suggest you consider the following: 1) ALWAYS purchase an EXTENDED WARRANTY for your machine...at least 2 years or more. These warranties (purchased through Amazon) have covered me twice when my previous machines have “konked out” at 18 to 24 months. Full reimbursement of purchase price, no hassles. 2) CLEAN your machine. In all the owner manuals I have read, not one of the suggests cleaning (or de-scaling) the machine. Amazon sells “ice maker cleaner” which is nickel safe, and will not harm the machine. I recommend wiping down the inside of the machine with the diluted solution, AND running at least a portion of it through several ice making batches to clean out the water tubes also. I clean my coffee maker monthly...but never thought about ice machine. 3) Change the water in the machine about every 3 month (or more). Regardless of your cleanliness when removing ice and adding new water, some dust particles (or possibly more) will settle inside the water in your machine. Just drain the water, and refill, before any of that sediment moves into the water pipes, if your water has sediment in it, filter the water before adding it to the icemaker.

Yes, the PM2.5 does respond to air quality. After sitting at zero for a few days, I was beginning to wonder if the PM2.5 sensor worked at all. In retrospect, it was displaying zero due to the HEPA air cleaner running in the room and my worries were unfounded.

As evidence, we burnt some food while cooking and I could see the PM2.5 reading increase steadily up to 30, even though the smoke was not visible where the sensor was located in the neighboring room. After opening windows and running air cleaners at maximum power, the number stopped increasing and then slowly declined over the next two hours. So anyone who is concerned that the unit is not working (and anyone buying this unit probably also has HEPA air cleaners in the room) could simply locate the unit in the kitchen for a quick experiment.

One annoyance is the clock. I don't think anyone needs another clock in the room and this clock has the annoyance of not having a battery backup, so any power outage means another resetting of the clock to placate one's inner OCD tendencies. Probably better to put some masking tape over the clock section!

Symptom was no water into the ice maker but it is this unit, not the solenoid valve.
You can test the solenoid water inlet valve by removing the square white cover on the end of the icemaker (pry the bottom edge down and out) and jumpering the N and V holes on the black housing using an INSULATED wire. DANGER - line voltage on these. Door switch needs to by held closed during this test.

The problem with these units, as others have pointed out, is the connection from the tray heater to the control housing. The tray heater has round pins engaging flat spring contacts on the housing which makes small point contact connections. This causes overheating and causes burning/melting.

A factory solution would be simple and low cost by creating different contact geometry or using wires like the motor uses.

FWIW I repaired my old one using a piece of wire, routed carefully to avoid the mechanism, to bypass the connection. Heater pin is nichrome or stainless so I could not solder to it (maybe with the right flux and solder you could). Instead I soldered the wire to the inside part of a "tip jack" and pushed this on the pin. You also might be able to use the contact from a large size disk drive power cable or something else in your junk drawer.

Although the outside stainless steel braiding on these hoses are good for preventing sudden blowouts, they do nothing to keep the rubber on the inside from eventually decaying and rotting. Which means, if you let enough time go by and the rubber rots on the inside, the hose won't burst but it'll start to leak through the cracks and the stainless steel braided lining on the outside can do nothing to contain the water. Then you come home to a flooded house and who knows how much money in damages. So keep in mind that this isn't a buy-once-and-forget-about-it type of product.

There's lots of different stainless steel braided hoses here on Amazon. It's pretty hard to figure out which is better than the other. And I'm sure they're all made in some foreign factory and shipped into the US. So I gambled and chose this brand since this is the brand I bought physically in the hardware store the last time I bought hoses and they have done well for the past 5 yrs without any issues.

Anyway, these hoses fit the washer and the water outlet just fine. The brass fittings are not super thin and cheap, and the hoses didn't have too much of a memory effect where they stay coiled. Hoses fit just fine and I noticed no water leakage. The 90 degree neck worked well for me so that I could get the washer closer to the wall and avoid kinks. Everything felt pretty durable and well made and good enough quality that I can forget about them for about another 5 yrs. Speaking of which, I make up a little label on a small Post-it note that says "replace hoses in 2025" and tape it to the corner of the washer, kind of like what they do at oil change places, so that every time I do a load, I remind myself of when to do the maintenance. $15 every 5 yrs is cheap insurance.

The good:
* It's compact and works in a condo development like mine where you're not allowed to have a washer or dryer
* It fits into a closet
* It doesn't use much water at all
* It saves you hiking all the way to the laundromat
* It really chugs away and gets clothes nice and clean
* The spinner is excellent, and gets clothes a lot dryer than most machines
* The price is right
* You can set the water temperature exactly how you want it (because you're filling it yourself and can adjust the water from the sink

The not-so-good (?):
* THIS IS NOT AN AUTOMATIC MACHINE. If you're a first-world person and you're used to things happening all by themselves when you push a button, then this is NOT for you. You have to pour in the water, set the wash cycle, pump out the water, pour in new water for the rinse, tell the machine to pump out the water again, move the clothes to the spinner on the right, etc.
* The machine is very powerful, so it's not really good for super-delicate things. I tried to put delicates in a mesh bag, like somebody else suggested, but the machine just tore up the mesh bag. So perhaps do delicates separately, and then only run the cycle for 2 minutes or so.
* Be careful not to add too much detergent. It's kind of hard to get all of the bubbles out at the end if you use what you'd think is a regular amount.
* You can't do a bunch of loads all at once, like you can at the laundromat, or do a super-big load. That said, I am able to wash a complete set of queen sized sheets, plus a towel, and it works just fine.

Bottom line: I was moving back to the US from the Third World, and therefore thought this thing was pretty nifty. My family, who has never lived outside the US, thinks it's quirky and funny, and wonders why I use it...

I purchased this beverage center to store my ever-growing beer collection in, and it is perfect for that purpose! I've addressed a few different items below to hopefully help prospective buyers (many of these have been mentioned in other reviews as well) -

TEMPERATURE -

The beverage center comes with an adjustable temperature knob. I would recommend following the instructions of initially running the unit at max cool temp for 3-4 hours and then turning it back to the 10 o'clock position on the dial. If you leave it there, it should keep the temperature in the mid to upper 40's while not requiring the fan/compressor to run constantly. Ambient temperature may affect this, but I have mine stored in a pretty warm room. This temperature falls within the desired range for most styles of beer. If all of your beer is fizzy and yellow and you prefer to drink it ice cold, then you need to take a step back and rethink your life choices.

By the way - this unit does NOT come with any sort of temperature gauge. You should purchase a refrigerator/freezer gauge to accurately monitor it. I went with this model - [[ASIN:B00875TVYQ Taylor Precision Products Digital Refrigerator/Freezer Thermometer]]

NOISE -

I have this beverage center sitting next to my couch in my loft / MAN CAVE. I can watch TV quietly at night and the sound from the compressor is NOT excessively loud or annoying. Also keep in mind, as I mentioned above - if you don't run the unit at max cool temperature then that will reduce the amount of time that the fan/compressor are running.

INTERIOR LIGHT -

Many people have complained about the warm white or YELLOW "old" looking interior light. I agree that it looks bad. Some have replaced it with strings of cool white LED lights. I recommend just replacing the bulb with a cool white LED bulb - one with an E12 size base will fit. I went with this model and it looks great - [[ASIN:B015O6UT6E Rayhoo 2pcs E12 Base LED Bulb 104-SMD LEDs White Light 5 Watt AC 110V Lamps Equivalent to 40W T3 Halogen Track Bulb Replacement LED Bulbs,6000-6500K, 300-320LM]]

CARPET -

The door will most likely drag if you put the unit directly on carpet. You should use a piece of tile, wood, or small table to get it up off the ground. Something that is at least 15.5" by 15.5" will cover all of the legs. I used an extra piece of kitchen tile that I had and it works perfectly.

SHELVES -

You will need to adjust the shelves to fit your needs. In my case, I removed 2 of them and kept 2 in there. I use the bottom (not a shelf) to store bombers and extra-tall bottles, the middle shelf to store regular bottles, and the top shelf to store cans and short bottles.I haven not had a problem with bottles tipping or not sitting properly on the wire shelves, but if you do, you can purchase some mats like these, cut them to fit, and place on top of the shelves where needed - [[ASIN:B00METEK0Q Flexible Chopping Mats 4 Pack]]

The only difference between this part and another more expensive part that comes up as the "correct" part for my fridge is the stainless steel cover. You can remove the cover from the broken paddle and put it on the replacement via 4 small tabs (I used a small flat-head screwdriver and needle-nose pliers).  To install, you just need to remove 1 screw (underneath and to the right of the dispenser hole). Pull out and then down on the control panel. No need to unplug or remove anything else. Place the right-angled end of the spring in the hole above the one where the pin goes in, put the pin in the spring but don't put it into the hole yet. Hold everything carefully and use a butter knife (or nail file or other thin flat thing) to move the straight end of the spring into the notch on the paddle. It will be toward the actual front of the paddle and you're moving it to the back side over the top of the pin. Carefully, while still holding everything steady so your spring doesn't come out, drop that pin down into the hole and then snap the other pin in. My spring popped out the first time so I had to take the pins back out and try again, be gentle. Once you get the spring in right and the paddle secured, just snap the panel up and in, replace the screw and you're back in business.

I purchased two different temperature and humidity sensors a little over a year ago. I’ve already reviewed them both, and I like them both very much.

One of them died recently, after lasting almost a year and a half.

I have never in my life seen the weird type of battery it used, so since I had no idea what to search for and figured the battery, being so unique, might cost as much as the original thermometer (I believe I paid $5.00 for it) I decided to start shopping around for a new one.

It’s pretty critical I have a relatively accurate thermometer because I use it to determine the ambient temperature around all of my AV equipment for my home theater, which is installed in a separate small room off to the side of the theater, down in the basement.

Unfortunately, this room doesn’t get any exchange of air and unless the AC is running, it stays really hot.

My old thermometer, until it died, spent most of its life saying it was 80 degrees.

The good news is that the second thermometer I purchased, for the actual home theater (which takes regular AAA batteries) always agreed that the equipment room was 80 degrees, so I felt even if they weren’t accurate, at least they were “relatively” accurate.

When the battery died, I started looking for a replacement and I came across this one available at a discount in exchange for my honest review. It looked like it would fit the bill, so I ordered it.

It takes regular batteries so it should last a lot longer than the previous one. The real test was to see if it also agreed on the temperature with the other two.

Sure enough, it’s 80 degrees!

I think the size and style of this thermometer is perfect and I may buy another one for the rest of the basement, outside of the home theater and equipment rooms.

It’s the exact size of a business card, in case you were wondering. It’s 2” by 3.5” which is the standard size for all business cards, credit cards, etc. It’s only 3/8” thick, too.

There are three buttons, all on the right hand side.

The first button (on the top) is to clear out the min/max readings. If you’re putting the thermometer in another room and wish to reset the min/max readings, this would be the button you press.

The second button scrolls between the min, max, and normal readings. Each time you press the button it will switch between displaying the min, max, and current temperature and humidity readings.

The bottom button couldn’t be simpler. Each time you press it, it switches the readout from “F” to C” readings.

This device takes a LR1130 button battery which you can find at any dollar store available in multi-packs for $1.00.

It has a built-in kick stand which is pretty cool, but I wish it wasn’t so flimsy. It works, though, which is good enough for me.

It’s not weatherproof, so it’s only for indoor use. Also, there is no backlight. It isn’t wall mountable. They could have easily put a keyhole mount in the mold so it could be wall mounted, but they didn’t. Additionally, there is no way to calibrate it, so it is what it is.

Those are the only things keeping me from giving it 5 stars.

I really like this new temperature/humidity sensor and while I cannot say for certain it is accurate, it does match my other two digital thermometers readings very well, so that’s good enough for me.

This is a good downdraft cook top for a 30 inch opening. A lot of the cook tops out there are too big and have 5 burners. I was concerned about other reviews stating the flame is sucked into the downdraft. The downdraft is indeed pretty strong (which is a good thing) but the flame-pull issue does not seem to be a problem at all on my unit. You can see a little slight tug of the flame, but no problems -- the heating is fine. Here are the reasons I gave only 4 stars: 1. Once when the water boiled over, it knocked out the flame. If I hadn't been standing there to notice what had happened, I'd have been none-the-wiser with the gas coming out. 2. If you turn the cooktop knob too fast, it bypasses the lighting of the flame, and then again, just gas is coming out. (My husband did this. He had too quickly turned on the cooktop to pre-heat the pan, but he never noticed that there was not an actual flame lit under the pan.) These both seem like safety issues to me. My previous gas cooktop had a continual clicking when the flame was either knocked mid-cooking out or not lit at start up. Therefore, you knew there was a problem and did not walk away until resolved. I feel people should be aware of this safety issue.

I was glad to find this vent and it can cure the problem of an improperly vented dryer vent. In my case, the builder had installed a dryer vent into a space between the ceiling of a small porch area and the roof. The vent pipe terminated at an ell that was suspended just above the ceiling in the porch area. A 4" diameter hole was cut into the ceiling and a makeshift vent cover was placed over that. Although much of the air from the dryer vent was able to escape, moist air was also distributed into the area and a very large amount of lint accumulated on the framing and plywood that formed the ceiling of the porch, and blocked the vent cover. This vent was the cure for that problem. The only thing wrong was that the inside diameter of the 4" inlet to the vent was too small to accept any of the off the shelf metal duct, flexible duct, or metal ells. You will need a 1/4" socket and ratchet (preferably in 1/4" drive) along with a 6-10" extension or better yet just a 1/4" nut driver to remove all the small screws, also a wire stripper to redo the wiring.

1.) Pull off the door, very easy, just open it to the first stop and pull it out, no screws or nothing.
2.) Remove all your baking shelves.
3.) Turn on the oven light for better illumination, you don't need to unplug the oven as long as you're not trying to bake while repairing it. If you electrocute yourself somehow you did it wrong. Go Darwinism... Seriously though, if you feel more comfortable unplugging it do so, just make sure to have good lighting available.
4.) Pull the bottom oven cover, might be two screws at the back you need to remove first, mine didn't have them, pull it back to release the front lip and then lift the back out and remove from the oven.
5.) Note the burner tube with the igniter bolted to it. Remove the single front screw that bolts the front of the burner tube to the oven body.
5.) The igniter is bolted to the burner tube with two screws that are miserable to remove at the angle they are installed at, don't waste your time or patience. It can be done but not without swearing, then you still have to deal with the wiring.
6.) So instead just pull your bottom pan storage drawer, comes right out.
7.) Get on the floor and look at the back of the oven from where you just pulled the storage tray. There are two screws that bolt the lower end of the burner tube to the back of the oven. Remove them.
8.) There are two wires that go to the igniter, one goes directly to the control unit with a spade connector, unplug that. The other goes to an inline connector, unplug that.
9.) Now you are free to lift the entire burner tube with the igniter attached from the oven compartment, pull it all the way out to where you can work on it.
10.) Unscrew the old igniter, screw in the new igniter. One wire on the new igniter already has a spade connector, that will go to your control unit. The other will need to be stripped and spliced with the provided ceramic wire nut to your inline connector from the old igniter, don't cut your wires too short.
11.) Feed the wires and burner tubes back end down to where you pulled it from making sure you get all the wires down underneath so they don't sit up in the oven section.
12.) Plug it all back in, spade connector to control unit, inline connector to your ovens inline connector. If you didn't leave yourself enough wire this is the time to find out.
13.) Position the burner tube over the gas orifice and line up your two mounting screw holes.
14.) Re-install those two burner mounting screws. Use a small piece of paper (tear a piece off your 'instruction' sheet) between your socket or nut driver and the screw to wedge the screws in place so they don't fall out as your trying to reach in to line everything up and get them started.
15.) Re-install the front mounting screw on your burner tube.
16.) Double check your electrical connections, make sure something didn't come apart while you were installing the burner mounting screws.
17.) Before you install the rest of the covers do a quick test to make sure your repair has worked. Turn your oven on to say 300 degrees..., the igniter should come up to a nice glow, a few seconds later the control module should sense everything is okay and turn on your gas. If it does, immediately turn off the oven as the burner doesn't burn well without the top cover in place.
18.) Congratulations! Put the rest of your oven back together and make a big deal out of it to whoever will listen to you.

Like I mentioned earlier these are specific to about an eight year old Kenmore oven, yours may be easier or harder but I suspect the process should be similar.

One last thing I wanted to mention is that I compared the old and new igniters closely and the factory stampings on them were very similar (almost identical) and so was the physical overall quality so I suspect whoever really makes them also supplies them to the retail manufacturers or supply houses who jack up the prices because well, that's what they do...

Review from October 23, 2017:
I've given this range 8 months of solid use, so I figured it was time to write a review. I would say I use the stove range at least 4 to 5 times a week if not more, and I use the oven portion at least twice a week. I often do soups and stews, so I tend to do a lot of simmering over long periods of time.

Aesthetically, this stove is a real crowd-pleaser. I would say that I get more compliments on the stove than anything that I have ever put inside my home. It is stainless steel, the oven is blue inside, and the cast iron stove top looks very well put together and polished.

Cooking wise, I have very few issues and everything has turned out very well. The one thing I can say is that if you have never used the stove like this before, which I had not previously, you are in for higher temperatures with a commercial gas range than you're used to, and that can result in some burning at the bottom of a pot until you get it under control. I've had to adjust the temperature a bit to accommodate for this in everything that I make.

The convection part of the oven works very well. I was told that gas stoves aren't ideal for things like baking because the temperature can't be regulated as well. R this oven, that is simply not the case. I made macarons using the convection fan on the oven, and they turned out perfectly. The recipe even accommodated for using a conventional gas oven, which involved taking the macarons out and switching the pan. That step was not necessary because the oven is well-insulated, and the convection fan circulated effectively.

I only have one small gripe, but this has been true of every oven I've ever owned that is gas, so I'm not even sure if it's singular to this particular model, but I can say that when you light one burner some of the other ones snap and pop like they are attempting to ignite. It's a bit alarming when it happens rapid fire and you aren't even moving the knob.

That said, I feel like this oven is totally solid and I would recommend it to anyone. It's simplistic in its controls, you aren't overwhelmed with a ton of options, and you can focus on what's important - cooking!
