We recently purchased this Samsung model (almost 2 weeks ago) and not wanting to jinx anything (knock on wood), it is working flawlessly (right now anyway). The 2 biggest complaints I have is the intolerably loud noise the ice-maker creates when ice is ejected into the bucket. It's even more frighteningly loud when the ice bucket is empty as the sound amplifies upon impact with the hollow plastic container. I read other reviews commenting on this and thought it was an exaggeration, it's not. Samsung should really consider re-engineering the container by adding some sound deadening material around it to help muffle the noise (yes, it's truly that annoying). The other issue is relatively minor and indicative of all stainless appliances... the never ending battle against finger prints and skin oil smudges.

All that aside, the bottom line to any appliance purchase today is akin to betting on roulette and expecting to win (worst odds ever). Like many, I did an inordinate amount of product research and read countless customer reviews prior to purchasing. Opinions and experiences are all over the map. And this is a fundamental problem for all brands not just Samsung. As mentioned elsewhere there is much outsourcing going on and it seems almost impossible for manufacturers to attain consistent quality levels. BTW, I was surprised to learn (after purchasing) this refrigerator is imported from Korea. I bring this up only because it supports many customer complaints concerning long wait times when breakdowns inevitably occur. The delays are primarily the result of long distance parts delivery. Several service repair companies I contacted are not even qualified to work on these appliances as Samsung strictly controls the qualification process along with parts distribution (exporting from Korea).

To be fair, this Samsung replaces a 12-year old Maytag side by side (with ice-maker) which I can't begin to relate just how horrible and unreliable a refrigerator can be! It was the first appliance I ever bought with an extended warranty (reluctantly). It was also the first appliance I inevitably recouped my money from using that warranty (and then some) due to abnormally frequent repairs and parts replacement (both costly to the insurance company). What I learned from this is warranties can be useful for offsetting expensive service and food replacement costs but doesn't instill customer confidence or improve product reliability... it is what it is. Factor in countless hours due to lost work time; aggravation with incompetent CSR agents; delays and missed appointments with repair ppl and outrageous amounts of wasted food... you can easily see where this is going.

So don't hate Samsung just because it's not assembled in North America (who is?) or you see customer complaints online. In fact, check any brand and it's pretty much the same for all. CR may rate some models and brands higher but unfortunately (and inevitably) they all have issues. There are only a handful of companies (worldwide) making compressors and major components for refrigerators these days and every manufacturer is buying from them. So no brand is immune and "inconsistent" quality has been around for awhile now. The days of buying a refrigerator (or any major appliance) and expecting it to last for 20 years are long over. And spending more money doesn't help either. High end brands such as Viking and Sub-Zero are notoriously problematic and appear even more unreliable.

The bottom line is no matter how much research and regardless what brand you prefer or currently own... you definitely will be rolling the dice and taking a bigger chance than you might expect on your next purchase. The days of "Maytag reliability" are long gone (I can most definitely attest to that). Long term reliability is not the norm, it is an anomaly. Don't expect your next refrigerator to provide more than 7-10 years of consistent reliability (at most). Like other "tech toys" refrigerators have become trendy fashion statements, several high end models have built in flat screens with wi-fi, so don't expect them to last long. In fact, the tech will easily become obsolete long before the warranty ends prompting many to upgrade just to stay current.

The best advice I can offer anyone is cover your bets and consider an extended warranty and use AmEx or Discover (check their respective policies) to extend it another year. Because unlike back in the day, it may not take years to see problems develop in new appliances and 28 cubic feet of food spoils real quick and gets real expensive...

Update: 07-29-12
A brief update: After more than 7 months there is no significant issues to report and that is really saying something these days...

The refrigerator continues to operate flawlessly albeit with the following very minor issues. Every so often the unit makes a slight humming, mechanical or vibrating noise emanating from the rear. If I give it a slight nudge or push, it stops but returns infrequently. My suspicion is there may be a lose line inside the back that vibrates in sympathy with the compressor when it kicks on. Still its only sporadic and not repeatable enough to call out a tech... yet.

Beyond that all areas of the fridge appear to operate normally maintaining correct temps within acceptable tolerances. I installed 3 small digital thermometers within the upper, mid and lower (double door fridge, pull-out drawer & freezer) sections. Depending on time of day and frequency of access, the temps rarely deviate beyond +/- 5 degrees, which is really good especially with the unrelenting summer heat.

Our electric utility bills appear slightly higher than last year but the utility's "smart meter" indicates outdoor temps to be almost 2 degrees hotter these past months. Factor in our utilities super high rate pricing or "peak demand" for July & August (thanks SRP) and abnormally higher temps and it's tough to know if the refrigerator's efficiency gains aren't offset by our home's dual AC systems which cycle more frequently this time of year?

Lastly, the annoying ice maker continues to do it's part, still functioning normally albeit loudly. We have come to terms with it and now view it as a "feature" enhancement as you always know when its working. Guess you can get used to anything, all in all no real regrets...

Final Update: 07-01-14
Unless there is a catastrophic failure this will be my last update of issues and solutions we've experienced now that it's been more than 2.5 years with the fridge.

On 04-25-13 the infamous water drip began to appear. It started with several drips throughout the day, now we only see an occasional drip once per week or so. Over the course of the next 6 months I estimate about 3 techs, 2 water control valves (bottom back of unit), 2 hose connectors (under top door hinge) and a left door water/ice dispenser were all "experimentally" replaced. Remember, these were all trial and error exercises performed over weeks by various techs since none actually knew the root cause. While the net result of all these "fixes" yielded varying degrees of success I cannot say with certainty which really fixed the problem as none actually have. That said if I had to narrow it down to one "solution" I must say it was the one I least expected... the door dispenser. After each item was replaced we waited several weeks to observe and only after the door dispenser did I see the best result.

On 11-27-13 ice sheets began forming on the underside of the freezer pull out drawer (clear plastic storage tray inside freezer). I tried to thaw it out with a hair dryer but inevitably it reoccurred within 3-4 days. After fully extending the main freezer drawer and peering inside (between bottom of drawer and inside the freezer) a massive ice sheet had formed. Ultimately it was determined a clogged refrigerator drain tube was backing water up into the freezer where it spread and froze into a sheet. A tech was sent out to clear it and they say voila, no more ice sheets.

To summarize, all of these issues in an of themselves are really not significant but can be annoying and certainly time consuming to resolve so welcome to the new world order of appliance quality and ownership. As I initially stated way back at the beginning of this review don't go looking for long term reliability anymore. We purchased a Samsung dishwasher soon after and within about a year required replacement of a plastic upper tray lift release part that broke without ever using it. Later another recent acquisition, a Samsung microwave (arriving soon after the dishwasher) needed a new door due to a malfunctioning keypad. That's right the keypad isn't replaceable so time for a complete new door (handle and all)!

I still maintain if you plan to buy a new appliance, Samsung or otherwise GET AN EXTENDED WARRANTY! I promise you 2 things, I am not getting any commission or kick back for these (wish I were) and you will not lose money on it as it will more than likely pay for itself over time. After helping my sister about 6 months ago move into a her first condo I found a deal on a similar (slightly smaller) version of this fridge. I also made sure she purchased an extended warranty too. So far she hasn't needed it but I'm sure it won't be long...

Finally I'll leave you with this thought.
Remember life is too short so don't sweat the small stuff... it can always get fixed.

When this stove cover arrived yesterday, I found it was just a solid piece of mat. It had no cut-out holes in it for the burners. At first, I was disappointed because I didn't know it. One of the reasons it took me so long to decide which cover to buy was that I wanted all the holes in the right places and of the correct size.
But this turned out to be a blessing in disguise. I knew the overall size of the mat was the size I needed because I measured the surface of my range. All I needed to do was measure and cut my own holes. I removed all my grates and burner parts, then laid the mat down over the open holes and taped it down so it wouldn't slide or move. I pressed the mat down on each hole for the burners and the ignitors to make an impression in the mat and also marked it with a felt tip marker. I then removed the mat and cut the holes first with a razor knife, then with a normal size of scissors. For the small holes I used a pair of manicure scissors. The mat is very easy to cut. After a couple of fine-tuning cuts, it fit perfectly.
Several of the complaints I read about mats with precut holes is that the the holes are too large. The advantages to making custom cuts was that with making holes in the mat the same size of the holes in the range top instead of the burner is that when the burner parts are reinstalled, they cover the inside edge of the mat, and the burner holds the mat down.
My wife had several friends come over for lunch today and cooked a lot of food last night. The mat worked out perfectly. If I had my choice, I would have preferred a mat just slightly larger for the outer dimensions so it would turn up at the edges and contain spilled food. As it is now, the mat protects underneath the cooking vessels, but liquid food tends to run off the side of the mat and underneath it. But that's not a big problem because it is not burned on the range surface and is still able to be cleaned up easily.
After several hours of cooking last night and this morning, the mat still looks new.
I'm very pleased with the mat and would recommend it.

I have had this fridge for just over 3 months and bought it because I have really like my GE Cafe gas stove. There are things I love about this fridge and things that are disappointing.
First what I love…
The hot water dispenser, it's fairly quick and gives me the temp I need. I thought it was silly at first, but am amazed by how often I use it and have come to love it.
The cold water and ice dispenser, I love that it measures the water for you, the water is COLD, unlike my last in the door water fridge. The ice functions are great, crushed is crushed, cubed is cubed, cubes are a standard size, pretty straight forward.
The digital picture function, I love it, and will admit that I thought at first it was a little ridiculous and overkill for a feature. BUT now that I have had it and used it for a bit, I love having the pics on the fridge without cluttering up the front of it.
Deli drawer, I love the fact that it is so wide and has a wide range of choices for temp setting. Easily this is one of my favorite features.
Door alarm may save us millions in wasted power.

Now for the disappointments…
The freezer, its drawer does not pull out nearly far enough, you have to have both of the fridge doors also open to get into it. Also, it has a tip out shelf against the front of the drawer that you practically have to do a handstand to see into. Even the tip out feature does not help. The two smaller drawers within the freezer are ok, but again hard to get into without opening the whole fridge up to get into.
Interior space, UGH, the veggie and fruit drawers are tiny, not nearly enough space for even basic salad makings. Because the ice maker is on the inside of the front door, the shelves are not nearly deep enough. This fridge has the same useful cubic measurement of my old side by side, but you would never know it. The shelves on the door that holds the ice maker are impossibly shallow, fine if you use teeny tiny containers of condiments, but anyone else will likely be disappointed.
In summary. The lighting is great, the outside dispenser is great, I have had no issues with noise as mentioned in some of the other reviews, I love the way it looks and much to my surprise, I love the hot water and digital frame features. The Deli drawer is the best. BUT the draw backs are pretty important to me, space and access to the freezer.
The extra features are great, but I would probably not buy this model again because of the size issues and like I said it is supposedly the same size as my last fridge, but the set up makes it seem smaller and less accessible.

Like all of these dryers at some point, my tensioner pulley seized and was squealing like a banshee. If yours is making this noise, I would recommend not running the dryer until you get it replaced. If you stop the dryer right away, the job is much easier. If you don't, the pulley can seize onto the shaft in which case you may need to buy the tensioner arm as well that the pulley mounts on. And you will likely break the belt.

All that aside, the job was pretty easy with some youtube help. I am so glad I did this job as it allowed me to vacuum a scary amount of lint from the inside of the dryer and also remove a thick cake of lint/hair/sand/bobby pins/gunk from the inside of the metal duct that connects to the lint filter assembly.

All of my drum support wheels and belt seemed fine, but I replaced them since they came in the kit. The bushings of these wheels are bronze oilite, so no lubrication is needed or helpful (it will only attract lint). I cleaned the shafts that the wheels mount to with automotive brake cleaner and a dry cloth to remove built up residue. I then installed the new wheels and they fit and spun very well. Yes, the clips are a bit of a PITA - but you can reuse the old ones (if you don't break them on removal) which are slightly more pliable. Just take your time and you'll be fine. Hope this is helpful!

Great product. We live in the city and have a communal laundry room in our apartment building, but after having a baby we realized that the $4 per load would quickly add up! We decided to invest in a portable washer and after hours of researching we chose Della. After just one week of use, I can already see the benefit of investing in this machine. It’s very practical, washes the clothes very well, and dries them almost completely. Here’s my process for a full load:
1. Add 1tbs of detergent to basin of washing machine (yes, that really is all you need!)
2. Add clothes
3. Add water to the wash tub using the sink attachment on the left intake valve, shower head, or bucket, completely covering the clothes.
4. WASH CYCLE: Turn the machine to the preferred cycle (gentle or normal) and time (I use the full 15 minutes since I’m dealing with soiled baby clothes).
5. Once the clothes have finished washing, turn the Wash Selector to rinse. Let the tub train completely then return the Wash Selector to normal.
6. Repeat Step 3 (adding water to the wash tub).
7. RINSE CYCLE: Ensure the Wash Selector is set to your preferred cycle, then set the timer for however long you’d like to rinse them for- I do 6 minutes.
8. Repeat Step 5 (draining the tub).
9. Move the sink attachment tube to the right intake valve (if applicable)
9. SPIN CYCLE: Remove half or part of your washing load, squeeze out excess water, and add to the spin dryer. Push the clothes down, and place the removable plastic cover on top of them. Set the spin timer to the full 5 minutes.

Water needs to be on or running over the clothes for the first minute of the spin cycle to ensure all of the soap was removed during the rinse cycle. If you’re using the sink attachment and intake valve, simply turn on the faucet when the spin starts and turn it off after one minute. If you’re using a bucket or shower head, keep the top (grey) lid open for the first minute while continuously pouring water over the white lid. In either scenario, close the lid after the first minute and let the cycle finish.
11. After the first spin cycle completes, I reset the timer for another 5 minutes before removing the clothes. I do not add water to the second rinse cycle, and instead just use this cycle to make sure the clothes are as dry as possible. Repeat this process for the remaining clothes in your washing machine, then hang them to dry. Everything should be completely dry within 2-3 hours of hanging.

- Makes ice quickly. It'll fill the bucket in a little over an hour
- Relatively quiet. It's no more noise than a fridge.
- Larger size "cube" is big enough (though smaller than you may expect)

Cons
- As others have mentioned, this is not a freezer, so you need to put made ice in a real freezer. This is fine, but the bullets stick together like crazy in the freezer. It's annoying and frustrating, you wind up with a big blob of ice instead of individual cubes.
- When it's "empty", there's still a fair bit of water in the reservoir. This means emptying then wiping down.
- There's a fairly strong chemical smell inside that hasn't worn off despite cleaning and a lot of use. The ice doesn't smell or taste funny, but the smell is strong.
- Ice is white, not clear. This is mostly aesthetic, but if you're expecting clear ice, you won't get it with this machine.

We purchased the Samsung front load dryer in 2010 and in 2015 it wouldn't heat. I bought a Heating Element, watched videos showing the step by step repair and switched out the element (the old one had a break in the coil) - easy! When it stopped heating again in Sept 2016, I was overconfident and just installed a new Heating Element. The dryer still wouldn't heat and I couldn't see where the old one had any type of failure. So I took out the voltmeter and tried to figure out if the thermistor or thermostat, connected to the heating element side, was bad (I didn't realize at the time that there's 2 of each). Back to the store to buy the part that I guessed was bad - I installed it and it worked!
In July 2019, the dryer stopped heating again! This time I wanted to see what was bad before I started replacing parts, so I took the dryer apart and saw one of the wires connected to the heating element was burnt and separated from the terminal (see red wire in 1st picture) . I looked up replacement parts online and found that all the wires in the entire dryer are on one wire harness, which was pricey. I also didn't want to attempt that repair, so back to the part's store where I showed them the terminal and wire to see if they had anything I could splice in. They did! It was a part for a different brand dryer and it had copper wire, so I had to buy a special connector for copper to aluminum wire splice (see purple box in 2nd picture).
Now it's Jan 2020 and the dryer wouldn't heat AGAIN! After opening the dryer back up I saw the other wire connected to the heating element was burnt (compare blue wire in each picture). Researching the problem online I realized I was the root cause of the problem - if you don't ensure the terminals are snug to the Heating Element then excess heat can cause the wires to overload and burn. I searched on amazon and found the same wire connection repair kit, but this one had aluminum wire so I was able to use the regular twist connector. The part is for whirlpool and it's called a "Dryer Heating Element Wire Adaptor Connecting Kit 279457". But, I'm writing about this so you won't have to buy it. When your Samsung Dryer won't heat (and your wires aren't burnt)- just buy this kit and replace everything (Heating Element and all 4 thermistors/thermostats) so you don't have to guess which part is bad and replace them one by one. When I replaced the second burnt wire the dryer still wouldn't heat. I saw this kit and for the price it's easier to replace all the parts at once so you don't waste your time. The burnt wire probably caused another part to fail but there was no need to determine what exactly happened as I replaced all the parts and now the dryer works again. AND, make sure you use a plyers to snug down the wire terminals connected to the Heating element coils, just enough so they aren't loose.

After 4 years of regular use (about 2-3 times a month), our washer flashed the "PE" error code (The water level sensor is not working correctly). LG's solution states, 'Close the water faucets, unplug the washer, and call for service." How convenient. I tried the reset route (after Googling for other solutions) -- unplugged, wait for a minute, plug back in and pray the error code would disappear. Nope. The error code won't go away. It was time to roll up the sleeves and crack open the unit.

Our washer and drier are located outdoor -- an open but roofed patio. So, they're prone to malfunctions from both the elements and uninvited nightcrawlers. Thankfully, the LG WT1501CW is easy to take apart for servicing and for DIY'ers like myself. Just a few house tools: Phillips screwdriver, scissors, a pair of wide paint scrapers, and in our case, a roll of electrical tape, a wire crimping kit & a multimeter/tester, were all I used. That plus basic knowledge of electricity/electronics would help. Always UNPLUG the AC power cord before even attempting to loosen the first screw.

We were prepared to fork out another $700 for a similar model washer but all we spent was about $30 for both this new water level sensor switch assembly ($21.39 tax inclusive) and a new dispenser hose ($7.72 tax inclusive). The hose connects from the bleach holder to the leftmost tube in the same compartment where the water level sensor is located -- the top, back end of the washer.

While we slept, 'friendly four-legged creatures' gnawed on the black, rubber hose that conveys bleach, a few wires that came out of the noise suppressor (a white square box that sits atop a removable metal plate - immediately to the right of the water level sensor (WLS)) & the violet-colored wire on the 3-wire connector that plugs into and powers the WLS. Further inspection showed that the mouse also gnawed a couple of small, blue wires at the bottom of the unit and a small area of the clear hose attached to the WLS.

The mouse was able to gain access to that seemingly sealed top compartment from below the washer, climbed up the unit via the metal rods that support the washer drum, gnawed the bleach hose to make a nice home inside that rear compartment while he feasted on those yummy wire harness.

After replacing all the chewed-up wires, the rubber bleach hose, and the WLS itself, the unit was immediately ready for the next load of dirty laundry. The replacement WLS unit was the same brand and had the same length of clear tubing and a small black pad as the original. Just use the same metal clip when connecting the other end of the clear tube at the back, mid-part of the washer (after you removed the metal back cover held by four (4) short, self-tapping screws).

The plastic rear, top cover that houses the WLS, noise suppressor, tubes, and an assortment of wires is held by only two (2) Phillips-type screws. Then use the wide paint scrapers to gently pry and separate the cover via the gaps once the 2 screws were removed. With the cover removed, you might be overwhelmed by the jumble of wires. You will easily sort everything out as the wires and where they connect to are mostly color-coded.

To remove the top cover completely, you need to remove four (4) screws - two (2) long screws (hidden by small, round plastic cover plates at both ends of the main control panel) and the two (2) fat but short screws on the vertical slats of the washer at the back.

The WLS clear tubing is bundled up with some other wire harness as it goes down the washer and wraps around twice on the left (when facing the washer from the back) metal rod that supports the washer drum. Use a sharp scissor to carefully cut the synthetic cloth (as extra insulation/padding) to separate the tubing from all the other wires.

Overall, in less than an hour (if all the rest of the wires & hoses have no issues or damage) or two (like ours with all the chewed-up wires and bleach hose damage (for that, I had to pry open the entire top of the washer to connect & clamp securely one end of the new black rubber hose to the bleach dispenser cup located under the top, left portion of the washer), you'll get your LG WT1501CW (or, similar LG model top-loading washer) back in action.

And, save yourself a lot of money in the process.

We have moderately hard water (15-20 grains), and even with a softener, the filter forms crusty nodules on the outside after a couple of weeks, so we alternate between two filters. Moisture output drops noticeably (i.e. the tanks empty more slowly) as the filter clogs up with mineral salts. We run our humidifier 24/7.

The filters can be cleaned in the kitchen sink (sanitize it first!) with a hot water rinse and 30 min warm water soak. Lay it flat in the sink to reduce water usage. Add 2-4 tbsp citric acid powder to help dissolve stubborn hard water crust/stains. Rinse thoroughly with cold water. They come out almost as good as new. You can clean them this way several times before dust doesn't wash out anymore and the paper mesh begins to fall apart.

Don't forget to clean the base of your humidifier, too. It can also accumulate hard water and dusty gunk over time. Use an air duster to blast dust out of the fan unit.

When I first purchase my dryer it took forever to dry to the point I thought that I had received a defective product. The dryer’s representative said that to check the dryer vent and that it may be the cause for the long drying time. I saw a promotion on those deal sites and even with the so called “professional” cleaning, the dryer’s sensor would run over the allotted time and the clothes felt damp. I didn’t think too much of it since the dryer was drying, but once I saw a dryer fire video, I knew I had to buy and clean my vents.

This product cleaned my vents wonderfully. I think I have a 25 foot vent, but I used the 12 feet one and it worked fine. I cleaned from the dryer to the outside first and then from the outside toward the vents. Then I connected the dryer and pushed out all the lint to the outside (it was lint all over). The rods were really flexible and as many alluded, pushing and pulling the brush with the drill throughout the process helped. Sometimes you may feel like it is stuck, don’t switch the drill in reverse, just continue to engage the drill and try to pull it out. I did use duct tape as the instruction and so many people mentioned as a precaution. You do need a drill since doing it by hand is not optimal (in my opinion). Overall, I strongly recommend this product to clean your vents for faster drying time and to prevent dryer fire.

TL:DR – Cleans vents super well. Use a drill and clean from both ends for effectiveness for vents longer than 12 feet. Rods are flexible, but use duct tape on the joints. Drying times is shorten and longer life span.

This is my first experience with a countertop ice maker, so I please keep in mind I do not have any history to compare it to. From my perspective as someone who has never owned one, however, I am very pleased with the KUMIO icemaker. I did not have to worry about having enough ice, running to the store to get ice, or about storing ice in a cooler, etc. And while I do not consider this ice maker bulky, it does have somewhat of a large footprint, so be mindful of the dimensions and your available counter space.

Ultimately, I am very pleased with this ice maker and offer a strong recommendation.

If you have a tiny freezer and little ice capacity, or just want the convenience of crunchy ice nuggets without a lot of noise, this is the appliance for you.

You can use it with or without the side tank - the side tank just feeds the internal water reservoir (under the ice bucket) through one of the two tubes on the back. I'm still trying to figure out what the other tube does. You could probably pipe it into fixed water sources, but you don't have to - this can plug in anywhere with a 3 prong outlet, and you can bring your own water.

The cleaning process takes about half an hour, practically speaking, and they recommend monthly descaling (although using filtered water may help with this). There's a mobile app that will track the status of the machine and give you control over ice-making as well as the light. But you can control those manually at the device if you prefer.

It's a fairly big appliance for countertop use, but not too bad for what it does. Soda can shown for scale, and you want 3 inches clearance on all sides (a bit more in front to remove the ice bucket).

I ran a full batch of ice after doing the bleach/cleaning cycle out of the box, then put it in its "final" place and started another batch. Right now it's at about 1/2 to 2/3 after two hours or so.

The app will let you schedule when to run it, and when the ice melts it goes into the reservoir underneath to be frozen again next time it starts up.

We'll see how the family takes to it, and whether we can disable the freezer's icemaker and get some more room for things like meat and ice cream. But for now, it should be nice for iced drinks, smoothies, and so forth.

I like to save money like everyone else. This SealPro part has a number of drawbacks that negate most of, if not all of the savings.

1. This part is smaller in diameter than the OEM part. This happens often with cheap knockoffs that are reverse engineered. They don't properly account for the shrinkage of the material when they build their mold. I can put an oem boot on in just a couple of minutes. This little guy took me about 25.

2. My part had a lot of flash in the sewer and drain. Trimming this out took me another 15 to 20 minutes using a scalpel. You will need a scalpel or exacto with a very sharp blade to get good results.

3. The drain tube connection is about .100" too short. See photos. After installing the original clamp, I was easily able to pull the white plastic tube out. Fit my Maytag Model MDBH955AWW perfectly and included the actual latch handle itself - most likely why you're buying this in the first place. It took all of ten minutes to install, and that included figuring out which circuit breaker turned off the dishwasher. Turn off the breaker or unplug the dishwasher and use a T20 torx wrench to remove the screws on the inside panel of the door - except the ones at the hinge; just loosen them to make putting the panel back easierl. The inside panel of the door will push back easily and you can remove the switch/latch assembly. Move the two wiring connectors to the new assembly, push it into place making sure the screw holes line up, pull the door panel back and replace the screws (the two screws holding the latch first). The screws are sheet metal screws going into plastic, so don't get carried away and over tighten them! Turn the breaker on and you should be all set. This replacement part seems to be a better design than the original, which had the actual latch handle attached using a design by Rube Goldberg - and doesn't come with the original assembly (part 99003347).

The problem you're dealing with is that to buy the Frigidaire version, even on Amazon & unless you find an incredible sale, you're going to pay $40+ a unit an item that requires changing monthly. Compound this the last such unit I purchased not operating as well (water quality was not quite to expected standard, and the filter was restricting flow from the outset), and I was interested in finding an alternative.

Enter the Smart Choice Replacement SCWF3CTO. Now, often, I have to admit I subscribe to the adage "you get what you pay for" in terms of costs, and at 25% less ... well, caveat emptor applies. But the Smart Choice, when it arrived, excellent in every respect. It was, indeed, a "Smart Choice."

A slightly more compact unit, the filter has operated superbly. It primed quickly and easily; and it cleaned up and has maintained the flow of fresh, filtered water exactly as it should. Indeed, it improved the water's taste over the previous Frigidair unit I had installed, and has kept taste that even despite a recent a recent water system chlorination by our local municipality. That, to me, is very impressive, indicative of the quality of Smart Choice's filtration, and I'll definitely be purchasing this filter again.

If you, too have a Frigidaire or similar unit using this style of filtration, I fully recommend you too make the "Smart Choice" for yours!

I purchased this to have ice at all times in a small corporate office. My first surprise was the enormous size of the unit. It seemed much more compact in photos than I'd expected.

The unit does make ice quickly, about 10 small bullet-sized cubes at a time, but is a bit noisy as the ice falls and clanks into the hopper. Coworkers were amazed at the unit and its cool convenience, but the noise every 10 minutes as more ice was made or the melting ice shifting became distractinging after awhile. I found I had to keep a cup under the two ice dispensers, because as the ice melts and shifts, it occasionally falls out of the hopper, melting on the shelf the unit was on. The little drain catcher was flimsy and the grate too narrow to catch excess ice, so I'd get little puddles on the floor or shelf without the cups in place.

Even in a better setting, the unit would have been fraught with problems. The unit was delivered on its side and with a back panel cracked. Customer service was pretty helpful and we determined the damage was cosmetic. But when I tried to put a 5-gallon water bottle on the unit, it had trouble filling, with the sensor often buzzing and getting jammed. The solution was to take the large cap off the bottle (most 5-gallon jugs now have a smaller hole in the cap with a pop-out piece; it's hard to explain), but then there's virtually no way to load the bottle onto the unit without spilling a few pints of water everywhere - very impractical for a business office. Nonetheless, once I got it running, it did make ice and dispense water as advertised.

I eventually got used to the unit's fussy character, noises and need to be turned on and off periodically, but still found the hygene of the unit to be problematic. If the unit was turned off for more than 4 days (like a long weekend), a mild but funky taste developed. With the drain hole being on the underside of the unit, filling it with a vinegar-water solution, running the clean cycle, emptying it, filling with clean water, running the clean cycle again (a few times), was very tedious. There was also no way to really open the unit and clean it manually (or figure out what the problem was when it sometimes jammed).

All said, I really loved my ice, and it was convenient having the water dispenser in my office. But then one day I noticed some water on the shelf it was on. I thought it was just a stray melting cube. It turned out the unit had actually sprung a leak. This was 13 months into the twelve month warrantee, so I was out 400 bucks. It was nearly impossible to determine the source of the leak the way the unit's designed.

(Oh, there's also a little floating red ball in the center "shaft" of the front of the unit to see how full the unit is. It got stuck for about 3 months at one point but finally reset itself.) Perhaps my unit was just haunted. I'd like to get a replacement, but the cost and size are just too big.

This is the perfect answer to the annoyance of buying expensive K-Cups instead of making coffee in an old-fashioned machine or a more time-intensive way. Here you have an abundance of small, reusable K-Cups that you can load with a couple teaspoons of freshly ground coffee if your choice, then store in the fridge until you’re ready to use them. It’s all the advantages of a coffee made by machine, brewed with a minimum of effort, but made just like traditional coffee machines always made your coffee of choice.

The cups open up on top, close with a satisfying snap, and stay ready to use for as long as you need them. I didn’t give five stars for the flavor because even locking the cups in plastic bags and putting them in the fridge will still not perfectly keep them from oxidizing, but it’s minimal and a small price to pay for convenience. They are easy to clean and durable. You can wash them in your dishwasher. They are quite reasonably priced for something that can be used hundreds of times and which saves you spending twice as much for each “cup of joe...”

Let’s be realistic: K-Cups tend to be 30-40 cents for each cup of coffee. This brings the price down to probably under 5 cents (depending on what coffee you buy, and what equipment you use). K-Cups are a VERY EXPENSIVE convenience, but these reusable containers allow you all the advantages of the K-Cup brew while being roughly no extra cost over a traditional coffee machine. For my money, it’s well-worth it.

You can pick from a variety of colors. I’ve used these in multiple machines and they work effortlessly. If you want to make Spiced Cider cups, or put loose tea in a K-Cup, or pre-mix coffee and chocolate and powdered creamer, you can perfect your beverage to your own standards.

You don’t have to be beholden to high-priced and limited K-Cup offerings at your local store. You can decide to pay roughly the same amount as you would for an old fashioned coffee maker, while getting all the advantages of K-Cup convenience. Personally this has made me very happy because I can use my rare, loose-leaf teas and still just turn on the machine and poke one button so my tea is ready as soon as I’m out of the shower. Nothing could be finer for the stumbling caffeine addict who needs their fix before they can think straight. Just hit a couple buttons and remember to put a cup under the spout!

This worked great to fix my dryer, and I only had one small problem with it, which I will explain later. I'll describe my symptoms below, so that others can see my situation and decide if this is the part they need.

I have a whirlpool dryer, supplied as part of my home rental, but not "covered" or warranted by the landlord. It is a gas dryer (obviously). It is pretty basic, but it does have a sensor-based (hot or cool) setting, along with a standard timer-based setting. That's pretty much all the dryer can do - like I said, pretty basic.

I went through every single component of the dryer, testing with a multimeter. Everything checked out as functional. I spent a lot of time assembling and disassembling my dryer. I learned A LOT about dryer repair during my trials and tribulations. Getting a repairman was not an option, as most quoted 100-150 JUST TO COME OUT. Never mind actual parts and labor.

Here were my symptoms. No heat and the moisture sensor setting didn't work. Nothing was clogged up. The gas line was functional and open. The timed dry worked, but without heat. The auto-sensing dry ran forever, though. I actually forgot to turn it off before going on a weekend trip and it was still running when we came home. The clothes would eventually dry, but the dryer wouldn't stop once dry. Also, if I peeped through the observation hole, the igniter would increase in brightness, get really bright, then fade out without igniting the gas and producing a flame. I also didn't smell gas, or hear a click of the valve opening.

This actually happened twice before, but it started working again after a week or two. This time the problem persisted for months.

Like I said, I tested every part and the resistance matched what I expected from videos and guides. I tested the high limit thermostat, the fuse, the igniter, the heat sensor, the solenoid coils, the igniter, and another part I don't remember the name of. I never found the moisture sensor or the thermistor.

While screwing around, I dropped the igniter and it broke instantly. I replaced that using a $15 part here on Amazon and it worked great, but my problem persisted. That would've been great, if it had been the problem part and I accidentally fixed it. But, it was pretty clear that the igniter worked since it was glowing quite brightly. Also, it was turning on, so it probably wasn't the heat sensor. Everything pointed to the solenoid coils, or the entire gas valve assembly. The coils worked electrically, though, giving proper resistance values on all 3 contact points.

I said "screw it" and just replaced the coils with this. After all, it was only $10, so if it did nothing I wasn't out much. My dryer immediately started working perfectly, and has since. The flame turned on, I got heat and the dryer started turning itself off automatically when the clothes were dry.

The only negative about this particular product was that several of the pins came bent at almost 90 degree angles. Not so bad that I couldn't bend them back and have it work just fine... but that's still pretty sketchy. They should probably fix whatever shipping and/or handling problem that led to that happening. That's why it got 4 stars instead of 5.

I've been dancing a little jig every once in a while ever since. A $10 part saved me from having to buy a $400+ new dryer, and having to figure out what to do with the old one (since it isn't mine...).

I was initially drawn to this machine by it's looks, but bought it for ease of use. Samsung and LG consistently get high marks but in everyday use they drive me nuts. For those not familiar with the Asian design aesthetic, it basically goes like this: More buttons + more blinking lights + more beeping noises = more better. Well, in the words of Stan Marsh, "I thought this was America!" It is, Stan, and this one is actually made in America too.

The controls are simple, just go from left to right. Set auto or timed mode, modify the default settings if you want, throw in some bonuses (like delay time), and press play. I did not really need to read the instructions to figure it out, and the silly noises can be turned off. This is also the first dryer I have ever used with an automatic dry mode that actually works. Although the modes are a bit goofy, "more dry" equals dry, I'm not sure how you can be more dry than dry but whatever. "Normal dry" equals barely damp, perfect for ironing, and "damp" equals damp for hang drying. It is really nice that the steamer has an actual water line, not just a tray you fill with water like many others.

This is easily the best performing dryer I have ever used. The first time I turned it on it blew decades of old dryer lint out of my 30' long exhaust vent, and it blows out so much steam you could build a sauna around it. This thing dries quickly, usually in 40 mins. And evenly, even fitted sheets are no match. It is also very quiet. The only noise that can be heard is the burner lighting, and that is when standing right next to it.

One final note is a weird warning on page one of the installation manual: "Place dryer at least 18 inches above the floor for a garage installation. Failure to do so can result in death, explosion, or fire." Now we all know garage floors are no more explosive than regular floors and I am not going to build a stand for it that is 18 inches taller than my washer, but since this little gem is not mentioned in any of the sales info I thought I'd pass it along.

If you are buying this as a set like I did, the features of the washer and dryer to not really match up. The 6000 dryer DOES have a steam cycle and interior light, if you also want that on your washer you will need to step up to the 7000. Also, unlike the washer this dryer DOES NOT come with all of the required connectors. It only comes with the water line, you will need a gas line and exhaust vent. Please don't use a cheap-o flexible vent tube, they reduce efficiency and can create a fire hazard.

I wasn't sure how these would work out.. but am delighted now that I've figured it out! The "pod maker" product is no longer available, so the best way to use these is this:  Buy a 2 1/4" hole saw and drill a hole or two in a piece of 3/4" or 1" thick scrap board. Set up a clothes iron on medium heat with steam. Set the pod in the hole, carefully full with 1 tablespoon + 1 teaspoon fine ground coffee. Brush away any grounds at the edges, fold the top over, then apply the iron covering all edges of the pod, for 5 seconds, let it rest, then again for 5 seconds.  Pod is now sealed and ready to use in a coffee machine.  I bought these to take on a cruise - NCL has this type of pod machines on their ships in balcony cabins.

This is, by far, my most often used brewing method for coffee. I'm a coffee snob, and can brew coffee at my house in about 12 different ways (Turkish, Vietnamese, Indian, Chemex, Percolator, Steam, French Press, Espresso, Conventional drip,Cold Brew, Bag filter, Instant, and Aeropress). So it's no small achievement to have earned such loyalty from me when it comes to coffee.

This device is the best combination of ease of use, brewing speed, easy cleanup, and most importantly, coffee quality.

First things first, it's easy to use. Once you assemble it, applying the filter and cap to the basin, and put it on top of your mug, then just deposit into the basin 4 tbsps of espresso ground coffee (i.e., fine grind; but regular grinds works too). Pour just-less-than-boiling water over it--you can go all the way up to the very lip of the basin, ignore the guide markings on the side of it. Then insert the plunger and steadily press it down till all the coffee has been pushed through.The result is about 12 ozs of coffee, at roughly the strength of 4 shots of espresso.

Second, brewing takes maybe 2 minutes if you have a water boiler or about 3 minutes if you are microwaving your water. Cleanup takes 1 minute. Only instant coffee brews quicker, but that's a huge drop in quality.

Third, it's easy to cleanup. It has basically three pieces to cleanup, the cap, the plunger and the basin. I never use the stirring wand or the funnel. so they never need cleanup. [Hint: if you poured the water evenly over the grinds, moistening all of them, then the stirring wand isn't necessary]. I can use the coffee scoop, but prefer the metal tbsps on the side of my coffee canister. Cleanup is as simple as unscrew the cap, pop the coffee "puck" and filter paper into the trash can, then rinse all parts in the sink. The basin and cap are diswasher safe if you prefer to do that. I would not recommend putting the plunger in the dishwasher, I suspect the rubber would deteriorate over time.

Fourth, the quality is the best you can get for the price and the brewing speed. The coffee quality is stronger than typical drip filter brewers (including Keurig, and typical office pots). Plus, since the coffee never sits on a warmer slowly overcooking the coffee after the pot is done brewing, it never has that bitter/burnt taste associated with truck stop coffee. The Aeropress brewing style tastes like mild espresso since it's closest, mechanically, to the espresso brewing style, but it's not designed to sustain the 15 bars of pressure required for standard espresso. The result is MORE coffee than with espresso machines, but it's a bit less strong. For most audiences, it will taste like a quadruple shot of mild espresso. If that's still too strong for your tastes, I recommend adding an equal portion of warm water (for cafe Americano) or warm milk (cafe con leche). So a 12 oz serving of black coffee becomes 24 ozs, fit for two servings.

Fifth, the price. At this brewing speed, and this quality, there's no better priced coffee gadget on the market. There are cost efficient ways to get a similar quality of coffee but they take longer to brew. A comparably sized steam espresso pots (the fashionable low-budget option in Europe) can be $30 if you get a good bargain. But it takes 2-3x's as long to brew with these. There are also quick brewing methods that give a similar or better quality of coffee, but they are much more expensive. A few exceptional espresso machines do a good job at the $80-150 range, but for the most part, a good espresso machine will cost you $200 to $500. Nespresso (and some knockoff brands) has an automatic brewer that uses coffee pods. It's a good machine, but their cheapest models are $100, they use more counter space, and you have to purchase expensive coffee pods. Besides the nespresso automatic brewer, all the espresso machines are more complicated to use, and all of them, including Nespresso models, are way more expensive than the aeropress.

Overall, I highly recommend this coffee brewing gadget for any and all serious coffee drinkers, coffee snobs, or anyone who just wants to "up their game" with their morning brew.

One, I called the service guy and he was not very friendly and did not ask enough questions to get accurate information to give proper advice, then he was short tempered with me.  I am a Electrical controls engineer and work with factory tech people every day on the phone so I am a good judge on good service.  The second issue I have with the unit is how it is wired.  I took one of the reviewers advice and added a 120VAC LED and mounted it just behind the dryer to have a visual that the fan is running when the dryer is (I located the fan just below the floor behind the dryer).  Anyway, when i went to hook up the LED, i was surprised to find the fan is wired backwards of what it should be.  The Hot wire should go through the pressure switch so when the unit is off, there is no power to the motor.  It is kind of a safety issue.  Of course there is a ground wire connected to the case, but it is always a good practice to switch the hot and not the neutral wire.  This unit switches the neutral and has power in the motor at all times.  If the motor has a grounding issue and the ground isn't good to the fan, the unit will be HOT (120vac) all the time versus only hot when it would run if it would still run.

I posted this review on another Maytag Gemini 5 burner listing. We haven't owned this range long enough to comment on it's cooking quality. But, living off-grid, we discovered that if you lose power the stove is unusable. I called Maytag and was told that there is no over-ride because it's a "safety feature". So, if you live in an area where you may lose electricity for any length of time, this gas stove is no better than owning an electric oven. You may be hungry (and surrounded by spoiling food), but you'll be safe...from something!

UPDATE: OK, I had some reasonable arguments against my original 1 star rating for the 5 burner Gemini so I thought that'd better update this review as well.

I have now lived with it a couple of years and have added a star.

I really like the 2 ovens and they cook reasonably well. I don't like the fact that you can only change temperatures in 5 degree increments. There are some things that I make where I need to be within a degree or two of boiling without boiling. I can't guarantee that with this electronically controlled stove.

As others have said on the other Maytag Gemini listings, the control panel often fails. Ours was replaced once under warranty but it still shuts off the gas line occasionally, even when not in use. That's not a problem, but if you are cooking something and it shuts off, what are you to do if time is important?

I know that many, if not most, manufacturers are selling electronically controlled stoves. If they would build in a manual over-ride, fine. But they don't.

Living off-grid, we have several backup power systems that most people don't have. In the early review, I just wanted to warn people who live in areas where they often lose power or in areas where they may lose power for extended periods, that they better have a backup plan.

UPDATE #2: OK, we just replaced this turkey. Over the last 9 months or so 3 of the 5 burner control knobs froze up (and not at the same time). I had the first one repaired and it cost $220. When the other two froze I decided that there was no way I was spending anymore money on this hunk of junk. I'm not even going to give it away unless someone needs an anchor. Replaced it with a Dacor Distinctive 30". Hoping for the best. Removed the last star that I'm allowed to.

UPDATE: After using this for almost three months, I've decided I like it better than my decades-long standby, the Toddy system. The fundamental reason is that its coffee tastes better. And this is even though I have been resoaking and filtering the coffee THREE times. I'm raising my star rating from 4 stars to 5.

My original review:

I’ve been making cold brew coffee for over 30 years with the Toddy Café system. (The current version is called the Toddy Cold Brew System.) I’ve always liked OXO products, so I thought it would be worth giving this new cold brew coffee maker a try.

As usual with OXO products, this is thoughtfully designed. The brewpot sits nicely balanced on a stand. You put the grounds in the brewpot, then use the carafe to measure the appropriate amount of water, and pour that (fairly slowly) into the “rainmaker” on top of the brewpot.

The rainmaker ensures that the water drops evenly over the grounds to get all of them wet. That’s the theory anyway. In fact, as with all cold brew systems, gobs of dry grounds tend to burp up to the surface as you go, and you end up using the flat back of a spoon to press the dry grounds down into the wet. That happens with this system and the Toddy, so I don’t consider it a flaw. Just as an aside, I find that it works best to put half the water in (both the Toddy and the OXO) and let it soak for awhile—say 20-30 minutes—then add the rest.

Once you’ve poured in all your water, let the soaked grounds sit for 12-24 hours and then you’re ready to filter and get your cold brew. Here’s where a clever feature of the OXO comes in. When you are ready to filter, you just place the included carafe under the brewpot. Then flip the brew release switch on the front and the brewed coffee liquid starts flowing through the filter and into the carafe. When you’re done, you just pull out the carafe, which triggers the brew release switch to shut and stop any remaining drips.

This OXO uses a built-in fine stainless steel mesh as a filter. A little packet of paper filters was included in the box in case you find that the mesh doesn’t filter well enough for your taste. I’m not using the paper filters because, even using store-ground coffee (rather than the coarser grind recommended for cold brew systems), I only see a tiny bit of sediment in the last few drops of the carafe. The booklet says you can also use this OXO to make cold brew tea, but I haven’t tried that. I will probably do it at some point this summer.

Features I like on this OXO compared to the Toddy are its looks, the brew-release switch, and the stainless steel filter.

APPEARANCE: I love my Toddy Café, but I don’t want that big white plastic pot sitting out on the counter if I have company. The OXO’s smoked color and streamlined appearance make it look just fine sitting out. And when you do put it away, the parts all nest together so that it doesn’t take up much space in your storage cupboard.

BREW RELEASE SWITCH: OXO’s brew release switch is a big advance over the Toddy plug system. With the Toddy, you have to lift up the brewpot and pull a plug out of the bottom, then sit it on top of the carafe. Because coffee starts flowing instantly and it’s a little awkward to pick up the brewpot high enough to see and reach the plug and get it on top of the carafe immediately, I inevitably end up with a few drops of coffee on the counter. With the OXO, occasionally there will be one drip that hits the counter as I pull the carafe out.

FILTERS: The Toddy uses thick felt filters. They work well and can be used multiple times, but you do have to keep ordering them. I like the steel mesh filter a little bit better.

One thing I like much better about the Toddy is that the neck of the carafe is ridged. That makes it much easier to carry the carafe by the neck, one-handed. The smooth neck of the OXO carafe means I don’t dare to carry it one-handed.

If you’re trying to decide between the Toddy system and the OXO, it’s a tough choice. Both work well. The Toddy is cheaper, so maybe you weigh that against the good looks, the brew-release switch, and mesh filter of the OXO to make your decision.

One final note for newbies to cold brew coffee making. Once I’ve made one carafe, I just put more water in the brewpot and steep the used grounds to make another batch. It’s a waste of the coffee not to give the grounds a second brew.

My title sums it up and here's the logic to support it:

First, I'll address the quality issue: The OEM Samsung brand filter, which is made in Mexico, a country with which we have direct involvement in the manufacturing of products that are exported to the U.S versus this brand, which is made in China, a country with which we have zero input into quality control. Let's look deeper: What do we control, regardless of where it's manufactured? We control, through the FDA, labeling. The Samsung brand filter clearly states the filtering capabilities on the package. This filter makes no water quality claims whatsoever. The Chinese are not stupid. If they made a superior product that sells for less money, the details, including the filtering data would be plastered in big print on the packaging. If you think you're getting an equal to or better filter then you're living in Fantasyland.

Second is the warranty issue: If you read your Samsung's refrigerator owner's manual thoroughly, you'll learn that using a non Samsung filter voids your refrigerator's warranty. If you bought an extended warranty this could be an important issue.

Finally, so many people write reviews claiming they buy these things thinking they're brilliant because they're saving so much money. Well, I suggest they sit down and do the math. On the day I'm writing this review, this filter is selling at Amazon for $26.99. The Samsung brand "Samsung Da29-00020b Refrigerator Water Filter, 1-pack" is selling for $33.27. Now, let's do the math. $33.27 minus $26.99 = $6.28 more for the Samsung brand. Assuming we buy one of these every six months that works out to less than $1.05 more per month for the Samsung brand ($6.28 divided by 6 months = $1.04666667 more per month). Looking closer we divide 30 days into $1.05 and Voila! buying this product will save us less than a whopping 3 1/2 cents per day! I don't think that saving would even be meaningful to a homeless person. So, if this is truly a meaningful savings to anyone, I suggest they find a container or sandwich-sized Zip Lock baggie and put a nickel a day into it for six months. When it's time to buy your new higher quality Samsung brand filter, not only will you have more than enough money to pay for the difference in price but you may even be able to buy a few sticks of chewing gum as well.

Please stop with the reviews with outrageously extreme views that are not supported by data and accept the fact, that in this instance, you may not be as smart as you think you are.

My intent is not to be rude but rather to show, that when reviewing products such as these it's not at all difficult to use common sense, logic, and basic math skills to prevent oneself from making claims that simply do not add up to meaning much of anything.

I'm no genius but I do have a college education with a degree in accounting, finance, and my favorite class in college was logic and favorite activity was participating on debate teams. I'm retired now but worked for thirty years as a finance estimator for a Fortune 500 company and made countless presentations on whether or not it made sense to pursue a project from a financial standpoint. Providing supporting data for conclusions was always required. Blanket statements that "we should do it because it's cheaper," just don't fly without common sense support. So, while I may come off as a snob; I'm really only trying to show the value in critical thinking and not making blanket statements based upon emotion as opposed to fact.

Another example I've seen on these pages is "The water quality is just as good because it tastes just as good and is just as clear". This is another fallacy. Water quality cannot be determined by looks or taste; When we're talking about PPM (parts per million) of things, which is precisely what we're alluding to with water quality, have the water tested; something that's relatively inexpensive, before making such claims about water quality.

Somehow, I made it through 41 years of existence without ever having my own place with a washer/dryer in the unit. I looked at "portables" off and on, especially after getting a countertop dishwasher (life-changing!), but I had it in my head that I'd need a dryer, and all of the small ones seem overly expensive for the headache involved with hooking them up. Finally, after delaying many loads of laundry because I didn't want to go down to the basement, it dawned on me that I could stand to hang things up to dry. $200 later, I'm the proud owner of this machine.

Key things I learned from other reviews, that I recommend everyone take to heart:
- Make sure the drain pipe is secure! It doesn't hold in place well, and if it pops out and pours gallons of water onto your floor (and maybe causes your downstairs neighbor's ceiling to leak, oops), you will regret it.
- Get a snap coupling adapter (the one I have is listed as being for dishwashers but works for this), a longer washing machine hose (I had to buy a 2-pack even though I only needed one, but it was worth it), and some plumber's thread tape. The thread tape is going to make all the difference in not having leaks.
- Read the instructions, even though the English translation isn't the best. They're still helpful.

One thing I couldn't find out before buying was whether there's a place to add fabric softener. There is! I hadn't used softener before because I was using dryers and dryer sheets (or, more recently, those wool balls), so this is new for me. One thing I learned is the softener only works in warm to hot water, so if you're doing a cold water wash, stay away. But the option is there.

I'm writing this review in the first blush of joy at how well the machine works for me, so I don't yet know how it holds up over time. But I'm FINALLY making progress on my laundry piles. One last note is that I'm still experimenting with the drying racks that work best for me--I think you'll also have to try a few and see what fits your space and items. But if you're on the fence, topple over and join us on the washer side. I predict you'll feel as 100% finally adult as I do.

This is a very well-made appliance from a little-known manufacturer. I had my "hired muscle", who's been my mainstay throughout a complete (down to the wall studs) kitchen makeover, help me with mounting this, and it took the two of us about four hours to install it. You MUST have wood blocking between two studs to install the body of the hood on, as it only has two "keyhole" slots 10" apart, and it's too heavy for sheet rock anchors. We were able to insert a 2x4 between studs when we opened the wall up. It comes with a 3' power cord and grounded plug, but I suppose it could be hard-wired (there's no knock-out on the electrical box to accept a cable clamp, though).

The telescoping chimney attaches to two steel brackets, which in turn attach directly to the wall, and spiral sheet rock anchors are provided for them (their load isn't as much as the body of the hood). There are venting holes at the top sides of the chimney which are only required if the hood is not ducted (i.e recirculating with a charcoal filter); I don't like how they look, so I'll probably turn that piece upside down and drill new holes for the mounts.

Included in the package is a length of 6" flexible aluminum ducting, which should prove adequate for most people's venting needs. We have wait to break through stucco to attach the duct and cap, so I can't test the efficiency by cooking something smoky and greasy (like rib-eye steaks seared in a very hot cast iron pan) yet, but I suspect one of the middle speeds (there are 6) will be all I'll need for most cooking.

The touch controls are nice, as are the bright blue displays. The 35 watt halogen lights, though in the back instead of the front, have three brightness settings, and the noise level is about what I expected from a 900 CFM blower (but only the highest setting could be called "loud"). I'm extremely pleased with it, and if you do some online research, you can find it at a very reasonable price, especially when compared to better-known brands with similar features.

We bought a 12 ounce bag of already ground coffee for $9.00. We got 24 servings which makes it 37.5 cents per serving which beats every retailer we could find.
Sam's Club offers a 96 serving for $39 which makes the servings at 0.41
Macy's offers 18 servings for $11.99 (onsale) - and sometimes you can get it for even bigger discounts to make it 0.48 per serving
Keurig offers 24 servings for $18.49 - making it very expensive at 0.77
Amazon offers 80 servings for $33.06 - making it 0.41 per serving

So this device does allow you to save money on each serving - and the more you use it- the more money you will save.

With every use, you have to clean the filter. Empty the grounds into your trash can; rinse it out (and make sure you don't get any grounds down your sink drain or it will plug it up).

I just had my new Bosch dishwasher installed and was very excited. However, I was quite disappointed when the first wash was complete.
Things weren't dry properly even though I have used JetDry. Some parts were dry, but some parts felt wet. (and I am not talking about water pooling on concaved bottom of cups or bowls. This is understandable.) Some areas were dry to the touch, but there are lots of spots with condensation here and there - on utensils, side of some bowls, and so on. (They weren't overlapping and weren't even touching each other.) Even the arms of the center sprinkler were dripping because of condensation and the bottom of the silverware rack was wet. As I open the door I could see mild condensation on the surface of the inside of the door as well.
On second load, I used "Extra Dry" mode hoping that it would fix the problem. It looked slightly better, but the condensation still occured and I had to take out the dishes and bowls and dry them on separate dish racks.

I think it cleaned decently and it is quiet as advertised, but my 8 years old JenAir dishwasher was already as quiet and it dried excellently compared to this Bosch. I guess it's because it doesn't have a heating element as someone already pointed out.
I am quite disappointed and trying to find a way to solve this problem. I chose this model especially because none of JenAir models have the front display panel. But now I'm seriously considering returning this one and get JenAir instead.

*** Update ***
I checked out several forums and found out it is indeed because of Bosch's unique drying system called "condensation drying." It basically uses the heat produced during the wash cycle to dry the dishes.
There's pros and cons to this system.
Pros: Since it is not using heating element, it reduces energy consumption quite a lot.
Cons: Since the drying relys on the heat of the dishes after the wash, those made of ceramic, glass, or metal will dry quite efficiently, but those made of materials such as soft plastic - that does not hold the heat for long - will not be able to dry completely.

There are few tips to handle this situation.
1) Run the kitchen water until it becomes hot, then start the dishwasher.
2) Drying agents like JetDry is a must.
3) Make sure the water temperature for the house is sufficiently hot.
(The water temp of my house is slightly hotter than warm currently, so I'm planning on raising the temp.)
4) Leave the dishes in for more than an hour (or a few) after the cycle so that the left over heat can dry them.

I do like having dishwasher that can dry very well like my old one, but once I understood how Bosch's system works, I am willing to give it a little more try.

This is a review of the GE WR55X10775 Main Control Board Assembly which I purchased from Parts Plus Company via Amazon. It was delivered promptly.

After 13 years of faithful service, my GE Profile side-by-side refrigerator-freezer (model PSCS3RGXCFSS) started misbehaving. In short, replacing the old main control board with this new one completely fixed all problems. It was a very easy DIY (do-it-yourself) operation. I was glad I didn't need to pay for a repair person.

The water dispenser would mostly not work, but then it would work from time to time. The freezer and refrigerator setpoint controls stopped functioning from time to time. When I would display freezer and refrigerator temperatures, the display would sometimes start flashing. One morning I came into the kitchen and my refrigerator greeted me with flashing zeros on the display. Together, these symptoms suggested a voltage regulation failure in progress. Luckily, the freezer and refrigerator temperatures were being maintained.

After watching several helpful YouTube videos, I learned that the most likely failure was the main control board (part WR55X10775). While the problem could have been with the dispenser control board (part WR55X10785), that was less likely. So I ordered the WR55X10775 main control board. The board came in a sturdy cardboard box wrapped in two layers of bubble wrap. It did not come in an anti-static bag.

CAUTION: Always unplug the refrigerator (or open the circuit breaker) prior to working on it.

After watching a couple of How-To videos on YouTube, I removed the old control board and installed the new one in about 15 minutes. My refrigerator was once again fully operational after the new control board was installed, with all problems fixed. If one watches the videos on YouTube, I think anyone could replace the control board. On a scale of 1 to 5 for Difficulty, I'd give the operation a 1 (easy).

Glad to have our refrigerator fully working again. Since it is 13 years old, I suppose we will buy a new one if something else fails in the future. However, I am pleased to have my refrigerator repaired for roughly one-tenth the price of a new unit.

But wait! I then repaired the old (failed) main control board with about 2 dollars in parts!

Having removed the old control board to install the new one, I found myself curious to know why it failed. I inspected both sides of the circuit board under an industrial bench magnifier. I did not see any signs of overheating on or near the electrolytic capacitors, the 2 fan resistors, or the relays. The electrolytic capacitors did not show any gross bulging at their tops. However, on one of the 470 microfarad capacitors, I noticed a teeny-tiny spot of electrolyte, and very slight bulging. In control boards such as this, the most likely cause of failure is the electrolytic capacitors. And the most likely capacitors to fail are the two 470 microfarad capacitors (with the two 220 microfarad capacitors next likely). Failure of these capacitors would fully explain the symptoms I observed. So I removed the two 470 microfarad capacitors and found electrolyte stains on the bottom side of the one that had the spot on its top. So I replaced both of the 470 microfarad (25 volt) capacitors, then installed the old board in the refrigerator. It worked again! Just think: two electrolytic capacitors can make an entire refrigerator inoperable.

Even if I'd known I could I repair the old control board for less than 2 dollars in parts, I would still decide to replace the entire control board with a new one (the new one is reinstalled now). Consider: the original control board is 13 years old. While the 470 microfarad capacitors failed this time, all the other electrolytic capacitors are also 13 years old (as well as the relays). In industry, it is common to replace all electrolytic capacitors every 10 years. So maybe it's a good idea to replace the entire board if it is over 10 years old. Of course, there comes a point when one considers buying a new appliance, instead of repairing.

The package included product information and the outer/ inner gasket rings. The removal of the old gasket took less than a minute. It was the installation that took awhile.....three hours. However, if I was to do it again, I could do the install in half the time.

My recommendations include removing the door, front panel, and concrete stabilizers on either side of the drum. I tried to get cute and do it first without removing the concrete blocks but I realized I couldn't assure that the gasket was seated properly without visualizing the gasket behind the concrete blocks. Therefore, I went ahead and removed the blocks to be safe. Once the gasket was seated, next came the retaining ring. My suggestion is to watch the You Tube video that shows the "how to" on a Bosch 300/ 500, especially the part where he braces the retaining ring with a screw driver wedged between the concrete block. I reinstalled the right side concrete block and installed the retaining ring identical to the video and it worked great! I didn't spend a lot of time on that part. I then reassembled the left concrete block and continued reassembling the rest of the washer parts that I had removed. After seating the other half of the gasket, I attempted several tries at placing the retaining ring over the gasket. I then found another You Tube video and watched how the person demonstrating this part completed the seating of the retaining ring. I then followed the same method and it worked perfectly.

I also took time to clean out the drain trap at the bottom of the machine. Again, there is a You Tube video on how to do this and though it is simple, I recommend using their technique of having a shop vac running as you're loosening the plug.

I bought this because I forgot my french press on one too many camp outings and had to try to make filters out of paper towels and a rubber band (not fun when you desperately need that coffee that's slowly wicking up the sides of the paper towel rather than falling into your cup). I considered an aeropress but didn't want paper filters, and by the time I added a mesh filter I'm looking a a $40 press that I'll only use while camping.

I stumbled across this, figured what the hell, and ordered the two-pack to give one to my dad who has had the same misfortune as myself. It came in today and I made a test cup of coffee with it and I have to say I'm super impressed. The design is slightly limited in that you have to fill your drinking vessel all the way up with water for it to brew, so for example you wouldn't be able to brew right in the camp stove unless you filled it all the way up.

But the amazing thing is that it's so easy to clean! Compared to my french press, I have to find some water, rinse the screen off into the press, dump the grounds, add more water, dump the rest of the grounds, and probably even a third splash to get the last couple grounds. At home because I'm paranoid of grounds clogging drains this means going down to the bathroom and dumping into the toilet. I've heard of composting it but the amount of grounds I build up would be entirely too acidic to be a suitable compost material on its own. Plus you still have the issue of separating the water from the grounds, compost can't be too soupy.

With this thing, you just wait for the grounds to drip dry, then dump it upside down in the trash. You run your hands over the inside-out mesh once to get the bulk of them off and then you can just rinse the last little bits down the drain. Beautiful.

As far as the coffee it makes, just as good as my $100 stainless french press. The screen is a touch finer so in theory there might be fewer oils making it through? Not sure, it didn't seem that way to me. If anything it just meant less sediment at the bottom of my cup, which I always tossed when making a french press cup.

I'm a diehard FP user and I'll never give it up, this thing doesn't give you a carafe for instance or a very convenient way to brew a whole batch at once. But for traveling, camping, and single-cup uses, I don't think there's a better or more inexpensive product on the market.

My house central AC/heat unit is equipped with Aprilair 400 humidifier. It worked properly, but I was concerned about stale water collecting at the bottom of the panel housing. Water did turn green, and introduction of in-line antimicrobial filter together with occasional sprinkling with tea tree oil (powerful antiseptic) help alleviating this situation to a degree.

I still wanted to convert 400 model into 600 model that uses running water. This particular maintenance kit helped me to achieve this. Previous reviewer described several stages of the conversion, I just want to add that the supplied funnel snaps into the humidifier housing, and fits perfectly. It has 1/2 inch diameter extension to fit a water drain tube (I got a transparent tube from HD to channel water into sump pump) Overall, this kit fits 400 housing with no issues, and I did not need to change 400 humidity controller.

My first results to use the converted humidifier were positive. I needed to maintain above 40% humidity level in my house during the winter period to help my newborn baby to breath easy through the night. I could see that humidifier was running water every time furnace got activated to maintain this relatively high humidity level.

But couple of month later, the setup had a harder time to maintain this level, it could barely keep it around 40%. I attribute this to wearing out of the humidifier water panel supplied with the setup. It seems that the panel (made of aluminum mesh layers fused together) had some sort of deposits that helped retaining steaming water. These deposits wear out with time, and the panel has much harder time to allow for proper water/air interaction. I had to revert to the original panel, No 45, designed for Aprilair 400 series as it has lots of paper layers to soak in water. After this, humidifier could easily increase humidity level to a desired value. So I subtract one star for the supplied panel No 35 behavior - it seems strange to me that it "wears out" so fast.
