Now I don't know what I'm doing wrong, as I'm using drip grind, filling below the max line, and ensuring that the cap is snapped shut. I do notice that the cap always has a hairline gap after it snaps closed. I can push the top down just a smidge further and then it's perfectly sealed, but it won't stay down. There are no coffee grounds on the lip, and it's been like that since I purchased it, so I'm not sure if that's an issue. I only need to use one DW gel pack for cleaning even though there is a place for 2 for dirtier loads.  I always rinse off food before the dishes go in it.  There is a tray to empty food particles that may gather during a wash cycle which should be cleaned out each time if needed.  Mine has never needed it.  It is very quiet while running, more so than any other DW I have owned.  Some friends stopped in recently, saw our little DW and all were impressed with it. The price is more affordable than many other Portable dishwashers that we looked at during out search. The rack is smaller than a single rack of a typical dishwasher but once I practiced getting my dishes in I am happy with the size of the load. When we are finished doing a load we turn off the hot water and empty the hose in the sink.  You need to push the little red button on the white sink nozzle attachment to release the water pressure before detaching the hose.  We then put a small pan on the floor and allow the hose to completely empty into the pan.  This just takes a second and removes all water left in the hose.  It will also sound a buzzer if you turn the DW on with the attached hose but forget to turn on the Hot water.  We did this once and were so glad for this feature.  We would not want to burn out the motor.  I tell my husband almost everyday, " Did I tell you that I love my new dishwasher?" This works for the 2 of us.

We just bought our first house, and we are DIYing a lot of things. The baking element in the oven that came with the house must've been left on for a few weeks - it was pretty much reduced to ashes. I bought this as a replacement because it looked identical, but I was just going by the picture.

It does not come with instructions. That's ok, as it's pretty common sense if the part is identical: unplug the oven, unscrew the old element, remove the wires from the connections, and put this one in its place. In my case, the original had straight connections, and this one has connections bent at a 90 degree angle. That would be fine, but the wires weren't long enough to connect at that angle from the inside of the oven, so I needed to do a little more work to get it installed.

I removed the old element, took the back plate off of the oven, and pulled the wire connections out of the holes so they were back behind the oven. I put this new element in and pushed it all the way back until the ends were poking out the back of the oven. I put the connections on that way, replaced the back panel, and then finished installing the new element inside the oven.

I was a little concerned (as anyone should be when they are winging installation on anything that uses electricity and particularly something that uses electricity to make heat), so I gave it a few test runs at lower heat while I watched for any problems. It worked perfectly. It's been a month now, and we use that oven all the time. We've never had any problems and I have no doubt it's working exactly as it should.

I've now had this machine for about a month and a half. I know it looks like it should come with an EZ-Bake oven, but this is no toy. I'm utterly serious when I say that the washer does a much better job of getting clothes clean than a "regular" North American type washer/dryer set. The water literally whips the clothes around in the tub (you have to see it to believe it) and my stuff has never been cleaner. My apartment doesn't have hookups and the laundry room is in the basement 10 floors down with ancient Speed Queen machines that are as old as I am--and $5.00 to wash/dry clothes was getting ridiculous, so I got this. First, I really thought my wife and I required as large of a machine as possible. The fact is this 26lb model could VERY EASILY accommodate a family of four. If you want to save some money, the 17lb model would likely be far more than you need for two people. I got this model because it had a drain pump. Put it on a small dolly that we just wheel into the kitchen on wash day, and put the drain hose into the sink--much better than the gravity-drain models.
ONE ITEM THAT IS A MUST: The hoses that come with this are meant I think for asian homes where the faucets are much smaller than ours. I bought something called a "RINSEROO", available on Amazon, which is a faucet adapter that fits ANY faucet and the hoses of which fit the machine perfectly for filling the unit. I can't overstate the fact that I "overbought" with this machine. While the dimensions suggest otherwise (it is very compact) it holds a LOT of laundry. Multiple towels (heavy bath sheet types), jeans, etc etc. The downside to all this capacity is that it takes about 10 minutes to fill the wash tub with our rather low-flow kitchen sink, and the next size down would shorten that time. With all that said, picture two 50-somethings watching this thing agitate their clothes in a whirlpool of sheer power! LOL. It really is astonishing that something this inexpensive does a BETTER JOB than a regular washer. It is, however, more labor intensive, and you have to watch it while it fills (no auto-shutoff, YOU are the water level sensor). We turn on the water, and set the kitchen timer for 10 minutes to avoid a flood. It's worth the time, because everything for us fits in one load with room to spare. Also: The spinner is NOT A DRYER!!!!!!! It simply gets the excess water out and does NOT dry--PEOPLE: READ ABOUT THESE MACHINES. I'm tired of people complaining that it isn't a heated dryer. With that said, clothing comes out of the spinner DAMP. You literally cannot wring any water out of them, and we hang dry for a couple hours which works just fine and likely saves a TON of electricity.
We are ASTOUNDED at how well this works, especially the agitation and how clean everything comes out.
It's hard to believe the cost when compared to standard machines, and yet get this result.
If you can't have a "normal" washer/dryer set, THIS IS A GOD SEND, works far better than advertised, and it is one of those things that is just so simple, it's a thing of beauty.
Have I mentioned the agitation? LOL. No other standard washer even comes close to moving this much water around, thus things are just so much cleaner.
After the detergent wash cycle which is up to 15 mins, we transfer the stuff into the spinner, and hook up the hose to the spin side of the machine, which rinses the soap out while it spins. We then fill the tub back up for a thorough rinse, but I suspect the "spin rinse" would actually have an acceptable result if you're short on time. In closing, if you don't have laundry hookups in your abode, this is exactly (more than) what you need! FIVE STARS. We are totally impressed and satisfied. Just know WHAT IT IS, and do yourself a favor and watch a couple you tube videos, and you'll be equally impressed, guaranteed.

Bought this washing machine because I truly despise going to the laundrymat. It takes up a good amount of precious space in my bathroom, but I think it's going to be worth it- eventually. Here is my list of pro's and con's about this washing machine:

PROS
- Looks like it can hold a decent amount of laundry. I think I could wash a set of full-sized sheets in there in one load at the highest water level (water levels range from 1 [smallest] to 10 [largest], or a king sized set in two loads. It would probably hold a small laundry basket full of clothes, or an armful. Big capacity for relatively low cost
- One of the feet can be adjusted to level how the washer sits
- I've only run it on one setting (Fast/Air Dry) and it left everything pretty wet, but it does appear to have a spin cycle. Might update this post when I've tried more cycles. That said, that setting was pretty quiet with minimal vibration- I couldn't hear it with the bathroom door closed if I was more than 15-20 feet away in my apartment. The noisy part is the chime (see "cons")
- If you want to run it without hooking it up to a water source (the water intake hose they supplied is very short), you can, but you have to just keep adding water until it finally kicks into action, depending on the water level. My test run was at level 1, and it took some time to get it about halfway full. Makes sense since the capacity is fairly big for a portable washer. You have to re-fill it to do the rinse cycle after it drains this way.
- Opening the back panel reveals a fairly simple setup- lots of plastic, but no leaks when I ran it.
- I've had bad experiences with ordering appliances to be delivered by mail and having them come broken, but this was well packaged and runs well with no leaks.
- Once I got the drain hose on correctly and put the washer on a table so that the hose only went downwards into the tub (needs to be flat or only downward, you can't have it go up over the edge of the tub or sink), it drained fully and the drain hose did not leak. The device comes with a round metal clip (called a "pinchcock" in the instructions... hehehe... that looks like what it would do literally... apparently that is the technical term for it) that fits around the tube and the drain valve to make the connection tighter. I put the hose on backwards at first and it leaked terribly- FYI, the wider end of the drain tube connects to the machine, not the end with the little L clip on it.
- You can also change what side the machine drains on through the back panel, which is nice. I didn't do it because it was on the correct side for how we set it up in our bathroom, but I did have a moment of panic when I was doing the first wash and I forgot if I had hooked the tube up to the correct side.
- The voltage it needs (110) is compatible with our janky electrical system in our apartment, it didn't cause the breaker to go off.
- The single tub design means you don't have to switch your laundry over to another compartment to do the spin dry (which only reduces the dampness in clothes, does not actually dry)- a lot of cheaper machines available have a dual tub design, but this one doesn't, which is one of the reasons I bought it even though it didn't have any reviews yet.
- Clear lid opens and folds down so that when the lid is open it doesn't add much more height to the machine, maybe 6-7 inches, leaving more room for a shelf above the machine.

CONS
- As a previous review said, the hose has to be laid flat or nearly flat to fully drain the washer. Since we have a tub and not just a shower, we have to build a sturdy wooden box for it to sit on so it is high enough for the drain valve to be higher than our tub (for us, it will be about 15-16 inches high and 20 inches square on the top and bottom). There is a product available for washing machines in general called a laundry pedestal but these are at least $200 to buy. The washer is pretty tall, so building a box for it to sit on will make the whole set up about 50'' tall. Not sure how the box will affect the noise/vibration (might act as an amplifier).
- Unclear policy about returns... unclear paperwork in general. The translation on the instructions is terrible, and it takes some time to work out.
- Intake hose is very short (4 feet maybe?) and connects to the washer itself very well, but the other end that you're supposed to connect to a water source doesn't fit anything we have- it might hook up to our handheld shower hose if we take off the sprayer, but that would be pretty inconvenient to set up every time we want to do laundry.
- The chimes it uses to tell you what its doing are kind of loud and annoying- I think there might be a way to turn it off, but I have to decipher the instructions further.
- Still not sure about how to use the control panel to select different wash and spin cycles, again, need to do some trial and error and creative interpretation of the instructions.

TIPS
- Let your stuff soak for a bit before you let the washer run to get your clothes cleaner, or pause the cycle during the wash part for a little bit.
- After you use the machine, leave the lid open for a bit to dry out the inside. It drains pretty well, but if you close the lid again any moisture left inside might sit there and mildew.

So I had the UL code on my Cabrio washer, which was about 6 years old.

I had a horrific time removing the tub and old bearings from the washer. The tub was fused to the axle assembly and required using a 2x4 wedged in the drum and a scissor jack between the axle and the 2x4 to remove. The axle it self required an axle puller attached to the metal ring that holds down the stator to remove (this subsequently bent that metal ring which also had to be replaced). The bearings came out ok after that using the metal rod included in the kit and a large hammer to knock out.

I then cleaned the channel for the bearing/axle and replaced everything with the provided items in the kit, using plenty of grease and glue on the bearing seal. The next day I ran a wash cycle but still had the UL error! I realized that the bearing tool in the kit did not make the 2 bearings sit completely flush and level in the tub and that the axle was not wedged fully into the upper bearing. I had to follow up with a large socket and hammer to straighten out the bearings and also had to hammer a bit on the axle to make it sit fully flush in the bearing. If using a hammer / socket on the bearings, make sure that the socket only contacts the outer lip of the bearings as hammering on the inside of the bearing will damage the races. After correcting this and letting the glue dry again my issue was finally resolved.

I have been running with the new bearings and axle for about a week now and about 5 heavy loads with no more UL error. The washer is much more quite now when going into ultra fast spin mode.

Issues with the kit:

-I did not get any instructions with the kit at all and had to google everything
-The glue and grease were not labeled (minor but could confuse some people)
-The grease seemed extremely thin, I threw it and used a known fully synthetic automotive grease
-The axle did not sit flush in the bearing without some convincing
-The bearing press tool did NOT do a perfect job of pushing the bearings in flush

I think this kit would be extremely difficult for someone to install without prior mechanical skills and expanded troubleshooting knowledge. It did however work out for me in the end so I am happy. Hopefully the bearings provided in the kit are not of a horrible quality, but only time will tell.

[[VIDEOID:37f46344adc61e10c6c5af363adc2de8]] I want to give this machine 4.5 stars but that isn't a choice. Overall, the machine is great but it definitely had a learning curve for me and I am usually very handy. I also have a few concerns about some of the other reviews, which I relied heavily on with making a decision to purchase this unit. It came packaged securely and was easy to assemble the bottom panel. Like other viewers, I did vacuum out all the loose Styrofoam pieces so they wouldn't later end up inside the parts of the machine somehow. As soon as I unpacked the machine and got it ready to install to my kitchen faucet with the [[ASIN:B008M6KBWG Danco 10512 Garden Hose Adapter, 55/64-Inch 27 Female x 3/4-in GHTM, Chrome]] which I purchased based on another reviewer suggestion, I found this 10512 adapter did not sit very deep and securely into the water inlet hose. It fit perfectly onto my faucet but due to a smaller end that goes into the hose and the way the hose is designed, it was almost impossible to connect to the hose. So off to the local hardware store I go to find a more suitable adapter. This adapter Danco 10513 [[ASIN:B008M6KFD6 Danco 10513 15/16"-27M / 5/64"-27F X 3/4" GHTM or 55/64"-27M Multi-Thread Garden Hose Aerator Adaptor, Chrome]] (see photo) works so much better and seals tightly to both the hose and the kitchen faucet.

Hooked the machine up and ran a short wash with a tiny bit of liquid detergent and a quick rinse to get the pungent smell out of the machine (hopefully). The drain hose u-shaped elbow device that is meant to hang the drain hose over the sink was useless on my kitchen sink because my sink is not at the very edge of the counter top but sits back a little further. The u-shaped elbow is not very large allowing it to hang into my sink as designed. Therefore, I removed the u-shaped elbow and just tied the drain hose to the water inlet hose with twist ties. (see photo) I will eventually try to find something to easily clamp/unclamp the drain hose to the water hose when in use or just use a zip tie to hold them together to ensure the hose doesn't go flying out of the sink when draining and spinning.

Everything looked fine, so I grabbed some laundry. Some of the other reviewers may be exaggerating a little about how much you can actually fit into this machine and expect it to be cleaned properly. I was able to fit maybe a 1/3 to 1/2 of a load that would fit into a normal older style top loading machine, which is fine for me since I am single. Then starts the issue of water flowing onto my floor and I was not pleased with that. My floor is tile so it was really no big deal except that it was a lot of water and pretty inconvenient. This didn't happen the first time I ran the rinse cycle mentioned above so needless to say I was concerned. After some tedious troubleshooting, I figured out what the issue was. I have really strong water pressure and if the water pressure is on too strong, the water tends to go into the machine too fast and erratic and drip onto the lip of the top of the tub. (see photos) The lip is not very thick and the water was filling up the drain hole at the top of the tub faster than it could drain back into the tub, hence overflowing onto my floor. I think Giantex could make this lip around the top of the tub a little thicker/higher to avoid this from happening so easily. After resolving this issue by turning my water pressure way lower and allowing the machine to fill slower, all was good.

The clothes washed great and the rinse and spin cycles are wonderful. The clothes came out damp and not sopping wet. I then tried to wash my queen size sheets and found that I really only felt comfortable washing the flat and fitted sheets together with no pillowcases or even better yet, wash the flat sheet separately with 2 of my pillowcases and the fitted sheet separately with my other 2 pillowcases. It just seemed to be overloaded with the entire sheet set in the machine. I think I read someone saying they could fit a quilt into this machine, but I don't see that happening. I ended up doing about 6 additional loads and everything works seamlessly now. I haven't washed towels yet so I am not sure how many bath towels will fit in a single wash. However, I did run a second spin cycle on one load and the clothes came out even more dry than before, which would probably work great for towels or heavier items that take a long time to dry.

Lastly, I also purchased this appliance dolly, [[ASIN:B00IF6YJAS Stalwart Adjustable Sized Telescopic Furniture Dolly Roller]] which I read fits perfectly. Au contraire mon ami! The smallest this dolly would go was still almost too large for the machine to set on without falling through the middle. I have a very small apartment and need the dolly to be exactly the same size as the washer. I took a hacksaw and shortened all four rods to the length needed to allow the dolly to shrink and fit snugly under the machine. Now all is great and the washer on the dolly fits snugly in its resting place and still fits under my countertop.

Overall, I am extremely happy with this washer after doing about 7 loads of laundry thus far. My suggestions would be to do more research on the adapters to fit your specific faucet because it would appear the provided water hose will not fit any sink in the USA - maybe if you are hooking it to a regular washing machine/laundry hookup, it would work fine. Also, do not turn the water pressure on full blast unless your floors need to be mopped and then you can just kill two birds with one stone. Haha! Additionally, if you want to purchase a dolly, try to find one that will shrink to a smaller size more suited for this machine unless you have a hacksaw to shorten the poles on the model mentioned above.

Before we get into the nooks and crannies of this machine, please let it be clear I really wanted to give the product a 4 star rating. However, due to the type of cheap plastic chosen for the internal construction, I felt it would be best to go sort of "neutral" on the star rating and give 3 "okay" stars. I'll explain later in this review.

The instruction manual is lacking some details and is wrong on other details, so you might want to read this review carefully.

First things first... The blue button on the right of the control panel turns the unit on and off. I'm only telling you that, because those with poor eyesight may have difficulty reading the faint red text on a bright blue button. I'm in that camp too. A green LED indicator on the far right of the control panel will remain steady when the power is ON, but blink slowly if the power is OFF [in other words "standby"].

If you're looking for a home appliance countertop bottled water ice machine for a family of 4 that will keep up with an ice demand, then you've come to the right place. This machine is certainly capable of doing that. It makes bullet ice sizes of small [6 minutes], medium [10 minutes], and large [15 minutes]. It has a very large ice bin which will hold 5.5 pounds of ice. It takes about 3 hours to fill up the bin on the large setting, which means the machine is very well capable of producing 40 pounds of ice per day. Most descriptions I've seen are truthful to that respect. However, I would recommend the medium setting, if you are a habitual ice eater. Yes, I'm a fellow ice cruncher too. The middle blue button selects the bullet ice size. A green LED indicator will move appropriately along the bottom of the control panel to indicate the size you are selecting.

The ice water dispensing feature is a secondary function which is on a spring loaded spigot. You press a switch on the control panel for the spigot to extend, but you have to push the spigot back in manually. The first blue button on the left triggers the pump for dispensing water. If you're going to use this machine for both ice and water dispensing, then I would recommend just leaving the spigot extended for quick water access. The machine does not have a drip tray for the spigot, but a folded paper towel works just as good for catching an occasional drip after using it [like I said... "secondary function"]. It takes a while for the ice water temperature to drop, but you can speed up the process by allowing the first 2 batches of ice to drop directly into the ice water reservoir below the ice bin. This also helps the machine make perfect ice by the third batch from first time startup [helpful tip and trick there].

There are no audible alarms on this machine, but it does have LED indicators. There is a red LED indicator in the upper left of the control panel that will illuminate steady if the ice bin is full. The machine will go into standby mode when the bin is full. This same light will blink slowly if an ice jam has been detected. Ice jams do occur occasionally, but it usually happens when the small ice size has been selected. Again, I recommend using the medium ice size.

There's also an "add water" LED indicator near the bottom-right of the control panel. I don't plan on letting it run out of water, and I certainly don't recommend deliberately allowing it to run out of water. Besides, if the unit gets low on water, then you will definitely know about it, because the pump will make gurgling sounds as it tries to draw on a low water supply. So, Hey, there's your "audible" alarm, LOL. Obviously, the machine will go into standby mode if it does run completely out of water accidentally.

On page 4 of the instruction manual [if you want to call it that], there is a weak clue on how to remove the ice bin. If you have large hands and fat fingers, then you're in for a difficult task here. You're supposed to be able to reach your hand into the bin, fold down the stop bracket, and pull the bin out. Well, I couldn't do that either. I had to use a duct tape trick and some slight-of-hand to get that funky stop bracket to fold down far enough to remove the bin. Imagine being in a hurry to clear an ice jam, and you'll probably also imagine breaking that stupid stop bracket completely off. Yeah, needless to say, the stop bracket is no longer on my ice bin. Works better that way anyhow, because now my WHOLE hand can get the ice scoop down in there properly. Apparently, the ice bin clearance was designed by midgets, but I digress.

By the time you reach page 5 of the instruction manual, you may come to the conclusion that idiots wrote the manual for idiots. There's actually a diagram of how to install a bottle of water, but don't laugh yet. Believe it or not, this step could be very critical depending on the cap thickness of the bottled water you are using. It's pretty tight, to say the least. You literally have to make sure you are completely square with the machine before dropping the bottle straight down on it. In fact, you may have to give the bottle a small tap down to complete the puncture, that's how tight it is. Unlike other small ice machines, this one will spit at you when the bottle neck reaches the bottom of the collar. So make sure you have a towel handy to wipe up the mess. The reason why it does this is because the machine doesn't have a secondary reservoir below the collar. It only has one reservoir below the ice bin and the water has to travel through tubing to get there. Hence, there's going to be a small splash for every new bottle placed on it since this machine uses a direct gravity fed method. In spite of this itty-bitty design flaw, I actually prefer the gravity method since it eliminates needless pumps along the water path.

On page 7 of the instruction manual it speaks of 2 filters behind the ice bin, under the bottle collar, connected to the water tubing, accessed by removing a clipper. Read this next statement carefully... THERE'S NO SUCH THING!... There's NO clipper, it's a zip tie. Not only is there not 2 filters, but there are NO filters, it's just a tube connection. That's okay though, because why would you need a filter for bottled water? Especially if you're going to use Spring Water? So, I can only assume that previous models may have had such a filter.

Ok, now flip back over to page 6 of the instruction manual where you find cleaning recommendations. Notice it is "strongly recommended to clean it thoroughly before use." They're NOT kidding! Make sure you do so specifically for the interior. Every black plastic surface needs to be scrubbed down, because of the type of black plastic they used for construction, which his heavily petroleum-based and it leeches something awful. In fact, it may smell like diesel fuel in there to you. You may have to scrub it down 3 times before getting the odor out of there. This odor also taints the taste of water and ice. I don't mind "a new machine smell", but whoever decided to use that black plastic to house drinking water needs their head examined. It may also take up to 10 gallons of water to flush it all out.

But, don't freak out or panic. There's an easy solution to cleaning the diesel out of there for good. After scrubbing it down with weak soapy warm water and draining the machine, Your best friends will be ordinary tap water, vinegar, and lemon juice for the rest of it's life...
1. Mix 1 cup of white vinegar and 1 cup of real lemon juice to 1 gallon of water.
2. Pour directly into the reservoir under the ice bin and scrub down all black surfaces including the area under the ice maker elevator [you'll see it], and don't forget the ice bin too.
3. Allow the ice maker to make large ice until it runs out of that 1 gallon of water.
4. Dump the ice, and drain any remaining water.
5. Pour 1 gallon of filtered or bottled water directly into reservoir.
6. Allow ice maker to make large ice with that 1 gallon of clean water in order to flush it.
7. Dump ice and drain machine again.
8. Repeat steps 1 thru 7.

Then from then on per every 5 gallons of bottled water until the odor/taste is gone, put 1 tablespoon of white vinegar and 1 tablespoon of real lemon juice in the reservoir. Allow machine to run 3 cycles before drinking any water. It's not going to hurt you and you can barely tell it's there. In fact, you're supposed to use these same cleaning procedures every 3 months for ANY home appliance ice/water dispenser, except you only do it ONCE. We're simply tackling a special exception monster here.

Overall, it's a good machine. I just hope they make some improvements for the next model and use better plastic too.

Hope this helps. Enjoy your purchase.

P.S. - One other thing I forgot to mention. If this machine begins to jam too much on Medium ice, then take out the ice bin and check the white tube running from the bottle source to the elbow connection on the right. If this tube is curved inward toward the elevator, then it can cause ice to bounce backwards and create a chained jam over to the left side of the elevator. To remedy this problem you'll have to twist the large tube connection at the bottom of the bottle collar towards YOU so the tube will curve away from the elevator. You may have to remove the zip tie to do this, but Walmart carries the same small zip ties to replace it with. It's an easy fix, but it also affects how you move the ice bin in and out. So, if you have to fix this problem, then remember to always move the ice bin at a forward down angle to avoid racking it up against the tubing all the time. Yes, this another design flaw they need to fix.

UPDATE - I found another glitch. During warmer weather the air pressure in the bottle increases slightly and causes a little water to purge around the collar. It only happens when there's about 1/4 of the water remaining and the increased air pressure is trying to push the water out. The valve in the water reservoir closes when the level is at max as designed, therefore the water pressure has nowhere else to go but up through the collar. It's not a whole lot of water, but it's enough to be irritating. It finally stops doing it when the pressure equalizes in the bottle. I haven't got my air conditioner running yet, but when I do, I hope it stops doing that. Yes, another design flaw.

UPDATE # 2 - Air pressure problem is eliminated by air conditioning. I keep my thermostat set to 75 degrees F.

UPDATE # 3 - On Sept. 1, 2014 the ice shovel malfunctioned (the white bucket that fills with water and dumps the ice). It behaves like a gear has been damaged. I prefer to repair things myself, so I'm planning to disassemble the unit and find out which part I need. While I'm in there, I'll let the review readers know if the unit has a low port for coolant recharging (always a good thing to know). I'll add another update as soon as I can, so stay tuned if you haven't made a purchase decision yet, or if you experience the same malfunction.

UPDATE # 4 - On Sept. 15, 2014 the ice shovel repair was completed. Apparently an undetectable ice jam had occurred which caused a plastic female shaft to shatter. The plastic female shaft is split-keyed for the metal male drive shaft of the motor to slip into and turn it. Technically there are NO gears, everything is direct drive and relies on micro switches to let the motor know when to stop turning. Since the plastic female shaft is permanently part of the ice shovel tray the only way to repair it is to order another ice shovel tray. The good news is the part only costs $11.00 including shipping. You have to contact...
CHARD INTERNATIONAL LLC
Email = customerservice@chardinternational.com
Phone = 888-815-4252 8am-5pm CST
Ask for an "ice tray with sled" for HZB-15/BF (product # IM-15SS).

I did all of my correspondence through Email and Customer Service was an excellent experience. No problems whatsoever.
Making the repair was time consuming, but overall it's pretty easy to do. If anybody needs help with disassembly, just post a comment and I'll reply with instructions.
Oh yeah, I looked for a low port for future coolant recharging and it does not have one. However, there's plenty of room inside for a tap. Refrigerant and pressure specs are on the back label. Warning: Refrigeration and safety knowledge is required!

Final Comments:
- I wish the ice shovel tray was all metal with plastic coating for the reservoir.
- I wish there was more clearance for the water tubing above the main storage drawer.
- I wish the ice tray dumped onto a permanent sled, instead of the sled being attached to the tray.
- I wish the water would cycle for cooling first from a cold start.
- I wish the bottle collar was wider and deeper in order to help prevent splashing with a new bottle.
- I wish I would have invested in a commercial ice machine, but this one still does what I want it to do for now.

I'm pretty happy with the Ekobrew if for nothing else than the fact that it's quicker and easier to use (and clean up) than the official My KCup insert. However, whereas you can use drip grind coffee in the official My KCup device (because of it's locking cover), the Ekobrew really should only be used with coarse grind coffee. The reason for this is mainly because the top of the cup doesn't hold in water pressure the way the official one does and the metal filter is a much smaller area. As a result, 2 1/2 tbsps of drip grind coffee will almost but not quite clog the Ekobrew (which is probably why a lot of people are having issues with leaks). My recommendation to people thinking about getting the Ekobrew is to experiment with your own grinds at home. If you don't have a coffee grinder and/or hate grinding your own beans, try coarse grind coffee and see if that works better for you. If you feel the coffee is too light, go back to drip grind only buy a stronger brew and use less coffee (say, 1 tbsps). If that doesn't work, you may have to stick with the official My Kcup insert.
Oh, and another thing, if you are using drip grind coffee, expect a small amount of fine grinds in your coffee; the Ekobrew filter is just the tiniest bit wider than the official one, so you will get a little bit of grinds in the coffee. This doesn't bother me (I actually think it kinds adds to the taste in certain coffees), but again this cup seems to be intended for coarse grind.

I would buy it again--that's the first thing. As with other reviews, it is best designed for 15-25 g, really only 1-2 cups. It does a good job; the fines are the consistency of talcum powder. Unlike others, I don't mind not knowing the sieve size. It's the taste that matters and that is improved. There is a slight but noticeable improvement in the taste of the coffee; somewhat smoother. I find that shaking it 'sideways' is best since it increases surface contact with the filter. As others have said be careful with the thin-walled inner filter--it looks delicate.

The static generated by the shaking makes the fines stick to the inner surfaces. A gentle tap on the counter helps free up most of the powder but there is still an annoying amount that gets out to the counter, your hands, and the immediate surroundings. It is best to do as much over the sink as possible. A slightly larger version would be useful as long as it can still be shaken by one hand.

ORIGINAL REVIEW: I installed this in a mid-1990s Comfortmaker furnace that had gotten quite noisy. The job took a bit less than 2 hours and wasn't especially tough. The new inducer fits like the original.

For those who track such matters, the box was marked Made in Mexico.

On my installation, the flue pipe was attached to the original inducer's outlet with 2 sheet metal screws. The new inducer's housing is sheet metal like the original's, so it was easy to duplicate the mounting. I'm not sure that would have worked with the cheaper knockoffs I've seen online with housings that look like they might be potmetal.

The furnace is much quieter now. I was surprised that one reviewer here complained about noise. I can barely hear the inducer blower over the main blower motor. Maybe that person got an out of balance blower.

Negatives: the motor is a cheap 2-pole, smaller and less electrically efficient than the original, but they all seem to be that way now. The gaskets included were about 1/4" too large in diameter; they fit, but just barely. I had to extend the existing furnace wiring to reach the new blower's terminals, and crimp on fastons -- not a big deal since I had all the parts on hand. Finally, the vacuum hose that ensures the inducer is running before lighting the burners fit looser than on the original, so I added a small hose clamp to be sure of a good seal. Again, fortunately, I had it on hand.

Overall, it's a satisfactory replacement, reasonably priced compared to local sources. I hope this one lasts 20+ years like the original did.

I previously used an Inkbird ITC-308 controller to regulate the temperature of my homebrew fermenters, and it worked great. However, I recently got a larger fermentation chamber, and coincidentally also happened to get into barrel-aging beers. I needed a new temp controller for the ferm chamber, so I decided to upgrade and go with the ITC-608T. While I don't need the full range of its capabilities just yet (I'm only using the temp control), it will be nice to be able to regulate humidity when it comes to extended barrel aging.

I've had the regulator hooked up to my keezer/ferm chamber for a little while now and it's worked just as well as the ITC-308. If you're familiar with how Inkbird controllers work in general, you'll be right at home. If not, the user manual might be a little confusing (fairly broken English), but there are plenty of secondary resources around the web to help you out. Basically, just set a desired temp, the amount you want to let the temp fluctuate up and down, and (if you like) temps on both the high and low end where you want an alarm to go off, in case something goes awry. (One thing to note: Unlike more basic Inkbird controllers, the two AC outlets aren't labeled Heating and Cooling, but rather "Work 1" and "Work 2." Just remember that 1 = heat and 2 = cool.)

Overall, I'm pleased. Inkbird makes reliable controllers and the price can't be beat. The build quality is also very nice on this unit: high-quality plastics and pleasantly tactile buttons.

-----------------------
Tap water: 489 ppm
Kenmore Filter: 482 ppm
Brita Pitcher: 436 ppm
Distiller: 4 ppm
Gallon of distilled water bought at Target: 4 ppm

Here is a guide to where the water should be:
-----------------------
0-50ppm = ideal drinking water
50-100ppm = carbon filters, springs
100-200ppm = hard water
200-400ppm = average tap water

So although this Kenmore filter is reasonably priced, it doesn't do what it should, which is filter water adequately.

Installed and did conversion on this range yesterday. Two comments: to change the oven gas orifice, installation guide instructs to remove oven door. I would not advise doing so, and I do not think it is necessary. Removal of the oven floor panel is necessary, but it looks possible to do without removing door. Of course, it is easier to position your body for doing the work if the oven door is removed, and if you attempt the work with the door in place you will have to be careful not to distort the door with the weight of your body. The reason I do not recommend removal of the oven door is that the latches which hold the hinges in the correct position for removal and installation are completely inadequate for the application. With the hinges is the latched-open position, a slight bump will cause them to release. Not only is it challenging to return the hinges to the fully open position with the door removed, the latches are not sturdy enough to withstand the force of the door springs, and will basically fold. This will make them unsuitable for holding the door open, and the distortion will make it impossible to close the oven door. Other methods will need to be improvised in order to get the door back on, and the distorted latches will need to be conformed to allow the door to close. The other comment is that all the installed orifices are tightened beyond what is necessary. Removal will not present a problem with the proper 7mm socket, however there is one orifice (on the center (double) burner that is positioned horizontally, without room to use a socket. In my case, it was installed so tightly that a 7mm box-end wrench rounded the facets. Since I did not expect to reuse the installed NG orifice, and since it was already rounded off, I used vise grip pliers to extract it. Most tap water is virtually undrinkable--but a good water filter eliminates the need for costly bottled water.

OEM filters in this form factor run upwards of $30 each. That's hardly a crippling expense for most, and still cheaper than bottled water, but $4 a filter is quite the discount. So the question is, are you getting the same quality with this 3-pack?

If you're used to OEM filters, you'll notice some cosmetic differences, mainly the colors. But size-wise, they're identical, and both have the same o-ring seals on the top. These filters fit exactly the same in my refrigerator, installation is a snap, and after running the appropriate volume of water through the filter, water appears to be equally clear with an equally clean taste. Taste is every bit the equal of bottled water. So they're the same as the OEM filters, right?

Well, not exactly. These filters are certified to meet NSF42 standards, but the OEM filters conform to the more rigorous NSF53 and 401 standards--meaning they are guaranteed to eliminate more dangerous contaminants. Do you need the additional protection? That comes down to your local water quality--but if you want maximum peace of mind, you need to pony up for the much more costly OEM filters. Personally, I'm comfortable with the cleansing quality of these discounted filters. Any differences between OEM and these filters cannot be determined by unscientific taste testing.

This IS a good replacement for a RPWFE filter. In order to use it, you NEED (NEED) HAVE TO HAVE the fridge read and authenticate the chip from another filter. It needs to be taped to the filter housing.

You can use a RPWFE filter's chip, but just know that it will take some time to remove. I tried using a knife to 'pry' the chip, but know that it is NOT a regular RFID tag. It's a literal chip that is surface-soldered to a RFID tag, then glued to the body of the filter. If you try to remove the RFID 'sticker', you will leave the chip behind and null/void the whole thing.

NO CHIP, NO WATER. Remember that.

Cut the body of the filter with a saw or something and then tape the RFID tag to the location in the fridge that reads the RFID. If you use the chip from the bypass filter, the fridge will read "Not filtered". Otherwise, from a RPWFE filter, the fridge will still say "99 days overdue"

Regardless, this filter DOES work with the RPWFE fridges, and it tastes delicious. Good luck!

I was looking to replace our over the head microwave/hood combo - which was loud and inefficient sucking the air out (maybe 250-300 CFM max) - for a more powerful range hood in the 900 CFM but most in this range are in the 9-10" thick and would restrict the cooking space. Found and bought this gem with just 7" profile, not the slimmest but definitely among the most powerful out there. I was concerned about the noise loudness due to reviews on other similar systems so besides the mfr. specification, I double checked and noticed that this particular one has an 8" duct venting as compared to 6" for the other ones and by physics, the larger vent duct should allow more air flow and less noise.

The width of the hood itself is 29-5/8" so you definitely need a 30" clearance side-to-side to slide it in. It fits the under cabinet space like a glove even though ours is quite small with just about 10-1/2" D x 28-3/4" W opening (under). I personally think that the provided fasteners (screws/bolts) are on the thin side so I replaced those with 1 size thicker and stronger hardware just in case. Self-installation was not simple but doable b/c it's made of heavy stainless steel and weighs in the 40-45 lbs so would require two persons (tips: we put it on a pneumatic office chair which sat on a piece of plywood on top of the range to help lift it up in place). The notice was clear but we installed the wood strips or stringers (10" x 1-1/2" x 1/2") on both sides and in the back as well for better support.

IMPORTANT TIPS:
- Make sure to install the stringers slightly above the bottom cabinet frame at about 1/8"-3/16" so that the mounting brackets can pull the hood all the way up to flush with the bottom cabinet.

- Also when the unit is still on the floor, make sure to set the (4) bolts (that will hold the brackets at the 4 corners) thru the top cover, then add washers and nuts (just a few turns) to hold the bolts in place. I didn't think about it and it was a pain to get the bolts up thru the tiny holes from underneath with very little clearance and visibility.

It looks beautiful once in place. I then downloaded a (free) sound meter app on my iphone and measured the noise levels from 3ft away at three different speeds and got 60dB @ 300 CFM, 64dB @ 600 CFM and 68dB @ 900 CFM - which are not noisy and bothering at all compared to our old one (probably 75-80dB @ 300 CFM as nobody can hear nobody when it was on). I believed that it could be even quieter if we'd enlarge our venting duct from 7" to 8" but not worth the effort for our needs.

Would definitely recommend it.

I love this dishwasher. I live alone as a single gal in a 1 bed 1 bath apartment - and it's perfect. I run it about 2 times a week & it takes care of everything. I tell people it's like having the top rack of a dishwasher only.

Before I bought this I read though a lot of the reviews... and I have a few comments regarding the critical reviews.

1. You don't have to buy anything additional to get this set up. Read the manual, it explains it. In my kitchen the little faucet end thing screwed off - and they provide another one that you screw on. Then the hoses hook up and hold on to that. You can use the sink while the dishwasher is running if you need to - just pause it & then press the red button on the side of the nozzle that hooks up to the sink.

2. It doesn't leak if the hoses are attached tightly. Be sure you screw them on TIGHT. Also, when you're ready to disconnect the dishwasher, be sure to turn the water off, then press that little red button to release the pressure.... or water will go everywhere.

3. After putting some pretty nasty dishes in there, your washer will get gunked up a bit.... but you can clean it out & it will work brand new. The manual explains this. There's this plate type thing underneath the arm and you can remove that - and a little drain trap that you'd need to clean out as well. Then you can either wash with a dishwasher cleaning packet/bottle thing OR you can use baking soda and vinegar. Run it through empty once before trying to wash dishes again. I've found that I need to do this once every 4 months or so.

4. As far as the smell goes, a bit of baking soda at the bottom of the dishwasher goes a long way - just make sure you get it out of there before doing the dishes (ie vinegar & a rinse cycle). Also, keeping the door slightly open when not in use also works. I've never had a smell in mine.

5. When the dishwasher is done it beeps.... but if you wait about 20 seconds (if that) it stops. It will not continue to beep.

6. It does pump all the water out of the hoses - but the hose that brings the water in is not drained once you turn the dishwasher off & disconnect. You'll need to drain the water out before storing.... have a bucket ready. It's not that much water, but it's enough to make a mess on the floor.

I haven't had any trouble with this dishwasher - it's about the greatest thing ever - vs having to do the dishes myself. Larger pots and pans will not really fit.... so you'll still have to do those by hand. There is an artful way to getting some of them in. ;) I store mine in my spare closet on a large rolling cart (bought here). It's perfect. I've had this product for 9 months now.

Having a Frigidaire refrigerator, we decided to go with the Frigidaire WF3CB filter. We used other filters in the past but decided to spend more for a OEM filter, thinking we would get better results. Wanting to drink the purest drinking water, we previously purchased a water distiller. This distiller produces water with a 0 - 1 ppm rating when using a calibrated water tester.
We changed out the old filter, which was a different brand altogether. (Aquafresh) Before that, I tested the water from that filter and the rating was around 135 ppm. A little high but okay for drinking. After replacing the filter with the Frigidaire brand, we ran the water for several minutes until it was primed. We filled about 2 gallon containers before we tested the water. Sadly, the Frigidaire water filter produced water at 225 ppm. Pretty high. We left the filter in the refrigerator, using it for several days, hoping the levels would decrease. They didn’t. Testing the water today, our water tested at 244 ppm. It’s actually getting worse. Here is a list, comparing this with other filtration systems and unfiltered water.

Unfiltered water - 215 ppm
Aqua fresh water filter - 135 ppm
Water distiller - 0 ppm
Brita UltraMax tank water filter 99 ppm
Frigidaire WF3CB - 244 ppm

The Frigidaire, somehow, makes the water PPM worse than tap water. These tests were conducted by me using a calibrated water tester. I checked and rechecked each sample and the results were consistent. So while your water from a Frigidaire water filter may make your water appear cleaner and better tasting, the PPM levels can not be ignored. Do the tests yourself with other water filters. The Frigidaire lacks here and I would purchase with caution.

I've done commercial and residential heating and air since '97 and have installed literally 100s of these, maybe more. Truth be told there is no difference between this and the other powered humidifiers. They all work off the same principle. These are very easy to service and simple to install and are my favorite just because parts are easy to get. The media pads are available all over the web as well as most hardware stores.

As for the other reviews indicating the massive water waste, they are not installing this properly. Any central humidifier (as in mounted to a furnace) needs the control wires to be tied into the heating circuit on the control board. In fact, most newer furnaces if not all of them also have contacts for landing the 110V wires on so that it can only run during a heating cycle (usually marked "HUM"). Set up properly, this unit will not use that much water. Running this humidifier when the furnace is not in a heating cycle (not just the fan running, but actually heating) is a complete waste of power and water- not to mention how much faster you will wear out the pads.

Four months later, the fridge started to make grinding noises nearly 24-7, as well as sounding like an airplane was taking off in our kitchen. We called GE to have a tech come out and look at it.

The next day we received a box from GE that contained parts for the repair. GE did NOT communicate with me that they were doing this. They also failed to inform their OWN technician they were doing so. When he arrived, he was very apologetic, but informed us that he was not going to be able to fix our fridge for another week. GE hadn't allotted him enough time for our fridge repair, which he said would take at least 2 hours. GE only gives their techs 1/2 hour for each service call, unless the tech lets dispatch know in advance that the call is going to take longer. The day of his 1st repair visit he was 1 1/2 hour late. I tried calling GE several times to find out where he was, and no one was able to put me through to their dispatch unit. None of the GE customer service reps seemed willing or able to help me. They just told me to wait and that he would be here soon.

He was also late the next week. This time when I called GE, they told me that they didn't have an appointment scheduled for our fridge until the following day - yet the automated system confirmed our appointment for when the tech told me he would be here.

So, I was waiting around, wondering if the tech was even going to arrive.

He did arrive that day, but he was again late. Please, it is NOT the technicians fault, he has to follow the dispatcher's instructions, and is given very little time to complete jobs, which means he is constantly overbooked and short on time.

He started the repair and accidentally broke the copper refrigerant line. We do not blame the technician, since GE used the cheapest copper they could get their hands on for this fridge. The slightest touch broke it in half. This discouraged us, we expected more from a $3000 American made, high end appliance.

So, the tech had to reschedule again since he had to order the part that he accidentally broke.

He came back the next day, did the repairs, which took nearly 3 1/2 hours, and started the fridge up.

He told me to give it 24 hours to start cooling again. I thought that was odd because it started cooling within 2 1/2 hours of delivery and installation. Well, long story short, it never cooled down. The internal temp of the fridge stayed at 62 degrees.

We called again, and we had to wait another two days for the tech to come out again. The poor tech spent another 3 1/2 hours trying to fix it. The fridge at this point was beyond repair, and he informed us even the GE manufacturing plant would junk it - they wouldn't even scrap it for material.

So we have a broken fridge, were given a case number, and given the name of our case manager. You'd think the case manager would have called us, right away, when she saw the notes and situation.

Wrong. WE had to contact GE to initiate replacing or refunding our money. I have talked to GE over the course of a week about 12 times, and have left message after message for OUR assigned case manager to give me a call. She STILL has not called us back.

Because this fridge is on back order where we live, they wanted to to replace our $3000 fridge with a less expensive model and NOT reimburse us the difference. When I declined, they then offered me a more expensive model, and I asked them if they were going to eat the cost, they said I would have make up the difference. Either way, GE was asking for more money from us on a product that was faulty the minute it left the factory floor - our technician admitted to that fact.

I did, however, manage to get through to one of the reps who I hope will help us through their buy-back process. I am still awaiting confirmation she received our faxes to start the process. I can only hope she comes through.

On top of this, we had MAJOR food loss over the course of 3 weeks, over $500 worth of organic produce and food. GE wasn't going to pay for any of this, we literally had to fight with them to get even a portion of this loss back. We did our best to keep our food cool in a cooler, but most food needs to stay dry as well, which is difficult to manage in a cooler. Produce is particularly vulnerable to wet conditions.

I could literally go on and on about this experience and the lies and runaround that GE IS currently putting us through. Our next step is to write a letter to GE Corporate Headquarters and seek legal counsel if they don't respond to us soon.

I would NOT recommend this product, nor any GE product, to anyone, not even my worst enemies.

I have attached two pictures. One is a before and after of a rust covered rag I used to wipe out all of the standing water and rust in a galvanized metal tray the Electrolux was sitting in. This product is a great purchase for compact refrigerators or larger sized refrigerators too!

Pros:

The amount of eggs that it can hold is great! I opted for the 2 tier (because I have a larger sized family and we go through eggs by the carton in just days!!!) I was able to fit 40 large Grade A eggs within this storage container! I've had refrigerators that had the egg holder in the door and I would always end up with cracked eggs for various reasons. I like this storage container because the eggs are protected on both sides, top and bottom with no way for them to be damaged unless physically removed from the container!

The way the storage container is designed allows for the eggs to drop down on an incline once an egg is removed. It's helpful so you don't have to reach inside the container to get an egg to search for one! Everything is easily accessible and within reach.

Adding onto the design of the container, when placing new eggs in the container, it's easy too! You just pop one in and when adding another just push the previous one back and pop the other egg in its place! No fuss, no mess, no worrying about stacking eggs on top of each other (or opening cartons for that matter).

Cleaning the storage container was a breeze too! The four parts included in the package are very easy to clean and dry. I would imagine if there was a broken egg, it would be very easy to clean and not a hassle in any way. It would be easy to spot any broken eggs since the eggs are on an incline and since the material is clear - you be able to spot a mess right away!

Cons:

I like the fact that the storage container is lightweight, however, when the pieces are unassembled, they did feel a little flimsy. Once put together, it did feel stronger and not as flimsy as when it wasn't assembled.

There wasn't a set of instructions on how to put it together. Initially, I was unsure of which piece was the top or bottom - but I figured it out! There were four pieces in the package so it wasn't a big deal, but some people might prefer to have some type of diagram or instructions on how to put together the storage container.

Overall, despite the slight flimsiness of the product I would definitely recommend this product! It has the ability to hold several dozen eggs without the worry of any damage to them.

Additional Info on Troubleshooting...
Igniter was glowing red and current flowing through it to the gas valve read just shy of 3 amps. Troubleshooting videos will generally lead you towards the igniter if the current flowing to this valve is less than ~3.2 Amps, so I replaced the igniter. We had been out of the country for over two years and had leased out our house.  After we returned to our home and dispensed water from the frig., we could see particles floating in the water.  Gross!  We have a GE built-in frig., and I'm certain that the tenants had never replaced the filter during their stay.  I'm inclined to buy authentic GE filters, but they are ridiculously overpriced.  Amazon to the rescue!  I decided on this filter for its price,its ratings from other purchasers, and because it's Prime eligible.  I replaced it as soon as it arrived, flushed the system as recommended, and then examined a glass of water directly under an overhead floodlight.  No particles.  Taste test was as it should be - it tasted like nothing.  The filter comes with month stickers, so you can apply one to remind you when it was installed.  At this time I can certainly give it four stars.  It's getting its job done.  It's been in place for only a week, so I can't speak as to its longevity.  Time will tell, and I'm hopeful that it will prove itself to be a five star product.  By the way, we were in a country where you wouldn't dare to drink water straight from the faucet.  We would reverse osmosis AND gravity filter our water for drinking, so I do have a concern for the safety of drinking water from a health standpoint.  However, it seems that many people here may be overly concerned - given some of the reviews.  It's just my observation, but the water from our faucet here is far better to begin with than the water in many other parts of the world.  Until such time as we live in a perfect world, we can't expect perfection.  That expectation, alone, can make us sick.

Old (+10 years) condenser fan motor had blown front seal and oil residue was creeping across motor. It also sounded a little rough. This new fan motor was over $50 less than I was seeing on other sites.  Received a very well boxed and protected product. This fan motor is same manufacturer and has the exact same model no. and information label as the old condenser fan motor on my American Standard 'Allegiance 12  2A7C2060A3000AB' air conditioner, except of course the serial number. The mounting holes for the new motor are not threaded, but are smooth. This motor comes with 4 screws that are to be used with the new motor.  Although they are not self-tapping screws, apparently they are of a hardness that will allow the installer to tap/ install them into this motor's housing when mounting/installing. The screws screwed/tapped into this motor just fine using a 1/4" drive ratchet, with reasonable effort.  Has been running like a champ for two weeks now, is quieter than the old +10 year old motor, and seems to push more air. Used a penetrant oil to loosen the existing fan blade (fan blade is reused) and fan blade screw from the old motor's shaft.  Cleaned penetrant oil from removed fan blade, screw, and screw hole using electrical contact cleaner.  Repositioned and installed old fan blade on new motor fan shaft using LocTite thread locker sealant on screw/ screw hole. Used a good quality (Proto) adjustable 8 inch wrench to tighten, as the shaft screw has a square head, as tightly as I dared.

We've purchased other LG electronics and had good experiences and thought that this brand was reliable. Our 4 y/o fridge burned out a wire that blew 2 circuit boards in the ice/water dispenser. We paid $427 to replace both circuit boards before they figured out that the wire was burned & we also needed to replace the entire door for another $360. The repair man suggested that I ask LG to foot the bill for the door. LG service refused consider my request because it was out of warranty (the warranty only is 1 year)so I demanded to speak to a supervisor, It was only at this higher level that I finally got them to consider my request. They made me jump through hoops producing the original sales receipt etc and taking over 3 weeks to respond. LG finally conceded and replaced the door but that was only after I told them that I was going to tell everyone i knew not to purchase their appliances.

During the 3 weeks i was waiting for LG to make up their minds if they would help me or not, I began speaking with my friends about my experience. I found that almost everyone I spoke to who had an LG appliance that was out of warranty had failure of those appliances and had to replace them. It seems that LG is making their products to last through the warranty and then fail. Refrigerator condensers seem to magically fail only months after the warranty expires. I've spoken to people whose driers failed after only 6 months of use, and my friend with a 3 year old LG dishwasher said it sounded like it would die any second and she couldn't find an appliance repair that would service it when they found out it was an LG. It finally died 6 months later and she has replaced it with a GE. Another friend's LG microwave died a month after the 1 year warranty expired.

The lesson here is that although LG appliances will work wonderfully for the first few years you own them, you should expect that soon after your warranty expires you will find that the appliance will fail and you will be footing the bill for costly repairs or replacement. this is not such a big deal if it's a cell phone, but when you are spending $2,200 or more for an appliance you expect it to last longer than 4 years. I now fully expect that the compressor will fail on my refrigerator shortly after it is 7 years old (end of compressor warranty).

Even though LG finally did the right thing and replaced the door, It was only after I demanded to speak to a supervisor and demanded that they do something for me. I will never purchase another LG appliance and I'm warning you about this. Before purchasing LG appliances I suggest you talk to everyone you know and learn their experiences. I'm certain that you will begin discovering that many people have had similar experiences as I & my friends have had with LG.

This was the exact OEM replacement part. The original one had a burned wire which was not clear until I tested with a multimeter and then removed the tape bundling all the wires. If you get the LE error on an LG washer, this cable is one of the common causes. Mine showed signs of water contact but otherwise looked okay.

I didn't think it would be possible for one of the individual wires within the bundle to have gotten damaged. The cable does undergo quite a bit of bending stress as the washer tub shakes, which mine was doing excessively. So the combination of water and overstress must compromise one of the wires enough to cause it to burn through its individual wire casing; the result is an intermittent connection which then fails with movement in the middle of a wash. The break was total, but was not apparent until I removed the tape which bundles multiple wires together. I first tested with a multimeter and noticed one set of pins gave a different value than the others, so then I cut off the tape. I could have tried soldering the one wire back together but it undergoes high stress and this part is cheap.

If I'm wrong about that, I will be sure to amend this rating (if I can't, I'll repost).

**UPDATE**
So, REALLY fine ground coffee fails, too. You need your coffee to be just between REALLY fine ground and coarse ground. At least with the K155, as there's not enough pressure for the water to soak through the REALLY fine grounds and make it into the cup. I have a 14oz. cup. Add some heavy whipping cream and I can use the 6oz. button twice with no flow-over. In this case, I had to use the 6oz. twice and the 8oz. once. And still didn't get a full cup. AND, it was weak. Weak as a day-old kitten. For this reason, I'm knocking off a star from four to three.

Needless to say, make sure you grind your beans to a 200-grit density. That may be the sweet spot. If I figure it out, I'll report back.

This is a wonderful little machine but there are a few issues.
1. Size. It is a great size to sit in the corner of my kitchen. The tub size however is smaller than expected. The listing does not give an accurate description of the actual size of the tub. I mean I understand it is not going to hold a full size load. I can do a few shirts, some underwear, socks and a pair of pants at once but it struggles with a pair of jeans and a sweater.
2. Controls. The controls are not the worst but also not the best. Once you set the load size and then select the load type, the load size resets to medium and you have to go back and set to large again. It's a bit frustrating.
3. Leaks. Yes, this leaks. It leaks at the faucet connection but a little Teflon tape takes care of that. The real leak is at the drain hose. Where is connects to the machine at the bottom more specifically. It does leak a bit there. I keep a Swiffer next to this to mop up the small amount of leak. It's not a large amount, just a few dribbles but its still annoying.
4. Foam Padding. On the inside of the machine, on both sides of the tub there is foam padding to help with the spinning and vibration. They are held in place with these tiny strips of like double sided tape. They do not stick well at all and are all the time sliding down to the bottom of the unit. I have to cram my hand inside, which is painful as its a VERY hard space to reach, pull them back up and restick them. A little bit of better tape will fix this issue.
5. Draining. Every now and again it just will not drain. It's almost like the pump just said "I'm tired right now, try again later". Taking the hose and lowering it into a bucket for a moment then back into the sink usually fixes it. It does not happen often but it does every so often.

Overall this is a great washer. It cleans really well. Just a few things to deal with but for the price I recommend it. I do also recommend getting the extended protection warranty just in case it is needed. It's worth the extra 18 dollars. I have gas heat and have monitored every floor of my home with hygrometers for years and every winter (we live in Virginia) the house would get pretty dry (around 20-25% humidity). A single room humidifier was way too much maintenance for me, so after many years I opted for the Aprilaire 700 whole home humidifier. I’ve been running it about two weeks in my 1971, three-level, 2400 square foot townhouse, and the entire place is now sustaining a lovely 45% humidity, which was exactly the goal.

The instructions actually say to have a professional install the humidifier, but I watched a lot of You Tube instructional videos and since I have a moderate ability with things like this, I did it myself. (If you can put on a slip on SharkBite connector, you can do this). One thing I cannot praise enough is SharkBite connectors, which I used for a secure tap into my cold water line. Their slip on (no solder) copper pipe connectors are amazing.

Also, I'd really consider the NEST as your controller. The Aprilaire 700 (Automatic) came with a fancy controller that has a wired outdoor thermometer that reports outdoor temp to the controller so it can intelligently drop humidity setting when it gets colder to below the condensation level (for your windows). That sounds great and I thought I'd miss not having that feature but unless you live in a region with crazy temp swings (In Virginia, we do not) then you don't need it. The NEST, though it knows the temp outside for your area), does not yet factor that into any intelligent humidity adjustment (though it easily could later if they wanted to push an update). For now the NEST humidity setting is "set it and forget it". If you plan to use the NEST thermostat as your controller, buy the Aprilaire 700m as the “m” (manual) version is about fifty dollars less because it doesn’t include the Aprilaire controller (which would not be used if you were to use the NEST in its place).

The wiring can be tricky and they try hard to prevent homeowners from installing it themselves. I had to dig around online to find documentation from NEST on how to integrate the Aprilaire 700 with their thermostat. I found a NEST Contractor manual online and that showed me the way. It all came together when I realized my Aprilaire 700 needs 24 VAC on its two brown wires (and not a separate relay like I had originally thought). As a reality check, I spent several days reading forums, printing out directions, and running back and forth to Home Depot (including one run to get Aviator Snips to make the hole for the humidifier in the HVAC Supply duct), before doing the install.

If your tap water isn’t too hard or if you don't mind adding a water filter in-line, you may want to consider a steam humidifier. Here are the economics: Flow Through type humidifiers like the Aprilaire 700 (when on) pass 1 gallon every ten minutes (I’ve read that and measured it myself), or 6 gal per hour. If (this is upper bound max) it ran 24/7 for a month, the Aprilaire 700 could use 4,300 gallons in a month. For every 1,000 gallon it costs me approximately $6, so figure the MAX cost at ~$25/month x 4 months =$100 for water. Flow through filters take no maintenance other than annual replacement, so figure that in too. All in all, I expect my costs will be less than Max (as the humidifier does occasionally shut off with humidity set at 40%), and I'm ok with the price point to avoid crazy dry skin. Steam is supposed to be a faster delivery mechanism (and even more efficient), but water line filter costs would likely exceed water cost of the flow through (if you needed to install filtration upstream of the humidifier). Since my water isn’t very mineralized, if I had it to do over again I would try a steam humidifier, but the Aprilaire 700 does the job fine.

Today, I got the place up to 50 percent relative humidity today while we were out and my fiancé could smell a faint odor of chlorine upon our return (In Fairfax, Virginia they heavily shocks the water with chlorine). Dialing back the humidity a little seemed to clear that up. If any chlorine odor returns, my next step may have to be either a humidifier line water filter, or perhaps a whole home water filter. But that has nothing to do with the humidifier and I only mention it for completeness. To close: The Aprilaire 700 (manual version preferred) connected to the NEST thermostat delivers long sought after humidity levels in my home and I only wish I had installed it years ago. Cheers and good luck to you! – Terry H (Fairfax, Va)

The first time I tried to brew a cup of coffee with this, I made a mess on the counter because this filter does not form a good seal the way a paper filter does and the water leaked through and overflowed the cup. It turns out that, since this filter has a little thickness to it, you have to turn the filter holder into the press *extremely tightly* in order to get an ok-ish seal. Incidentally, this also makes it extremely difficult to remove.

It turns out that this filter is essentially useless unless you brew your coffee in the 'inverted method', which means erecting a precarious tower of scalding coffee slurry with the aeropress plunger on the *bottom* of the tower. You then add your coffee beans, fill half-way with hot water, stir for about 45 seconds, top the water off, and then screw the filter apparatus (with a good amount of torque) into the precarious tower of scalding hot coffee slurry. You then have to *invert* the top-heavy tower onto your cup and then depress the plunger - which is easy to do, because the filter is extremely porous.

The end result is much weaker coffee made with a lot more effort than a paper filter takes. I had high hopes for this, but I'll be sticking with paper filters from here on out.

It works.  However, the hose was terribly kinked, which could have been avoided just by packaging it rolled instead of folded.  This created a difficult installation and uncertain drainage.  Also, I wish it could be a closed system instead of an open reservoir.  The short hose coming from my dehumidifier simply lays into the pump's reservoir through a simple oversize hole in the top of the reservoir, then as the pump detects a certain level of water it turns on and pumps the water out through the attached longer hose, which I have running out of a hole in my foundation.  The situation this creates is that if the pump ever fails, my dehumidifier will continue to dump water into the pump's reservoir regardless of whether it is getting pumped out or not, which means it could eventually overflow into my crawl space.  If it were a sealed drainage system, the pump's reservoir would fill up but not overflow, and instead would backup into the inlet hose and push back into the dehumidifier's reservoir eventually causing it to turn off once that reservoir is full.  Having said all that, I am enjoying not having to go into my crawl space twice a day to empty my dehumidifier.  As long as everything keeps working, it's great.  So I'm happy... just a little nervous.

I purposely selected these ovens because I wanted even heat for baking.  After about 1 1/2 years of use, and MANY service calls, I am working with it, and here is how:  When I want to bake anything where even temperature is necessary, I must preheat it for ONE HOUR!  Anything less and the wild fluctuations in temperature around the set temp will interfere with baking.  I had many baking failures before figuring this out with a GE repairman.  When you turn the oven on to 350F, for example, the tone will indicate that it is at that temperature when it is about 290F.  Then it cycles between 290 and about 400, with long periods at temperatures that are not even close (e.g. 310 or 390).  After about an hour the range of temperatures is down to about 20 degrees on either side of the set temperature, which allows for even baking.  I have also added baking stones to the bottom racks, which helps stabilize the heat, but subtracts one rack from baking.  According to the various repairmen I have had look at the thing, ALL of the new ovens from the American makers are made in China and are pretty much the same.  When I have finally had it with this one (and gotten over what we paid for it), I will be researching the German ovens.

The Tee fits in/on 1/2" water line whether copper, PVC, CPVC or PEX.

It's super easy to install, just cut a half inch section out of the water line to make room for the tees extra length and then just push the tee onto one end of the cut water line and then feed the other cut end into the other end of the tee. Make sure to push hard until you feel it move past the first resistance and up against the firm stop on both sides.

The Tee has a ball valve built in that allows you to shut off the water to the fridge without shutting off the water to the whole sink or the whole house and seems to work fine. (note it took some pretty good effort for me to open it after having water pressure on it).

The 1/4" tubing seems like good heavy weight line which should last a long time.

To hook the tubing up you only have to push one end into the 1/4" line of the tee and it's done. As for the refrigerator end there are a couple ways to hook it up.

First being just using the white coupling seen in the picture, it works just like the tee does when inserting it in the 1/2" water line. Just push it onto one end of the tubing then onto the end of the 1/4" line coming out of the refrigerator. (if you have a fitting on the line coming out of the refrigerator you'll have to cut it off first). That is how I did it as the refrigerator didn't have the middle part of the compression fitting attached so I would have had to go buy one.

The second way is to use the compression ferrel (little white ring) and the compression nut on the end of the line. Again this requires the fridge has the compression fitting and the part this kit compresses onto.

But these slip type fittings work very well, I'm not sure exactly how there made and work so good but they do... the kit with the slip type tee and 1/4" line parts make this kit so easy to use... I highly recommend it.

On a side note. My kit didn't come with the red "lock" clips you see in the picture. The bag lists the contents inside and didn't list those pieces either. But it appears it would be very rare that the line would come out without it. I first tried taking out one line after inserting it and it was a bit of a struggle as you have to hold down the little lip that the line pushes into to be able to pull out the line.
