Another thing to note is that there is some additional maintenance with condensation dryers: you have to clean the heat exchange unit every month or so, depending on usage. One night my wife set our GE Dryer Model DHDSR46GG7WW on automatic and went to bed. In the morning, it was still tumbling. I did some internet searches and found all sorts of possible causes of this issue. There could be a build up of lint causing problems with the moisture sensor, a bad gas burner valve, etc. However, the clothes were dry, so I didn't think it was a blocked vent or gas heating issue (besides, I had recently cleaned it out). I decided I needed to test the timer itself. There are YouTube videos to do a "dryer timer test", but they all passed just fine (you measure a few resistance values with an ohmmeter). So to test the timer for sure, I set it to a timed cycle (the non-auto ones) and used "No Heat - Fluff". The time did not advance even in the regular timed mode, so I knew the timer was broken.

Getting to the timer is a cinch - you remove the knob, remove 3 screws from the back of the front panel, tip it forward, lift up a small tab and rotate the old timer counter clockwise and it comes right out. I recommend putting in the new timer (just put it in the same spot and rotate clockwise) before you remove the wires from the old one. Move the wires one at a time from the old to the new so you know where they go.

Just like that, my dryer is fixed and I saved hundreds in costs having to call a repair man or buy a new dryer!

This was purchased to use with my North Trail 21RBSS travel trailer, which is a 22 foot sized trailer. Between uses, it resides inside the small shower stall in the trailer's bathroom.

When it is time to do laundry, I either use the little washer inside the shower, and let the dirty water and rinse water drain into the grey holding tank, OR I set it outside on our little portable camp table. We tend to 'boondock' (dry camp) off the beaten path, so we normally do not have a sewer hookup when we camp.

If we use the washer outside, we drain into a 5 gallon bucket. We always use the same biodegradable, eco-friendly detergent that I use when backpacking. https://www.amazon.com/Sierra-Dawn-Campsuds-Biodegradable-Soap/dp/B000LDMQ7G/ref=sr_1_3?dchild=1&keywords=Sierra+Dawn&qid=1606073320&sr=8-3

The actual amount of detergent used is tiny. With the agitation-action of this washer, very little detergent is needed for clothes cleaning. This not only reduces the amount of biodegradable soap in the water, but it lessens any potential lingering scent for animals to pick up on if the water is disposed of into a dug out hole, away from the campsite. (Yeah, yeah. . For those self-righteous and scientifically illiterate know-it-alls, who want to fit-foam in knee-jerk reaction about dumping that water, please attend a remedial Environmental Sciences 101 class before commenting).

I limit wash loads to 6 pounds of minimally water absorbing clothes, like shorts, socks, t-shirts, etc. For highly water absorbing items, like towels and sweats and long pants, I will eyeball the load so that about half of the wash tub is filled with items to be washed.

Keep in mind that this is for camping-travel use, which means that it is really easy to do washing every two to three days of fewer items, rather than saving up a large pile of dirty clothes over a 5 or 7 day period for a trip to a laundromat. Or go to an RV Park laundromat and wait your turn for a scheduled time slot.

It was simply amazing to see how clean our clothes would get in the short, timed wash cycle. If you watch how vigorous the agitation action is during a wash or rinse cycle, it becomes clear how such a thorough 'clean' is achieved. Within the first minute, the water, for a load of clothes which has no really visible soiling, turns gray then brown in color as dirt and oils are removed.

The first time using this machine, a couple of older t shirts came out far brighter than they had been when I had packed them for camping. Dinginess was gone and they looked closer to their original new colors. The same thing with my lightweight fleece thermal layers, sheets, pillowcases, zipoff pants/shorts, etc.

Here's the only downside, which is manageable and not really a big deal - - - for t shirts, especially, I learned to use the 'Delicate' setting, along with a shorter timed cycle for both washing and rinsing and centrifugal spinning. It keeps the collar area from becoming a bit 'relaxed' from stretching. This is never an issue for other clothing items. I will do all of the t-shirt garments together separately from other clothes for a wash.

We found that we have the best results for most clothes, with the shortest time-frame, by doing a ten minute cycle for washing, followed by a five minute rinse cycle, and then five minutes in the centrifugal spinner compartment. For t-shirts, I will do a 5-5-2 (minutes) cycle using the Delicate settings.

Since I do wash when I am doing other chores, like cooking or trailer cleaning, I can set a cycle timer on the machine and then go about other chores while each cycle does its thing.

The centrifugal spinner section will take sopping wet clothes, and get them to a 'damp-dry' state. Drying time on a line is FAST, especially if it is a bit breezy or sunny outside. If conditions outside do not allow for drying, then I use a retractable clothesline inside the shower stall and open the overheard skylight a bit and turn on the vent fan.
https://www.amazon.com/Little-World-Retractable-Clothesline-Adjustable/dp/B07CV6P1K7/ref=sr_1_8?crid=C05196OQ0G2Y&dchild=1&keywords=rv+clothesline&qid=1606076503&sprefix=rv+clot%2Caps%2C227&sr=8-8

When I need to use the shower, it is a fast and easy task to move this washer unit out of the shower and into the living space, and out of the way.

While I love this little washing machine for RV camping, I can see this also being used by a single person as a regular washer in place of even a 'compact' style residential washing machine IF they are willing to do washing frequently enough to not have a pile of dirty clothing, towels, etc.

For use as a residential washing machine for more than one person or a small family. . Nope, not for me. It would take far too much time, constantly washing clothing due to the volume restriction to a wash load, to make it a real viable option.

My problem with the Samsung RF266 Twin Cooling system is common. Icing of the drain used to transfer water to the evap tray and icing of the defrost air duct to the timer behind the fresh food tray. I took the step of ordering the complete set of sensors and the evap fan access cover and the heater element. This revised drain clip is much larger than the OEM clip and should provide better heat transfer to the drain, but I also added a length of 16 gauge bare copper wire to the heater element, securing it with small gauge copper wire for better contact. I positioned the larger wire down into the catch tray and about an inch into the drain hole. Hopefully this will add more heat to the catch tray to avoid freeze up. If you do anything to the defrost system, make sure the drain duct is clear of ice by using hot water to melt ALL present ice. You will know the duct is clear by water rapidly exiting the catch tray. We recently remodeled a rowhouse built in 1875. During the remodel I insisted we move the washer/dryer out of the low ceiling basement with the leaning steps to the 2nd floor.

I had the choice to redo (and repay my contractor) the ceiling to install more bracing or try a shock pad.

I ordered these based on reviews and insisted my contractor put them under the stacked washer/dryer he installed. He was skeptical but humored the crazy owner lady and slid them under before we tested the washer. And we were both amazed - there is hardly any vibration transfer to either the tile floor or the party wall. I felt a little vibration when it was spinning at the highest speed possible but when I used the next lower spin speed there was nothing. I highly recommend these if you have vibration concerns in an older building.

Note: I’m using these with a 24” stacked Bosch set, which do weigh less than full size units. I think this makes the stacked unit sway a bit more during the start & stop of the spin cycle but I’m going to put pieces of foam between the units and side walls of the niche to help with that.

As others complained about, the water supply hose that comes with the machine does not necessarily connect to your kitchen sink faucet and it certainly does not connect to a standard washing machine supply spigot if you have a laundry room. I had to purchase a normal size washing machine water supply hose from the hardware store for $16.00 but I anticipated this problem from other reviews and it did not bug me.

I would have been more vexed had I not had the standard sized washer hookup in the laundry room. Since I have the standard hook up, all I needed was a water supply hose with two female ends. Had I had to use the kitchen sink there would have been problems since the supplied hose did not fit it even when I removed the kitchen sink faucet aerator. I feel it would have taken me a long time to find a hose or a conversion kit that did connect with the kitchen sink faucet in my rental. Most landlords aren't going to let you change out the faucet in your kitchen sink so that it will fit the hose that comes with the machine. So consider this fact if you don't have a standard hook up for a washing machine and have to use your kitchen sink. The people at the hardware store's plumbing section might have some conversion suggestions so look into that first before buying.

The machine is simple to use and does a wash/rinse/spin cycle twice in 40 minutes. Make sure you get the water drainage hose deep down and otherwise firmly wedged into the drain because if it pops out you will have water everywhere. You turn on the power button, hit the "start/pause" button, and walk away. There is a timer telling you how long until it is done and a chime goes off to tell you it is done. You can also set it to soak and to use less or more water, but I don't use those features.

The machine senses when there is enough water in it to start washing and turns the flow of water into the machine off automatically. The bottom of the machine goes back and forth during the wash cycle. It pumps out the water for both cycles and spins the rest out. I only use a half cap of liquid laundry detergent and that gets everything clean. I can get about five tee shirts, five pairs of underwear and five pairs of sox in a load.

I could three pairs of jeans in along with some other small clothes. I could likely get more in but I am not challenging the device to do what larger ones can as that is not what it is designed for.

If you have a laundry room, hook up the water supply line to the hot water, that is what you get you clothes washed in. Hook it up to the cold water, then that is what you get. The device does not choose between hot and cold water. You do that with your hook up choice. But it is just a matter of unscrewing the supply line and attaching it to the other supply spigot if you want to go back and forth depending upon what you are washing.

Even though there is no agitator arm sticking up from the bottom through the middle like the normal sized machines, it gets everything clean all the same. Some people tell you to get these plastic agitator balls but I don't think they are necessary. There is a trap for wet lint but though I check it each time, I have yet to have to take out the screen and clean it off.

When I ordered it, I was frustrated to learn that it would take three and half weeks to ship to me, but it got to me in about 10 days so I was happy. I received an email when it was delivered so I knew to go home and get it off the porch. I am 55 and not an athlete but I was able to carry it into my house easily without a dolly and set it up as it does not weigh much. It has adjustable pads to stand upon so it won't vibrate when it spins but mine did not need adjusting.

Some people have put in their reviews that there was a little water in the drainage hose when it came out of the box, prompting them to think they got a used and returned device. But I think this is just from testing the device before shipping it to make sure it works and doesn't leak.

I have had it for about two and a half months and I have no complaints other than the anticipated problem with the water supply hose. I don't have an RV but one of these machines would be good for that sort of thing.

Measurements: It is about 27 inches tall by 15 inches side to side and 15 inches back to front. It is an inch or so taller in the back than in the front. The opening to put in the clothes on the top is 12 inches but narrows down to eight inches inside the cannister which is about 12 inches deep (the washing cannister widens out after a slight bottle neck to about ten inches). Once the water gets everything soaked it looks like you could have gotten several more shirts and stuff in, but again, I am not trying to push the machine beyond what it is designed for.

I am happy so far with the product. I don't have a dryer so I hang up all of the clothing to dry in my closet. While the clothing is wet when it comes out, the clothes are not dripping wet. Just very damp.

I took two stars off on my rating for noise level since it is as loud as a normal sized washing machine (which is not a big deal to me but it might be useful information to others). I also took off one star for ease of use because of the initial anticipated problem with the water supply hose. But once you have that taken care of, it is extremely simple to use.

You're no doubt thinking what I was: $20-something for the same part the appliance part websites are selling for $40+? Sounds great, right? Well, kind of. Read on...

First off, the part I received was in my opinion not an actual Whirlpool OEM part despite language in the description implying it would be an OEM part. The labeling on the part I received was minimal and no Whirlpool official logos or text was present on the label, which is different from other appliance parts I've ordered that I know were genuine OEM parts.

Second, we have an old (circa 1997) Maytag dishwasher (model DWU7602AAE) with the hard plastic lip around the outside of the door perimeter where the door meets the gasket. As other reviewers here have mentioned, older machines having such a lip on the door can be problematic with this gasket because the gasket it too think/bulky and renders the door impossible to close (will not latch, even when slammed shut).

Some tips if you have the same door style:

(1) Start by marking the midpoint of gasket by folding it in half and drawing a line at the fold (midpoint) using a permanent marker. Let the marker ink dry for a couple of minutes before moving on to step 2.

(2) Before trying to install, soak the gasket in hot water for 10 minutes or so. This will make it more pliable.

(3) Now install the gasket by placing the marked midpoint underneath the door latch and pushing the gasket into the groove starting at the midpoint and heading around and down each side toward the bottom. IMPORTANT: **stretch the gasket** as you push it into place! This is key to getting the door to close when you are done.

(4) The gasket is several inches too long even if you didn't stretch it, and definitely because you *do* need to stretch it as you push into into the groove. Plan to trim off several inches from each end, but do this only after you've installed the gasket within a half inch or so of the door bottom so that you can be sure how much to cut. I cut off in increments until the gasket just barely reached the bottom of the groove, just touching the base of the door opening on each side.

(5) With the gasket installed, try to close the door. I found the door would latch, but only by pushing it very, very firmly. It's also difficult to release the latch to open the door. I am hoping this difficulty eases a bit over time as the door is opened and closed and, presumably, compresses the gasket somewhat.

In the end, the new gasket did fix the leaks we were having, and I hope the steps above are helpful.

Our 10-year-old GE Profile fridge ran beautifully until a few days ago, when outside temps soared to the 90s (high humidity as well). The dreaded CA-CLICK...CA-CLICK...CA-CLICK started one evening and continued intermittently over the next 48 hours -- it seems to be triggered when the heat/humidity rises. As mentioned by other reviewers, the clicking comes from a relay on the main board. With each click, the interior lights go dim and a low whirring sound seems to emanate from a fan (inside the fridge?) as it tries to spin up.

Called GE at (800) 749 6629 and was quoted a discounted price of $60 + shipping for this circuit board. The phone agent was very helpful and explained that the board was indeed subject to a recall and was replaced free of charge for the first five (or so) years after date of manufacture. She went on to say that board failure after 10 years is "expected" and therefore GE won't replace it for free at this point. It's disappointing that manufacturers nowadays expect key components in their high-end or even mid-range appliances to fail within ten years, but I guess that's just business.

Anyway, we were happier paying the discounted price instead of the much higher price offered here on Amazon.

A RO system will run you about $0.02 per gallon and isn't hard to install yourself, consider that route early and save a lot of money over the long run.

Beware of mid life filter failure! Note your flow rate when the filter is new. if the flow significantly increases during the life of the filter (eg sprays out of fridge at much strong pressure) then the filter may have failed internally and is just bypassing your tap water. Had a roller go bad in my dryer so ordered the complete set of these November 2, 2019.

First run after the install they were nosier than the stock units they replaced but acceptable.

It gets progressively worse and then April 2020 it starts rattling and squealing so bad it's unusable.

Takes some time to chase down a replacement that I can get quickly.

Needless to say I spent for one OEM wheel $15.00 more than this complete set.

When replacing the wheel the difference in quality was brutally obvious.

The tolerances between the axle and hub on the wheel with this set no where near tight enough. They are loose and sloppy. The OEM feels tight and solid.

After pulling the bad wheel out I inspected it and as you can see in the pic the chrome coating is worn off so you have metal on metal hence the squealing.

I pulled the other three apart and they showed since of the same wear but not as bad, still usable but it is only a matter of time until they fail. I give them maybe another 2 months at best.

The problem it seems, and all 4 replacements showed this, is the such sloppy tolerances allow grit to work it;s way between the axle and wheel hub where it accumulates and starts grinding down the axle.

I would avoid this set, spend more the first time because in the long run these will cost you more if you have to replace them every 6 months.

This kit did a fantastic job cleaning a corrugated 8' dryer vent hose which has several sharp bends.  It had many years of accumulated lint stuck inside the undulations in the walls of the vent. My shop vac hose is a standard 1.5" diameter and the hole in the suction cap is way too large to be usable.  If I had known this I would have just purchased the much cheaper similar kit with just the brush head and rods for half the price.  The rotating brush moved back and forth will pull the lint out of the vent without using a vacuum as I thought it would need. I found this filter and was a bit nervous after reading the reviews.  But, given the alternative, even if it only works for one season, I'm ahead of the game. We are on the second week now, and the filter does not show any signs of getting choked, it is still quite clean, no sign of lime or calcification.  I took the filter out and cleaned it anyway.  The manufacturer recommends cold water and dish soap for light calcification, vinegar of moderate, and muriatic acid for heavy.  I bought some muriatic acid just in the event it is needed.  I was so impressed by this filter, I purchased a second as a backup.  My plan, swap filters every two weeks, clean and store the cleaned filter and treat them the same as the disposable filters, change every two weeks and keep going.

Like others I have seen here, we have a garage refrigerator that we bought used off Facebook marketplace.  One day the freezer side started only cooling on the bottom, and the stuff at the top of the freezer side started to warm up.  Initially I went to repairclinic.com to lookup what parts fit in that and common problems with the unit. It was suggested to test the evaporator coil fan, which is just an electric fan that pulls the cold air from the cold coils up to the top of the refrigerator.  I took a digital multi-meter and tested continuity across the motor of the fan and no-beep meant it was bad.  When I tried to go to normal part suppliers all these parts were expensive like $90 etc.  Amazon and this particular company to the rescue, I was able to get an evaporator fan for $18 and a defrost heater for $15.  A post had recommended checking the board being reviewed here for burn marks near resistors. Another user had said that when the fans burn out in these units, they take the resistors with them.  They were right.  Buying a refurbished board from this company turned out to be the final piece in my puzzle. The refrigerator is now functioning perfectly.

This is a review of the Vegavo brand compatible filter for the Winix C535 air purifier. I received a free filter for evaluation as part of the Vine program, however this did not influence my review.

The box contains one replacement HEPA filter along with 4 activated charcoal prefilters (each bagged separately) along with an instruction sheet. The replacement filter is quite similar to the OEM filter. They both use high quality filter material that's supposed to remove particulate matter down to 0.3 microns in size. It was simple to open the unit, remove the prefilter screen, then the charcoal filter and finally the main filter. I installed them in reverse order: first the new replacement HEPA filter, then a new activated charcoal filter and finally I clicked the prefilter screen back into place. Don't forget to reset the filter replacement indicator (I used a safety pin to depress the recessed button for 5+ seconds). After powering on the air purifier, it operates normally once again.

Pros: similar quality HEPA filter to the original (MERV 17 rating), less expensive than the manufacturer's replacement filter
Cons: activated charcoal filters are thinner than original

Depending upon your usage, the HEPA filter may need to be replaced sooner or less often than the 6-12 month recommended lifetime (I leave my unit running on "auto" all the time). The only noticeable difference between this filter and the original is that the activated charcoal prefilter is a bit thinner. Now that the new filter is in use, I'm glad to be able to breathe easier once again.

The Samsung microwave this handle was used on has a pretty bad design flaw. A lot of stress is put on the anchor points (where the screws screw into the handle) when the door is being opened and closed. The anchor points are strong plastic but they appear to be surrounded by weaker plastic so, over time, they will break out from the handle. If you buy these things from Samsung they can be pretty expensive. This was a cheap solution and fits perfectly, as well as being a good match for the original handle.

One word of caution when installing this. Be careful not to over-tighten the screws as you risk breaking the anchor points from the handle. As soon as it is flush with the door and there is no movement stop tightening. If not, you'll hear the surrounding plastic start to splinter and crack. That's the anchor points breaking out of the surrounding plastic in the handle.

YOU WILL HEAR A GUSH OF WATER RUNNING THROUGH THE FILTER UNLESS THE WATER SUPPLY IS TURNED OFF!  If you do not hear this, the filter is not installed properly. Beware, you might not be getting the product you expect. For years, GE sold the MWF filter. Now they offer two similar-sounding products, the MWF filter and the MWFA filter. Even though I have purchased the MWF filter from Amazon since 2010, this time they shipped me model MWFA (I ordered the MWF "three-pack" from a related product page). There is a very significant difference. See the manufacturer's link (shown in the photograph). The old MWF filter is being sold as "Pharmaceutical Filtration" while the new MWFA filter is being sold as "Standard Filtration." The implication is that the only difference is the MWF filter also reduces certain listed pharmaceutical compounds, while the MWFA filter removes everything that the MWF does except for the pharmaceutical compounds. This is NOT the case. The MWF filters that Amazon shipped to me did little or nothing to improve the taste of my water. I was not convinced that I could actually get the old MWF filter from this website, so I went to Home Depot and found the old MWF filter (sold as the "Pharmaceutical Filtration" model) at a price higher than from Amazon. I installed the MWF filter and once again my system supplied water with good taste.

If you want the best tasting water, and likely the highest contamination removal, be sure to use the MWF "Pharmaceutical Filtration" model and avoid the MWFA filter. Unfortunately, I don't know if the MWF filter is available from Amazon, and which filter will be shipped if you order from this product page). If Amazon ships you the MWFA filter and you've ordered the MWF filter, be sure to return it for a refund within 30 days.

Unfortunately, GE jacked up the price of the MWF significantly, so if you've used the MWF filter in the past, expect to pay a lot more for it now.

If you recently ordered this product from this link, let us all know (by commenting to this review) if you got the MWF or the MWFA, as this will be helpful to others. Thanks.

I wanted to give instructions on how to deal with the dreaded "E4" drain flow error. I have had to troubleshoot this a few times and each time, I learn something new. When one encounters this, it happens at the end of the rinse cycle. The dishes will be clean but they won't be dry. You may find water at the bottom of the dishwasher.

Steps
1. Siphon the water out. This is useful to have. https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B06XKGYJHR/
2. There are a series of filters that you will need to remove. There is a diagram of these things here. https://www.manualslib.com/manual/1461560/Edgestar-Dwp62bl.html?page=20#manual Make sure you clean them really well.
3. Underneath the metal filter, there is a plastic piece on the left that you can unscrew with a Phillips head screw driver. Behind that is a propeller. Spin it with your finger and make sure it is still moving. This is where the water comes into the dishwasher. On the right side is another piece that is removable. It snaps in and protects the area near the drain hose that removes the water. Make sure those are clean and there is no debris in it. (There shouldn't be.)
4. Make sure the drain hose is not kinked. Check behind it, and wherever the hose goes. When you push the dishwasher back into it's normal position, you may inadvertently kink it. So check that again.
5. If it still doesn't work, either you have not unleashed the clog or there may be water in the unit. Water will often be in a reservoir inside of the dishwasher just before the propeller. There are two ways to get it restarted. a) wait for it to evaporate out which could take days or tip it over and drain it out, which is cumbersome.

Note to manufacturer. You should have something in the software that will allow people the opportunity to recover from an E4 error. A button sequence that says, please reset and drain whatever remaining water is in the cavity. It would be a lot easier than tipping it over to drain the water.

I have an LG model WM3170CW and 6501KW2002A is the correct part number for this. So ignore any comments from vendors that it is not the correct part. My washer stopped rotating, but moved, so not the motor. There are several YouTube videos that showed the exact same problem I was having and how to fix it. Replace this part. I disassembled the washer to remove the part to confirm the part number. It arrived with 36 hours. BUT the rubber seal / cover that protects the circuit board was broken. No way could the seal break and yet the rigged plastic housing be intact. Came sealed in the package. (I should have taken a photo). So the manufacture knowingly shipped it this way. Since this was only the cover I decided to install it anyway to see it the board itself was OK. The disassembly / reassembly only takes 15 minutes in all, and a better test than relying on using a multi-meter (also covered on YouTube). And it was fine. Since this component does not move, and is not exposed in any way, I do not see a real problem the defect. But be warned if you use this vendor that they will ship defective parts. Also judging by the number of people on Amazon alone who have rated this part from several vendors this does seem to be a vulnerability in the reliability of these washers. Not uncommon it today’s world that sensors (instrumentation) are the weak link. My last 2 washers each last 16 years before failing. This managed only 8.

Overall Score: 4.5/5.0 Stars

Pros:
*Removes ~90% of water from clothes: Nylons, polyesters, and mixed blends come out almost bone-dry. Cottons, towels, and jeans still feel damp but air dry in only a few hours.
*Whisper quiet: unit is extremely quiet when operating. I stood right next to it when taking the video and my microphone couldn't even pic up the noise :)
*Minimal vibration/walking of unit: Rubber/silicone tri-legs eliminates vibrations and walking/shaking of unit. I live on the 3rd floor of my apartment and never had any angry neighbors come after me. Roommate didn't even know when I was running it.

Cons:
*Leaks even when not spinning due to gravity: As soon as you place wet clothes in the dryer, water will start leaking from the outlet even before the unit is turned on or a bucket is placed below it. Would have been nice to see a better design to prevent accidental floods and potential floor damage
*No timer: Would have liked to see a timer (clothes dry anywhere from 1-5 minutes. Had to set a timer on my iphone to remind myself. Forgot once)
*No on/off switch: As soon as you close the lid, the unit begins spinning and will remain spinning until lid is opened or unplugged from wall. Potential safety hazard if you forget.
*Unclear operations for stopping spin: Not sure how long the brake will last for, but only way to stop unit is to open lid (while its spinning) to engage the emergency brake or unplug from wall and allow to free-spin. Instructions were unclear on this and it is not intuitive
*No pump: Would have liked to see a pump or internal storage reservoir for water that is spun out. Spigot design is inconvenient to empty without making a mess on the floor, as there is a small air draft created when the unit is spinning, which sends small droplets of water flying everywhere

Overall: Clothes get more dry than a traditional spin cycle on a classical washer, but as newer HE washers and front loaders are reaching RPM speeds of 700-1200 RPM, the differences will begin to become unnoticeable. At the current price tag of around $120, it can compliment a classical washer or a twin tub/single tub washer to aid in reducing drying times (which will save money in energy costs for your dryer), but if you have a newer modern washer (topload or front load) with a spin of 700+ RPM, you will notice minimal differences in drying amounts.

I was one of the unfortunate ones that purchased a Kenmore refrigerator model 11173039910 two years ago.
I had the infamous "bottom freezer cold refrigerator warm" symptom. Repair man was called and he diagnosed that the refrigerator temp sensor had went bad. $350 later still no refrigerator. I decided to take matters into my own hands and being no appliance repair person I started an extensive search on line for info. I found one of the most common faults was the evaporator fan failure ( fan assy. part # 30120-0031900-00 fan motor part # 60159-0013600-00 ). This is the fan that blows cold air from the freezer to the refrigerator compartment. Supposedly the fan fails do to a drip or drips' of water at some time?!?!?, entering the fan and freezing causing resistance on the fan which intern starts a nasty growling sound and eventually burns out the fan. Of course the OE fan / motor (mentioned above) are on nationwide backorder with lead times of a possible year before you will be able to get one.....mind you for a 2 YEAR OLD refrigerator!!! I was NOT going to except that!!!! I found on a appliance repair blog that this motor 50240401000 / BCD-330WTV can be used in place of the 4W 12V OE Daewoo motor. It looks different but fits fine in the plastic support holder as long as you double wrap the wire around the wire holder slot to prevent the motor from turning back and forth. You also have to change the series of wires. The OE plug is wired Red (hot)(left), Yellow (signal)(center), Black (ground)(right). The BCD-330WTV comes wired Red (hot)(left), Black (ground)(center), Purple (signal)(right). So you have to move and cross the ground and the signal wires around. I installed mine 3 days ago and it's working absolutely fine. Freezer temp at 0 degrees fridge at 34 degrees. I will post an update on this after a few weeks/months to see if the reliability/dependability is there but from what I have read they seem to be lasting. Hope this helps save someone some time, aggravation and money!

Just like every other review for these suspension rods, our Whirlpool Cabrio HE washer had been going on the fritz after a few years of decent service. It started out that only a few loads would result in the UL (unbalanced load) error message, and this was usually when washing towels or comforters or other bulky items, so we assumed it was our fault. As time progressed (I'd say over a few months), this problem got worse and worse until every single load we put into the washer resulted in the UL error message.

We were pretty desperate at this point and started looking online and read on a few forums that the suspension rods on these types of washes sometimes get worn out and this could be the problem. We were fairly skeptical about this at first, but the price was certainly right to give it the old college try.

Installation was pretty easy. It helps if you have narrow arms and a friend to help lift the basket up to remove the old suspension rods and install the new ones. These rods use plastic bushings instead of grease, which supposedly helps them last longer than the old ones, and the bushings were at the very bottom of the narrow box they arrived in, so be sure to check the box before throwing it away! Be sure to clean all the grease off of where the old suspension rods sat. I hate to pay $35 for an original Samsung filter. So I was very excited to find "compatible" filter for only $10. However we all know the saying "You get what you pay for". There must be a reason for the huge difference in price. Hence I did some research and found out there are 2 standards: NSF 42 and NSF 53 certified.

NSF 42 certified means it is only for aesthetic purpose (i.e. reduce odor, improve taste).

NSF 53 certified will reduce health related contaminants (i.e. heavy metals like lead, mercury, arsenic). For the health of my family, I would gladly pay for the latter. Given that we only replace the filter every 6 months....we're talking about a $50 savings /year. This is one area I won't compromise on. Hence I would recommend everyone to avoid such budget filter and get one that is more effective.

The good: Start-up takes only 1 minute, then it kicks out a batch of 9 ice "cubes" every 7-8 minutes.
The bad: There is no refrigeration to keep the ice cold; unless you are going to use it immediately, the ice needs to be transferred to your freezer frequently (at least once an hour). The "cubes" (actually more a a fat thimble or bullet shape) are wet and freeze together in the freezer--similar to ice you buy in bags at the store. If you don't empty the ice bin, it will fill up in about an hour and the machine will shut down until you remove some ice, or until enough melts (and drains back into the machine's water reservoir) to lower the ice level below the sensor.
The ugly: after a couple of months of using it every couple of weeks (using distilled water), it would give a false "add water" indication and quit working (ice-making chamber fills with water, then low water light comes on and it dumps the water and shuts down). A combination of repeatedly cycling power and thumping the unit (to dislodge a stuck float?) gets it running for a while, but it seems to take more restart attempts each time I use it. From reading reviews from other sources, this appears to be a common failure.

This product is top notch and resolved the issue I was having with my refrigerator, which was a bit different from the issues in other reviews...  My refrigerator was achieving the proper temperature, but my freezer was maintaining -9 degrees when set to 0.  The unit was also running almost constantly except when it would go into the defrost mode.  After some trial and error, I theorized that the damper assembly door was not opening and that the fridge was able to achieve 37 degrees by the fan inside the broken damper running continuously along with the fridge.  This allowed the fridge to bring over just enough cool air from the freezer to achieve 37 degrees, while never making it "over the hump" and permitting it to shut off (thus the constant running and freezer temp of -9).  After installing this new damper assembly, the refrigerator is maintaining the exact set temperature in both the refrigerator and the freezer +/- one degree.  My main reason for posting this review is to let people know that this damper assembly can solve many, if not all problems relating to air flow between the refrigerator and freezer section of these GE side by side refrigerators.  It's use is not limited to solving only the "fridge too cold/freezing fresh food issue".  My refrigerator model is GSS23WSTASS.

One nice feature was the water tray on the top. My kitchen faucet has the built in sprayer, so hooking up the hose to the faucet isn’t an option. ORIGINAL REVIEW:

I thought about buying one of these for a long time, and would periodically check for new reviews and watch the price fluctuate quite a bit. Finally I looked at the site one day and the price was as low as I'd ever seen it, so I pulled the trigger. The manufacturer boxes these units up quite well, and mine arrived without any damage. It was easy to prepare the unit for use; there is a metal quick-connect fitting which replaces the aerator tip in a standard kitchen or bathroom faucet, and the hose set clips onto this. Some reviews mention using Teflon tape on the hose fittings on the back of the unit to prevent leaks, but I did not find this to be necessary. The oddball-dimensioned cabinetry in my kitchen precludes countertop use, so I have the unit on a cart. I attached a piece of 2X2 lumber with a coat hook on it to the cart to hang the hoses on when the machine is not in use.

I use Oxi-Clean powder (only a small amount is needed per cycle) and a rinse aid product, as directed by the manufacturer. The standard cycle which the unit defaults to works fine, as do the shorter ones intended for glassware and lightly soiled dishes. The noise level is fairly low, other than when the wastewater is being pumped out into the sink, and the shrill beeping when the cycle is finished. For the most part, items placed in the dishwasher emerge clean, spotless, and fairly dry, notwithstanding the fact that the unit does not have actual drying capability. (I assume the rinse aid is helping here.) Very small glasses can be "missed" by the sprayer arm if placed in a corner.

The two shelves above the glassware section can be unclipped and moved up or down, or taken out entirely, or be placed across the base of the rack as supplemental support to prevent items from falling through (there is almost no clearance between the bottom of the rack and the spray arm, so you have to guard against it being balked). The cutlery basket is made of two sections which can be separated, and there is also a removable grid across the top which is probably better suited for chopsticks than it is for forks, spoons and knives. I am using only one section of the basket, without the grid, and have it placed closer to the center of the unit; this works well, and has the added benefit of seeming to enable the detergent dispenser to function more reliably. (I had a couple of instances in the beginning when the dispenser door opened, but the detergent only seemed to get wet enough to clump up and remain in the dispenser.)

My only mild reservations about the unit are based on its size, and lack of tweakability. I assume that the manufacturer felt constrained to limit the overall height of the unit to make it fit underneath wall cabinets in a standard kitchen, but If it had even as little as one additional inch of interior height, its useability would be enhanced substantially -- full size dinner plates could be accommodated easily, and items like baking pans and cutting boards cut fit upright. The unit's dish rack has one small removable section, but is otherwise unadjustable. The instruction manual has a photo of a full set of presumably munchkin-sized plates and bowls neatly loaded into the dishwasher, but most of the items in my kitchen -- e.g., my clunky Crate&Barrel "cafeware" plates and bowls -- are too large and too thick to fit into the narrow spaces between the tines of the rack. A reviewer here recommended using Correlle square salad plates, and I can concur that these do work well. I am still trying to find bowls that can fit properly into the bowl rack.

I have purchased several varieties of capsule lids from this company. I’ve been using their solid aluminum lids for over a year with great success. Initially I was skeptical about this new silicone lid. I’m happy to say it has replaced the aluminum lid as my all-time favorite. I find the perforated holes around the perimeter are slightly larger thereby allowing a stronger flow of coffee to pass through. Also, the silicone lids, because of their flexible nature, are easier to clean. And lighter in weight which creates less stress on your machine. The most important things to know:
1. Choose a quality coffee that is ground just slightly coarser than espresso so it doesn’t clog.. Alternatively, I prefer using 3 scoops espresso grounds covered with a scoop of slightly coarser ground coffee. This makes a stronger flavor cup of coffee without clogging the perforated lid holes.

2. Fill the capsule leaving just enough room for the cap to be comfortably pressed into place. Overfilling will stress the machine. Under filling will make weak coffee. Tamp very lightly, then press silicone lid into place. Be sure it sits properly without a void felt between the lid and the coffee grounds.

3. Experiment with different capsules. Each variety has a different printed code that programs parameters such as intensity, temperature, spin rate, etc. I find the best coffee is made using empty Nespresso chocolate fudge capsules. Awesome crema!

Each empty capsule should last about 50-100 cups before the printed code wears off.

Have fun exploring and experimenting!

This is a very nice Bearing/ Seal replacement kit. It fit perfectly and has lasted well. I have read some other reviews that state these are junk, they are not. You have to be careful how you install these or any bearings. You cannot install these bearings by hitting on the inner ring of the bearing, it will instantly ruin them and shorten the life span. I put my bearings in the freezer for 5 hours to shrink them before installation . Then I used the old Bearings on top of the new bearings and hammered on the old Bearing as the driver until new one was seated. The seal has a joining seam where is connected that you will need to install on top of the drum , this is due to the fact that this is the weakest point of the seal and water does not sit on the top of the Drum. These Bearings are rated Washer Duty and are better than OEM as they have rubber seals as opposed to the steel seals that will rust when water comes into contact with them and let the Grease out. Admittedly another failure will occur but you will definitely get longer life out of these. I had 15 years out of the original so I expect as much from this set. This is a great dryer if you have only one or two people, and have limited space to set up a washer and dryer. I bought this to complement the Black and Decker mini-washing machine I had recently purchased. This is a very easy machine to set up, Requires little space or technical expertise to set it up and, once it's running, it dries clothes as fast as a full-sized dryer, just not as many at once. It is really quiet, and the filter is easy to clean after every load.  For me, a one person household, it works great, and saves me a ton of money and time versus going to the laundromat. I didn't have the space to set up a full-sized set, so I opted for the compact washer and dryer, and it has turned out to be just the ticket to suit my needs. Now, it is so much more convenient, because I don't have to take the time out of my schedule to load everything up and head to the laundromat and to have to sit there for almost an hour, between washing and drying, This will dry a full load of clothes in about 30 to 35 minutes. As I said, it's great for one person, or maybe two, as it only handles a smaller load, but the functionality and convenience more than offset the limited capacity, and it will pay for itself, in time and hard money savings, in less than a year. It is very quiet, for a smaller machine, I thought it would be somewhat noisier, but it's actually more quiet than the full-sized dryer I used to have. I have it only vented inside, yet it doesn't seem to put out much lint beyond the filter, and hardly affects my temperature or humidity in the house at all. I did opt for the secondary filter to add additional filtration on the exhaust, but haven't gotten around to installing that yet. If you have limited space to set up a laundry system, I would definitely consider one of these. I put up a shelf in my bathroom and put it on that, and it works fine; it's out of the way, at a comfortable height for me to be able to get things in and out, and it's located right over my washer, so it's a nice compact laundry system, perfect for one or two people with only limited space to install a machine. Very satisfied with my purchase.

I hope this review helps anyone with this model dryer who is unsure regarding the fit. NOTE: while labelled as a WASHER Door Switch Kit, the Whirlpool instructions state the actuator WON'T work on washers, and to reuse the old one. If you have a washer and the actuator is broker, check out the part number needed for that.

I've had this item for about a year now. I have no regrets buying it and it has certainly helped relieve the stress of one of my most hated chores.

Size: It is big enough for a few days of my dishes and my small dog bowls. It is also big enough for the majority of my pots. I have Ikea dishes and the large dishes are definitely a tight fit, but they do fit.

Noise: I think this thing is very quiet. I usually put it on before bed, and I live in a studio apartment. It can sound like a very light rain. It does beep to indicate the drying cycle has started, but not when the full run is done.

Cleaning: at first I was thrilled with the quality of the wash cycle. Everything came out exceptionally clean. Having it for a year now though I've experienced a handful of cleaning cycles that have done a poor job. This could be user error as I think it happens more when the dishes are oily rather than having 'stuck on' food. It can feel like the dishes are washed in oily water. When that happens I can't just run the washer again (if I do the dishes come out in the same state). I have to hand clean the items to get any film of oil or dried soap off of them before putting them in the cycle again. When I do that, the dishes come out clean the next cycle. Occasionally it seems like the soap doesn't get all the way out of the soap section either. I'll rerun the dishwasher when that happens and the second cycle in that situation has always worked. They aren't super common but it has happened a handful of times over the year.

Drying: the first drying cycle dried these dishes incredibly well. That being said it's now more often than not that the dishes are still very wet when the cycle is done. I think this happens when I don't open the dishwasher soon after it is done. If I leave clean dishes closed in there for a day the dishes will usually come out soaked. As I mentioned earlier, the machine beeps when the drying cycle has started but not when the entire cycle is complete, so I have to be a bit more vigilant of watching when the cycle is done to open the door and not let the moisture sit in there.

This machine isn't perfect, but considering where I was at with dirty dishes before I bought this the overall quality still makes this one of the best pricey purchases I've made for my own quality of life. I think the full size dishwashers Ive used in the past can have similar problems as I listed above, so I think it is more of a dishwashers aren't perfect situation. Overall, definitely recommend.

Many reviewers have been complaining about not being able to recycle used K-cups.  They can be easily recycled!  Here is how: First slip the tip of a table knife under the foil seal on the K-cup and lift up until the seal tears.  Then lift off the foil seal with your fingers and discard.  Take the ground filled K-cup over to a waste can and tap out most of the coffee grounds.  Pull out the paper filter inside the K-cup and discard.  Rinse the remaining grounds out of the plastic cup and you have an easily recycled K-cup.  No more clogging landfills!

As our freezer ice maker could not keep up with demand for my family, we started looking at small ice makers. Amazon offers so many but they all kind of look the same until you read each review and look elsewhere for more details.

The DELLA is awesome! Ours arrived well packaged and protected. Took it out of the box and let it sit for the hour it suggests in the manual. After cleaning the inside and items as suggested, we began making ice. It's fast and consistent during this process. You can set two sizes and I suppose if you used one of those water bottles, the small would be great for this. For us, the large was the way to go.

After tossing the first cubs made just to avoid the plastic taste, we just let it run all day long. For us we learned it drops new cubes about every 7-8 minutes like clock work. The only issue we have found is that the cubes are a little wet and if you juts tossed them in the freezer, they will clump together. A simple fix for this, we place new cubes on a cookie sheet in the freezer and wait for the next batch before dropping them into our ice bucket. This seems to work out well for us.

Yes, it's a little more work but worth it as this little gizmo makes ice like crazy unlike our freezer ice maker. They are wet I assume by the process and speed it makes ice. Our freezer ice maker does the same thing just quite as bad as it's in the freezer. If you leave the cubs in the bin until the process stops on it's own... You may have a big chunk of ice instead of cubes. With this in mind, we let it drop 4 or 5 times and then pull them to cookie sheet.

The cubes are just right for us made in a good size for glasses with a round shape with a hole in the top of each one. Oddly, this shape and size appears to melt slower in the glass. Much easier to grab and get into the glass without dropping any on the floor.

All in all and for the price, we feel this was a great buy and is proving to be a great ice maker. A couple of small adjustments to habit and we see this being a trusty ice maker that will help us get through the summer months here in Arizona without ever buying bag of ice.

OK so the Whirlpool Washer wouldn't drain the water.  There are basically 2 "blink" codes.  One means something like "there might be an electronics failure" that is 8 blinks and the 9 blink one means "I couldn't drain".  In the manual, if you get either the solution is "Call for help!".  hah.  Anyway, from what I can gather, there could be a variety of things than can lead to the washer not being able to drain the water effectively.  At a certain point, it may recognize (via a sensor) that it is failing and it just gives up.  Step one is to use a shop vac on the drain pipe and pull the water out that way.  Forget trying to open up a front load washer full of water and trying to catch it!  You may be shocked how much water is actually in there.  After you've got all that out, check the trap first - mine was FULL of dang corroding bobby pins.  I figured that was the problem but it wasn't.  The problem was the impeller shaft was badly bent and the impeller itself was rubbing into the housing.  I couldn't tell this from sticking my finger in and rotating the impeller.  It seemed to be moving the way you would expect with partial turn snaps.  It wasn't until I took the whole assembly apart and inspected the motor that I realized it was damaged.  Even then I didn't know if it was THE problem, just A problem.  I ordered this motor, swapped it, and everything has been working great since.  This motor is powerful and quiet.  A note on the electrical connections - there weren't good instructions.  This motor is an Alternating Current (AC) motor so the polarity does not matter.  So it doesn't matter which of the supplied wires you connect to the wires inside the washer.  It wasn't intuitive how to actually jam the leads in but I figured it out I guess.  I didn't want extra slack from the wires rubbing against anything so I sort of wrapped them up and covered them in pipe insulation.  I also added a piece of pipe insulation around the tube for the water sensor.  One of the things I've learned about this Washing Machine (a failure 6 years ago and reading testimonials) is that the wires and the tube for the sensor can rub up against things if they come loose and over time they can be worn down to failure.  If you are having a control issue (intermittent control panel etc) that could be the culprit.  So check the wires for signs that the insulation is being worn.

Wash comes out so clean and fresh smelling--no laundry additives needed. Spin-dryer works exceptionally well to extract excess water. Hang to finish drying, or toss in a dryer. There was a learning curve in the beginning, but nothing drastic: In no particular order:
👁 If you are not planning to semi-permanently hook up the washer, then you don't need any new hardware, and you do not
need to add any hosing to the machine unless you want to. I prefer to add water using my handheld shower attachment,
so I did not use the separate hose included with the new machine.
👁 Only 1 teaspoonful of liquid laundry detergent per load. I used a half capful and ended up having to rinse and rinse and rinse.....
👁 There will be LINT.
👀 There will be lint in the wash water from the drain hose, so cover the end of the hose with some net-type cloth. I used a
lingerie washing bag as lint trapper.
👀 There will be lint on your clothes. The machine cleans like a powerhouse but is not very efficient at filtering out loose
fibers. Strongly suggest that you do NOT mix lights and darks. If there is lint on the finished load of wash, then running
the load in an electric dryer should trap the lint in the dryer filter. It worked for me, and I had LOT of towel lint from
washing light towels with 2 pairs of dark leggings. 🤭😬
NOTE: the toss-into-the-washer lint trappers had lousy reviews from just about everyone EXCEPT those people using them
in one of these portable washing machines, so I ordered them, will use them, and will edit to add my review here.
👁 The spin-dryer will make an awful racket if you unevenly load your wash into it; otherwise, it is whisper quiet. It is a hit-or-miss
situation--either they are evenly placed in the spinner, or the load is not balanced properly. If it starts rattling, just lift the
lid, rearrange the load, and close the lid.

All in all, this little machine works better than I thought it would. If you have a small space and need a washing machine, this should do the trick.

The spark module (P/N WB13K25) fixed the problem with our gas cook-top range (JGP932TEC1WW).

Issue Description: Turning on the range caused the kitchen ground fault interrupter (GFCI) to pop. We were able to continue to use the range by unplugging the range and lighting the burners with a "long nosed" utility lighter. Clearly not ideal, but it worked until I was able to fix the real source of the problem which was the shorted spark module.

I purchased the spark module from Seneca River Trading. They processed the order very promptly and the module was received within a few days of the order placement.

Brief instructions on range top disassembly (It was not immediately evident to me how to disassemble the range to gain access to the "guts" including the spark module. Hopefully this is helpful.)
FIRST: For the sake of safety, shut off the gas valve under the range and unplug the range top!
1) remove the four plastic gas control knobs by pulling them straight up.
2) set the two burner grates aside
3) remove the burner spreader and cosmetic burner spreader cover (round disks that make up the top half of the burner)
4) VERY carefully extract the ceramic igniters by pulling straight up. (The igniters are held in place by spring clips attached to the burner assembly under the range top.) Be forewarned, these ceramic components are as fragile as glass. If using tools be very gentle!
4b) Disconnect the igniter wire from the bottom of each igniter (pull the wire off of the igniter)
5) Remove the two Torx head (T-15) screws for each of the four burners (8 screws in total). These screws hold the range top to the lower assembly. Note: In my situation, both screws for the main burner had seized. The screws were corroded and soft. Unfortunately, the heads of these two screws came off. Fortunately, after the top was out of the way, I was able to remove the screw stubs with penetrating oil using vise-grips on the bottom of the screw (below the burner).
6) With the screws removed, it should now be possible to separate the glass range top from the lower assembly. With the glass top out of the way, you will have access to the internal components... and in-particular, the spark module.

Good luck!

I've used this stove and it's predecessor from "the other' manufacturer from which Solo appears to have borrows its design. This stove has no moving parts, is lightweight, silent, and runs on nearly ubiquitous alcohol fuel. That said WHICH alcohol fuel you choose matters.

I've read a number of the negative reviews and most of them involve dissatisfaction around boil times, soot, or leaking. Quick thoughts on each:

Boil times This is not a pressurized fuel stove system. It's essentially a ported cup for burning alcohol. Just as an acetylene torch burns hotter than a wood fire, so too will an unpressurized pool of alcohol burn cooler than a pressurized cannister of IsoPro or white gas. BUT....why is everyone in such a damn hurry in the back country? This fixation with "boil time" always seemed strange to me. Light your stove, put you water on, then go prep your tent and sleeping system....or maybe just sit back and enjoy the sunset??!! What's this fixation on "clocking" your stove every time? Okay, longer boil times can mean more fuel use over time but goodness....if you're that obsessive about 2 additional ounces of fuel to get you through your trip.....get a debris stove (which will blacken every piece of gear you own.)

Soot: This is a fuel "type" problem. The isopropyl you find in your CVS drugstore burns dirty and can leave soot. Denatured ethanol (e.g. alcohol fuel specifically made for stoves or lanterns) burn much more cleanly. Another option is the yellow bottle of HEET found in almost every gas station in the U.S. which burns soot free. Right fuel = problem solved.

Leaking: Neither of my alcohol stoves have ever leaked when storing them with fuel in them but then again neither have a fuel reservoir large enough for multi-night trips. So unless you are going out for just one night and looking to carry ONLY your stove...you are likely carrying extra fuel in something. Solution = if your solo stove leaks don't store your fuel in the stove and just carry it in that extra something.

Lastly, there are all sorts of other things to consider like low temp/high temp, high wind conditions etc. I won't go into all those considerations here as they are covered extensively with a simple google search like "best camp stove for......" The point is, there is no "one stove" to rule them all. Different stoves have different strengths and weaknesses and excel at some things while falling short on others. But as an all around simple stove that boils water and can simmer food, with no moving parts other than the simple flame limiter, has silent operation, and uses a nearly universally available fuel.....this simple little gadget is an absolute stand out. Highly recommended.

My Whirlpool dryer stopped heating, so while I was looking for a new element, I came across this package and decided that I might as well replace everything while I had the back off. For the price of the kit, it's pretty much a no-brainer.

Got my package the next day, but it was only the element, so I asked for a replacement. It arrived two days later, so I pulled the dryer out of its cubby and replaced everything. It was pretty quick to complete. Took longer to get the dryer to a place where I could work on it than it took to replace everything.

I started it up, element glowed and was getting nice hot air out of the vent, so I called it done and put it back together and maneuvered it back in place. That's when the problems started. It ran for a little bit and then stopped tumbling and the dryer got really hot, so I turned it off. After it cooled, I pulled it back out and discovered that the thermal fuse did its job and shut it down. Luckily I still had the old thermal fuse, so I put it back in place. I checked all the thermostats and the element for continuity and they all were good, so I plugged back in and ran it. It heated back up and seemed to be doing good, until the high limit thermostat cut the power to the element and I noticed that only half of the element shut off. That's not what it's supposed to do. I turned on the air dry cycle that uses no heat, only air and I noticed that the same side of the element heated up. That's when I knew I had a problem.

The one thing I didn't check before I put everything in place was for continuity between the element and its cover. Sure enough, it was bad. Looks like one or more of the insulators on that side was not working properly and it was getting juice as soon as the dryer was turned on.

Luckily, I had been lazy and hadn't returned the other original element that I had received, so I checked it and it was good and put it on. Problem solved and I have a working dryer again.

Long story short, when you check the element, make sure you check for continuity between the posts and between the post and element case itself. That will help save you any headaches later on.

The element that I am putting back in the return box has obviously been used, so I am putting a note in the box to let the seller know why it's been used. Hopefully they won't charge me for element. If they do, I'll update this post with my observations about their customer service.

FYI, I know you will read a lot about having lots of towels around when replacing this pump, and if your location is in the basement, or concrete floor with drain near by that works fine. But since my washer sits on original solid oak wood floors I had to find the dryest method, naturally, so this is what I did. First, use a shop vac to empty washer drum where the clothes sit, to minimize what comes out below. Then at the pump, I found slowly releasing the tubes to pump assembly, one at a time emptying water into pyrex dish. As the pyrex dish got full, I would push hose back on to stop flow, and they shop vac to empty the pyrex dish, and then repeat until all water is out of tubes and pump. That last step I had to do by myself, but would be easier if you had someone else handling the shop vac duties. If you try to pull out the pyrex dish and empty by hand you will spill it all over because you have no room to pull it out level. Kept hardwood floors nice and dry. Hope this helps.

This egg holder looked like a great idea for managing the eggs from our small flock of hens. Turns out it looks better than it works.

Pros:
- Holds a good number of eggs. I bought two levels, to hold 3 dozen eggs.
- Rigid top allows non-egg items to be stacked on top of it with no harm to eggs

Cons:
- Stock rotation (first in, first out). It’s challenging to rotate your stock if you use (and/or if the girls lay) less than six eggs at a time. Only the eggs at the front of each row are accessible unless you take off the lid, making it difficult to put new eggs behind older eggs. Which leads me to…
- Gravity. This is designed with a gentle slope so that when the first egg in each row is removed, the remainder should roll to take its place, leaving the empty space in the back. In practice, this rolling effect does not reliably happen. One of my girls lays medium-sized eggs, and hers tend to roll not-quite-straight and end up resting at a slight angle, holding up everything behind it. The large eggs from the other girls roll better. Usually.
- Use of fridge space. Because eggs are accessed from the front, this holder needs to be on the front edge of your fridge shelf if you want to use eggs from it. For me, that means I lose other fridge items that are inadvertently pushed behind it, and ultimately end up with more spoiled food (out of sight, out of mind!)
- Moisture. Because this egg holder isn’t sealed, and egg shells are porous, the eggs lose moisture in the fridge. This isn’t noticeable until you use the egg, and isn’t specific to this egg holder - but something I didn’t think of until I realized it was happening.

While this adapter did drop the voltage to 120V as designed, it does not provide for a proper ground.  When tested with an outlet tester, it showed as an open ground.  The GFCI included with the device will provide some protection from electric shock if the GFCI is working, but I am told it will not necessarily protect sensitive electronics that are part of most new appliances.  Lack of a proper ground may void warranties.  GFCI devices also sometimes fail with age or as a result of surges.  With this device behind the stove, it would be difficult to test or verify whether it was working or not.  If it was not, and the circuit remained energized, a short could energize metal parts of your appliance resulting in a nasty shock should you touch it and ground yourself.  I am also told to operate safely, the 240 combined breaker in the service panel needs to be changed to a single 120v breaker.  Though more expensive, I plan to play it safe and have an electrician change the outlet with a proper ground and properly sized breaker in the breaker panel.

I have owned this dishwasher for 1 year this month and I despise it. My 15 year old dishwasher was so noisy we couldn't run it while we were in the room but it did a good job of cleaning the dishes even if they hadn't been pre-rinsed. We looked at many dishwashers and this one came highly recommended by the salesman and the sound rating was impressive. That's where the positive part ends. It is very quiet and I like that. We have not misused the machine and our children are all grown and out of the house so we can't even blame "the kids."

Some of the other negatives are as follows:

The racks are fine if all you have to load are plates and glasses or cups. Serving bowls, small bowls, serving spoons, or odd shaped items do not fit well making loading a challenge. Even when nothing is in the way, the dishes have to be pre-washed before loading to insure a clean wash.

The control panel is hard to read (black controls on black background) and is so sensitive just brushing against it may start a cycle or cancel and drain when it is washing.

If money was no object this dishwasher would be at the recycler with my old Maytag. Since I can't afford to replace it now I am resigned to suffer in silence with this quiet beast! I'd gladly take some noise over the frustration I have had with this "quiet" Kitchenaid.

This is the real McCoy of reviews. I know this product front-to-back, it's positives and shortcomings. I used to work at an industrial aircraft part warehouse, and this product, in various lengths, was THE sealer we used. So I've operated this and the other length options THOUSANDS of times.
This is how it works: there's a piece of teflon tape on the bottom covering a wire heating element/filament. This flat wire is removable, as is the teflon strip, making replacement easy, which is good, as both do not last forever (think of a lightbulb filament, only one with much more electricity passing through it, and the teflon tape is only teflon-coated paper, which will burn and crack after a number of uses, possibly 100, depending on the heat level and care it is treated with). The heat is controlled by a dial knob. The element heats up when the upper bar is pulled down, which compresses the two plastic sheets. The thicker the sheets, the longer you need the bar down and the higher you need the heat. Again, the filament is on the bottom, and both sheet's need to be melted enough to adhere, so plan the heat level accordingly. I've sealed thin, sandwich bag-thick bags, bubble wrap, potato chip bags, as well as thick industrial strength vinyl bags.
The sealer's casing is of strong metal design, industrial, and durable to a moderate amount of disgruntled employee abuse (heh).
There is an indicator light for when the sealing is "done", but it is only a combination of heat and a predetermined time limit. Once the indicator lights up, the heating element switches off. So, there were times when I was sealing a half dozen vinyl bags together and had to compress the bar multiple times to get the filiment to seal through all the layers.
Anyhow, if you're going to need a sealer for a lot of uses, want to keep it for a long time, have a modicum of finesse, and are okay with changing out the filament and tapes from time to time, this brand is the way to go. If you're need is only of the "once in a while" variety, the get one of the plastic, handheld, $6 ones from another supplier. In closing - this one is legit, but seriously vulnerable to user error.

First machine arrived and wouldn’t even turn on... not a great start. Returned for a replacement. Second machine spun the clothes and they came out quite dry- great! We liked that it had a five minute auto shut off, but we never ended up needing it as our clothes were dry enough before then. It's also great that it has a stainless steel drum.

HOWEVER, we ended up purchasing the Laundry Alternative’s Nina Soft and returned the Panda. In comparison to the Nina, we felt the Panda construction wasn’t very sturdy- the transparent lid was flimsy and wiggled around. We thought it might break the first time it slammed shut. We planned to store the machine under a shelf and needed the door to remain half open to air out between uses. The Panda door was was either open or shut- no spring to keep it half open, like the Nina. The handle to turn the machine on/off felt like it’d be the first to break. The spout is quite low, and it was difficult to find a container that was low yet large enough to contain all the water that came out of the clothes. This machine doesn’t have prongs (or whatever you call them!) that allow you to wrap the cord around for storage . The stainless steel exterior looked dirty after just having taken it out of the box- you’d definitely have to wipe it off constantly. It felt like it would dent and scratch very easily. Yes, it did spin our clothes *ever so slightly* drier than the Nina (Panda is 3200rpm vs the Nina 1800rpm), but the overall machine didn’t have the sturdy and quality made features that made us feel like it would last very long! We also felt more confident with the Nina because it has a three year warranty- the Panda only has a one year (from what we understand anyways! This information wasn't easy to find). And if you're wondering about overall size- they're generally the same size- the Panda is slightly taller, but the Nina is a bit wider at the base. How does the Panda's 22lb capacity compare to the Nina's 12lb? I thought it would be a lot, but it only ended up being around two men's medium Hanes t-shirts, or a pair of women's size 32 jeans- not much! In any case, opt for the Nina- much better construction!

I'm definitely not getting paid to promote the Nina Soft- I couldn't find a comparison online and had to comb through hundred of questions and reviews just to find the information I was looking for. Hope this review is helpful to anyone out there trying to decide between the two!

So I bought these because my grandpa has stage six dementia. I added some Gorilla Glue super glue to the adhesive and it works like a charm. I can't even pull it open with both hands! Grandpa can't raid the fridge now and my wallet is thankful for not having to replace groceries so often!
I can see how this would work for little children with the original adhesive. But if you are like me and trying to keep your dementia riddled grandpa from raiding the fridge, these locks are going to go well with Gorilla Glue. They need the extra strength. Seriously, throw some in your cart along with these locks, that way you can get it all done in one go instead of waiting the hard way like I had to.

Also, to remove the adhesive, just dab some nail polish and it should remove the super glue. With dementia, child locks are temporary, so don't be afraid to apply a good amount of glue to get these locks working at peak potential. The nail polish will undo all the glue when you're ready to uninstall.

I have owned this range for a little over a year now and it has been great, with one exception…the center cooking grate is slightly higher than the 2 outer cooking grates.

Cooktop:
• Burner performance is very good; a lot of options for high heat and slow simmer applications.
• Easy to start and large, hefty knobs make it quick and easy to adjust as you are cooking.
• Cleaning is relatively easy, with respect to a gas stove; cooking grates are easy to remove and put back in place.
• The only glaring issue is the unevenness of the center cooking grate (slightly higher) compared to the 2 outer cooking grates.
o This makes it a challenge to move pots around the cooking surface easily; you have to slightly lift part of the pot or pan…it is not truly a continuous surface.
o Large/heavy stock pots, filled with liquid, are a challenge to move or adjust on the burner, if not placed exactly in the spot you want them.
o Also, when you have a fry pan bridging the center and outer cooking grate, any oil will tend to pool a bit to the opposite side of the pan.
o At first this was a minor inconvenience, but after a year it has become a glaring issue for me.
Oven:
• The oven performance is very good; heat distribution is pretty even and temps seem to be accurate with respect to the corresponding settings.
• Convection performance is excellent and the air fryer setting works well.
• There are a lot of rack locations, so you have a lot of options for cooking multiple items at once.
• Cleaning pretty easy, but I have not tried the self-cleaning option yet.

Overall, I have really enjoyed this range, but wish there was a fix of the uneven cooking grates.

I read all the reader’s reviews and it took me ~1 month of practice to finally get the brew just right. Here are my tips for best results and to limit the amount of grind in your cup.
- use espresso grind (must be very fine)
-use 1 rounded scoop (scoops provided)- I wish the scoop was perfectly sized so you wouldn’t have to round it, as that adds variability to the process.
-once the scoop is in the Nespresso tin, use the back end of the scoop to create a center channel in the coffee grounds. *this is a critical step and the one I figured out on my own after examine how the grounds in the new Nespresso tins appear when the lid is removed. This allows the water to go through the center and by doing this, greatly reduces the ground in the brewed coffee.
If you follow these steps and you are willing to take the extra time, then this product is worth it. To me, it is a bit of a hassle, but when I run the numbers it’s well worth it. Because you are only using 1 scoop per cup, your pound of coffee goes a long way!
Good luck!

I needed a small fridge for a "granny" apartment, and I always try to buy Energy Star. In a rare fit of supporting the local independent mom-and-pop store, I bought one of these in July. It took them over a month to get one from Frigidaire.

When first plugged in, it would run for maybe 15 minutes and then stop for at least that long. Took it over a day to get the fridge section down to 50F. With normal food inside, it won't go below 39F even on the very coldest setting. The off-to-on hysteresis is 10F, so at the coldest setting it cycles between 40F and 50F. The freezer will go to -18F if you turn its knob cold, but the refrigerator averages around 45F. If you take out all the liquids and heavy stuff, the fridge will freeze your lettuce to death before shutting off, while still waiting for about 50F to come back on.

It also makes a wide repertory of amazing noises, loud enough to be heard all over the house. Sometimes it is a "boink-boink-boink" sound from the compressor or the gas bubbling. Way louder than the normal soft boiling sound refrigeration sometimes makes. Other times it is a loud buzz from the air circulation fan - you can tell because it stops when you open the fridge door. And sometimes it is normally quiet, but totally unpredictable.

The local repair guy keeps replacing fans and sensors, and the behavior changes a bit each time, but there doesn't seem to be a real fix. I'd love to hear from anyone else who has one of these, working well or not! Frigidaire, if you're listening, I'm not very hopeful about hauling this back to the store on my dime and waiting another month to see if a replacement would be any better. I'm thinking serious design flaw...
