My fridge had stopped cooling, and began to make a loud click sound approximately every 5 minutes, preceded by a few seconds of a wind up buzzing sound that ended after the click. After doing some research, I found out that the likely culprit was the start relay.

Opened up my fridge, and removed the old start relay, which had part number 8EA14C3 (3 long pins with connections, and a small unconnected metal stub where the 4th pin would have been). After some googling, I found out that a 2262181 part is just another id number for the same 8EA14C3 (and other relays with similar ids all similarly have an analagous Whirlpool number), so no point in ordering the more expensive and harder to find 8EA14C3.

Unlike other commenters, my relay didn't have a rattling sound when shook. However, if you squeeze the pins on the sides of the relay, you should be able to open up the relay. After opening, and upon removing the disc held inside, I saw two scorch marks on one side where the metal pins made contact, confirming that the relay was in fact damaged. Likewise, for those that hear rattling sounds, it's an indicator that the internal disc is shattered (fragments from mine broke off after lightly touching the scorched areas).

While waiting for the replacement part to arrive, I re-inserted the disc so that the metal pins only made contact with the unburnt (white) areas (despite the chipped edges), and I was able to startup the fridge again. However, as I don't know of any potential long term damage or risks that come with using a faulty component, I wouldn't recommend this as a long term solution. But it might come in handy to preserve some of your food until the new part arrives.

These come in a two pack, and sit in the two pod holder provided with the standard Senseo brewer. My wife and I both like the idea that they also come from the Netherlands, which is where the Phillips Senseo coffee brewer comes from. The cost is very reasonable, especially when you buy as many of the pods as we have. (Less than $10) After giving them a gentle wash in running hot water, they are ready to use right from the bag. Don't be worried about the packaging they come in, it looks cheap - but they are really very well made.

To fill, you just pop the filter top, add coffee to the cup, pack a little with a spoon, and replace/snap on the filter top. Then place into the Senseo brewer basket, so that the tab on the bottom of the eco-pad fits into the base of the two pod holder. It fits a little snugly, but it will fit when pressed in. Place the brewer basket into the brewer and close the lid as you would normally, and brew with either the one or two espresso button.

At first, we used drip ground coffee and got fairly weak results when we used the two espresso button. I tried one, then waiting, and one again - but still got weak (tea) results at the end of the run. Then I ground fresh beans into a very fine espresso grind level, almost like it was a fine powder - and tried it. That made a HUGE difference in coffee quality from beginning to end. It almost started black, and ended looking like good coffee I still would have drunk. And the taste was 100% better as well, even better than the standard pods you buy in the store. Plus you only use about 2 teaspoons of coffee per cup/serving.

After use, you want to remove the eco-pad, dump your grounds (we put ours into a composting bin) and wash the pod with warm-cool water. It comes out clean, but a good wipe out with a finger or a paper towel is advised every few cups of coffee to keep it looking like new.

All in all, I was very impressed with the results - and am looking forward to a simple cup of fresh brew every morning as I head into work. This is definitely the way to go, unless you want to take the time to make a full pot of coffee or espresso. Of course, if you are in a rush, you can still grab your regular Sesneo store bought pods and make a quick one for "on the run" coffee too. No modifications are made to the brewer or the pod holder what so ever.

Bottom Line: EcoPads really work well - if you use fresh, fine grind espresso coffee and take a little care in cleaning afterwards. And far faster and easier than making a full pot of coffee.

This dual valve kit fit my 20 year old whirlpool refrigerator perfectly, and it works just fine. I had a leak that started to flood my laminate flooring behind the refrigerator. Thank goodness that I have drop ceiling installed in my basement , so I was able to temporarily move it out the way to easily trace the leak through the water line tubing. It was visually obvious that this leak was dripping rapidly and getting some of my floor boards wet while damaging underneath my laminate floor. Did tons of research, many so called experts pointed to the dual valve that may have a bad solenoid on it. So not only did i pull up some of the extra tubing through the hole where the tubing was installed and cut it with a sharp razor behind the area that was punctured. I installed the new valve and some new tubing as well that I purchased at home depot. The valve is much more quiet than the original one, and there are no more leaks. The hardest part for me was threading the metal compression nozzles to the tubing. You have to do this part perfectly and cut the new tubing perfectly straight or it will continue to leak. Remember the water dispenser & ice maker is working with a water pressure of 30-120 psi , so take plenty of HD pictures of the old connections before installing the new parts. Looking at the old parts and the HD images showed me that i was threading the tubing under the compression connector instead of threading it over the connector. It was a learning experience but with a few tedious hours and putting our glasses on, my wife & I figured it out. If your tubing keeps popping off within a few seconds, then there is a 99.9% chance the water pressure is knocking the tubing off because it is not properly threaded.. The price of this valve was $60 less than Sears parts online, and it looks exactly like the original one (just alot cleaner) and it works great!!

Mechanically this is a very solid and well made range hood.  None of the problems I experienced were related to the manufacturing process.  This company definitely needs to reassess their packing method.  Those three baffles are heavy and need to be individually wrapped and secured inside the box.  They also need a better inspection process before the hood leaves the factory.  The missing spring clip and inoperable light would have been obvious flaws an inspection would have found. (By the way, switching out the bad light for good light was an easy process).  On the positive side, the fan motor is a heavy duty and powerful unit.  The six speeds offer all the air removing volume you could need.  It is a heavy unit (around 40lb) and should not be attached to just drywall.  Even if you have to order two hoods to make one perfect, it could be worth the effort.  In the end you'll have a very solid and attractive range hood.

If you're into non paper filter brewing methods such as french press, you know that paper filters will retain a lot of the oils from the grind that gives coffee it's flavor. Another plus is that you can use this with a really fine grind (I use in between espresso and auto-drop coarseness) without getting grounds in your cup. Try with both paper and stainless filters to taste the difference.

My perfect cup, americano style:
2 heaping tbsp (varies) fresh fine ground coffee in the aeropress (non inverted position).
Boiling water up to the 1.5 line.
Stir immediately, brew for 20 seconds.
Press slowly over 20 seconds into the cup.
Add desired amount of hot water for the strength of the cup.

Alternatively, press into a pint glass, add a little less volume of cold water, finish with ice to yield a great iced americano. Add a twist of lemon peel for an Italian flavor. Great for the summer.

I desperately needed to get one of these portable ice makers, since I live in an apartment where the fridge does not have an ice maker and getting one is not an option. I waited until I found a unit for a price I was willing to pay and this Emerson unit fit the bill.

Yes, the unit is big and heavy. But it is so great to be able to have as much ice as you want whenever you want. The unit makes ice beautifully, in three different sizes. The cubes are a bit smaller than I expected, but that's OK. You can always select the large setting for bigger cubes. (I usually use medium.) The unit makes 9 cubes at a time, and it takes maybe 20 minutes to make the first batch of ice, maybe 10-15 minutes for consecutive batches.

The cubes are tubular in shape, with holes in the middle. The design makes them easy to put in Ziploc bags and store in your freezer until needed. (No need to run the machine every single day!) If they stick together, a little whack should separate the cubes.

A couple of things to keep in mind:

Before using the unit for the first time, add a little vinegar to the water and let the machine run. Dump the ice and and drain the water. Then, do a run with some lemon juice in the water. Again, dump the ice and drain. Then do a few runs with clean water. If you don't do this, the ice will have a bit of a chemical taste, even after several runs. (I thought several runs of plain water would clear up the taste, but it didn't. The vinegar and lemon juice, however, did the trick beautifully.) Also, you should probably use filtered water for a cleaner taste. (I use water from my sink that has gone through my Pur facuet filter.)

The plug for the water drainage is VERY small. Be careful with it. Also, because the plug is so small, draining the water takes a while. Gently tilting the unit (carefully!) will help to slightly speed up the process.

So yes, the machine has a few minor flaws, but the convenience more than makes up for it. It is great to have ice whenever needed, and it is so cool to watch the machine in action, when the built-in "spatula" scoops up the ice and tilts it into the basket! This is one of the best kitchen appliances I have ever bought, and I'm hopeful it will last for many years!

UPDATED REVIEW 8/4/2022: The problem with this unit that I had reported earlier with insufficient power to draw air has been solved--the culprit was the venting configuration in our wall that interfered with the operation of the unit. Ours was configured with a rear venting option, and the unit is designed for that rear vent to push air directly out the back to an exterior location. However, our exhaust vent first detoured upward 90 degrees then had a second 90 degree elbow outward to vent to the exterior. In this configuration, a flap at the rear of the unit that would normally prevent cold exterior air from backflowing into the unit would almost completely block the exhaust flue when the unit was turned on. This is why an insufficient volume of air was being pushed out. The solution was simple: we took the unit down and simply removed the exhaust flap from the back of the unit. When reinstalled, the unit drew air perfectly and I'm exceedingly happy with it. So I am amending my previous review (included below)--the unit now draws air perfectly fine. So I'm moving from three stars up to five stars--the only thing I'd change are the controls for resetting the clock, which are very unintuitive.

ORIGINAL REVIEW: I'm writing this several months after purchase because I've had some challenges to overcome with the original unit that was shipped to me. First, I really like the design of this exhaust fan--well-engineered, easy to keep clean, seems like a high-quality build. That's all to the good. Second, the company stands by their products. I had extensive interactions with two members of their customer support team, and I'm extremely impressed with their responsiveness and desire to make the customer happy. So far so good. Third, at least in the rear-exhaust configuration, the fan does not draw as much air as I was led to expect by the CFM rating. WIth the first fan I ordered, there was clearly a problem with the ability of the fan to increase output at higher fan settings. I cook with a wok and need a strong exhaust. I bought this model to replace my old fan, which worked fine but was in need of replacement, and the more than 1.5X increase in CFM over my old fan was a major selling point for me.

Instead of drawing more air, the new unit drew considerably less. I was setting off my smoke detector almost every other time I used the wok. The company worked with me to first send a replacement transformer, which helped a little but didn't fix the problem. They then shipped an entirely new replacement unit under warranty, which also helped a bit more but I'm still setting off my smoke detector probably one out of 12 times that I cook. One thing that may be a factor in my case is that I use the wok on a front stove burner, but the two fan units in this exhaust system are set far to the rear. That distance might be an additional factor that makes this particular fan less than ideal for my situation--if I was cooking on a back burner, the fan position would be much better at picking up the smoke and vapors. But even with that design aspect in view, it's not drawing as much air as my old unit, which had a much lower CFM rating.

So I have a mixed experience to report. I'm sticking with the replacement unit they sent, because I'm tired of replacing my exhaust fan and this is working okay (but just "okay"). My experience with their customer service as first rate--they are very responsive and immediately worked to address the problems. But in the end, if I had known what I know now, I wouldn't have chosen this particular model.

I feel like all these people complaining have purchased this machine without understanding the trade-offs of a single washer-dryer machine, so to set the record straight:

1. re: mold; I have owned this machine for 3 years now and I have never had a problem. The trick is to keep the washing machine door and drawer OPEN when the machine is not in use. This way the inside of the machine dries completely. You also need to run the tub-clean feature once a month with a washing machine cleaner or just plain water/bleach. All of these are described in the user manual and if people just took time to read it then they wouldn't have a problem.

2. re: wrinkles and drying. This is simple, DO NOT OVERLOAD THE MACHINE. Again, this is stated in the manual. If your clothes are coming out damp, wrinkled, and taking too long to dry then you are overloading, plain and simple. If I am washing dress shirts and pants, I set the machine to perm-press and only load half of the capacity of the machine; for normal clothes I will put two-thirds full but that's it. I don't think this is a big deal; I don't wait for the weekend to do a big pile of laundry, I just do several small batches throughout the week. For bulky items like comforters, you may need to pause the machine mid-drying cycle and rearrange so that your comforter will dry evenly.

3. re: lint. The machine does not have a lint trap, so after each wash-dry cycle you need to take a damp paper towel and wipe the inside of the machine, particularly the rubber seal on the door. This is also why it is important to run the tub-clean cycle regularly. I have also needed to take a pair of tweezers and pull out lint from the soap dispenser (the orange thing where the soap comes out). I only needed to do this twice in the 3-year period that I have owned the machine, so again no big deal, you just need to observe your wash cycle if it looks like soap isn't coming out.

This machine has served me well and if I ever need to, I will happily buy another LG washer-dryer combo.

All told, I spent 16.5 years in various apartments without washer and dryer hookups. That's a long time to go to the laundromat, and even when I didn't spend the time doing it in the laundromat, I paid a fortune for wash and fold. And about a year ago, I received this washer as a Christmas gift. I LOVED it! It took me a few times to figure out how to get it to complete a cycle (hint, all the lights have to be on, wash, rinse, spin. Otherwise, it will only wash). I found it held approximately 1/3 of a "normal" washer load, so for my family of 4, to keep up, I did 3 loads a day. It could even do King Sized sheets, but only one at a time. The only thing I couldn't fit were king sized comforters.

What I liked about it was it was super customizable. You could run any combination of cycles, water levels and you can even control the temperature from the sink. I was able to do a hot wash and a hot rinse. I've since moved to a house, and I miss that feature on my new full sized washer. Don't let the size fool you. This is a "real" washer, and your clothes come out clean and not sopping wet. I've never felt the need for the spin dryer step that other reviewers have mentioned. If you are really concerned about it, just run another cycle on spin.

PROS:

Sink Hook-up
Regular house current (110V)
Custom water levels and cycles
On wheels

Small load size
The sink connection was sometimes leaky, but a washcloth over the faucet kept it from spraying all over the place.

I hate doing dishes. Passionately. So much so that I have been searching rental ads, looking to move to a different house, specifically one that has a dishwashwer. Turns out a better investment was buying the EdgeStar portable dishwasher - purchased in a fit of frustration after using the last clean dish in the house. This little device is amazing. I can't believe how well it cleans even caked-on or sticky, etc. dishes. It also holds my large plates, wine glasses, smaller pots & pans... the only things I have to wash by hand anymore are cookie sheets and large pots/pans. I was able to install it myself, just screwed the attachment onto my sink faucet with no additional hardware needed. (You clip a second hose attachment on/off the screwed-in attachment when you need to use the faucet.) And it's so simple - just put in the soap, clip on the hoses, turn the machine on, turn the water on, and that's it.

Only drawbacks (but it still gets 5 stars because it works so well overall):
-Installation was a little confusing; I didn't think the directions were clear, and I ended up figuring it out by trial & error. I also had to use some electrical tape to wrap around the screw-in fixture to keep it from leaking at the connection to my faucet. Could be my old faucet hardware that is the problem.
-At first, my dishes came out spotty and/or filmy and not that clean. After the first couple washes, I was really disappointed. But then I switched detergents, and it made ALL the difference. Now my dishes come out crystal clear and squeaky clean. I recommend those little combo detergent/rinse agent packets - they work great for me.
-It's bigger and heavier than I expected (yes, I read the dimensions, but I have pretty poor visuospatial skills). If you have limited space, make sure to measure carefully because it is much bigger than a microwave (which is how I had kind of pictured it).
-The connection to the faucet still isn't great, and for me, a bit of water trickles out and runs down the side of the clip-on attachment while the machine is in use. It is not a lot, and certainly a lot less water than I would use washing a sinkful of dishes otherwise. Again, could be my faucet.

All in all, I love this dishwasher more than I ever thought I could love a kitchen appliance. It works brilliantly and has made such a difference in my life. I cook more, my husband and I never argue about the dishwashing chores, and I don't have to move to a new house!

For those who don't know, its best practice to not re-use washing machine hoses once they have been disconnected. In this scenario, the delivery team made the correct decision.

The final issue is that the delivery team quickly left once they realized the gas and water could not be hooked up, and failed to install the exhaust tubing or test other functionality of the dryer.

While my installation experience was bad, the machine itself works well and dries quickly. The only feature I haven't been able to test are the steam features, I'm still waiting on new hoses from Amazon. I'll update this review in a couple months to see how the machine has broken in.

*2 YEAR UPDATE****

I now have a gas furnace and I am entering my second winter with the gas furnace and my 3rd winter with the humidifier. I also switched my humidifier over to hot water. Performance has improved slightly, but I still find myself swapping pads every 4 to 6 weeks or so in the winter. Still using the rag in-between the pad and humidifier water distribution tray. Still very happy with this unit all things considered. Highly recommend if your application is similar to mine.

****ORIGINAL REVIEW****

Alright. I've had this thing installed for about a year now so I feel comfortable writing a thorough review. A little background on me, I'm a professional engineer with a license in HVAC and Refrigeration. I certainly don't claim to know it all, but I'd like to think I know a little more than most when it comes to HVAC applications. First off some background on my house and HVAC: 1970's construction, 2 story, 2,200 sqft house with new windows. Northeast US winters. All electric heating (heat pump with electric element backup/aux). I did not install the provided humidistat and instead run this off of an Ecobee smart thermostat. My house has a septic system, so I was worried about sending gallon after gallon of water into my basement sump (also over working my sump pump) and then running that water through my septic system. So I elected to install this over the 500 series. I connected mine to cold water, and after doing it I regret not hooking into the hot water, something I will expand on later in this review. I installed this myself in a full day, but I needed to do some minor plumbing re-configuring and run an additional wire to my thermostat. Humidity in my home would usually sit in the 24% to 28% range in the winter before installation.

First off for my particular house, the unit works well. And by well I mean it keeps the edge of low humidity off. We definitely experience fewer dry throats/noses/skin and the dog appreciates not getting zapped from static all the time. With a fresh water pad installed the unit can maintain around 34% to 38% RH in my house with temps in the 20s outside. I have it set to maintain 40%, so it pretty much runs whenever the heat kicks on. As the pad degrades and gets crusted you can see the performance drop as the house will only maintain low 30%'s (30% to 32%) with similar weather conditions. On extremely cold days where the electric elements are running more often and the available humidity is even lower outside the house can get down into the lower 30% as well despite the pad condition. Since installation I rarely see RH below 30%, except when I run my wood burning stove, another point I will expand on later in this review. If someone in the house is sick, I still find myself setting up a table top humidifier in their bedroom in order to improve overnight breathing conditions, but for day-to-day, this thing does its job.

Some general tips and points to consider:

-I've found that pad life is grossly overstated by Aprilaire. I don't think our water is overly hard, but 1 or 2 pads a season is far too infrequent to maintain reasonable RH in my house. I'm probably around once a month, maybe once every 6 weeks depending on weather/HVAC system cycles. I'd consider a heating season here in the Northeast to be at least 6 months. No way you're getting that kind of life out of 1 or 2 pads. I've found deals online to get pads in bulk for around $10 a pad, so the cost isn't too terrible for maintaining good RH. When I can tell the system is struggling to get above 32% I'll usually go down and check the pad and it's brownish/dried out and not wicking/holding water well. I'll swap out for a fresh pad and within a few hours the house is back up into the 35% to 38% range. This could just be something with my particular install, but I'm finding pad life to be key in maintaining reasonable RH. Something to consider if you have this unit and are having problems.

-After my initial installation I was somewhat underwhelmed with performance and went searching for potential solutions. I was finding that the top of the pad was drying out very quickly and the wicking action was only keeping the bottom 1/4 of the pad wet, essentially reducing the capacity of the unit by 1/4. Until the reservoir level had dropped sufficiently to cycle the water valve and wet the top of the pad, this was essentially reducing the capacity of the unit by 1/4. Some people have essentially converted this unit to an Aprilaire 500 by duct taping or somehow holding the magnet floats in the down position. Water will then constantly overflow the reservoir and go into the drain and the full pad will constantly stay wet. Again, I was concerned about overworking my sump and septic system, so I combated the lackluster performance in a few ways:

- I think the biggest improvement came from taking a small cotton rag, folding it and placing it between the top of the pad and the black plastic distribution tray. You don't want to block any of the pad face, as that will reduce airflow, so keep the rag small and folded, but you want to enough rag to hold some water and distribute it over the full width of the pad. The rag acts as a sponge and retains some water, allowing the top 1/4 of the pad to stay wet. This helped improve the output of the unit. You'll want to be mindful and and change this out relatively frequently (every month/6 weeks along with the pad seems to be good for me), since mold might grow on it.
-2nd thing I did is crack the ball valve I installed supplying the humidifier just barely. I opened the valve the smallest amount I could until I could hear water flowing and left it. The idea is to get water flowing very sloooooowly. This increases the time it takes to fill the reservoir at the bottom, and increases the time the pad has the soak up water when the control valve opens. Blasting water over the pad that just rolls off into the reservoir does no good.
-3rd thing I did was check the level of my humidifier. I was finding that one side of the pad was drying out faster then the other. I don't know if this was just due to airflow patterns, but I failed to check level during installation, and found that the humidifier was indeed slanted to one side. So I can't stress this enough to people who are looking to install this: MAKE SURE THE HUMIDIFIER IS LEVEL DURING INSTALL! I tried to rectify the problem by shoving some cardboard under the filter pad holder on one side. I can't tell if this helped much or not. If the humidifier is tipped to one side the water won't distribute evenly over the pad, resulting in one side getting soaked and water running off into the reservoir, and the other side just barely getting wet, allowing it to dry out shortly after the water flow turns off.

-If you're looking to install this, just connect it to hot water an be done with it. There's pages and pages of forums out there with people debating the merits of hot vs cold water evaporation rates. Aprilaire claims the benefits of hot water will be reduced due to the style of this humidifier (water will cool after the reservoir is full). Since I think my humidifier is just a tad undersized for my house when connected to cold water, I think whatever small benefit from connecting to hot would have helped. I am considering changing my connection over eventually. I was worried about higher electric bills, but after seeing the small amount of water this thing uses, I wish I would have just connected to the hot. If you're installing a different "flow through" model (i.e. Aprilaire 500 or 600), your electric bill may very well be impacted, assuming you have an electric water tank. If you have a gas water heater you should most likely be connecting to the hot water side. At least in my locality, gas prices are an order of magnitude lower than electric on a per BTU basis, even considering the lower efficiency of gas water heaters. The added cost to heat the small volume of water with gas should only be a few bucks a month.

- Wood burning stove owners: If your wood burner takes combustion air from inside, it's a tall order for any humidifier to maintain upper 30%'s RH when a wood burning stove is sucking a ton of humidified air out of your house up the chimney. It's then getting replaced from somewhere in your house (door/window cracks, etc.) with dry outdoor air. If your wood burner has an outdoor air intake for combustion air this should improve your situation, but the heating system should still run sparingly when the woodstove is going (which is good for your wallet!), so maintaining relative humidities in the 30%'s may be difficult. Even if I set my Ecobee thermostat to run the humidifier and the fan only, there's not a lot of heat to help evaporate the water. Typically I will set up a table top humidifier when the wood stove is going and that will usually keep my RH above 30% at least and will help the house recover RH faster after the fire dies out.

Keep in mind all this experience is based on my house and my HVAC system. Base your own assessment on your own home construction and HVAC system compared to mine. Newer/tighter homes or smaller homes will probably be better off holding onto humidity and will likely be really happy with this unit. Larger/older/leakier homes may not get enough out of this unit to keep RH where they want it. I feel like my house is just on the edge, since the unit runs all the time, maintains a reasonable RH, but can struggle if the pad gets excessively old or temperatures outside are below zero. I am hoping to switch to a gas furnace in the future and hope that the elevated temperatures compared to my heat pump will help improve evaporation off the pad

I never wanted a dishwasher.  It was hard to justify getting one for just 2 people and the drawers and outer door take up a lot of space and make loading awkward.  My tall version of the single dishdrawer is great.  The only draw back is that it is an uncommon dimention and I had to customize my Ikea cabinetry to support the machine and add a draw below it.  I found the manual online and was very confused since they make about 4 models, each with unique installation yet the published all of the instructions in the same document.  It took a while for the delivery to be sent out so I changed my order to the standard face (non-designer with recess handle) since I was concerned about the upper clearance that is needed on the designer model.  I think it was 5/8" difference and $100 less, the only difference being the fancy stainless steel face.  Oh in case you hadn't inferred this is a DIY job.  This NJ based company didn't do installation of dish drawers.  I learned a lot about plumbing and customizing Ikea furniture, I had to measure everything about 10 times.  One sales woman in IKEA actually told me that my configuration wasn't possible, then I found a built in microwave of the same dimentions on the showcase floor.  I had to cut the top off of the 24" frame to make it work.  I really wanted to use the predrilled holes to set the height so I wouldn't make I level holes that cause rattling or improper draining, but it made the process difficult.  I took a few days to finish the job, not including the week worth of research.  I'm sure I would do it differently if I had to do it again.  Did I mention my wife really didn't like the idea of getting a half sized dish washer?  She pushed me to get this "tall" model that is about $100 more and a few (2?) inches taller.  I am happy because it even fits our large roasting pan.  She really loves it now, since I love it and care for it like a child.  Did I mention how efficient this thing is?  2 gallons a load.  I calculated that it takes a minimum of 18 gallons for me to wash a comparable amount of dishes.  Because it is smaller than normal machines the energy star rating is literally off the scale. Only 141kw per year.  I haven't calculated how many watts it takes me to wash one years worth of dishes, so don't ask.  I just remembered one issue.  In the installation instructions there is an image of the hot water hose rubber gasket going on the mouth of the flange, this caused serious leaking on the first run.  I simply moved the gasket to the dishwasher side of the flange and I haven't had an issue since.  The company is based in New Zealand so maybe the fittings differ there.  I believe that this could be a cause for the complaints that accumulate for the F&P dishdrawers.  It also "feels" flimsy since it is made from polyethylene, but in truth, the stainless steel that goes into less expensive machines is probably low quality and will rust in a few years.  If you have the time and are up for a challenge that will result in a machine that you can brag about, get this one.

-Plug power cord into an outlet

-Once wash timer has completed, set cycle dial on "Drain"
-Drain soapy dirty water to prepare for rinse
-Once water has drained, change cycle from "Drain" back to "Normal" or "Soft"
-Fill up left side with water for rinse cycle
-Set wash timer to 6 mins

-Drain dirty water

I have now had the Purewash installed in my home for six months. I was skeptical at first. I tried a full load of towels in my front-load washer using no detergent and no softener. The towels came out clean and smelling VERY fresh. Since the smell is not an artificially added smell, it actually lasts longer than if you used a scented detergent or softener. The first time is used one of these newly cleaned towels after a shower it was like I was using a brand new towel. I was more absorbent than it previously had been and also seemed fluffier. Six months in and we still use no detergent, softener, bleach, or hot water.

One of the big things that interested me in this product was that it could eliminate foul smells in the washer. I tend to forget laundry over night, and it always came out smelling rank. I tested a load by leaving it in the washer for two days straight and it came out still smelling fine!

Pros:

Cleans well (stains do need to be pre-treated, just like normal)
Clothes smell VERY fresh afterwards
No (or very little) detergent use
No hot water use
Easy installation
No more smelly washer
Towels dry like new
Clothes last longer

Cons:

Slightly louder operation than I imagined (still quieter than a washer though)
Some loads will still need a dryer sheet to combat static. I wear slacks and button down shirts to work every day, and if I don't use a dryer sheet these clothes stick to me and attract every bit of lint or hair imaginable. I don't know if this is due to the Purewash or not, as I had always used softener or dryer sheets before, but once I stopped when I got the Purewash, I immediately had to go back to dryer sheets.

Overall, this unit is well worth the money just in the savings from no hot water or detergent/softener/bleach use alone. Add in the fact that towels dry better and it is better for the environment, and I can't imagine not having one of these in my home. If this one ever quits I will immediately purchase a replacement. Amazing product.

Update: 6/20/14

After having this product for almost two years, I still love it as much as when I first got it. My first unit did develop a small leak, but Purewash sent me a new one. I have solved the problem of static by simply adding a small amount of vinegar to loads that I know will be problematic. This does a very good job, and does not leave behind any residual smell. Plus it is safe on clothes and the environment. Still love my Purewash!

Removing the old igniter could not have been simplier: just remove a couple of hex screws and unplug the spade conector and the male connector from their respective mates.  I cut off the male connector from the old igniter and used one of the included ceramic electrical joiners to join the two wires.  I put the igniter back in the oven, attached the spade end wire to its post, attached the male end wire back to its female counterpart, put the oven back together and turned it on ... it works and my wife is happy.  Only about an hours work.  Saved $50 if I had bought it from the local supply store, and $175 if I had someone install it. I was looking for a frugal option to the very expensive Samsung OE filters and stumbled across these. I went for the 4 pack, thinking it would save me money and time over the long run. Boy, was I wrong. Seller shipped quickly, there were no problems there. The first filter installed and worked fine. I could tell these filters were perhaps not as effective as the OE filters - the flow rate was very high, suggesting to me that the water was moving through the carbon awfully quick (therefore maybe not as much carbon?). The first filter lasted a very long time, which struck me as odd, as I thought it should bugger up after awhile. Anyway, the real trouble started after I replaced the first filter. The morning after I changed the filter, I can to my kitchen to find my refrigerator and floor flooded. The filter was not seating properly. Removing and reinstalling the filter did not correct the problem. So I tossed the second filter and went for a third. Same issue - it leaked all over the fridge and floor. There were no visible defects or issues, but the filter was not seating and locking properly.

At this point, I said screw it and paid the full price for a Samsung OE filter. Worked perfectly and without issue.

I cannot recommend this in good faith to anyone. I don't believe the carbon filter itself is anywhere near as effective as the Samsung filters and there were clearly manufacturing/quality issues that proved to be a big headache for me. If motor is running well and electrical systems seem to be otherwise okay, the cause of noisy fans is the connection of the metal axle of the motor to the small hole for the plastic fan blower wheel.  Over years the D shaped plastic hole strips and the fan blower wheel does not stay tightly affixed to the metal motor axle as it should.  Then when the exhaust fan is turned on, the motor runs fine, but the plastic fan blower wheel slips, vibrates, makes noises and works inefficiently.  This new plastic fan blower wheel makes a very tight attachment to the the axle which not only eliminates vibration/noise but makes the fan work much better....like new.  Also, don't get confused with the crazy old numbering systems that NuTone had for its exhaust fans, motors, and fan blowers.  Just measure your old plastic fan blower.  If it is 6 inch by 2 inch and looks like this, then buy it.  Folks who replace the motor with the fan blower wheel pay for a new motor when they do not need it!!

Great care must be taken to keep the cutter firmly seated against the top of the cup to prevent any side-to-side forces on the blades. I needed to replace my front loading washer. This is the second front loader that I've had to replace in the past 10 years. The first was a Frigidaire which was purchased because I needed a stackable unit and it was the only one that fit my budget and was not teeny tiny. I never liked the Frigidaire. It was replaced with a Whirlpool Duet. I liked the Whirlpool and felt it did a much better job than the Frigidaire, but when it also kicked the bucket after several years, I decided not to go with a front loader again. They are way to expensive to replace every 5 years.

I was hesitant to go from a high efficiency washer back to an old style washer with an agitator. I like the idea of saving electricity, water, detergent, but the cost of replacing front loader every several years is not environmentally friendly either, and it is certainly not good for my budget! I looked at high efficiency top loaders, but was unimpressed with reviews. The 25 year life expectancy of the Speed Queen convinced me to give it a try.

I was concerned about the size of the Speed Queen, since it is so much smaller than my front loaders. I do laundry for 7, so I have lots to do! The Speed Queen takes about 30 minutes to wash a regular load and a little longer for heavy duty loads. This is about half the time for my front loader. I can wash and dry two loads of laundry with the Speed Queen and my old Whirlpool dryer in about the same amount of time as one load it my front loader. Two Speed Queen loads are more than one front loader load, so the size hasn't been an issue. The Speed Queen will not wash a king size comforter, but I did wash a Queen comforter. It was a quite full, but it fit.

The Speed Queen only has three cycles; Heavy Duty, Normal, and Delicate. I wasn't happy to give up all the different options my front loader had, but honestly I probably used one of these three options 95% of the time anyway. I've had this washer for 7 months and I've not wanted a different cycle.

I feel that my clothes get cleaner in the Speed queen than they did in the front loader. I think it is because the Speed Queen fills up with water, so the clothes actually get to soak in the water. As long as your expectations are realistic, you will love this little icemaker! At this price point, you will NOT:
1. Get an icemaker that will last for many years.
2. Get an icemaker that has a large storage bin with temperature controlled to below freezing to store all the ice it keeps making.
If that is what you are looking for, multiply the price of this icemaker x10, and start from there. Don’t want to spend that much? Then you ain’t going to get what you want.
All that being said, we have been using these little countertop style ice makers for about 10 years. We go through a lot of ice. We have many activities that require keeping a cooler of drinks on ice, (weekend landscaping work, softball tournaments, boating). We keep 2 countertop icemakers running at all times, and we purchase the drawstring ice bags to store the ice. Our two machine sit on a shelf in our dining room and we keep a large pitcher of water next to each one to make sure the water bin stays full. A couple of times a day, we empty the ice in the baskets into an ice bag we keep in the kitchen freezer. When that bag is full, we tie it off and store it in the big freezer in the garage, and start a new bag. Easy peasy. Having 2 little machines running, it doesn’t take long to fill a bag of ice.
I explained all this to show that we know a thing or two about these icemakers. We have used many different brands through the years. The lifespan of these icemakers is 1-2 years. Any less than 1 year, then we warranty them out. The IGLOO (IGLB33BLK) we have now is almost 2 years old and going strong. It has outperformed every other little icemaker we’ve had. We had this same brand/model before, and it died just before the warranty ran out so had it replaced with this current one. Our 2nd icemaker (we run 2) is a little Frigidaire we bought at Costco. We bought that one a little over a year ago and it just died yesterday. We will replace it with this model IGLOO. The IGLOO ran circles around the little Frigidaire in the quality and quantity of ice.
For those who have never used one of these type icemakers before, you fill a small bin with water, the machine makes a small tray of ice, then drops the ice cubes into a basket suspended over the water bin. If you don’t remove the ice, it begins to melt and drips back into the water bin to be reused to make ice again. It takes abou 7-8 minutes per ice drop. This model basket will hold a good bit of ice before it fills up. When the basket is full, the machine stops making ice until the ice melts down or is removed, making room for more ice. There are sensors that tell it when the ice basket is full or not, and also when the water bin is empty and you need to add more water.
Hope this helps! We’ll be sticking with this model IGLOO for now until we can’t find them anymore.

After too many trips over the last couple of years to the grocery story to buy ice for our family, I purchased the ES IB120SS ice maker after extensive research. I also bought the 3-year extended warranty policy. The unit was delivered several days ago, and I set it up yesterday in our basement, connecting the water line to our existing reverse osmosis water filter system.

Within 40 minutes, the first batch of ice was produced. It continued producing ice steadily. (After 3 hours, I threw out all the ice, and thoroughly washed out the ice bin, as instructed in the installation steps.)

However, this morning, I discovered that the ice maker itself had stopped producing ice sometime during the night. (The condenser seemed to be working fine, and the interior of the freezer unit was cold.) The metal arm that detects a full bin was partially up, and the white "arms" that rotate and push out the ice cubes had stopped in an odd position. After some inspection, I discovered that a bit of ice had formed at one spot on the white plastic top rim of the ice mold, effectively jamming the white arm at that location. I carefully broke the ice away, and the white arms immediately started rotating, and a moment later the ice mold filled with water.

I'm not sure how water could have dripped or splashed onto that location. My guess, however, is that as the white arms rotate, they carry with them a drop or two of water. In that particular location, the drop accumulates on the rim, and quickly freezes. More drops of water accumulate and freeze, until the bit of ice there is large enough to finally stop the white arms from rotating.

I"ll continue to report on what happens.

Update 2017-09-02:
The ice maker module continued to accumulate ice on its top plastic rim at one end, jamming the white arms that release the ice. This occurred about every 4-5 hours. I called EdgeStar customer support, and they were very helpful. The support rep first said that they would send out a new ice module and find a locale technician to install it (all covered under warranty). A few minutes later she called back and said that the module was not in stock and that they would send me a complete replacement unit (yes, the whole appliance). It arrived a few days ago, which I immediately installed.

So far there have been no problems with ice build-up on the ice maker module. I also noticed that the compressor seems to run a bit quieter than the original appliance. (Or maybe I'm just used to the sound now. We have it in our basement, and it cannot be heard in the next room or upstairs.) Only downside is that I need to pack up the original unit and ship it back. But fortunately I kept the original box and packaging, and EdgeStar is paying for the return shipping.

I'm upgrading my rating from 3 to 4 stars, because of the good customer service and prompt shipping of the new unit, and because this new unit seems to be working well.

Update 2018-02-03:
Since I received the replacement unit from EdgeStar, this unit has continued to operate flawlessly, cranking out a bin of ice (about 6 lbs) every 12 hours

That being said, defrosting the unit every 4-6 weeks is critical. (It is not a self-defrosting unit; but I knew that when I bought it.) Otherwise, ice will build up on the interior from frost and water splashes, and jam the mechanism.

Defrosting the unit, however, is easy. I simply turn the unit off, open the door, remove the ice bin, and place a large cloth towel in the interior, making sure that the towel is pushed against all sides and corners. (This prevents the ice water from running out of the interior compartment and onto the floor.) Leave the door open for about six hours, and it's defrosted. Toss the wet towel in the laundry basket, put the ice bin back in, and turn the unit back on. Twelve hours later, the bin is again full of ice.

I contacted Aeropress at: info@aeropressmetalfilters.com and they informed me "Some (about 5%) have a really tight locking system and won't fit our filter."

I would think that they would increase their quality control and assure that all their Aeropresses would conform to a single standard. Thus, once the new filter was sent out to the few customers who needed them, they would be scrapped. A cost that Aeropress was willing to incur to satisfy their customers.

3) Finally, something I have always been satisfied with; the resulting coffee using the Aeropress with the paper filters is the best homemade coffee I have ever experienced drinking. Only in a few coffee shops have I had better coffee and at $3 (2 Euros) a cup, they weren't that much better. Especially considering that they were probably using a machine costing upwards of $6,000. I live rural being well-surrounded by a large farming and lakes community. Despite having a very deep well, I've had concerns about the water-table levels depleting in the region from intermittent drought; pesticides and herbicides became the primary concern. I was debating whether I should just splurge on the premium GE MWFP or shop a budget-friendly alternative that is also certified to the NSF/ANSI 401/53/42 standard(s). After much research (they're all made in China regardless), I elected to try the "WaterDrop plus WDP-F13". I verified their certification via NSF and the reviews were impressive. Here's some observation and tips that WaterDrop recommended with their included instructions when replacing the filter. TURN OFF THE WATER VALVE TO YOUR REFRIGERATOR BEFORE REMOVING AND REPLACING THE OLD FILTER! I had never applied this recommendation in the past thus I always got a little blow-off when removing the old filter. It's a simple no-brainer and is much gentler on the water-lines and system as a whole I'm sure; I won't ever skip this step again! Also, I primed the new filter (filled the new filter with water before re-installing). This helps to minimize blow-out at the dispenser. I was absolutely ecstatic when I began to purge a couple of gallons from the dispenser. My flow-rate quadrupled compared to the "Glacier Fresh" and the "Original basic GE MWF". I'm thinking I had air in my line all this time; or quite possibly, this new "WaterDrop plus" is just "that good". Time will tell, but I'm impressed. Cheers!

Turns out it was a quite simple replacement.

The original motor is 5KH26JJ064S that does not have a harness and all wires are individually inserted. Take a picture before you unplugged them (pic1).

Clean up the dust, you can clearly see the terminal number for each wire on the white socket (Pic2).

WE17X10010 has a jumper harness. Insert the white end in and you can match the corresponding terminal number for each wire (Pic3), Install the black end with two screws and not hard to find another end of each wire and now you know the terminal numbers on the black end of the harness (Pic4)

Last step, just simply plug all wires into the correct terminals on the new motor.

Someone said the new motor is very noisy. I encountered the same problem and finally solved it: when install those two motor mounts (they are not included, and need to use the old one), you need to sit the four (two on each bracket) tiny locator tabs tightly into the blue areas of the metal bands (pic5). If you leave them out (red areas), the motor will vibrate and become very noisy.

I purchased this unit after recommendations from several relatives. We all have them for our RV's. When I received it and turned it on, it would not work. Unfortunately, due to a delay in our first trip after purchase, the Amazon free return period was past. I checked and found it was going to cost me $70.00 for return shipping.

I contacted "NewAir" and after a two emails with "standard responses," was put in contact with "Mireya" in Customer Support. I explained the issue and she obtained authorization for "NewAir" to provide return postage.

I returned the unit and "Mireya" notified me that the unit was defective and they would replace it with a new one and ship at their expense. I received the new unit a few days later. It works perfect and I am very happy with the product.

Two lessons reinforced. When you receive a new product, try it out before the free return period expires. There can always be a defect, but in my opinion, what counts is how the company reacts when you tell them.

In this case, "NewAir" could not have been more responsive and "Mireya" could not have been more helpful.

The Samsung DV448AEP dryer is a poorly designed machine. Lint can easily escape from the lint compartment -- and from the poorly designed dryer drum -- and onto the bottom portion of the dryer where the electrical components, the heating element, and the motor are located. They're in the business of being able to detect poor design. And not one repair tech said - "Hey - major amounts of lint - like this - should not be located in this bottom area." It wasn't until our fifth fire - when we took the dryer apart ourselves that we discovered the design flaws. Any idiot can see where the lint is escaping. Why the machine was designed this way is beyond me. Why no one has contacted us about a recall -- or to tell us this machine is a fire hazard is beyond me. Why professional experienced repair techs did not know about this issue - or couldn't figure it out by looking at the machine is beyond me. Samsung should notify every consumer who has purchased this machine and offer a fix - or a newly redesigned dryer. You cannot tell me they don't know about this issue. Do not buy this machine. . . . don't give up without some experimentation.  I finally achieved good results with 2 supermarket brands:  Maxwell House Slow Roast and Seattle's Best Breakfast Blend.  I added coffee almost to the top of the mesh, tapping the filter on the counter to settle the coffee uniformly with each spoonful.  The key is to get as much coffee as possible into the filter without packing it in too tightly or allowing any grounds to remain on the rim of the filter basket.  Use the small cup setting.  Near the end of the brewing process there is a spurt of what looks like clear water.  If you remove your mug before this final spurt, the coffee will be stronger.  I simply swap out my mug with another cup and dump that last ounce or so down the drain.  Now that I am happy with the taste of my coffee using My K-Cup, the only negative comment I can make about this accessory is that there is some slight splashing during the brewing process.  But dealing with that still takes far less time than it did to clean my old conventional coffeemaker.

To any one thinking about purchasing this for use with Home Assistant or any Open Z-wave based controller, I was not able to get this device to ever report properly for motion detection, which was what I bought this for. It appears to be the only semi-outdoor z-wave motion sensor not built from cheap plastic.

This gets one star for form factor, and another star because it did report humidity, temperature and light, but as others have mentioned, Aoetec needs to go back to the drawing board on the action button design. The "action" button on the back of the device is simply an thumb indentation that physically forces a piece of cheap plastic down onto a tiny button on the internal circuit board. It is cheap and bends and eventually becomes unusable, making the device unable to be included/excluded properly from the network.

This particular sensor has a lot of complicated config, and the although picking up the sensor did trigger the led to blink as if it were detected a change, the changes never get reported properly to OZWCP. In Home Assistant, my sensor's tamper/burglar was stuck reporting "3" after repeated use of the action button, and even after a factory reset and firmware upgrade, multiple add/remove from the networks (secure and unsecure) I still to this day was never able to get this working in Home Assistant as a simple outdoor motion sensor.

I will be returning this and looking into waterproofing a different device. I will consider trying a Gen 6 if reviews look promising.

Although not the fault of the product, I had opportunity to interact with Whynter's Customer Service process. I say process because it moves at its own speed and the more patient you are the happier you will be. Ultimately I was very happy.

While the landlord was making electrical "improvements" they managed to disconnect the neutral in the supply wiring to my space. Not unexpectedly, one side of my panel jumped from 120 volts AC to 240 volts AC. Understandably, some of the appliances did not react well to double voltage. That would include the subject refrigerator.
In the interest of time, I I ordered a duplicate from Amazon which arrived in a day or so. The landlord and I came to financial terms. But what to do with the dead fridge? I reasoned that the failure might be limited to the main power control board, and it would be a shame to toss an otherwise good refrigerator which might be simply repaired.
If you call Whynter, they really want you to email them. So you may as well start that way. Expect a response the following day. They wanted to ask me a bunch of warranty and troubleshooting questions which I didn't think fit my circumstances. Our email correspondence took place over several days. They did offer me some help with purchasing a new one. But, I explained I was past that point. What I really wanted was a power control board. They don't really anticipate that customers will perform their own repairs. If I had to pay someone to do it, it wouldn't be as satisfying a story. They had an owner's manual available (which I already had). But, there doesn't appear to be a technical manual. Fortunately, there's a wiring diagram on the back of the refrigerator which along with an exploded parts diagram gave me enough clues. Whynter furnished a power control board and I finally got around to playing technician.

The damaged board had a blown disc capacitor which gave its life to prevent further damage. I took some pictures before I disconnected the wiring and consulted them while reconnecting the new board.
When I powered up the fridge, the display and lighting came on. It quickly chilled to the set point and has been in service ever since.

So, my thanks to Chenie with Whynter because everything worked out.

The ugly; the most frequently this thing will check temperature or push a report is 15 minutes (confirmed via user manual and Aeotec support). For my bathroom fan application this was seriously inadequate. This 15 minute limitation meant my bathroom fan would kick on anywhere from 15 to 30 minutes after I started taking a shower. To make matters worse, the way the logic works means the fan might not get shutoff in a timely manner (hours after dewpoint became acceptable). Also, using 15 minute reporting killed 10% of the battery in less than a day of use (though the battery it came with was down to 30% out of the box).

If you agree with me, then I'd recommend getting the Aeotec 6in1 sensor and plugging it into USB for better humidity/fan control performance.

I should've bought this sooner b/c it saves me a lot of stress, money, and time! No more going to the laundry mat all day or having to wait for the community washer. This washer is super easy to use, a little more work, but definitely worth it. Just a few tips to know:

WASHING:
- Have a decent bucket ready (I use a large kid's bucket but a mop bucket will do fine). Just remember, the larger the bucket, the heavier it'll be so get a size of your preference to your needs. You'll nees the bucket to fill/drain the water. You can use the hose but you'll need to find the right size to fit your faucet otherwise, it'll come off and fillung the water takes longer w/ the hose. Trust me, a bucket will do.
- Place the washer next to a source of water/sink and a place where you can drain/pour the water (I have mine next to the bathroom)
- Use Hot-Warm water during the initial wash.
- Direction states that you should place clothes in the spinner before rinsing - no, you don't. Save time by just draining the initial cycle and untangling your clothes before adding the water for rinsing.
- Make sure you drain immediately soon after the cycle stops - you don't want your clothes sitting in dirty water
- Rinse with cold water and run for another full cycle
- Drain/Squeeze out excess water from clothes
- Place clothes in spinner in small increments (saves you drying time plus makes sure that you only use one drying cycle). You can hang dry the delicates soon after. IMPORTANT: Make sure you have the bucket underneath the drain hose while activating the spin cycle as it will continue to drain water (I made the mistake of not doing that and there was water everywhere, so make sure you do this.)
- Dry in dryer as normal

CLEANING:
- Rinse the washer side with hot water after use
- Clean the plastic lint box to make sure there's no dirt
- Wipe down

I got these several weeks ago and I wanted to try them out repeatedly before doing a review on them. I generally don't review items but I really relied upon them for these capsules and I wanted to offer one for someone doing their research as well.

I bought these for our Nespresso DeLonghi Lattissima Pro- mostly because the features of the machine were perfect for what I wanted but I wasn't a fan of the one time use capsules. Enter these reusable capsules. I purchased 5 2-packs of these because I work 12 hour shifts and I don't have the time to always refill my capsules. Having 10 on hand is much easier and well worth the expense. I ordered my favorite espresso beans (Lavazza Super Crema) and spent about 2 hours perfecting my grind (you want a fine to medium fine grind using a burr grinder) and tamping (lightly tamp the coffee, do not pack the grounds). By round 6 of testing, my ground espresso was almost identical to a Lavazza one time use Nespresso capsule- I compared color, taste, and even crema to make sure I was doing it right.

I read several reviews with the following issues:

1. Several said that the capsule was noticeably smaller than a Nespresso plastic capsule. The box of the item explains why- so it doesn't damage the metal capsule or the machine. It's pretty common sense but again, the box explains it.

2. Several reviews said their coffee was weaker or they had grinds in their coffee post-brew. You have to leave a tiny bit of room for your seal ring and make sure it's not pressed all the way into the ground coffee prior to putting the foil seal on. Also, do not pack the grounds in and don't make them so super fine or super coarse. Experiment with your beans. It's worth 6-10 shots of practice to know what you're doing.

3. This is not a cut and dry, grab a pod and go system. You do have to grind your own beans, seal them, clean them, etc. If you don't like that, don't buy it. It's worth it in the long run. The taste isn't 100% like a Nespresso pod but after using these daily since I bought them on May 29th, I've said an obscene amount of money vs. buying out and the taste is so much better than Starbucks and my other go tos.

I absolutely love these little capsules. I may purchase more in the future but if you're looking for a quality way to save money, help with environmental impact and more, you won't be sorry purchasing these. Just have patience if you haven't done it before and do your research so you don't blame the product without any prior experience.

The Easy Way to get Higher Water Levels if you desire, is to use the BULKY Selection.

Even without the Bulky Selection, the Washer does a great job in Washing all types of laundry, both BIG & Small.

To deepen the Water Level in the Normal Cycles, I added 3 ft of 1/4" Vinyl Tubing with a Brass 1/4" Barb Splicer to the Water Pressure Transducer tube Connection on the Control Module (in about a 3 inch coil beside the Control Module). 2. This washer machine may be small, but it uses a LOT of water. Think you're saving money buying this thing? Think again- you'll be spending much more on your water bill using this washing machine as compared to an eco-friendly one. How do I know? Look at fact #1 above; it dumped water all over my kitchen, and it flooded my 7 x 5 ft. kitchen with around 1/2 inch deep water, and some water even got into my dining area. It did all of this when I had it set to a medium load. THAT'S A LOT OF WATER FOR A SINGLE MEDIUM LOAD.

3. You'll need to buy a rolling pallete if you plan on using this washing machine, because it is rather heavy and unless you plan on leaving it in front of a kitchen sink or a bathroom sink, you'll be moving it around a lot. You'll also need to buy an extension for the drainage hose, because it isn't long enough AT ALL to reach a standard-height kitchen sink. As noted (now) in the description for this product, these filters do not include the RFID chip and are not suitable as a direct replacement for the RPWFE filter. The only issue is the refrigerator will not recognize that the filter has been replaced and will still indicate that the filter is expired by "X" number of days/weeks/months. If you can live with that (I can) you can continue to use these generic filters and just keep moving the OEM chip from filter to filter. Based on my very recent experience I would advise that you continue shopping and NOT purchase this cheaply constructed and highly priced unit unless you plan to NOT cook on it. It is a nightmare to clean and has the durability of a china tea cup. I purchased this unit and had it installed on May 31, 2016. Less than 2 months later, I ACCIDENTALLY dropped a light-weight aluminum lid from only a few inches above the unit. The lid hit the edge of the cooktop and shattered a good-sized piece of the glass. I had purchased an extended warranty from the store along with the cooktop so I contacted them about what had happened. After waiting a week for their review they decided it was my problem as accidents were not covered and they refused to help me in any way. I then contacted customer service at KitchenAid thinking that such a “reputable” company would surely be concerned about the quality of their products and their reputation with their customers but I got the same response from them – basically, “too bad, your problem”.
Aside from the total lack of customer support from both the store and the KitchenAid Co., my biggest issue is with the delicate construction of the cooktop. I’m pretty sure I’m not the only person to have dropped something accidentally on a stove. The unit should not have shattered so easily. In addition to the flimsy glass, there is definitely a design flaw in that the top and bottom edges are covered with a stainless steel strip but the sides are not which causes both the uncovered left and right sides to be elevated above the countertop with no support under them. I am sure this contributed to the break. I wish I had noticed this flaw before I bought it. This cooktop cost me over $1,701.00. Biggest waste of money ever. In anticipation of selling my home within the next few years, I am in the process of renovating my kitchen. I wanted to install quality products and mistakenly believed that KitchenAid was the way to go – big mistake. I purchased scrapers specifically made for glass cooktops and a good glass cooktop cleaner. I don’t cook very often but whenever I do I clean the cooktop every time. Neither the scrapers nor the cleaner would remove the surface debris sufficiently as I was trying to keep it looking like new. The only thing that removed the burnt on spills was a new razor blade but that left tiny scratches on the surface which would not buff out with additional cleaner. So if you prefer to ignore my experience with this cooktop and its manufacturer and purchase it anyway - and then plan to actually use it every day, be prepared to spend a ½ hour cleaning it - but don’t expect it to be perfect. Above all treat it like the delicate tea cup that it is and do not have any accidents (as if that was possible) because you will be on your own with no support. I am now in the process of searching for a remedy to cover this crack in the way of stainless steel strips but will no doubt need to buy yet another cooktop to replace this piece of junk before I decide to move. I also need to buy a range hood, dishwasher, microwave/convection combo, a refrigerator and a wall oven sometime in the near future. To be sure, I will NEVER again purchase another KitchenAid product – or JennAir either as they are part of the same company.

I sell appliances for a living, so I know quite a lot about them. I bought one of the first little Haier washers 6 years ago, and ever since, I wished there was a matching dryer. Since my washer has held up so well all this time (never a problem and I use it LOTS), I decided to buy this dryer right away once I discovered it. I've had it about a month.

Let me tell you about dryers: Get the biggest one you have space for, same as for washers. and you'll be happier. I move often and I tend to rent small places, so this is the only one to consider; It's either this or drying racks! All the other portables currantly out there are bigger and more cumbersome than this one. This one truly is portable in that I can pick it up and carry it easily. But, it will not hold as many clothes as the bigger ones. It is, however, perfect for the little Haier washers.

If you want faster drying times, be prepared to have a 220v or gas line installed. (Your landlord will go for that, sure!) Otherwise, 120v portable dryers are going to take, on average, 90 minutes per load. The flip side of this is that you can operate it almost ANYWHERE, and your landlord doesn't even need to know you have it!

120v dryers also do not have to be vented outside. They do not produce nearly the lint of larger dryers. You can if you want.

Tinier dryers may produce an extra wrinkle or two over largers ones. They don't have as much room for tumbling, so, be sure not to overload this one. That will also affect drying time. No dryer should be filled more than half full of wet clothes, unless you like ironing out wrinkles.

I ordered this from Amazon, thinking that I was getting the one with the window and the dial. Instead, I got the one with the electronic controls, which is the nicer one. I'm not sure the window/dial version is available anymore. This has all electronic controls with many little lights. Very hi-tek! It has a sensor dry feature that is usually accurate. Sometimes, I'll need to add some manual dry time afterwards, especially if I've mixed lightweight with heavier weight fabrics, as that throws the sensor off a little. Of course, keeping like-weight clothes together would be better.

There are 3 auto-dry cyles: Normal, Heavy, and Delicate. Use Heavy for Jeans and Towels. I'm not sure when I'll ever use Delicate, as 120v dryers only dry on low heat! That is why they take longer to dry. I believe that cycle uses an even lower heat. There is also timed dry available. Drying status lights (drying, cooling, done, and check lint filter) are helpful. It has an end-of-cycle signal. It does not have a drying rack, as some descriptions on the web have stated.

This, like my little washer, is surprisingly well-built! It has a metal body (I was expecting plastic). I think it will last a long time, hassle-free, just like my washer has.

My only real complaint is the lint filter. It seems fragile and it is the most bothersome one I've ever had to clean! There are two filters nested together, one fine and the other course, and both have to be cleaned. It is located on the back of the drum and doesn't pull off that easily. I imagine this is necessary, though, because of the dryer's small size. I wish Haier would have made a stronger, more convenient filter. THIS IS THE ONLY REASON I AM GIVING THIS DRYER FOUR INSTEAD OF FIVE STARS.

Overall, if space and portability are your chief concerns, Haier's small washers and this dryer are very, very good! I highly recommend them. However, if you have more space, and stay put for many years, get something bigger.

There was a weird smell right out of the box. Not strong enough to be off-putting, but it was noticable. I'm usually a wimp when it comes to smells but it wasn't so bad.

As other reviewers pointed out, there's no way to connect to a faucet unless you go to the hardware store to buy a part to go onto your tap. A little annoying, but I use an old jug to fill up the tub. I'll probably be headed to the hardware store later today. The electrical cord is a bit short, so I have to awkwardly stage it in my bathroom, but if you have multiple outlets, that's probably not such a big deal for you.

The dryer basket is small, MUCH smaller than I anticipated, and three pairs of jeans and two shirts was a little bit much for it. I put two pairs of jeans and a shirt and it did great. The washer is larger than I expected and can handle larger loads fairly well, but the dryer can only handle a few items at a time. Also- pro tip, invest in a color-catcher. If you have dyes that run, it will stain the inside of your machine.

Now, the drain.
The drain is badly designed. The pump isn't strong enough to get all of the water out if you use the drain hose to drain into something like a bathtub, so I need to lift the machine to get the last bits of water. If I don't, the second the hose touches the ground, it sprays all over. Like a full cup or two of water. Minor design flaw which is mostly gravity's fault, so I can deal with that.

But when you're spinning something in the basket (anything- oversized load, undersized, ANYTHING), the hose will discharge whatever water is left in it without the machine set to "drain," even if the hose is flat and you have what you think is all of the water out.
Invest in a good towel and/or a command hook/zip tie situation to keep the hose in place.

Why four stars then? Because this thing actually gets my clothes really,really clean. Much more than the community washer in my complex. It's a pain in the ass, but it's light, fairly inexpensive, and it does the job credibly.

If you're on the fence and don't mind minor hassle and a trip to the hardware store, it's 100% worth it. If you're looking for something you can just walk away from, invest in a full set.

This replaced an old 3 tap Beverage Aire Commercial kegerator I had go out on me. I didn't want to spend $1500.00+ for a new commercial quality one, so I opted for this unit. I'll list the Pros and Cons as I see them.

First the Pros...
1) Has (2) taps.
2) Looks good.
3) Good range of temperatures (approx. 33-40 degrees F.)
4) Uses half the power of my old kegerator.
5) Actually hold (3) home brew kegs (5 gallon).
6) Good quality dual gauge regulator.
7) So far seems to be reliable.

Now the Cons...
1) Co2 tank is too small (2.5 lb). It should come with a 5 lb. tank. (I have a couple of 15 lb. tanks so not a big deal for me)
2) Cheap quality beer lines. (I recommend you replace them w/ 5-6 feet of 3/16" I.D. high quality beer line)
3) Cheap quality gas line.
4) Standard brass faucets. (I replaced w/ my S.S. Perlick forward seal faucets)
5) Black plastic top seems cheap.
6) Drip tray does not fit properly around the beer tower. And it just sits movable, not fixed on top.
7) Casters are too small and don't rotate well.

Of course these are just my opinions and going from a commercial quality kegerator to a residential type, I have lots of nit pick things about it.
All in all, I would recommend this to people who would like a little variety instead of the single tap single beer at a time.

Note: I wrote this immediately after successfully brewed a satisfactory 8oz cup of coffee after 1 week of trial and error. The following instructions are for brewing an 8oz cup of coffee only, I haven't tried this on 14oz and higher. It worked for me, let's see if it works for you.

First, buy [[ASIN:B00USGQVY0 EZ-Carafe Paper Filter Refills - 3 Pack]] so you won't get silt from finely grinded coffee. The other important role of the filter is create some hydrodynamic resistance in order to keep the hot water contacting the ground coffee longer. When you get a weak cup of coffee, the fundamental fact is you didn't extract enough soluble content out of the ground coffee, which could almost always be attributed to these reasons: low water temperature, coarse grind, only few of the ground coffee actually met the hot water, or low extraction time.

Here's how I met these requirements.

To grind whole beans: I used a manual grinder, [[ASIN:B01328Q51E The Abundant Kitchen Slim Coffee Grinder and Burr Spice Mill | Moneyback Guarantee | Glass Bottom | Perfect Size for a Cup of Joe]]. I filled it with beans, screw the nut all the way to the end, then reverse 1 whole round. That's how I set the fineness of the grounded coffee. If you purchased ground coffee, their grind might be too coarse. You can fix this by regrind the ground coffee to finer grind, or use the "bold" option in brewer setting.

To fill the filter: put the filter in the eco-carafe, and PUNCH THROUGH THE PAPER LID OF THE FILTER USING THE SPIKE (HOT WATER DISPENSER) OF THE LID. The manual printed on filter package told you not to do so, but I believe they were wrong. If the paper lid is left intact, I believe the majority of the hot water will go through a shortcut: filter lid -> top layer of the coffee -> outside the filter. Water chose this way because they go where resistance is lowest, and finely grinded coffee generates a lot of resistance. One possible, permanent way of fixing this might be moving the metal filter screen from the side to the bottom, which will force all water flow though all of the coffee, which is how traditional drip machine works. Also, I've seen a picture of a dissected K Karafe pod which contains a plastic spike with holes on it. This spike will dispense hot water evenly throughout the pod so you can get a whole carafe of coffee in satisfactory strength. This spike may improve the dispersion of hot water in eco-carafe pod. Pour ground coffee in the filter until it reaches the top, then press them using a bottle cap (or something with a flat head but small enough to reach into the filter, your finger for example) to 1/2~2/3 of its original volume. This will increase the amount of coffee loaded in the filter. Keep filling to the top, but no pressing this time so the spike has some room to fit.

Brewer setting: the difference between "Strong" and regular setting is the difference in water temperature and the flowing speed of the hot water. In "Strong" setting, the water pump works at a significantly lower frequency, this, as mentioned before, will increase the time water and ground coffee contacting each other. In my opinion, if you use a fine grind and punched through the paper lid, the regular setting would be fine. But if you use a coarse grind (as found in our regular, bagged, ground coffee for drip machines), "Strong" setting may fix it.

Enjoy your coffee.

I bought this machine, and it is now working well at my home, but you will want to know the full deal, which I figured out by persistence.
This dryer is a commercial Speed Queen, essentially identical to the entry-level consumer machine. Buying it online saved me $300 or so, vs buying from a dealer locally.
The box that it came in was intact, and the dryer looked good coming out.
I hired a reputable dryer repairman to install it. At that point we discovered that it would not light. His inspection showed a shattered igniter, and singe marks inside, suggesting that it had been turned on before. Possibly was defective and shipped out to a consumer via amazon rather than repairing it.
I paid for the repair and the hookup $250. I don't know what a local dealer would have charged for hookup, but probably a lot less.
I talked to Speed Queen. Consumer machines come with three years parts and labor. Commercial machines come with three years parts but no labor. They do not authorize sale of their commercial machines over the internet, and thus do not cover parts either.
So, at this point, I am saving a few dollars vs having bought locally. If I have any additional problems in the next three years, this may be a more costly way to buy a Speed Queen.
In my case, since I hire a skilled technician for repairs and installation, if I had it to do all over again, I would buy local. If you are handy and confident, you might do better financially buying online.

The app is not complicated and gives the time vs. temp information as either a graph or as a table that can be downloaded. I found the tempCube so useful that purchased 3 more (from the tempCube website rather than from Amazon because the tempCube lite had become listed as unavailable from Amazon at that time - the price was the same on the tempCube site). In my experience, the tempCube lite is a well-engineered product that is simple to use and reliable. When I called customer support, my call was answered promptly by a helpful individual who answered my question and made sure that I was satisfied - the availability of such excellent customer support is reason enough to buy this product.
